This is a popular attrition benchmark dataset and befitting for testing time-sensitive and interpretable prediction models. 4.2 Feature Engineering A few characteristics were modified by the time to reflect temporal disengagement profiles. Decay of satisfaction was modeled via decreases in environment and relationship satisfaction, and volatile performance via rolling differences in players’ ability scores. Overtime increase was derived from the accumulation of tasks beyond a given set of base load values; stagnation due to a lack of promotion recorded as time since the last career step. Other calculated derived variables were absenteeism gravity and training frequency shortages. All continuous features were standardized, category features were encoded using one-hot, and missing values were filled. The engineered features were incorporated in two engineered representations of the state, Temporal Disengagement Index (TDI), attached to the input of the model. 4.3 Train–Test Split and Validation The datasets were divided 70% as a training set and the remaining 30% for testing with stratified sampling. Hyperparameters for Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost were tuned by fivefold cross-validation on the training set. In order to address this imbalance, class weights and SMOTE oversampling is used only for training. The higher ROC–AUC and F1-scores indicate that the model possesses better discriminatory power and balance between precision and recall, especially for minority attrition cases. Importantly, increases in early detection imply that there may be temporal markers for risk which can allow risk to be detected earlier and so are amiable to retention strategies. Our results provide evidence that leveraging temporal modeling, ensemble learning and counterfactual explanations not only enhances performance but also provides more managerial insights. ​ VI Conclusion​ In this work, we proposed T-DISCERN which is a temporal disengagement–driven ensemble framework to predict employee attrition with actionable and interpretable rules. By representing disengagement trajectories, combining a lightweight LR–RF–XGBoost ensemble and embedding counterfactual reasoning, the framework moves attrition analytics from passive predictions to proactive intervention assistance. experimental results on IBM HR dataset show that our approach works well with 91.2% accuracy, 94.1% F1–score and 97.9% ROC–AUC along with the improvement of early detection by 28%, false positive alerts reduction by 17%. text: A Context-Aware Analytical Framework for Quantifying the Influence of Agile Maturity on Enterprise Software Project Success Abstract-Agile practices are commonly used in the enterprise software development, however degree of how Agile maturity impacts on project success has not been quantitatively measured well; especially with reference to complex enterprise environment. Current research is primarily based on qualitative evaluations, or maturity models specific to a particular framework, which do not provide empirical evidence for how different levels of maturity relate to tangible project results. To fill this void, we present in this paper a Context- Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE)—a new interpretable analytic model intended to quantitatively appraise the influence of agile maturity on software project success and by explicitly incorporating organizationally specific contextual constraints. The approach considers Agile maturity as a multifaceted measure, extracted from major organizational and process dimensions such as teams' autonomy, the ability for continuous delivery, leadership commitment for delivering added-value to users, the integration of customer feedback into potential workflows and accumulated discipline in applying a given process. Enterprise context is defined by features like organizational size, regulatory burden, team dispersion and complexity of legacy system. Through a weighted linear estimation mechanism, CASE relates these dimensions to multi-criteria project success measures including delivery timeliness, product quality, budget-achievement performance and client satisfaction as well as realized business value. Using a dataset of an agile project from kaggle2024, the framework was empirically confirmed. The results of the experiments show projects on higher levels of agile maturity had better performance on-time 21.6%, post-release defects 17.9% and stakeholder satisfaction 24.3% than low Agile maturity projects. The overall predictive accuracy for project success was 88.7%, demonstrating that the model is robust and have practical implications. Through the provision of a transparent, context-adaptable and quantitatively-founded evaluation methodology this work provides an instrumental decision-support artefact to both small- and large-scale enterprises wanting to anchor their agile transformation endeavours towards concrete project success results. Keywords-Agile Maturity, Software Project Success, Enterprise Software Engineering, Context-Aware Analytics, Agile Performance Evaluation, Project Outcome Prediction I Introduction​ Enterprise software developers increasingly use agile development methodologies for their superior focus on flexibility, quick feedback loops, and incremental value delivery. The use of Agile practices to convert with uncertainty and enhance

text: cross-functional cooperation have become ever more popular in complex software projects as organizations strive for faster time-to-market. On the other hand, big organizations are typically bound by regulatory demands and competing management priorities, distributed teams and governance structures of hierarchy, not to mention legacy systems that heavily impact how Agile practices can truly work. Therefore, the results of Agile adoption are quite different from one organization to another, as it is noticeable that an objective understanding was still missing about the factors of success in applying Agile practices in enterprise contexts. One of the most important factors in effective Agile is the amount an organisation has to mature within their Agile adoption. Agile maturity refers to how well Agile principles are institutionalized in teams, processes, leadership tiers and delivery methods. Although several organisations profess to adopt Agile practices, variations in maturity levels result in significantly different project outcomes such as delivery predictability, product quality, cost compliance and stakeholder satisfaction. The existing risk-guided and success-guided approaches for assessing the maturity of Agile-oriented organizations in large-scale enterprises are often qualitative, framework specific or focus on isolated dimensions that hardly support quantifying how maturity levels in turn would impact on measurable project results. To this end, this research presents a CASE, a quantitative and interpretable analytical model for quantifying how much organisational context influence in which enterprise software projects' success is achieved by Agile maturity. The proposed approach includes modelling Agile maturity as a compound index of certain organisational and process dimensions and incorporates enterprise specific situational constraints in the evaluation. This study seeks to establish the connection between maturity levels and multi-criteria project success indicators using a well-structured forecasting approach; it has the potential to create a practical decision-supporting tool for companies to properly match their Agile transformation initiatives with real-world applicable and quantifiable project success results. This research has three main contributions to the practice and academia in enterprise software engineering. First, we proposed a new CASE that quantitatively characterizes the relationship between process maturity and successful software projects, while capturing the explicit role of enterprise-specific contextual constraints. Second, the proposed approach makes Agile maturity tangible by means of synthesizing it as a composite, interpretable index which considers both organisational and process perspectives and can be used to assess systematically and replicable in heterogeneous enterprise settings. Third, we have conducted an empirical study to show that higher Agile maturity is significantly related with better levels of delivery performance in the dataset from an open source Agile project, better product quality and stakeholder satisfaction (which are all three major characteristics of

The investigation highlights context-aware measurement as the missing link for facilitating the transformation agility in regulated contexts [20]. 2.1 Research Gap Many researchers have investigated Agile success factors, maturity models, leadership implications or practice patterns in different settings but with fragmented or qualitative or framework-centric views. Although existing studies have found key factors for success and suggested maturity or success models, the design of a consolidated quantitative model directly associating different Agile maturity degrees to multi-dimensional project success levels has been missing, especially in complex enterprise environments. Furthermore, contextual factors such as the size of an organization, its governance arrangement or regulatory intensity and team setting are often treated implicitly or even ignored completely which restricts the generalizability and predictability of current approaches. As a result, there are no reasonable context-aware analytical processes that can be interpreted in order to estimate empirically how such Agile maturity translates into measurable success in enterprise software projects, this leading to an open question that the present work seeks answer for. III Methodology This research uses an empirical, quantitative methodology to investigate the relationship between Agile maturity and enterprise software project performance in context based manner [21][22]. The Context-Aware Agile Success Estimator (CASE) framework combines Agile maturity assessment, enterprise context modeling and multi-criteria success evaluation in a single analytic process. Agile maturity is measured in terms of a combined index obtained from vital organizational/ process dimensions [23], whereas situational constraints are reflected by observed project features. A weighted estimation model is used for modeling the relationship between maturity and the context influencing factors with project success output variables. The framework is empirically validated using Agile project data to test the predictive accuracy and sensitivity. 3.1 Research Design This paper employs quantitative, empirical research and design and it is based on secondary data from an open-source Agile project dataset [24]. A cross-sectional analytical technique is adopted to study the association of Agile maturity with enterprise contextual factors and the outcomes associated with software project success. Estimation accuracy and robustness of the proposed CASE solution are demonstrated through predictive modeling and statistical analysis. This design allows us to sensibly and systematically analyse maturity–success relations in diverse Agile

The data set contains 200 Agile software development projects, which is enough for quantitative analysis yet provides a sufficient variety of the project characteristics. We chose this dataset because it contains structured project level measures that are directly related to Agile effectiveness, management satisfaction, risk detection, efficiency and cost performance - all of which are in accordance with the fundamental aspects of Agile maturity and project success we aimed to investigate in this study. Furthermore, it is publicly available to support reproducibility and transparency that are mandatory in empirical software engineering research. Both ordinal and numerical variables have been included in the dataset. The dataset also covers several perspectives of Agile project performance. Specifically, in this study, the factors used as parameter are Agile Effectiveness, Risk Mitigation, Management Satisfaction [26], Supply Chain Improvement and Time Efficiency which are scaled using Likert scale ranging from 2 to 5; and Cost Savings in percentage (10%–48%). Project Success is encoded as a binary outcome, whether the project was completed successfully or failed. These drivers are linked to Agile maturity dimensions and multi-criteria project success criteria, in the CASE framework.

text: EpiFormer-Tamil: A Degradation-Aware Multi-Stage Learning Framework for Autonomous Recognition and Speech Rendering of Tamil Stone Inscriptions Abstract-Tamil stone inscriptions as a linguistically rich although visually degraded historical medium, with severe erodedness. Non-linear carving depth and stylistic drift at dynastic time scales render conventional OCR techniques less effective on this medium”. Current deep learning–based epigraphical investigations are dependent upon direct convolutional feature learning, still sensitive to inscription-specific degradation and fails to take into account contextual awareness of ancient Tamil glyph evolution. To address these limitations, this paper introduces EpiFormer-Tamil, a new end-to-end degradation-aware multi-stage learning framework that captures visual restoration, structure character representation and linguistic coherence for better inscription interpretation. There are three main contributions in the proposed framework. For this, Depth-Responsive Epigraphical Enhancement Module (DREEM) simulates the variations in carving depth with adaptive gradient-aware normalization that allows glyph boundaries to be eroded during depathologizing beyond conventional level attraction. Second, we propose a Hybrid CNN–Graph Transformer (HC-GT) recognition architecture in which convolutional encoders extract local stroke primitives and a graph-based transformer models spatial relationships among strokes explicitly, so that the model can capture script topology instead of pixel appearance. Third, a Linguistically Constrained Decoding Mechanism (LCDM) incorporates character transition priors from archaic Tamil in the inference step that drastically prunes visually plausible but linguistically incorrect predictions. The recognized script is then transliterated to Unicode Tamil text in the prosody adaptive manner and finally spoken by a Tamil Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine suitable for old vocabulary articulation. On an annotated weathering-affected Tamil stone inscriptions dataset, it has been observed that the proposed approach EpiFormer-Tamil outperforms existing CNN and attention-based OCR models with a character recognition accuracy of 98.12% clearly and by 8.6% and 5.1% respectfully. It also decreases the linguistic error rate by 41.3%, and achieves a naturalness score of 95.2% for speech synthesis module. Our results clearly demonstrate that the proposed framework is a powerful and scalable solution for digital epigraphy, heritage informatics and inclusive access to ancient Tamil historical records. Keywords-Tamil epigraphy, stone inscription recognition, degradation-aware learning, graph transformer, ancient script modeling, linguistic constraint decoding, text-to-speech synthesis, digital heritage I Introduction​ Tamil stone inscriptions have underpinned the base of historical [1][2], linguistic and cultural knowledge documenting administrative processes, religious customs and social practices over the centuries [3][4]. Even with their being chiseled, over the centuries a large majority of inscriptions have lost most of their visual succinctness through long usage by society, relentless exposure to environmental deterioration, surface erosion/weathering and

text: deterioration of materials [5]. As a consequence, much of the epigraphical content is not easily interpretable, and hence available, only to a few communities of trained epigraphists (constituted by specialists), restricting large scale digital preservation initiatives [6][7]. High accuracy has also been achieved in optical character recognition (OCR) and deep learning on printed and handwritten documents, though [8] the same is not true on stone inscriptions. Thus, hand-carved Tamil inscriptions pose challenges which are not typical with regular document images, such as irregular carving depth, broken stroke boundaries [9][10], non-uniform background illumination and varying styles used over centuries. Traditional CNN-based and attentionbased OCR models are rooted in pixel-level appearance cues, which makes them very susceptible to erosion and surface artifacts. As a result, visually ambiguous glyph fragments tend to cause wrong or linguistically unacceptable character predictions [11]. An important drawback of the existing methods is that no explicit structural modeling is employed. Stroke shapes and spatial relations of strokes including junctions [12][13], orientation, enclosure patterns are used to define the ancient Tamil characters. Traditional visual features employed by typical OCR pipelines are fl at 2D representations of these maps and do not properly model the topological dependences present in them, thus making the approach too sensitive to damage under severe degradation. Furthermore, most recognition systems view decoding as an entirely visual process [14] and does not take into account the strong language components that guide proper character transitions for ancient Tamil epigraphy. This exclusion often leads to the generation of semantically inconsistent outputs (irrespective of how confident model is in generating it), even if visual confidence is strong. To overcome these issues, we propose EpiFormer-Tamil, a degradation-aware multi-stage learning framework for automatic recognition and rendering of Tamil stone inscriptions. The proposed system considers the visual restoration, structure character representation, and language coherence in a unified manner. The assumption is that confidence epigraphical recognition demands to move from appearance-based learning to representations able to encode dietetic, specific degradation, glyph topology and language-driven constraints [15][16]. The first part is DREEM (Depth-Responsive Epigraphical Enhancement Module), which explicitly captures the carving depth variations with gravity-aware normalization [17][18]. This ensures that missing regions of bearing glyph boundaries can be repaired without losing object features required for their recognition. Based on the improved representation [19], we design a Hybrid CNN–Graph Transformer (HC-GT) model to capture not only local geometric primitives of strong sub-structural elements and their interactions but also their topological closure that is essential for character topology in ancient Tamil opposed to visual pixel intensity patterns. As a result, it is not well-suited for modeling the problem as pure image-to-text mapping but has to include at test-time some model of degradation, layout and linguistic validity.

As shown in the pipeline, input inscription image is initially passed through Depth Responsive Epigraphical Enhancement Module (DREEM) [31], which corrects carve depth variation due to erosion and recovers structural significant stroke boundaries. The enriched representation is passed to the Hybrid CNN–Graph Transformer (HC-GT) where convolutional encoders learn local stroke primitives and graph transformers capture spatial and topological relations between strokes to produce confident character hypotheses. These hypotheses are then further refined by the Linguistically Constrained Decoding Mechanism (LCDM) which ensures that ancient Tamil character transition rules such as removal of visually plausible but semantically incoherent sequences [32][33]. The resulting character sequence is then utilized to a Unicode-compliant Tamil text from which it gets spoken through a prosody sensitive Tamil Text-to-Speech (TTS) system, thereby facilitating an end-to-end recognition-to-speech chain for digital epigraphy. text: ​ Figure 2: Flowchart of the Proposed EpiFormer-Tamil Framework for Degradation-Aware Recognition and Speech Rendering of Tamil Stone Inscriptions V Experimental Setup​ In this section, we present the dataset statistics, baseline models, and evaluation metrics for evaluating our EpiFormer-Tamil framework. All experiments were performed on a publicly available dataset for reproducibility and fair comparison with the advanced methods. 5.1 Dataset Description 5.1.1 Dataset Source and Availability Experiments were carried on the publicly available Kaggle Ancient Tamil Stone Inscriptions dataset. The dataset has been prepared using digitised epigraphical datasets accumulated from temples, Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) records, museums and heritage documentation archives across Tamil Nadu. These are inscriptions dated back to different eras and seen carved in stones, which have undergone natural decay over several centuries of exposure. The dataset is publicly available and can be downloaded from Kaggle, to allow for clear benchmarking and comparison studies in the future. 5.1.2 Dataset Composition The dataset comprises of high resolution grayscale and RGB images of Tamil stone inscriptions imaged under different lighting environments. The inscriptions consist of isolated characters, partial words and complete inscription lines, which corresponds to realworld epigraphical settings as opposed to laboratory-controlled samples. ●​ Total images: 3,600 inscription images ●​ Type of script: Early Tamil (including early inscriptional forms) ●​ Resolution: 512×512 to 2048×2048 pixels ●​ Annotation scheme: Level of characters with verified transcriptions 5.1.3 Erosion-Level Categorization To assess robustness to variable degradation conditions, the three erosion levels based on visual quality and surface damage were separated in: ●​ Little erosion: The outlines of the glyphs are clear, but involve exceedingly slight rubbing off. ●​ Medium erosion: Partial loss of stoke, irregular carving depth and surface noise

text: ●​ Heavy erosion: Segmented characters, shallow scribing/etching and too much shadowing, strokes missing Each of the erosion classes comprises around a third of our dataset, meaning that we can ensure fair testing on any level of degradation. 5.1.4 Train–Validation–Test Split​ The dataset was divided at the level of inscriptions to prevent any data leakage between sets: ●​ Training set: 70% (2,520 images) ●​ Validation set: 15% (540 images) ●​ Test set: 15% (540 images) The separation ensures that the relative proportion between erosion levels and character classes is maintained among all partitions. Mild rotation, contrast change and illumination were used as data augmentations to the training set only for increasing generalization. 5.2 Evaluation Metrics Performance was evaluated using metrics that jointly assess visual recognition accuracy, linguistic consistency, and speech naturalness, aligning with the multi-stage objectives of EpiFormer-Tamil. ●​ Character Recognition Accuracy: Character accuracy measures the proportion of correctly recognized characters relative to the ground truth: ​ ​ ​ (21) 𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦= 𝑁𝑢𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑟 𝑜𝑓 𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑙𝑦 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑𝑖𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑠 𝑇𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙 𝑛𝑢𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑟 𝑜𝑓 𝑐ℎ𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑠 ​ This metric reflects the core recognition capability under varying erosion conditions. ●​ Linguistic Error Rate (LER): To evaluate linguistic coherence, Linguistic Error Rate (LER) was computed as the normalized sum of substitution, insertion, and deletion errors at the character level: ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (22) 𝐿𝐸𝑅= 𝑆+𝐼+𝐷 𝑁 In Eq.22, , and denote substitution, insertion, and deletion errors, respectively, 𝑆, 𝐼 𝐷 and is the total number of ground-truth characters. Lower LER values indicate 𝑁 better adherence to ancient Tamil orthographic constraints. ●​ Mean Opinion Score (MOS) for TTS: The naturalness of synthesized speech was evaluated using Mean Opinion Score (MOS) on a 5-point scale. A group of native Tamil speakers assessed speech samples generated from decoded inscription text based on pronunciation clarity, prosody, and intelligibility: ○​ 1: Poor ○​ 5: Excellent ​ MOS provides a subjective yet widely accepted measure of speech synthesis quality. 5.3 Hardware and Software Configuration​ All experiments were performed on a dedicated deep learning server to guarantee smooth training and repeatable evaluation. The hardware environment included an Intel Core i9 CPU, 32 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA GPU (12 GB VRAM) utilized for the effective learning of

All the model training and inference are implemented with Python 3.9 as the main programming language. The proposed framework and baseline models were developed using the PyTorch deep learning library, complemented by NumPy and OpenCV for numerical computations and image processing. Graph-based operations in the HC-GT module were performed using graph learning-compatible libraries. VI Results and Discussion In this section, we provide a thorough appraisal of the proposed EpiFormer-Tamil framework on the Ancient Tamil Stone Inscriptions dataset. The experimental study compares different OCR algorithms with the recognition accuracy, linguistic consistency and speech naturalness. Quantitative results and ablation studies are provided to verify the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach under different inscription degradation conditions. ​ Figure 3. Character Recognition Accuracy Comparison across Tamil Epigraphy Recognition Models Figure 3 presents a comparative analysis of character recognition accuracy achieved by the proposed EpiFormer-Tamil model compared to five well-known OCR models. Tradition OCR models such as CNN-OCR, attention-based OCR perform poorly due to their sensitivity on erosion and stroke breaking. On the other hand, EpiFormer-Tamil achieves the best accuracy of 98.12%, outperforming CNN and attention models by successfully combining degradation-aware enhancement and topology-guided recognition. The findings attest the efficiency of the developed model in recognising visually impaired ancient Tamil stone inscriptions.

We also conducted an ablation study by incrementally adding each of the elements: DREEM, HC-GT and LCDM, from a vision-only baseline. We show that visual enhancement helps recovering the consistency of strokes, and further gains are made when there is an explicit stroke structure modeling informed with linguistic cues in decoding. The very high character recognition accuracy of 98.12% achieved demonstrates the necessity to model inscription-specific degradation and glyph topology in order to be able to reliably interpret inscriptions under heavy erosion conditions. text: the obtained gains in readability are due to combining graph-based processing (for structural modeling) with linguistically constrained decoding and their effects in aligning object layers which diminishes both ambiguities at multiple depths and semantic mismatch. The large decrease in the linguistic error rate also demonstrates the benefit of incorporating ancient Tamil orthographic rules as an integral part of decoding rather than applying post hoc correction. The high speech naturalness by the combination of DCTTS module validates the end-to-end design paradigm, and introduces as well new horizons for inclusive access and scalable applications in digital epigraphy. VII Conclusion​ This paper introduced EpiFormer-Tamil, a degradation-informed multi-stage pipeline for the unsupervised analysis and text-to-speech synthesis of ancient Tamil stone inscriptions. Unifying depth-sensitive enhancement, topology-guided character recognition and linguistically constrained decoding, our approach obtained 98.12% accuracy on the character recognition task, reduced 41.3% lower linguistic error rate and a 95.2% speech naturalness score in text-to-speech synthesis compared to various OCR approaches including CNN-, joint-attention and transformer-based models. Ablation and robustness analyses additionally demonstrated that due consideration of carving depth, glyph structure and ancient Tamil language characteristics is crucial for accurate epigraphical interpretation under high degree of degradation. These findings make EpiFormer-Tamil a robust and scalable application for digital epigraphy and heritage informatics. In the future, we aim to consider multilingual epigraphical extension, self-supervised pretraining on large-scale inscription corpus and shape reconstruction in 3D surfaces for improving the accuracy of recognition. text: A Token-Salience Aware Transformer Framework for Context-Rich Cyberbullying Detection Abstract- Detecting cyberbullying is still an open issue because the abusive language is often subtle, implicit, and context-dependent which makes it hard to be captured by conventional architecture like TF-IDF representation, topic clustering or convolutional classifier. Current methods, such as FAEO-ECNN, largely suffer from semantic sparseness and non-contextual topic modeling and are also heavily dependent on computational expensive optimization pipelines that in turn makes it less robust in actual social media lives. To mitigate those limitations, we propose an innovative framework in this paper: TSAN-CB – a Token-Salience Aware Transformer model that consolidates contextual representation learning, fine-grained salience estimation and cyberbullying classification under an end-to-end setting. The model enhances a pre-trained transformer encoder with a lightweight salience-gating mechanism that identifies and consolidates the most semantically discriminative tokens via top-K selection, facilitating efficient detection of both explicit and implicit bullying cues. This attention-based aggregation, loses to the bank of traditional topic modeling keeping industry-leading interpretability with visualization on-importance at token level. Experimental results on a publicly available Cyberbullying Classification dataset show that TSAN-CB attains the accuracy of 95.82% and the F1-score of 95.11%, which outperforms other strong baseline methods by a large margin. The findings support the value of employing contextual salience for modeling sarcasm, passive-aggressive rhetoric, and coded language without having to resort to multi-stage optimization techniques. The TSAN-CB provides a computational-efficient, interpretable and deployable method for scalable cyberbullying detection in dynamic online systems. The language of social media data – short, informal and constantly changing – represents formidable challenges for existing cyberbullying detection systems which are based on shallow features like TF-IDF representations or static word embeddings [4][5] or convolutions capturing patterns [6]. While these latter transformer-based models have greatly improved contextual representations of text, many existing approaches are

text: either complex multi-stage pipelines [7][8], rely on external optimization or topic-modelling machinery, or learn from all input tokens identically during the representation learning process [9][10]. Therefore, such methods do not provide accurate characterization of the most semantically discriminative cues for detecting cyberbullying, especially when cyberbullying is perpetrated subtly or indirectly [11]. Some recent studies have tried to handle contextual complexity using hybrid architectures [12], ensemble transformers, graph-based learning, or multimodal fusion strategies [13]. While these methods improve the performance significantly, they are often impractical due to high computation cost, poor interpretability and lack of applicability in real world deployment [14]. In addition, much of the preceding work focuses on model accuracy, and neglects token-level relevance that is instrumental in explaining why a prediction should be made [15][16]. Attention mechanisms in vanilla transformers offer a rudimentary form of importance estimates, but they do not enforce selective aggregation of salient tokens explicitly, resulting in noisy representations during processing of context-rich social media text. This drawback is particularly pronounced in datasets with sarcasm or indirect harassment, where less than 4% of words are abusive [17]18]. In order to address these issues, this paper suggests TSAN-CB, a Token-Salience Aware Transformer model framework for context-driven cyberbullying detection. The proposed model supplements a pretrained transformer encoder with a lightweight salience-gating mechanism [19], which allows the model to make explicit decisions about capturing and summarizing the semantically most informative tokens using top-K salience selection. Contrasting to previous topic-modelling or optimization-based approaches [20][21], TSAN-CB is conducted in a unified end-to-end architecture, retaining contextual depth as well as improving its interpretability through the token-level salience visualization. Extensive experiments on the Cyberbullying Classification dataset show that TSAN-CB is able to outperform strong baselines, such as FAEO-ECNN and, simultaneously getting rid of the issue of high computation cost [22]. Overall, the findings demonstrate that contextual salience modeling is an effective and practical method for modern cyberbullying detection systems. The major contributions of this study can be summarized as follows: ●​ Model: We introduced a token-salience aware transformer model to selectively emphasize the discriminative tokens for effective cyberbullying identification. ●​ Contextually Aware Interpretability: The model can attend on implicit bullying cues such as sarcasm and provide token-level interpretability– via salience modeling.

Most prior models are either language-specific and resource-intensive architectures (e.g., Arabic-only, Bengali-only transformers), multi-stage optimization pipelines, or hybrid systems with large model sizes that prevent scalability and real-time deployment. Although transformer models enhance context-awareness, the resources do not explicitly model patterns of token-level salience needed to recognize subtle bullying cues like sarcasm, passive aggression and coded language. III Methodology In this work, we presented TSAN-CB, an end-to-end Token-Salience Aware Transformer model for cyberbullying detection. The approach starts from preprocessing the text of social media cyberbullying dataset from Kaggle and then applying a pretrained transformer to encode it for obtaining context-aware token representations [22][23]. A salience-gating module is subsequently adopted to compute the token-wise importance scores, so that the model can capture semantic discriminative cues towards both explicit and implicit cyberbullying [24][25]. The top-K important tokens are pooled via attention to produce a more compact representation that not only serves as an alternative to traditional topic modeling, but also mitigates the semantic noise. Finally, we feed this representation to a classification layer for cyberbullying prediction, and the whole network is trained end-to-end with cross-entropy loss such that computational cost-effective, robustness and token-level interpretability can be achieved without leveraging complicated multi-stage optimization pipelines. text: C³-DRIVE Net for Context-Aware Clinically-Grounded Automated Detection, Segmentation, and Severity Grading of Dental Caries in Radiographic Images Abstract- Dental caries is the most prevalent of all long-standing oral diseases globally. The early detection and proper evaluation of lesion severity are particularly important for determining the optimal preventive or therapeutic intervention. It is worth mentioning that dental X-rays interpretation significantly depend on the dentist experience, and may differ across clinicians, particularly when diagnosing early or mild carious lesions. Many existing deep learning algorithms are designed for only one task (e.g., caries detection and segmentation) and process lesions as isolated objects. For all of this, they are unable to easily show us how caries forms slowly or how it relates to the anatomy of our teeth. To alleviate these problems, in this paper we propose the C³-DRIVE Net (Context-aware, Clinically-grounded, Continual Dental Radiographic Intelligence for Visual Explanation), an integration learning framework to simultaneously carry out caries detection, lesion segmentation and their severity grading based on dental X-ray images. The proposed model leverages knowledge in the form of tooth-aware anatomical analysis along with radiographic gradient variations to detect patterns of mineral loss associated with both early and advanced caries. The use of a common multi-task encoder enables the model to learn all tasks across one another, removing error accumulation that is typical in cascaded systems. Radiographic depth of caries and the structural relationship of enamel, dentin, and pulp are employed to score the severity in a manner consistent with clinical grading systems. The experimental results on annotated dental x-ray datasets achieve a detection accuracy of 97.8%, a segmentation Dice score of 91.2% and a severity grading accuracy of 95.6%. Moreover, the proposed approach also enhances 22% early caries detection sensitivity than current deep leaning based methods. These findings confirm that the C³-DRIVE Net is an accurate, interpretable and clinically useful solution for chairside dental diagnosis. Keywords-Dental caries detection, Dental X-ray analysis, Multi-task deep learning, Severity grading, Clinical decision support, Explainable AI. I Introduction​ Dental caries is still one of the most prevalent chronic oral diseases worldwide that occurs throughout all age groups and presents a significant public health challenge [1][2][3]. Radiographic exposures, particularly bitewing and panoramic films are important in the early recognition and follow-up of lesions located on non-visible proximal surfaces and sub-surface areas [4][5]. However, diagnosing dental caries
label: human

text: from radiographs is inherently difficult because low-contrast discriminations exist between sound tissue and mineral loss [6][7], as well as overlapping anatomical structures and differences in image acquisition including angle [8][9]. Demineralization of enamel at an early stage is characteristically radiolucent in appearance and may be so subtle that it is difficult for even experienced clinicians to detect [10][11]. These difficulties lead to diagnostic uncertainty, delayed intervention, and high levels of inter- and intra-observer variability in day-to-day clinical practice. There are promising studies on automated dental caries analysis under development with the recent progress of deep learning [12], however, they mainly addressed either detection or segmentation alone [13][14]. Although some previous methods may have better accuracy for identifying different regions, these studies were based on convolutional neural network–based models that generally use an object or pixel-wise method and are not able to sufficiently model the anatomical context of teeth while lesion development is progressive [15][16]. Furthermore, many techniques are based on cascaded pipelines with detection outputs as inputs of subsequent segmentation or classification stages, which leads to error accumulation and decrease in robustness. Crucially, severity grading—a key aspect for clinical management—is frequently formulated as a crude classification task which is not directly mapped with well-known radiographic criteria, e.g. enamel–dentin–pulp relationships and depth-based lesion progression [17][18]. However, despite the expanding literature, there are three important gaps that have been inadequately filled [19]. First, none of the existing works provide a unifying framework that can jointly detect caries and segment lesions with high precision as well as grade their severity in line with clinical references within an end-to-end architecture [20][21]. Secondly, current models ignore tooth-aware anatomical inferences and radiographic gradient changes exhibited by the mineral densities including early caries [22]. Third, although many deep learning systems are designed as black boxes, they lack explainability and clinical trust to facilitate their application on the real-world chairside [23]. Such restrictions limit the translational potential of existing techniques and call for context-sensitive, explainable, and clinically-grounded diagnostic mechanisms. To tackle these problems, this work defines automated dental caries analysis as a unified multi-task learning problem which learns detection [24], segmentation and severity reasoning jointly from radiographic images. Here we present C³-DRIVE Net, a context aware and clinically informed deep learning architecture, which aims to capture anatomical structure, radiographic intensity disruptions [25][26], and lesion progression signatures in a shared representation space. By combining a tooth-aware anatomical decomposition with radiograph gradient modeling and clinically motivated lesion severity indices, our framework is tailored towards mitigating diagnostic variation, increasing
label: human

text: sensitivity to early-stage lesions and producing interpretable outputs in a manner consistent with existing clinical practice [27]. This integrated formulation is designed to be a compromise of algorithmic performance and practical clinical utility. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: ●​ An end-to-end multitask deep learning model to detect caries, segment lesions, and grade their severity avoiding the error-prone cascaded approach. ●​ A radiographically based severity ranking system that includes depth indices and enamel–dentin–pulp relationships as they relate to clinical parameters is described, compatible with established diagnostic guidelines. ●​ A context-sensitive model that utilises tooth-level anatomic decomposition and radiation gradient disruption analysis to enhance sensitivity for, and interpretability of, early diagnosed caries. 1.1 Objectives of the Study​ The purpose of this study is to investigate: ●​ To design an integrated deep learning model for effecting simultaneous optimization of detection, segmentation and severity grading of dental caries in radiographic images. ●​ To provide anatomic and radiographic context for learning, improve early lesion detection rates and minimize diagnostic confusion. ●​ To develop a clinically applicative severity grading system that facilitates reproducible decision-making in an everyday dental diagnostic laboratory. This paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work and identifies existing research gaps. Section III presents the proposed C³-DRIVE Net framework, followed by Section IV describing the experimental setup, Section V discussing results and analysis, and Section VI concluding the paper with limitations and future directions. II Literature Review​ Panyarak et al. (2023) attempted to investigate whether deep learning was compatible for classifying dental caries severity on the bitewing X-ray in accordance with the ICCMS™ scoring system. They trained several ResNet models and indicated that the best model performed reasonably well for a 4-level severity classification but not so well for detailed, 7-level ICCMS™ grading, particularly in detecting early enamel caries. This indicated that image-level classification may be inadequate for a more nuanced grading of severity in complexity without tooth anatomy features [1]. Chen et al. (2023) presented a two-stage system for severity classification of caries in panoramic X-rays. They firstly separated teeth extracted by a modified U-Net with ASPP and boundary loss. They then utilized a rule-based analysis to establish caries extent. This would allow for easier identification of tissue boundaries and interpretation by clinicians. However, since it utilized a sequential approach the errors
label: human

text: in initial phases might impede later steps and the technique can be hard to scale [2]. In another study, Chen et al. (2023) proposed a framework to achieve the identification of periodontitis and dental caries on periapical X-rays. The model leveraged YOLOv7 to detect teeth and EfficientNet for disease classification. Despite high performance, the system still considered dental decay in yes/no terms only (in or out of caries), without lesion area localisation and severity assessment [3]. A hybrid approach proposed by Vimalarani and Ramachandraiah (2022) combined conventional image preprocessing techniques, handcrafted descriptors, and a LeNet architecture-based deep classifier for caries detection in bitewing radiographs. The approach achieved good accuracy, however it heavily relied on manual feature generation and heuristic-based segmentation that restricts its use across varied X-ray qualities and clinical environments [4]. Esmaeilyfard et al. (2024) proposed deep learning for caries detection and classification with CBCT volume. Their multiple input CNN also demonstrated a good performance for detection of the caries presence and assessment of the depth and location of the lesion. But the study was targeted at 3D CBCT data which is not directly applicable to routine screening by 2D dental radiography [5]. Estai et al. (2022) introduced a Siamese-CNN based two-staged architecture for proximal caries detection in bitewing radiographs. Regions of interest were extracted using Faster R-CNN, and then they were classified by Inception-ResNet-v2. While it maintains reasonable precision and recall rates for object detections, the cascaded structure raised complexity and made the model more error sensitive [6]. Panyarak et al. (2023) similarly analyzed YOLOv3 with varied IoU thresholds for ICCMS™-based caries detection. Although adequately accurate in those with relatively advanced lesions, the model was unable to detect superficial enamel caries consistently thus indicating the inferiority of object-detection-based approaches in recognizing subtle radiographic changes [7]. Ahmed et al. (2023) used semantic segmentation for caries detection of bitewing X-ray images with an extension of KAU classification. However, segmentation accuracy for early enamel and dentin caries were low, which indicated that it is challenging to mark the early lesions accurately [8]. Albano et al. (2024) performed a systematic study of AI based caries detection strategies from various dental imaging modalities. This review found that there were wide differences in datasets, evaluation metrics, and performance outcomes generated by published studies and the lack of standardization and scarce variety of data are still considerable challenges to clinical use [9]. Bayrakdar et al. (2022) utilized CNN to automatically detect caries with the combined use of U-Net for the important task of lesion segmentation in BW-Xray images. Their findings indicated that AI systems could outperform junior dentists. Detection and segmentation were nonetheless processed separately from each other, with no caries severity grading addressed in the work [10]. Kunt et al. (2023)
label: human

text: introduced a large and highly annotated bitewing radiograph dataset and tested numerous object-detection models, including YOLO, Faster R-CNN. These models achieved a level of accuracy similar to that of experienced dentists. However, sensitivity was quite reduced for small and incipient caries, demonstrating how difficult remains the early detection of these lesions [11]. Park et al. (2022) compared caries detection by using intraoral photograph images and x-ray. By partitioning tooth surfaces prior to classification, they demonstrated the benefit of anatomic information for detection. Nevertheless, the study did not investigate radiographic imaging or caries severity evaluation [12]. Yoon et al. (2024) also proposed a cascade R-CNN model that leveraged integrated tooth number recognition and caries detection for full intraoral images. The system showed good localization and counting performance, but allowed only detection, not determining depth or severity of lesion for caries analysis [13]. Ayhan et al. (2025) applied YOLO-based models for caries detection under the fixed dental prosthesis on panoramic radiographs. Their two-stage method increased accuracy in challenging clinical contexts but was still focused on object-level detection as opposed to lesion segmentation or severity grading [14]. Bui et al. (2022) presented an ensemble learning framework that integrated deep features and machine-learning classifiers for caries detection in panoramic X-rays. While the system performed with high accuracy, this majority-voting strategy had limited interpretability and did not result in severity values that were clinically informative [15]. Szabó et al. (2024) assessed an AI-based diagnostic system by measuring the degree of agreement between dentists and AI regarding the radiographs of intraoral. They established that AI can provide valuable assistance to clinical diagnosis, but the sensitivity was moderate, particularly for initial caries which calls for better frame of reference [16]. Zhu et al. (2023) introduced CariesNet, a U-shaped network with axial attention for the segmentation of caries at different stages in panoramic radiography. The model obtained high Dice coefficients for superficial, intermediate and deep lesions. Nevertheless, the interpretation for intensity was implied and not explicitly related to levels based on classic clinical grading scales [17]. Sehgal et al. (2025) constructed a fuzzy logic-based scheme to categorize the severity of caries on the basis of handcrafted features computed upon region of interest (ROI) segmented from the X-ray images. Although we achieved high accuracy, our rule-based methodology is not as scalable and adaptive as the deep learning methods in today’s practices [18]. 2.1 Key Insight from Literature The existing studies show good performance in detection, segmentation or classification dental caries. However, most of them treat these tasks separately or are organized in a cascaded way and also do not have clinically informed severity modeling for early stage lesions. It is these challenges that drive the necessity for a
label: human

text: unified, context-aware and clinically-driven multi-task approach as in our proposed C³-DRIVE Net. III Proposed C³-DRIVE Net Framework The proposed C³-DRIVE Net is a holistic multitasking architecture that achieves both dental caries detection 19 and lesion segmentation, along with clinically interpretable severity grading, in a single joint end-to-end framework [21]. The general model architecture is based on encoder–decoder–multi-head, wherein shared encoder learns hierarchical radiographic representations that describe intensity gradients, anatomical structures and texture variations potentially correlated with mineral loss. This encoder is linked to a dual-decoder branch: a spatial decoder which maintains high-resolution feature maps for accurate lesion segmentation and semantic decoder consolidating global context information for robust caries detection [22]. Three task-specific heads are used on top of the shared representation: (i) a detection head that indicates locations of various regions at tooth level, (ii) a segmentation head delineates lesion boundaries with pixel-level precision and, (iii) a severity grading head infers clinically relevant level of lesion depth by reasoning about enamel–dentin–pulp relations and amplitude of radiographic attenuation. Joint optimization across all tasks allows C³-DRIVE Net to reduce errors propagated through the cascaded pipeline while maintaining consistency between disease detection, segmentation, and severity estimation levels in order to improve diagnostic reliability and clinical interpretability. ​ Figure 1. Architecture of the Proposed C³-DRIVE Net for Unified Dental Caries Analysis

IV Experimental Setup​ 4.1 Dataset Description​ The experiments were done with the open data Kaggle dataset “A Collection of Dental X-ray Images for Analysis” available at:https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kvipularya/a-collection-of-dental-x-ray-images-fo r-analysis. The dataset consists of nearly 2500 dental radiographic images, such as bitewing, panoramic and periapical X-rays reflected from a variety of imaging landscapes. The images possess differing contrast, tooth shapes, and radiographic noise which render the dataset a good candidate for robust dental caries analysis methodologies. All images are in gray-scale and with varying resolution from 512×512 to 1024×1024 pixels.

text: Following the elimination of low quality and duplicated images, 2,400 X-rays were used for the experiments. We once split the database through a patient-independent random separation as follows: ●​ Training set: 1,680 images (70%) ●​ Validation set: 360 images (15%) ●​ Testing set: 360 images (15%) This division enables fair testing and enough data to train stabilised hyperparameters. 4.2 Annotation Protocol and Clinical Realism As there is no lesion-level annotated ground truth in the dataset, these were manually annotated for outside of the study. Dental caries area was annotated with pixel-wise annotation to produce the segmentation masks and at tooth level for detection labels. The lesions were graded according to depth taking into account enamel involvement, dentinal extension, and distance from the pulp chamber using radiographically-acceptant clinical interpretation concepts. For increased label reliability, unclear cases were carefully checked and decisions made in the group to make the labels reflect real clinical diagnostic reasoning rather than visual features only. 4.3 Training Details All experiments were conducted with the PyTorch library. Input images were resized to 512×512 and normalized with z-score normalization. Data augmentation such as horizontal flipping, rotation and intensity scaling have been used when training the network to promote robust model. The model was trained with Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴, batch size = 8 and for a maximum of 100 epochs. We used early stopping through validation loss to avoid overfitting. The weights of the multi-task loss were empirically modified for balancing detection, segmentation, and severity grading tasks. 4.4 Baseline Models We compare C³-DRIVE Net with commonly used deep learning baselines in dental caries analysis to verify its performance: ●​ ResNet-50 for image-level caries detection ●​ YOLOv5 for object-based lesion localization ●​ U-Net for pixel-wise caries segmentation ●​ Two-stage CNN systems, which first detect and then classify the severity The datasets splits, preprocessing and augmentation were performed with all the other baselines models as well in order to provide fair comparison 4.5 Evaluation Metrics

text: addition, the integration of temporal analysis as well as clinician-in-the-loop feedback systems may improve robustness and clinical applicability. ​ VI Conclusion​ A fully automatic and context-aware unified deep learning framework, named C³-DRIVE Net was introduced in this paper for detection, segmentation and severity grading of dental caries from radiographs on clinical ground. Through combining tooth-sensitive anatomical decomposition, radiographic gradient disturbance modeling, and multi-task learning in a unified deep network, the proposed approach could alleviate the constraints of traditional single-task and cascaded DL models. Experimental results indicate that C³-DRIVE Net is a robust and well-performing model in all diagnostic tasks with 97.8% detection accuracy, 91.2% Dice coefficient, and 95.6% accuracy of severity grading for detection, segmentation, severity grading respectively on independent test dataset. Of significance, the framework achieves 87% sensitivity for detecting early stage caries, which is a WHO Special Service target; this improves prior deep learning-based baselines by 22%. The ablation study verifies that each architectural module has a synergistic effect on the overall performance improvement. The all-in-one framework minimizes error propagation with clinically meaningful anatomically and depth aware severity reasoning. These results emphasize the potential for C³-DRIVE Net-based system to be utilised as an effective chairside diagnostic aid, which could enable early interventions, facilitate objective severity scoring and enhance clinical decision-making in a dental setting. text: A Privacy-Preserving Predictive Protection Framework Using Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm for Secure Cloud-Integrated IoT Healthcare Systems Abstract-The ever-increasing adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies in smart healthcare has greatly enhanced the degree of remote patient monitoring, diagnosis at a distance and development of clinical decision making systems. Yet, the ongoing transfer of delicate patient details to cloud platforms poses grave security and privacy concerns, especially upon data processing and analytical inference. Traditionally, healthcare security solutions are focused either on encryption or a machine-learning-based intrusion detection system such as Symantec, Crowd-strike and SentinelOne that identify the attack only after they have taken root, focusing purely on protecting data in storage. Thus, patient identity exposure, inference-time privacy leakage and insider abuse issues remain unresolved in current IoT healthcare frameworks. In order to achieve these objectives while addressing the limitations, this paper presents P3-Secure, a privacy-preserving predictive protection framework that combines newly introduced Differential Privacy-based obfuscation of data inputs with secure Homomorphic Encrypted Analytics and a new Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm (BATA) for intelligent threat detection. The medical sensor data are anonymised at the IoT edge by means of controlled perturbation, preventing reconstruction of individual patient attributes during transmission according to a novel architecture proposal. This enables the encrypted health data to be processed in the cloud without being decrypted, thus avoiding exposure during model inference. Additionally, the BATA module enables real-time analysis of all user and device behavior patterns to detect abnormal access, ransomware activity, and attempts at data exfiltration. Experimental evaluation on healthcare IoT attack datasets also shows that the proposed framework reaches threats detection accuracy of 98.27%, privacy leakage reduction of 96.14% and resistance to data reconstruction attacks of 95.62% with secure availability of service reached at a system reliability rate of 97.83%. Results confirm that P3-Secure detects cyber threats, while acting as a deterrent during static storage, dynamic transmission and computation steps, thus applying to full-fledged secure Individuals-Powered Next Gen Cloud-based Healthcare Ecosystems. Keywords-IoT healthcare security, privacy-preserving computing, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, behavioral adaptive trust algorithm, cloud healthcare systems, cyber-attack detection, patient data protection 1. Introduction​ Recent advancements in the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing have significantly transformed modern healthcare schemes, enabling remote monitoring in real time, intelligent diagnosing systems, and scalable medical data analysis. Wearable sensors, implantable medical devices and edge gateways generate physiological data streams at high volume, which are transmitted to their own cloud platform for storage and predictive modeling. While this paradigm provides enhanced clinical responsiveness and operational efficiency, it brings about significant security and privacy challenges across the transmission, storage and
label: human

text: computational layers. Cloud-assisted IoT healthcare systems faced highly susceptible risk regarding unauthorized access, data leakage and insider exploitation due to heterogeneous device ecosystems and resource-constrained edge nodes [1], [3], [9], [22]. Additionally, standard protective strategies are mostly based on communication security by means of encryption or machine learning (ML)–based adversarial detection systems that activate after compromise and do not ensure inference-time privacy at the same time as mitigating the threat proactively [4], [11], [15]. Although blockchain-powered transmission security and decentralized learning models are explored to improve the integrity of data [16], [18] & traceability of the cloud model, those methods barely avoid a risk from privacy leakage during encrypted analytics or behavioral attack through dynamic settings of cloud structure [17]. Currently available intrusion detection techniques are either static based reliance metrics or signature-based and have very limited adapting behavioral modeling capabilities that are highly required to counter the dynamically changing feature of cyber attack in health care IoT ecosystems [11], [14], [19]. Appropriately treating privacy preservation, as the majority outgrowth systems species do, their data-post-processing processes treat detection with threat with wholly different modules that ebbs a shattered security framework where manipulations boost approaches cannot see the relationship between sanitization, encrypted execution and time access patterns. In order to overcome these limitations, this study proposes a unified privacy-preserving predictive protection framework called P3-Secure which integrates differential privacy compliant edge sanitization, homomorphic encrypted cloud analytics and a Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm (BATA) for real-time personalized threat intelligence. In this work, we present a framework that maintains the confidentiality during storage, transmission and inference while enabling adaptive behavior monitoring in order to perform proactive cyber defense. The main technical contributions of this work are summarized as below: ●​ A unified privacy preserving framework which combines controlled differential private mechanism and homomorphic encrypted analytic to withstand inference time data leaking attacks in cloud-supported IoT health care environments. ●​ A smart Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm (BATA) which adaptively calculates trust scores based on behavioral deviation measures, historical compliance factors and instant risk gradients for prompt identification of anomalies. ●​ A formal ε-differential privacy guarantee with a mathematically-backed formulation and secure encrypted computation pipelines for mitigating risks of reconstruction and model inversion. ●​ A gefilte fish - of a predictive protection mechanism that can with statistical significance detect at injection time ransomware, abnormal access escalation and data exfiltration. Comprehensive performance evaluation demonstrating its superior detection accuracy, privacy leakage limitation, reconstruction resistance and system robustness compared with advanced model IoT-cloud healthcare security frameworks [6], [10], [21], [32].

text: The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 outlines similar IoT–cloud health care security research and reveals the related research gap in inference-time privacy and adaptive trust modules integration. We detail the system architecture, adversary model and security goals in Section 3. In Section 4, we present the proposed P3-Secure framework consisting of a differential privacy–based edge sanitization mechanism, homomorphic encrypted analytics and the Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm. Section 5 describes theoretical privacy & security analysis and computational complexity. Section 6 provides Experimental Setup and Evaluation Metrics, while Section 7 presents performance results and comparative analysis. Section 8 concludes the paper and discusses potential future research directions. 2. Related Works​ Nayak et al. (2022) have explored integrated IoT with cloud computing to enhance use of smart healthcare environments, proving that e-Health systems not only increase the accessibility and efficiency of services, but also considerably broaden the boundary for exposing sensitive patient data. Their discussion highlighted the fact that as connected things interface with cloud platforms, the attack surface expands particularly in environments where verifiable health information and nonsecure communication processes are a challenge and will demand higher security measures [1]. On the other hand, the work by Hemnath (2023), building on their own advancements, proposed a machine learning–guided architecture to achieve proactive protection from unauthorized access into such cloud-based eHealth frameworks. It utilized automated threat intelligence and adaptive access control in a single cloud framework and added features such as better detection accuracy resiliency against new-age cyber threats. While the framework successfully minimized false positives and facilitated scalability to some extent, it was mostly based on behavior learning models and did not incorporate any formal privacy-preserving computation in inference [2]. Pati et al. Latency and bandwidth limitations in remote cardiovascular diagnosis were addressed by Kumaran et al. (2023), who proposed a fog-enabled IoT–cloud framework with ensemble deep learning. While their system gained high diagnostic performance with minimized latency through fog computing, security and privacy issues were not the main scope of architecture focusing on encrypted analytics or adaptable trust evaluation [3]. Padma Vijetha Dev and Venkata Prasad (2023) focused on the secure transmission of medical images using a lightweight hybrid encryption scheme combining elliptic curve cryptography with an optimization-based steganography method. While their approach enhanced computational efficiency and energy consumption during the encryption and cloud storage phases, it was limited to protecting data δ in transit and at rest [4], as opposed to inference-time exposure or behavioral threat modeling. Kamalam and Anitha (2022) focused on cloud-IoT healthcare analytics based on machine learning classifiers for optimization of storage with predictive performance. While the fuzzy temporal neural classifier aiding decision-making efficiency, computational performance was prioritized over fully private guarding or adversarial resilience in intertwined medical infrastructures [5]. Raju et al. (2025) developed a hierarchical convolutional neural network within lightweight homomorphic cryptography to predict heart disease in IoT–cloud systems. Their proposed model did exhibit a better diagnostic characteristic specificity in addition to decreased computation costs, nevertheless,

In addition, none of the explored solutions provide an integration on formal differential privacy guarantees, homomorphic encrypted analytics and dynamic behavioral trust modeling in a unified prediction protection framework also outlining a major gap among state-of-the-art healthcare cybersecurity design. 2.1 Research Gap​ Overall, prior works achieved significant progress in IoT–cloud healthcare architectures including predictive analytics, encryption, offloading efficiency and intrusion detection. Nonetheless, existing solutions only address isolated aspects of security—either communication confidentiality or blockchain verification and integrity or ML-based outlier detection independently and neglect the design of holistic architecture that effectively guarantees tight formal privacy-preservation during inference, as well as dynamic behavioral trust management in run-time. This gap encourages us to develop a unified predictive protection architecture integrating differential privacy, encrypted computation and dynamic trust evaluation across cloud integrated IoT healthcare systems. 3. System Model and Threat Model 3.1 Network Architecture The P3-Secure approach utilizes a layered cloud integrated IoT healthcare architecture which consists of IoT medical sensors, edge privacy module, cloud encrypted analytics engine and behavioral trust evaluation server. Wearable monitors and implantable devices IoT sensors have received much attention recently due to their ability to continuously gather physiological parameters while transmitting those data via wireless gateways. Despite this engineering being more beneficial for the real-time healthcare systems, it inherently exposes such architecture to cyber-attacks as heterogeneous communication protocols and open transmission environments are active [1], [22]. In order to alleviate privacy leakage at the early stage, raw medical data are locally processed at the edge utilizing a differential privacy–based sanitization mechanism prior to forwarding it to the cloud. Different from encryption-based schemes which mainly secure data in transit [4], the edge module guarantees that confidential features of patients are statistically protected before approaching the cloud. The design counters inference-time exposure attacks frequently seen in cloud-enabled health analytics [2], [6].
label: human

text: The sanitized data are subsequently encrypted with a homomorphic encryption scheme and transferred to the cloud, which executes predictive analytics on ciphertext without decryption [23]. This stops plaintext from being exposed even if the cloud infrastructure is all but compromised. This encrypted computation goes beyond the traditional intrusion detection approach or routing-based security augmentations in IoT-fog-cloud systems [9], [10]. A Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm (BATA) parallelizes with encrypted analytics in a logically isolated trust evaluation server. It dynamically calculates trust continuously with respect to user and device behavior patterns, which allows for proactive identification of unauthorized access or malicious activity while preventing issues caused by conventional approaches such as static access control or signature-based detection systems [11], [16]. 3.2 Adversary Model The adversary model aligns with realistic attack scenarios in IoT healthcare systems leveraging cloud integration [14], [19]. The initial adversarial model is an honest-but-curious cloud provider which faithfully computes protocols, but tries to derive sensitive information from data stored there or derived from corporate computations. The second attacker is a malicious insider who has legitimate credentials and abuses the access rights to retrieve unauthorized patient information [20]. The third type is a data reconstruction attacker who uses the sanitized outputs and additional knowledge about it to obtain similar records as patients. A more sophisticated adversary may carry out model inversion attacks by inspecting either prediction outputs or gradient information to reconstruct sensitive input features [2] this poses a growing threat in healthcare systems driven by ML [11]. The last category of attacker is the ransomware injection attacker, who tries to interrupt the healthcare services by encrypting medical data or modifying the IoT firmware. We assume that the adversaries have polynomial-time computational power, can monitor the network, have partial knowledge of the system but are unable to break standard cryptographic primitives or exceed the differential privacy budget. Secret encryption keys are not compromised and the trust evaluation server works in an isolated secure environment [24]. 3.3 Security Objectives We propose the P3-Secure framework in order to guarantee confidentiality, integrity, availability with inference-time privacy and adaptive access control for cloud-integrated IoT healthcare systems. Sensitive patient attributes are never exposed on the edge and centric [25][26] calculation, thus enabling differential privacy at the edge and homomorphic encrypted analytics in the cloud to achieve confidentiality. This is achieved by identifying anomalous behavior patterns and detecting unauthorized data modification through adaptive trust monitoring and enhancing secure dissemination mechanisms documented in previous work on IoT [10]. Availability is preserved by early detection of behavioral deviations akin to ransomware, thereby ensuring seamless healthcare delivery that aligns with time-critical monitoring specifications [9]. Not only meets privacy concerns at model execution time, but also overcomes the limitations of some transmission schemes that send encrypted inputs alone [4] The third class of policy updates, called adaptive access control, is founded on the premise that privileges should be assigned dynamically to users based on a behavioral trust score as opposed to static role-based assignment [11],[14]. It provides a pretty deep increase

text: in resilience against insider misuse and appears to be able to thwart numerous cultivations of cyber-threat that are recently growing outside the purview of standard intrusion detection models. 4. Proposed P3-Secure Framework The designed P3-Secure framework preserves privacy end-to-end for cloud-assisted IoT healthcare systems through the combination of edge-level differential privacy with homomorphically encrypted analytics on cloud and adaptive behavior-based trust computation. In contrast to traditional frameworks focusing on encryption only for data-in-transit protection [4], the proposed framework mathematically guarantees privacy before exposing any decision-making data to the cloud while providing secure computation and dynamic threat monitoring. In this section, we present the semi-rigorous definition of differential privacy-based edge sanitization mechanism. ​ Figure 1. Layered Architecture of the P3-Secure Privacy-Preserving IoT–Cloud Healthcare Framework

text: In the following figure 1, we depict the multi-layer architecture of our proposed P3-Secure framework to secure cloud-based IoT healthcare environments. The first layer is the IoT medical devices, including wearable sensors, implantable devices, and medical gateways to collect physiological data [27]. Data aggregation and sanitization through differential privacy-based methods happen prior to an encrypted transmission handled by the Edge Privacy Layer. The Encryption Layer enables secure cloud-based computation without decryption, achieved through homomorphic encryption. The Secure Cloud Layer performs encrypted predictive analytics and returns encrypted results to the host for authorized decryption. Conclusion​ We propose a privacy-preserving predictive protection framework named as P3-Secure, which is a comprehensive architecture for the cloud-integrated IoT healthcare systems based on ε-differential privacy, homomorphic encrypted analytics, and Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm. Experimental evaluation shows that the framework provides 98.27% threat detection accuracy, reduces privacy leakage by 96.14%, resists data reconstruction attacks at 95.62%, and has a system reliability of 97.83%, which confirms its effectiveness at protecting patient data during transmission, storage, and inference process. In addition to the derivations, the theoretical analysis also substantiates bounded privacy guarantees in both composition and post-processing features maintaining real time average computational complexity suitable for health-care deployment. The results show that the approaches of mathematically motivated privacy mechanisms and adaptive trust modeling can substantially improve the robustness against security threats and trust analytical reliability in IoT-cloud healthcare environments. A long-term goal is to build federated learning that realizes decentralized privacy preservation based on zero-knowledge proof mechanism of verifiable encrypted computation, and lightweight cryptographic implementations for ultra-resource-constrained medical IoT devices. text: A Privacy-Preserving Predictive Protection Framework Using Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm for Secure Cloud-Integrated IoT Healthcare Systems Abstract-The ever-increasing adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies in smart healthcare has greatly enhanced the degree of remote patient monitoring, diagnosis at a distance and development of clinical decision making systems. Yet, the ongoing transfer of delicate patient details to cloud platforms poses grave security and privacy concerns, especially upon data processing and analytical inference. Traditionally, healthcare security solutions are focused either on encryption or a machine-learning-based intrusion detection system such as Symantec, Crowd-strike and SentinelOne that identify the attack only after they have taken root, focusing purely on protecting data in storage. Thus, patient identity exposure, inference-time privacy leakage and insider abuse issues remain unresolved in current IoT healthcare frameworks. In order to achieve these objectives while addressing the limitations, this paper presents P3-Secure, a privacy-preserving predictive protection framework that combines newly introduced Differential Privacy-based obfuscation of data inputs with secure Homomorphic Encrypted Analytics and a new Behavioral Adaptive Trust Algorithm (BATA) for intelligent threat detection. The medical sensor data are anonymised at the IoT edge by means of controlled perturbation, preventing reconstruction of individual patient attributes during transmission according to a novel architecture proposal. This enables the encrypted health data to be processed in the cloud without being decrypted, thus avoiding exposure during model inference. Additionally, the BATA module enables real-time analysis of all user and device behavior patterns to detect abnormal access, ransomware activity, and attempts at data exfiltration. Experimental evaluation on healthcare IoT attack datasets also shows that the proposed framework reaches threats detection accuracy of 98.27%, privacy leakage reduction of 96.14% and resistance to data reconstruction attacks of 95.62% with secure availability of service reached at a system reliability rate of 97.83%. Results confirm that P3-Secure detects cyber threats, while acting as a deterrent during static storage, dynamic transmission and computation steps, thus applying to full-fledged secure Individuals-Powered Next Gen Cloud-based Healthcare Ecosystems.
