text: I. Introduction
label: human
source_file: A Hybrid AI-Based Model for Enhancing Energy-Efficient Resource Allocation in Cloud Computing Environments-1.pdf

text: Cloud computing has revolutionized the IT industry by offering scalable and flexible computing resources. However, the exponential growth in cloud service demand has led to substantial energy consumption, contributing to high operational costs and environmental impacts. Efficient resource allocation is a critical factor in addressing these challenges, as it directly influences the energy consumption of cloud data centers. Traditional resource allocation methods, such as rule-based algorithms and heuristic approaches, have been effective but struggle with the dynamic and complex nature of modern cloud environments. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based techniques, such as Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), have emerged as powerful tools to optimize resource allocation. DRL learns optimal policies through interaction with dynamic environments. However, DRL suffers from high computational overhead and slow convergence. To mitigate these challenges, we propose a hybrid model that integrates DRL with Genetic Algorithms (GA), a heuristic optimization technique known for its robust global search capabilities. This paper presents a hybrid AI-based model designed to enhance energy-efficient resource allocation in cloud environments. The model leverages DRL for adaptive decision-making and GA for fast convergence to near-optimal solutions. We compare the proposed hybrid model's performance with traditional approaches, demonstrating its potential to reduce energy consumption while maintaining resource allocation efficiency.

text: VisioSense: An AI-Based Smart Glasses System for Real-Time Assistance to Visually Impaired Individuals Abstract- Visual impairment imposes severe constraints on an individual's capacity to see, maneuver and interact with the environment without risk of harm leading to reduced independence and quality of life. Traditional mobility aids, such as white canes, may provide only rudimentary assistance for mobility needs without “context-aware” functionality and real-time knowledge availability that are useful in situational contexts. This paper introduces VisioSense, an artificial intelligence smart glasses to offer the real-time visual to audio support for visually impaired people through computer vision and speech intelligence. The system records video using an embedded camera, runs the YOLOv5 deep learning model to detect objects in real-time, utilizes The Tesseract OCR engine for extracting environmental printed text from the scene and finally makes use of a text-to-speech synthesis to generate spoken words. A voice interaction module allows issuing commands and asking context-aware questions by users, which are then handled accordingly by an AI-based decision and question-answering module using visual context that has been pre-stored to avoid unnecessary visual operation. A time-controlled announcement mechanism silences redundant alarms to minimize cognitive load. Experimental results in indoor and outdoor realistic trials show 93.1% object detection accuracy, 90.4% OCR recognition accuracy, and a mean end-to-end response latency of 1.2 seconds. User interaction assessment also indicates a 35% reduction in unnecessary audio alerts, evidencing that VisioSense can offer accurate, prompt and context-aware assistance and thus is an affordable, practical and scalable technology to improve safety situation awareness and support for blind users. Keywords: Assistive technology; Smart glasses; Visual impairment; Object detection; Optical character recognition; Computer vision; Speech-based interaction; Artificial intelligence 1. Introduction​ Visual impairment is an important public health problem that limits independency, mobility and access to information worldwide [1][2]. The World Health Organization reports that more than 2.2 billion people worldwide suffer from some kind of vision impairment – with over 40 million classified as blind [3][4]. A substantial fraction of these people experiences daily difficulties to travel through the environment, identify objects in their surrounding as well as read regular text like signboards, labels and print [5][6]. These challenges not only diminish quality of life, but also increase risk for accidents and dependence, social reliance and isolation, as well as financial exclusion [7]. The safe human navigation, understanding environments and
label: human

text: the reading have been long-time challenges to visually impaired people. In unknown or changing surroundings [8][9], lack of vision to obstacles or moving objects and spatial orientation may result in accidents and reduced confidence. Depend on reading material that is posted in public spaces such as transportation centers and places of employment. Such concerns underscore the value of assistive technology which can offer real-time, context-sensitive environmental comprehension, instead that rudimentary distance reading [10][11]. However, conventional assistance techniques only partially solve the problem. The white cane gives no contextual or semantic information about the environment. Smartphone-based assistive apps have brought object recognition and text-to-speech technology to these devices, but have been associated with higher latency because of cloud processing, usability issues by means of requiring manual manipulation, or online consumption of the battery [12][13]. Furthermore, a device you constantly have in your hand is not conducive to seamless mobile assistance. Recent developments in smart glasses have made visual sensing hands-free; however, existing approaches are often costly, computation-intensive or cognitively burdensome. Many systems produce a constant stream of context-free audio alerts, which can become overwhelming and tedious for users. Furthermore, the majority of existing methods are framing by frame manner and do not have contextual memory. The users are having repeated notifications for the objects, so people don't interact with the system in a natural way by just conversational questions. Second, the realtime latency of service in both indoor and outdoor is seldom evaluated systematically, which reduces confidence for real deployment [14][15]. This gap is addressed by recent advances in the field of computer vision, deep learning and speech technologies. Light-weight deep learning models allow for real-time object-detection, while recent OCR systems can robustly read text across different lighting conditions [16][17]. When integrated with speech-centric interaction along with edge-level processing, such systems indeed enable continual, hands-free aid. However, seamlessly integrating these components into a single wearable system while being responsive, context-aware and cognitively efficient, is still an on-going research problem. This paper fills the gaps and envisions an AI-based smart glasses system which will be designed by embedding real-time object detection, text recognition and speech based interaction in a single framework. The proposed system possesses short-term visual context memory, which differentiates it from the contemporary methods and thus facilitates intelligent information filtering and context-dependent question answering [18][19]. A time-based alerting mechanism is presented to reduce the number of repeated notifications, while ensuring important safety material is dispatched in a timely manner. We validate the system in realistic
label: human

text: indoor and outdoor scenarios with focus on latencies, usability and robustness. Our main contributions are as follows: ●​ Development of an AI-powered smart glasses assistive system in real time with deep learning–based object detection, optical character recognition (OCR), and speech interactivity for the visually-impaired. ●​ Design of a context-sensitive help system with the visual state memory and timed suppression alerts feature to mitigate repetitive audio feedback and cognitive load. ●​ Extensive real-world investigation of the proposed solution in indoor and outdoor applications, focusing on responsiveness, user-friendliness and operational effectiveness. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on assistive technologies, OCR, and vision-based systems for visually impaired users. Section 3 describes the proposed system architecture and methodology, followed by experimental setup and performance evaluation in Sections 5 and 6, while Section 7 concludes the paper and outlines future research directions. 2. Literature Review Tang et al. (2023) introduced an integrated Optical Character Recognition (OCR) system that is dedicated for in-field reading of text from the iron plates. Their approach included following stages in a pipeline: text region detection, camera alignment, text line segmentation and character recognition that utilized fusion from vision-based as well language based networks. By adopting synthetic data generation and strong augmentation methods, the system overcame lack of data and demonstrated additional robust performance on real-world industrial scenes. While applicable for fixed industrial implementation, the scheme is designed under ideal conditions and lacks features considering mobility, real-time user interaction or wearable assistive applications [1]. Shahin et al. (2024) studied the use of existent OCR-based machine identification systems in Lean 4.0 manufacturing scenario. Their proposed method, MBID-OCR system, aimed at recognition of printed identification numbers with poor lighted conditions by applying image preprocessing and character segmentation methods. With a low character error rate the system achieved high precision and showed that it is applicable in industrial automation. But the method is specially designed for immobile camera and production line, which limits its portable use in dynamic user-centric assistive systems [2]. Fateh et al. (2024) considered document layout analysis and text line detection as important preprocessing steps for OCR, with a focus on the Persian script documents. The research boosted OCR performance of the deep learning models on complicated document designs by using voting models and geometric correction. Although the work improves OCR performance for structured documents, it is mainly designed for offline document analysis and does not
label: human

text: address real-time use or assistive scenarios with impaired users [3]. Patil et al. (2022) introduced a semantic segmentation preprocessing pipeline for enhancing OCR on documents with mixed printed and handwritten content. They proposed a pixel-level text region identification approach, which is followed by standard OCR engines for better recognition results. Considering the fact that this work is focused on simple prepossessing, it still uses traditional OCR backends and does not take into account real-time perception and audio sense requirements for assistive technologies [4]. Batra et al. (2024) for a comprehensive comparative study of OCR engines on medical report digitalization also tested several preprocessing and OCR frameworks. Their observations highlight the crucial role of preprocessing towards OCR accuracy, especially for domain-specific (e.g., medical history) documents. Although this work influences OCR optimization it only applies on an offline document digitization and do not cover the wearable or real-time assistive system [5]. Khosrobeigi et al. (2022) proposed neural OCR framework for Persian printed and handwritten texts based on CNN and a Bidirectional LSTM. The proposed system obtained the good recognition rate on both Persian and mixed-language using large-scale multilingual data. Although that approach illustrates the power of deep sequence modeling for OCR, it is still discriminating in terms of text recognition accuracy rather than end-user assistive interaction or environmental perception [6]. Mukhiddinov and Cho (2021) developed a smart glasses system for helping the visually impaired, especially in dark environments. The structure of their system included image improvement, object recognition, text recognition and tactile feedback. The experimental results demonstrated the competitive performance on some challenging datasets. Nevertheless, the system consist of several independent modules and does not specifically deal with context awareness, alarm repetition or conversational interaction with users [7]. Kuriakose et al. (2023) proposed DeepNAVI, a smart-phone based navigation assistance system that utilizes deep learning for obstacle detection and audio-based guidance. The system was portable and convenient, providing information on object type, distance, and motion. Although these methods are successful for navigation, the utilization of smartphones causes usability limitations and does not have wearable vision, contextual memory and text reading capabilities [8]. Xie et al. (2022) presented a multi-modal guidance strategy that brings together YOLO-based object detection and ORB-SLAM for indoor navigation. Realized as a smart cane, the system utilized both tactile and auditory feedback to support obstacle avoiding and path planning. Though this approach enhances on the accuracy of indoor navigation, it adds to hardware and mostly concentrates over the navigation instead providing a comprehensive view about environment or recognition of text [9].

text: Ouali et al. (2023) have utilized deep learning to develop a handwritten Arabic text recognition system augmented with audio output and augmented reality for blind users. The system had good recognition performance and showed the possibility of reading out complex handwritten text. However, the method is not language-independent and lacks continuous perception of the environment as well as wearable deployment for daily navigation [10]. Bala et al. (2023) developed a portable cognitive assistant based on freely wearable and multi-sensor fusion for navigation and obstacle avoidance. The system was tested with several environmental elements and conducted real-time user studies. However, the device is multifunctional and uses several sensors, which does not have an integrated vision-based context-aware intelligent framework, meanwhile it may increase the complexity and cost of the system [11]. Dos Santos et al. (2022) investigated the perceived stigma of support technology, specifically white canes and smart glasses. Their results indicated that device acceptance is highly sensitive to aesthetics and modern design. This paper highlights the need for unobtrusive wearable assistive systems, but does not deal with system design and technical intelligence aspects [12]. text: 2.1 Research Gap Collectively, the current research work reveals that there is remarkable achievements in OCR technology, navigation support and wearable aids for blind persons. However, such works tend to concentrate on single-task (e.g., text recognition or navigation), use static or smartphone-based systems or do not incorporate context-aware intelligence and real-time interaction. Research is still clearly lacking in an integrated, wearable smart glasses (generally under the name of a new generation) system which integrates real-time object detection, OCR for text identification on those objects and following apps as well as speech interaction with contextual memory and alert management – this is what motivates the present work. 3.Methodology 3.1 System Overview and Architecture​ The system we present is an assistive wearable real-time framework to endow visual impaired people with outdoor scene understanding, rendering the environment through audio information (Fig. 1). A smart glasses-based forward-looking camera records video frames processed locally using an edge-based pipeline, in order to reduce latency. Every frame is processed in parallel for two purposes: (a) to be analyzed by the YOLOv5 based object detection module, detecting relevant elements such as obstacles, people, and navigational cues; and (b) also by the OCR module to extract text information from signboards or printed content [13][14]. Objects detected and text recognized is maintained in a near-recent context memory, which can be used to stifle recurring alerts and inclusive user interaction. The extracted information is converted into phrased spoken response through a speech synthesis engine, and voice-command loop enables a user to make queries about memorised items hands free. The implemented architectural decisions: lightweight object detection, OCR integration, context memory and local speech interaction were designed to achieve a good balance between real-time response status, cognitive comfort level and practical utility of such system addressing shortcomings in current assistive systems.

To ensure practical usability, the system is designed to operate continuously for several hours under normal usage conditions, emphasizing energy-efficient inference and duty-cycled sensing. These hardware design choices enable a compact, low-latency, and wearable assistive platform suitable for real-world deployment while maintaining sufficient computational capacity for deep learning–based perception. 4.2 Object Detection Module​ The object detection module in the proposed system is realized based on YOLOv5, which is characterized by a good compromise between detection accuracy and real-time inference speed on edge devices [18]. Unlike two-stage detectors, YOLOv5 combines the object localization and classification into one forward propagation and is therefore more favorable for use in wearable assistive applications that have stringent latency requirements. In this paper, we use the YOLOv5s model to meet a trade-off between computational cost and accuracy so that real-time detection can be performed on embedded devices. The model is pretrained on COCO with the pre-trained weights, and then further fine-tuned on a task specific dataset combined of everyday indoor and outdoor classes that are relevant to navigation for the visually impaired (i.e., pedestrians, vehicles, doors, staircases, obstacles). Input images are rescaled to a resolution of 640 × 640, offering sufficient spatial information with an efficient inference speed [19]. During testing, a confidence threshold of 0.5 is used to suppress low-confidence detections and then non-maximum suppression to remove redundant bounding boxes. Tesseract OCR engine is used to recognize the text after applying target

text: pre-processing steps which increases recognition accuracy under real-world scenarios. These steps include grayscale processing, adaptive thresholding, contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization and noise reduction to alleviate the negative impact of varying illumination and background clutter. Text regions are filtered based on the confidence of detection and the spatial relevance, so that only meaningful and readable text content is passed for narration. The app also features multi-language text processing by offering dynamic language model selection and switching between languages as per a user's preference or sense of occasion. The output text is turned into audio with a small, embedded TTS engine chosen for its quick synthesis time and supported on many popular platforms. To minimize the end-to-end response time [22], OCR is restricted to areas of interest returned by the visual pipeline and speech synthesis is only initiated given new or user-species text. These designs allow auditory output to be provided in a timely and intelligible manner, without jeopardizing real-time operation of the guide or overloading visually impaired users' cognitive resources. 4.4 Voice Interaction and Context Awareness The novelty of the proposed work consists on the context aware voice interaction system that provides intelligence help, by not generating unnecessary audio feedback [23][24]. Experimental Setup​ The AI-based smart glasses system described here was tested through indoor and outdoor experiments in a real-world environment to verify its effectiveness and robustness. Indoor tests were conducted in hallways, classrooms, offices, stairwells and public buildings whereas outdoor experiments were done on sidewalks, highway shoulders, parking lots and campus walkways to represent common pedestrian scenarios. Experiments were carried out under different lighting conditions, such as sunny weather at daylight, dark indoor environment, and shadowed locations to verify the performance in shadows and varying illuminance. The camera was installed at eye-level for natural field of view during user locomotion. Object detection was tested on the related categories such as pedestrians, vehicles, doors, stairs, obstacles and furniture etc., while OCR module was evaluated with environmental text such as signboards, labels and printed notices with different fonts and backgrounds. All experiments were conducted with a wearable prototype hosting a 720p (30 fps) RGB camera, an incorporated edge-processing unit (Raspberry Pi 4 or equivalent), and bone-conduction or in-ear audio output – ensuring low-latency and robust operations with all computations executed on-device. Conclusion A study that used an AI-based smart glasses system for real-time assistance to blind or visually impaired users using combined object detection, optical character recognition and speech interaction was demonstrated. Benefiting from a YOLOv5-based perception module, an improved OCR pipeline and a context-aware memory mechanism, our system attained the high retrieval rate for object detection (93.1%), the excellent performance of text recognition (90.4%) as well as the low end-to-end latency (1.2 s) in both indoor and outdoor scenes. The time-based alert suppression helped reduce unnecessary audio alerts, and significantly enhanced the usability and cognitive convenience of the system compared to assistive tools available today. In summary, the experimental results have shown that the developed system provides an effective, scalable and user-friendly approach to improve independent navigation and environmental awareness. In future we aim to include temporal scene understanding, increase the scope of multilingual OCR support, incorporate more environmental sensors as well as optimize for power-efficient runtime on edge hardware to allow sustained real world deployment. text: A Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Framework for Contextualized Augmented Reality Interventions in Autism Behavioral and Cognitive Development Abstract-Augmented Reality (AR) technologies, combined with Artificial Intelligence, are increasingly explored to enhance cognitive, behavioral, and social skill development in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). However, current systems predominantly rely on black-box personalization models, lack transparent intervention planning, and demonstrate limited ecological transfer to real-world contexts. This research proposes NSCCA-AR (Neural-Symbolic Curriculum for Contextualized AR), a novel hybrid framework that integrates lightweight neural perception modules with a symbolic curriculum planner to deliver explainable, constraint-aware, and context-adaptive intervention sequences. The system employs Bayesian belief updating to track individualized skill progression across domains such as joint attention, emotion recognition, and turn-taking, while a symbolic task-graph planner generates safe and developmentally appropriate sequences under attention, fatigue, and safety constraints. AR overlays dynamically scaffold engagement through on-device inference, ensuring privacy preservation via ephemeral feature representations without storing raw sensory data. In preliminary simulations with clinically validated task models, NSCCA-AR demonstrated a 31.6% improvement in targeted skill acquisition, a 24.8% enhancement in engagement duration, and a 19.3% increase in ecological generalization compared to baseline AR interventions. Additionally, clinician trust scores improved by 27.1% due to the transparency afforded by explainable decision traces. This work establishes a foundational paradigm for shifting from isolated AR tasks to structured, goal-driven developmental curricula, while ensuring privacy, interpretability, and real-world transferability. Future clinical pilots will further evaluate longitudinal outcomes, caregiver acceptance, and adaptability across diverse severity levels of ASD. Keywords-Autism Spectrum Disorder, Augmented Reality, Neuro-Symbolic AI, Curriculum Planning, Bayesian Skill Modeling, Cognitive Development, Behavioral Intervention, Explainable AI, Privacy-Preserving Sensing, Real-World Generalization I Introduction Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) face a wide range of problems in social communication, emotion recognition and executive functioning. Generalization of treatment gains Children with ASD frequently have difficulties in generalizing acquired skills from therapeutic or experimental settings to everyday environments and this affects long-term effectiveness of interventions [1][2]. Conventional behavioural and cognitive treatments rely on controlled environments, expert guidance, and structured exercises with translation to naturalistic settings limited by resource requirements and redundancy for the caregiver [3][4]. Augmented Reality (AR) has clearly shown promise as a path for scaffolding learning in ecologically viable settings through the use of overlays of interactive cues on top of real world scenes [5][6]. However, while promising, the majority of current AR approaches

Filling these gaps requires a hybrid model that combines the flexible, perceptual abilities of neural architectures with the structured, constraint enforcing reasoning capabilities of symbolic planning for facilitating developmental interventions that are transparent and contextually updateable. Existing AR-based ASD systems are seen to suffer from severe limitations in terms of flexibility, explainability and generalizability. Although deep neural models are excellent at recognizing multimodal cues, beer gaze gesture facial recognition interpretable decisions and clinician interpretability is also impeded by their black-box nature [9][10]. On the other hand, symbolic planners give computationally interpretable deduction/justification and hierarchical task planning, but suffer from limited robust open-loop replanning for noisy or even unpredictable sensory environments [11][12]. Several other models[13][14] also assume fixed task hierarchies and do not account for temporal and the physiological state including level of attention variation, fatigue, cognitive overload etc. In addition, such systems do not update their knowledge of a child’s progress in real time and as the level of skills evolves, then one has no way to recalibrate interventions [15][16]. As a consequence, the static and fragmented intervention models which emerge can lead to under workforce for both dissatisfaction and combined with or ‘over’ training where ecological validity is diminished. To bridge this gap, we develop an intelligent curriculum model that dynamically adjusts to the learner's behavioral and cognitive trajectory while ensuring interpretability and safety through symbolic reasoning. The proposed framework, Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum for Contextualized Augmented Reality (NSCCA-AR), establishes an unified structure which incorporates neural perception, probabilistic reasoning and symbolic task planning [17]. Such neural modules transform multimodal input streams, comprising visual, gestural and vocal signals, into representations of task-relevant states such as gaze direction, emotional state or turn-taking. Finally, a symbolic curriculum planner builds adaptive task sequences according to explicit development, attentional and safety related constraints. Bayesian belief updating keeps a probability distribution over the learner’s ability levels in different domains— joint attention, emotion recognition, and reciprocal interaction—and enables real-time adjustment of task difficulty. As skill estimates change, the planner promotes or demotes tasks to ensure engagement with reduced frustration. All the inference is conducted on-device, and we keep only temporary feature embeddings to guarantee privacy preservation [18]. This blend of neuroplastic adaptability and symbolic transparency paves the way for transparent, context-sensitive, ethically sound developmental interventions in AR. Real-world deployment of this technique requires methods that are interpretable, scalable and capable to handle non-stationary learning environments. AR interventions need to overcome the constraints of static task design and demonstrate real generalization to daily behaviors [19][20]. The main issues are the coordination between perceptual inference and constraint-based reasoning, the reduction of sensory noise, overcoming conflicting adaptation signals and maintaining belief stability along non-stationary behavioural trajectories. The present proposal aims to overcome these challenges by developing an intelligent, privacy-preserving curriculum engine to support longitudinal developmental progress in children with ASD. Adaptive behavior and mastery of emotion increased following the consecutive weeks of AR intervention as planned, providing evidence for the feasibility of using AR as an early intervention medium through caregivers [20]. 2.1 Research Gap Although the literature broadly supports AR interventions across behavioral, cognitive and emotional domains, clear gaps in empirical work are evident. The definition is somewhat vague and poorly defines the training schedule and involves a task-specific setup or seeks minimum curriculum sequencing, refusal to adapt over time. The personalized factors are largely based on inscrutable neural models without clear explanation of decision making, reducing the confidence of clinicians and interpretability. In addition, there are limited methods that jointly plan for real-time AR task execution and awareness—accounting for focus change, fatigue, or safety limitations. Ecological transfer in real-world settings is weak as well, with the intervention having limited generalization beyond laboratory or classroom. Privacy preserving and explainability are other unexplored dimensions, especially when AI-driven components are deployed with sensitive developmental populations. Taken together, these limitations suggest the need for a neuro-symbolic architecture that can reconcile adaptive perception with symbolic reasoning in order to facilitate explainable, contextually-aware and ethically-guided AR interventions for supporting the developmental trajectories of children with ASD. III Methodology The current proposal contributes with NSCCA-AR, a Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum for Contextualized Augmented Reality that integrates perceptual intelligence, probabilistic adaptation and symbolic planning to provide explainable and context-sensitive interventions in children with ASD [21]. The architecture includes small and efficient neural networks for on-the-fly translation of multimodal sensory cues — such as gaze, facial emotion, and gesture recognition — into engagement and task performance signals 22. These perceptual inferences are integrated throughout time with a Bayesian belief model to dynamically estimate progress toward each child’s development over social interaction, emotional recognition, and attention regulation. Symbolic planner then schedules AR-based learning tasks based on explicit policies regarding mental load, tiredness thresholds and safety boundaries which lead to explainable and ethical decision making [24]. As privacy intervention, the system does not capture raw sensory data but only keep high-level feature representations in order to comply with common standards of personal data protection [25]. The NSCCA-AR system will do this by capitalizing on adaptive scheduling of practice and embedded feedback loops to appropriate levels that promote the trade off difficulty-of-progression toward mastery with motivation-to-practice, and enhance generalization from virtual practice to ecology. This combination allows the development of an interpretable, adaptive, and sustainable AR intervention to support individualized developmental trajectories..

NSCCA-AR System Architecture The multilayered structure of the NSCCA-AR framework is shown in Fig. 1, where neural perception, probabilistic belief representation and symbolic curriculum planning are combined into an adaptive AR environment. The multimodal sensory data (gaze, facial expressions, gestures, audio cues) are fed to lightweight neural networks for generating privacy-preserving feature embeddings. The Bayesian model can also dynamically infer a subject's developmental skill state, which provides the symbolic planner with information to monitor task ordering under cognitive, fatigue and safety constraints. The generated task plans are presented as AR overlays, providing context-aware, explainable and ecologically valid interventions for children with ASD. 3.1 Participants and Study Setting The subjects will include children who have been diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) according to the criteria of the DSM-5 and will be representative of a spectrum from mild to moderate functional levels. The focused age group of participants will be the 6-to-12-year- old children, as this is a developmental period in which gains are often made on social communication skills, attention-regulation and cognitive learning following structured interventions. Eligible criteria will involve children with preserved, good quality vision and normal hearing in order to be able to effectively interact with AR stimuli as well as follow simple instructions under supervision. Exclusion criteria will be participants with profound intellectual disability, uncontrolled epilepsy, or neurodevelopmental disorders other than ASD that could hinder AR-based interactions. An initial baseline assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical team of a psychologist, therapist and occupational specialist will be carried out whereby developmental levels on the three areas are recorded for each child: level of joint attention, emotion recognition, and compliance with task requests. The intervention will be tested in three controlled settings: a clinical therapy room, an inclusive classroom and a home-based AR training setup to assess ecological validity of learning to the generalisation

All contexts will use the same sequence of tasks, with sensory and interaction parameters being adjusted based on environmental cues to guarantee similar levels of data collection and personalisation dynamics across different environments. 3.2 Data Acquisition The procedure of collecting multimodal data used in this study is created to record and analyze behavioral, cognitive, and affective signals from children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) when they receive augmented reality (AR)–based intervention. To train and advance the neural modules of emotion detection (EMO) and engagement level prediction ENGA., this study includes a preparation training database named CK+ with 920 gray face images from its parent Extended Cohn-Kanade (CK+) image, video databases. The choice of this dataset is motivated by its quality annotations of prototypical facial expressions as well as because it provides a relatively balanced distribution across fundamental emotional categories that are so important to the domain of emotion recognition tasks related to autism. In this study, the proposed dataset is in contrast to previous large-scale emotion datasets which tend to suffer from irrelevant noise or uncontrolled poses, and such a curated CK⁺-based database ensures that the test images are consistently with aligned faces and illumination control. Its pre-computed form using haarcascade_frontalface_default for face cropping and normalization on 48×48 pixel resolution also enables the model training to be fast, influenced by a minimum of preprocessing overhead. Furthermore, the presented database is in good agreement with NSCCA-AR framework goals as it enables neural networks to generalize emotional recognition models while reducing computational burden and keeping intervention real-time responsive and interpretable. The augmented dataset includes 920 annotated facial images spanning eight emotion categories: angry (45), disgust (59), fear (25), happy (69), sad (28), surprise (83) and neutral(593) and contempt(18). Whereas each image is then flattened into a vector of dimension 2304 having gray scale pixel values (48×48) to achieve the same input dimensions for the convolutional feature extraction process. Three subsets of the dataset (80% for training, 10% for public testing and 10% for private testing) by partition split allows both model optimization and unbiased evaluation. The noisy samples marked by light and skin tone variations, hair occlusion were transformed during pre-processing to be clear and consistent in display so that it can be traced easily using the Haar classifier. This allows facial detection with high precision and emotional inference under uncontrolled visual conditions. The dataset’s small and different setting makes it well suited for the lightweight neural perception model presented in NSCCA-AR, which leverages real-time facial emotion recognition to forecast an adaptive scheduling curriculum. Therefore, the pre-processed CK+ dataset becomes a building block for system training to accurately interpret affective cues that can be contextually responsive and emotionally aware AR-based interventions targeting children with ASD. 3.3 Signal Preprocessing and Feature Extraction AR Sensors to be memorized The multimodal cultural-AR data from the interventions including facial image, gaze position, gesture and audio are preprocessed in a structured

text: comprised the iPad Pro (M2 chip, 8GB RAM, LiDAR sensor) for depth-aware AR overlays, Microsoft HoloLens 2 to provide a head-mounted immersive experience and Android smartphone (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2; 12GB of RAM) to enable wider reach. For Software: development, we used Unity 2023.1 for AR scene rendering, AR Foundation and Vuforia SDK for cross-platform AR object tracking, as well as PyTorch 2.1 to implement lightweight neural perception models. The neural modules were quantization-aware, trained and accelerated by TensorRT with latency of less than 100 ms for emotion recognition and gesture tracking. Hyperparameters were chosen to be: convolutional layers ranging from 3–5 layers with kernel size of 3×3, learning rate =0.001 with Adam optimizer, batch size of 32 and early stopping at validation loss plateau in order to prevent overfitting. The probabilistic belief modules (Bayesian update engine) were integrated with symbolic planners using RESTful APIs and on-device SQLite storage for the ephemeral feature embeddings, to provide privacy preserving real-time feedback. The system delivered visual, auditory and haptic perception cues under belief thresholds and task sequences to keep individuals engaged while tracking their cognitive load & fatigue instantly. 4.1 Experimental Protocol The experimental design included three phases: pre-intervention, intervention, and post-intervention. Baseline measures comprised cognitive, social and attentional tests and engagement monitoring (eye-tracking, interaction logs). Participants underwent intervention twice per week for 8 weeks, approximately from 20 to 30 minutes, in which task sequences were flexibly adjusted according to the probabilistic belief updates and symbolic constraints. A post-intervention assessment replicated the baseline probes to assess skill acquisition, engagement, and generalization. Retention of learned content for long-term use was assessed at 4 and 8 weeks post-intervention. The protocol was intended to strike a balance between demanding data collection and ecological validity, providing informative results on both short-term learning effects and longer-lasting behavioral change. 4.2 Evaluation Metrics A constructivist approach to the assessment of intervention effectiveness was used. Performance metrics Performance was quantified by the accuracy, completion time, and consistency presented in Eq. 30 and Eq. 31: ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (30) 𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦= 𝐶𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒𝑠 𝑇𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒𝑠 ​ ​ (31) 𝑅𝑒𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑒 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦= 1 −𝑉𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 𝑖𝑛 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑠 𝑀𝑒𝑎𝑛 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑇𝑖𝑚𝑒 Engagement measures consisted of duration of focused attention and gaze fixations as well as the frequency of active task interactions recorded through AR sensors. In comparison to current AR interventions, the NSCCA-AR led to greater gains in skill acquisition, engagement, ecological generalization, and clinician confidence which demonstrated promise of explainable, adaptive and context-aware task sequencing. The ablation study further validates that each module provides unique benefits to the overall effectiveness, with symbolic schedule construction being crucial for systemic and safe intervention control. These results indicate that real-time perception with probabilistic skill tracking and constraint-aware planning allows personalized, goal-directed AR experience that fills the gap between virtual training and real world utilization in a better manner than other solutions. Besides, the privacy-preserving nature of the system using ephemeral feature representations allows “safe” deployment without sacrificing personal customization. The implications of this work are relevant to clinical practice as well as education, and demonstrate a move away from static black-box AR tasks towards dynamic interpretable curriculum that can promote longitudinal developmental trajectories in children with ASD. The proposed model successfully combines lightweight neural perception, probabilistic belief space representation modeling as well as symbolic curriculum planning for realizing explainable, adaptive and privacy-preserving interventions. text: A Proactive Risk Anticipation and Multi-Agent Orchestration Algorithm for Benchmarking Clinical AR Assistants in the AR-ClinAgent Framework Abstract-Augmented Reality (AR)–assisted clinical systems are increasingly being adopted to support healthcare professionals during complex procedural workflows; however, the absence of a unified evaluation standard continues to limit their reliability, safety validation, and scalability. To overcome this limitation, the AR-ClinAgent framework is introduced as a benchmark and assessment platform applicable to both simulation laboratories and manikin-based clinical environments. The framework operates through a structured perception-to-action cycle that involves capturing egocentric video input, retrieving clinically validated procedural steps through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounding, planning and executing context-specific actions, rendering real-time AR overlays for clinician guidance, verifying procedural outcomes, and logging detailed performance metrics for assessment. A major advancement within this framework is the integration of Proactive Risk Anticipation (PRA) and Multi-Agent Orchestration, which enables predictive error detection and intelligent task division among specialized AI sub-agents to enhance workflow reliability and operational efficiency. The platform employs privacy-preserving, high-stakes clinical datasets focused on ultrasound-guided intravenous access, central line insertion, and medication verification, ensuring both realism and compliance. Evaluation metrics include procedural accuracy, latency, intervention frequency, safety incidents, and energy consumption, enabling a multi-dimensional analysis of system performance. Baseline experiments show that PRA-empowered AR agents reduce clinical oversight interventions by 31%, improve step-wise execution accuracy by 26%, and decrease near-miss incidents by 22% compared to non-predictive systems, while latency is lowered by 18% and device-level energy usage improves by 14% due to distributed task processing. With its standardized schemas, scoring mechanisms, and reproducible baselines, AR-ClinAgent establishes a reliable foundation for fair comparisons between AR-assistant models, providing explicit insight into the trade-offs between safety and efficiency. By combining regulated procedural grounding with anticipatory intelligence, the framework accelerates the evolution of trustworthy AR assistants, advancing their readiness for seamless integration into real-world clinical practice. The use of AR application with clinical workflows supports overlay guidance during high-risk procedures (central-line insertion, ultrasound-guided intravenous access and medication

Whilst positive results have been shown in simulation-based settings, current AR-assisted approaches suffer from several shortcomings such as failure to ensure procedural consistency, over-delayed interventions and lack of common evaluation frameworks [5][6]. Conventional subjective evaluation and small scale of objective performance metrics are used in most assessment techniques that do not present a holistic view to the procedural dynamics which are as dynamic and context-specific [7][8]. The lack of this discrepancy has slowed the scalability, reproducibility and regulatory validation in AR-assisted technologies [9][10]. Recently, some AI-based methods have attempted to cope with workflow optimization or error reduction but few frameworks have comprehensively considered proactive risk anticipation and cognitive task allocation in terms of specialized sub-agents [11][12]. Bridging this gap calls for a coherent framework that can assess AR assistants in controlled yet realistic clinical settings, while considering both safety-critical results and the system efficiency. It is well-known that the PRA can significantly contribute to reducing errors and improve procedural consistency in clinical AI systems 13. PRA and its pre-emptive failure prediction work as an early warning system enabling interventions to be introduced early enough, decreasing near misses [15][16]. As a PRA variant, multi-agent orchestration seeks to partition various cognitive and perceptual tasks among specialized AI sub-agents with the expectation of saving system latency and energy consumption at the expense of high accuracy [17][18]. This combination of characteristics could be implemented in AR-assisted systems for real-time adjustment to different clinical scenarios with reliable responsiveness and patient safety [19][20]. The MenTOR framework draws together RAG-based procedural grounding, egocentric perception and AR overlay delivery to create a structured process of perception leading to action, which supports correct task performance following clinically approved guidelines. This integration also allows performance metrics to be logged in real time for quantitative benchmarking, yielding a benchmark standard by which AR assistants can be evaluated within simulation- and manikin-based scenarios. Assessment of AR-assisted systems cannot be limited to completion rate only — but rather that a multivariate approach must be used, including intervention counts, safety incident counts, latency and energy efficiency [1][3][5]. Pioneering studies have shown that predictive AR systems with PRA mechanisms can decrease the clinical supervision interventions by more than 30% and increase step-wise procedural precision by 25–30% [6][7]. It has also been demonstrated that multi- agent orchestration can improve resource assignment, minimise device-level energy usage and continue to support real-time behaviour under highly complex behaviours [8][9]. These findings emphasize the requirement for minimal benchmarking that also considers the intricate balance of safety, efficiency and usability in AR-based clinical environments. In addition, we require standardized datasets and scoring protocols to permit reproducibility, inter-system comparison, and regulatory scrutiny 10. Moreover, these frameworks can provide insights into design tradeoffs by revealing when optimizing for predictive accuracy or latency results in the best patient centered workflow. The AR-ClinAgent framework addresses these limitations by integrating PRA, multi-agent orchestration with RAG-based grounding and real-time AR overlays [12][13][14]. It serves as a benchmark for intubation accuracy, intubation time-lag, the number of attempts involved in the process, complications such as safety incidents and energy expenditure in a vast range of

II Literature Review Augmented reality (AR) has gained attention of late in terms of improving precision during surgery and minimizing operative accidents. Stewart et al. (2022) found that 3D AR headsets enabled in-room robotic assistants were able to decrease the time of task completion and error rates, allowing non-expert staff to perform at the level of attending surgeons [1]. These results reinforce the idea of AR skill augmentation and assistance during complex intracorporeal procedures. In orthopedic surgery, AR imaging technologies also enhanced task efficiency and reduced cognitive load. Furman and Hsu (2021) investigated applications such as pedicle screw insertion and found improved operative accuracy with a reduction in radiation exposure in pre-clinical models, but acknowledged that clinical use would still be technology dependent based on user learning curve and procedural complexity [2]. Outside of the operating room, AR has penetrated rehabilitation and telemedicine. Yang et al. (2022) developed a hybrid AR-based VR rehabilitation system for stroke patients, which reduced human trainer burden and contact rates though gained functional improvement were significant [3]. Gouda et al. (2021) have recently highlighted in their publication that digital technology using voice support for cardiovascular trials can enhance transitional care and patients‘ monitoring as an example of multimedia digital aids used in clinical settings [4]. It also has the potential to transform neurosurgery and spinal procedures. Roethe et al. (2022) found that the use of heads-up AR displays cancelled out the requirement for pointers and navigator, as in PS selections were diminished. Such reduction was not associated with other groups despite a decrease in surgical demand and continual visualization of important anatomical structures [5]. Liu et al. (2021) reported an accuracy of 98% using AR during pedicle screw implantation in different regions of the spine, which emphasizes its reliability and clinical safety in higher risk procedures [6]. Moreover, Battineni et al. (2024) further expanded the integration of AR and AI to maritime medicine offering predictive health monitoring and on-the-fly remote support outside traditional medical facilities [7]. For post-market surveillance, Khinvasara et al. (2024) showed that AI-based systems can facilitate risk detection and anomaly recognition to optimise device monitoring, such as possible AR workflow for continuous AI informed optimization [8].

Additionally, albeit other emerging fields such as telerehabilitation, space medicine and extreme environment applications, the potential for AR in remote guidance would be beneficial, there are still limitations with lack of measurable real - time performance assessment (other than qualitative user feedback), reproducible benchmarks or privacy-comtrait datasets to train / evaluate on [3][11][12][16]. III Methodology In this paper, we present AR-ClinAgent, a structured framework that combines Proactive Risk Anticipation (PRA) with Multi-Agent Orchestration to improve the performance of clinical AR assistants. The system builds upon a perceptor to effector loop that processes input and egocentric visual and sensor information, while mapping the latter into clinically validated procedural steps 19, by using a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism. Specialised AI sub-agents are assigned specific cognitive tasks, such as path prediction, result validation and anomaly detection (see above), which enable task division to further optimise the latency and power over head without т compromising procedural realism [21]. Real-time AR views will be overlaid on the projected workflow to help clinicians through each step, and performance factors (such as accuracy of interventions being performed, number of interventions per individual imaged KE region and near misses) will be logged throughout for later review [22]. The approach uses privacy-preserving data across the range of human procedures, including ultrasound-guided IV access, central line insertion and medication verification to meet regulations while protecting patient health and safety. Simulation and manikin-based validation scenarios are used to compare baseline and PRA-amplified agent workflows, enabling reproducibility for comparisons with any future AR- assisted design [23]. text: Figure 1: Layered Architecture of the AR-ClinAgent Framework for Proactive Clinical Workflow Assistance 3.1 Data Acquisition We used the Surgical Workflow and Activity Recognition Dataset (Cholec80) – a validated, publicly available video dataset of laparoscopic surgery for procedural understanding and automation [19]. It was chosen as it is a comprehensive dataset with high-quality visual data, and its surgical phases are well annotated to efficiently develop and evaluate AI guided AR systems. Cholec80 is a dataset of 80 laparoscopic cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal) videos, recorded at a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels, featuring synchronized metadata and extensive procedural annotations. These labels organize each surgery video into 7 different procedural phases: Preparation, Calot-Triangle Dissection, Clipping and Cutting, Gallbladder Dissectioning, Gallbladder Packaging, Cleaning/Clipping and Closing. Such frame-level annotation enables fine-grained temporal segmentation and contextual comprehension which are crucial for AR aided intraoperative guidance. The achievement rate of execution step has the largest reduction without RAG grounding and also latency and energy consumption are increased significantly for MAO removal, and safety is deteriorated for PRA removal. Results validate the significance of individual mechanical components in terms of effectiveness and safety for clinical practice. 5.2 Discussion The evaluation of AR-ClinAgent demonstrates that the integration of PRA, MAO and RAG in procedural grounding allows for significant improvements over clinical safety and operational efficiency. The PRA significantly cuts down by 22%, the proportion of near misses and clinical oversight interventions by 31%, confirming the necessity and benefits of predictive error detection in complex procedural tasks. MAO to sub-agents and splitting the computation load MAO is less latent by 18% and consumes (device-level energy consumption) less energy by 14%, this provides a good insight of gains in efficiency when employing levels of intelligent task allocation. RAG- based grounding provides a 26% improvement in step-wise procedural accuracy, justifying its capacity to bring AR guidance closer to a protocol scrutinised by clinicians. Comparison with other AR-enhanced models demonstrates that AR-ClinAgent surpasses state-of-the-art systems on all the major indicators, demonstrating the synergistic power of predictive intelligence, structured multi-agent coordination and procedural grounding. These findings demonstrate that AR-ClinAgent is not only helpful in assisting clinicians to follow the prescribed procedure accurately but also in improving the resource efficiency, so that it can be scaled up to use cases of simulation labs, manikin-based training and real-world clinician environment. VI Conclusion The AR-ClinAgent framework coupled with a set of PRA, MAO and RAG-based procedural grounding shows significant gains in the efficiency, accuracy and safety of clinical workflow. text: Meta-Adaptive Quantum Protocol Synthesis for Secure Communications under Dynamic Adversaries Abstract-In this work we introduce QMetaSyn, a meta-adaptive framework for synthesizing and evolving full quantum cryptographic protocols in response to dynamic channel conditions and adversarial behavior. Unlike traditional approaches that embed machine learning modules into fixed quantum key distribution (QKD) pipelines, QMetaSyn treats the entire protocol stack (basis selection, sifting, reconciliation, privacy amplification, decoy strategies, error thresholds, etc.) as a reconfigurable genome to be optimized. Over successive epochs, a population of candidate protocol variants is iteratively evaluated on real or simulated quantum channels, rated by a composite fitness metric balancing key throughput, error resilience, and security margin under adversarial perturbations. High-fitness variants are mutated and recombined, while unsafe candidates violating baseline security constraints are discarded. In simulated experiments under a variety of channel drifts and stealth eavesdropping attacks, QMetaSyn achieves 15 % higher key rate relative to a static BB84 baseline while maintaining comparable security margins, and reduces abort rate by 30 % over 1,000 adaptation epochs. Against adaptive Eve strategies simulated post-hoc, the meta-synthesized protocols exhibit 20 % lower information leakage compared to conventional parameter-tuned QKD. These findings indicate that structural/meta level adaptation of quantum cryptographic protocols can result in significant improvements with respect to performance, robustness and security. Our approach also sheds light on the theoretical challenges of obtaining composable security proofs for protocol morphing; we present design requirements that lead to safety against “fallback” behaviors. Our method suggests a different approach in quantum cryptography: not just learning to tune cryptographic protocols, but learning to design them on the spot. Keywords-Quantum Cryptography, Meta-Learning, Protocol Synthesis, Adaptive Security, Quantum Key Distribution, Adversarial Robustness, Protocol Morphology I Introduction As one of the central quantum cryptography protocols, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is developed in order to gain secret keys between two spatially separated parties with the security that is provided by the laws of physics [1],[2], [3]. Two representative QKD protocols (BB84,B92) were treated in detail and implemented experimentally as the first step forward to quantum cryptography [3]. But, the existing protocols assume known/common behaviors of the environment and adversary that can't be true in practice given dynamism of communication channels[4],[5],[6]. With the advent of quantum networks and threats from advanced attackers, adaptive QKD protocols and QKD resistant to hostile environments are vital [7]. Now QML (Quantum ML) indeed has the potential to give birth to new paradigms of flexibility and robustness in the quantum domains. QML can adapt the QKD protocols to varying channel conditions like crosstalk and noise levels especially if the eavesdropping strategy may change [8],[9]. This integration is fundamentally different from the case of

text: fixed-parameter states, and makes possible flexible quantum communications systems that can be applied even in cryptography. While the prospect of QML in quantum cryptography is exhilarating, there are many open problems. Scaling of existing ideas which are based on quantum systems [10],[11], real-time, and the shift towards provable security against adaptive single photons of high fiberoptic fringe rates attack scenarios to build secure trigger functions is nontrivial [12]. In addition, quantum protocols are updated and need to be designed carefully not to break security when interacting with machine learning algorithms [13],[14]. The endeavour of providing an experimental testbed for quantum cryptography over satellite links can only be met with a mission scenario where the synthesis, testing and improvement of quantum cryptographic protocols is inbuilt into changing environmental parameters due to adversaries [15],[16]. In this sense, we propose to replace at least the QKD protocol stack with a new reconfigurable QKD protocol stack that will be able to offer similar security levels but adjustable via meta-adaptive techniques [17]. In [18], [19], motivation is similar but population based candidate variations of the protocol are sampled and refined iteratively by an aggregated fitness criterion including key throughput capacity, security error tolerance resilience and a form of security entropy slackness. This is not only used to enhance the QKD protocols of its implemented robustness in terms of performance and security but it also introduces a learning- driven, dynamic protocol adaptation together with design. The main contributions of the paper are: ●​ Meta-Adaptive Framework: A meta-adaptive framework is proposed which interprets the entire QKD protocol stack as a reconfigurable unit allowing for modiﬁcations based on evolving channel conditions and adversarial correlations. ●​ Evolutionary Optimization: We present an evolutionary optimization framework that uses a population based approach to iteratively scrutinize and evolve candidate protocol variations, trading the main throughput, error resilience and margin against security. ●​ Empirical Validation: Evidence through emulation experiments for the power of such a strategy to achieve better key rates, lower abort rates and information leakage than any static QKD protocols in dynamic adversarial settings. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces preliminaries, including the background work on adaptive QKD protocols and quantum machine learning applications in quantum cryptography. Section 3 describes the methodology, focusing on the implemented meta-adaptive framework and the adopted evolutionary optimization. Section 4 presents experimental and simulation based analysis to evaluate the proposed method along with the setup and simulation parameters. Section 5 presents the results and compares the meta-adaptive protocols with existing legacy static QKD protocols. Finally, Section 6 ends the paper with conclusions that include a discussion about limitations within the study and some future research ideas. II Literature Review

text: Semantic communication systems have been improved using deep neural networks for efficient transfer of meanings from sender to receiver. Sagduyu et al. (2023) proposed an autoencoder-based structure with a semantic task classifier through which structural information could be transmitted compactly while the amount of semantic loss was minimized. Yet, they also suggested susceptibilities to multi-domain adversarial attacks (with embedded perturbations seen at the transmitter and receiver) and thus provided a motivation for developing robust protocols in DNN-based communication systems [1]. Dynamic key management schemes have been proposed for security in IoT networks, especially for use cases of Industry 4.0 and 5G/6G. Pothumarti et al. (2021) presented a lightweight cipher and adaptive key generation scheme in NB-IoT network to guarantee the authentication and access control with resource efficiency simultaneously. Their approach is that a unique key is calculated on the fly, continually without being bound to anyone determining server (constantly establishing server) facing problems of heterogeneity, scalability and device resource constraint [2]. Moreover, the physical layer security has been developed under adversarial conditions. Letafati et al. (2022) analyzed PHY-layer secret key generation with a man-in-the-middle attack and hardware impairments. In the setting of device imperfections, their scheme enhanced achievable secret key rates by around 25% using randomised pilots, and provided engineering perspectives to secure protocols for key generation against active adversaries [3]. IoT in healthcare applications needs to be supported with lightweight, secure and robust communication protocols. Jan et al. (2021) proposed LightIoT for secure pairing using wearables and gateways with remote server, which is divided into three steps (initialization, pairing and authentication). Such a strategy reduces computational burden and communication cost significantly, while resisting different attack types, preserving data integrity and privacy in patient monitoring applications [4]. Wireless sensor networks have great advantage using identity based authentication and privacy preserving schemes. Hu et al. (2022) suggested a two-factor elliptic curve-based scheme with formal security assurances [5], and Kumar et al. (2023) proposed a source location privacy-preserving dynamic routing scheme(SLP-DRA), which injects bogus messages and selects paths dynamically [6]. Mezrag et al. (2022), IBAKAS: where ECC and identity-based cryptography to establish mutual authentication as well as secret key agreement with lower energy and communication overhead in clustered WSNs [7]. The Uyghur community uses drone networks and chaotic communication systems which have been reinforced with authentication, machine learning protocols as well. Wani et al. (2023) presented an identity-based secret scheme for the UAV-enhanced HetNets with centralized directories to secure data [8], and Hwang et al. (2023) presented an ML-based chaos-encryption scheme for wearable devices with the use of intelligent algorithms in robust, efficient communication systems and this promoted secure communication with the properties of signal synchronization and noise suppression [9]. Authentication and security issues have been a major challenge for ITSs. Shawky et al. (2023) suggested a cross-layer authentication strategy specifically designed based on short-term reciprocal channel characteristics for re-authentication with low computation, communication overhead and active as well as passive attack resilience. Their PHY challenge-response designs provide effective security for real-time V2V communication and pave the way for low-latency,

(2023) introduced blockchain integrated DFL for WCPNs using a new consensus proof of accuracy and evolutionary game which aims to strengthen the FL security against malicious nodes [14]. Prediction and safety for automotive communication systems are being moved to the edge-of-the-network, machine learning has been recently added. Ali et al. (2021) presented a blockchain-based federated learning for predicting vehicle destinations and emergency response scheduling for optimized service requests while maintaining privacy [15]. For Wireless Body Area Networks, secure, anonymous and mutual authentication with the help of SAMAKA was proposed by Narwal and Mohapatra (2021) [16]. Luo et al. (2024) used blockchain and digital twin guided Proof-of Network Coding (PoNC) concepts to advance security and efficiency [17]. Cryptographic techniques have been employed in enhancing home and IOT security frameworks. Uppuluri and Lakshmeeswari (2023) presented MHE-IS-CPMT with elliptic curve cryptography for secure smart home communication, focusing on key management and attack resistance [18]. Al-Mohammed et al. (2024) used Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) for the secure communication of IoT devices on high-speed trains without impacting throughput [19]. In the context of medical IoT, Al-Mekhlaf et al. (2025) introduced a quantum-safe lattice-based architecture, based on lightweight cryptography, zero-knowledge proofs and homomorphic encryption in order to protect sensitive healthcare data to traditional and quantum adversaries [20]. 2.1 Research Gap However, there are still a number of important open semantic communication issues in the IoT security, Vehicular networks, UAV systems and Post-quantum cryptographic community. Recent models address the efficient compression and transmission of information (semantic communication) [1], but are still extremely vulnerable to multi-domain adversarial attacks with few defenses implemented against DNN-based ones. IoT and WSN security protocols [2][5][6][7] have advanced authentication and key management, but most still do not consider the dynamic channel conditions or both in near real-time adaptability and resource limitations of their heterogeneous devices. Federated learning techniques in ITS and ad-hoc networks [11][12][14][15] are designed for privacy and poison-resilience but do not perform

text: well under high mobile environments, latency challenges and adversarial attack. Moreover, prior auto- mated vehicle and UAV authentication protocols [8][10][17] sacrifice the trade-off between computational efficiency, secure key exchange and resistance against emerging attacks. Quantum-resistant implementations suitable for 5G/IoT and healthcare [19][20] provide postquantum security without considering an adaptive threat model or performance optimization with real-time operational behaviour. Combined, these gaps illustrate the urgent requirement for more integrated models allowing for dynamic(meta- level) adaptation of cryptographic protocols that satisfy high throughput rates, low latency and strong security guarantees (diverse) adversarial strategies. Indeed such an approach could act as a bridge between existing static or focused solutions within this space. III Methodology The proposed approach designs a meta-adaptive synthesis framework for secure quantum and classical communication protocols, which applies dynamic adaptation to enhance key generation, error correction, and privacy amplification against channel variation in real time and adversarial strategies. The adaptive protocol design allows the protocol stack to be seen as a configurable genome, so that over successive evolutions we can search for optimal ad-hoc solutions according to combined fitness metrics, such as throughput, safety margins and latency under certain attack profiles [20][21]. Every proposed protocol variant is either simulated or deployed in heterogeneous network scenarios such as IoT, WSNs, vehicular and UAV-assisted systems to investigate the robustness against adaptive adversaries and resource constraints [22][23]. As high-quality solutions are repeatedly recombined and mutated, unsafe or inefficient variants are removed, which guarantees the convergence to both robust as well as efficient configurations. The approach also blends federated learning and quantum-resistant primitives: distributed model updates with lattice- and QKD-derived protections are employed to ensure privacy, integrity, and post-quantum resistance [24][25]. Combining evolutionary optimization, real-time evaluation and dynamic security features, this framework overcomes the limitations of static protocols, thus providing a flexible high-performance defense against multiple domain challenges. text: A Bayesian State-Space Observer Framework for Integrated Fish Stock Estimation, Disease Prediction, and Fertilizer-Driven Nutrient Impact Analysis in Deep Sea Fisheries Abstract-Sustainable deep-sea fisheries require simultaneous understanding of stock dynamics, emerging disease risks, and the ecological impacts of nutrient fluxes driven by fertilizer runoff. Existing approaches largely address these dimensions in isolation, rely on black-box multi-model pipelines, or fail to integrate heterogeneous observational data such as eDNA signals, CPUE records, and satellite-derived environmental indices. This research introduces BESSO (Bayesian State-Space eDNA-Sensor Observer), a unified probabilistic framework that models fish biomass, disease prevalence, and nutrient load as a coupled latent state vector. The system fuses multi-source observations from environmental DNA assays, acoustic catch data, in-situ water-quality probes, and satellite chlorophyll and SST proxies within a single sequential Bayesian inference mechanism. Unlike adaptive or federated architectures, BESSO employs a streamlined yet mechanistically grounded state-space formulation that captures logistic biomass growth, nutrient-induced stress effects, and disease propagation dynamics with quantified uncertainty. Preliminary evaluation using simulated data and retrospective calibration scenarios demonstrates a 22.8% reduction in biomass estimation error, a 19.3% improvement in disease outbreak prediction accuracy, and a 24.7% increase in explanatory power for fertilizer-associated nutrient impacts compared to baseline regression or single-sensor models. The framework additionally produces actionable probability forecasts and counterfactual projections, enabling early intervention, responsible catch allocation, and nutrient mitigation strategies. BESSO’s interpretability, computational feasibility, and modular structure position it as a next-generation decision-support system for fisheries management, providing a robust, data-integrative alternative to multi-complex or adaptive ensemble methods. Keywords-BESSO, Bayesian State-Space Model, eDNA, Fish Stock Prediction, Disease Forecasting, Nutrient Load Analysis, Fertilizer Impact, Deep Sea Fisheries, Environmental Sensing, Sustainable Management I Introduction Anthropogenic impacts on the deep sea are not limited to (over)harvesting, but also include widespread nutrient enrichments and disease emergence [1], [2]. Fish stock dynamics previously required models of populations coupled to some data on catch or surveys, while seldom considering external perturbations [3]. On the other hand, in aquatic ecology studies on fertilizer runoff and its consequences on nutrient loading are discussed; these have been reported to bring about changes in microbial or plankton communities and secondary stress through higher trophic levels [4],[5]. Also in parallel, marine epidemiology has described disease epizootics (e.g., viral, bacterial) in open water systems occasionally associated with environmental stressors [6]. However, these strands remain largely siloed: fish stock assessment models seldom incorporate nutrient or disease modules, and disease or nutrient

text: impact models rarely feed back into biomass estimation. The absence of an integrated modeling framework limits the ability to generate coherent system-level inferences under uncertainty [7],[8]. Moreover, available observations span heterogeneous types — environmental DNA (eDNA), acoustic sensing, catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE), satellite-derived chlorophyll or sea surface temperature (SST) indices — yet most modeling pipelines stitch separate modules loosely, rather than embedding them in a single probabilistic latent process [9]. A unified latent-state approach can overcome modular disjunctions while quantifying uncertainties coherently [10],[11]. Using Bayesian state-space models in previous works, it has proved effective to integrate process and observation noise (for instance non-linear dynamics) [12] as applied to ecological or epidemiological data. In fisheries, the Bayesian state space approach has been used to connect depletion models to CPUE time-series data or spawning biomass which improves robustness compared to deterministic assessments [13],[14]. However, limited studies exist to simultaneously model disease dynamics or nutrient effects in the same latent vector especially in deep-water marine systems. The combination of eDNA signals (which have proven to be a sensitive index for the presence or absence of species) with conventional CPUE or acoustic data allows more flexible estimation of latent biomass. However, there are challenges: strong non-linear coupling, measurement disparity and potential identifiability problems. Tackling them requires delicate pre-elicitation, regularization and inference of the prior (e.g. particle filtering, sequential Monte Carlo) [15]. Here we develop a Bayesian state-space eDNA-Sensor Observer (BESSO) to simultaneously estimate fish biomass, disease prevalence and nutrient load in deep marine systems [16], [17]. The latter are guided using mechanistic process equations: logistic growth with nutrient-dependent stress terms, pathogen dynamics and nutrient flux partitioning. Observations go through sensor models: concentration of eDNA as a stochastic proxy to biomass, CPUE/acoustic catch as noisy readings and satellite/in-situ probes for nutrient or chlorophyll signals [18]. The posterior state distributions are processed using sequential Bayesian filtering (e.g. particle MCMC). BESSO is benchmarked in simulation and through retrospective calibration experiments against naive decoupled models and simpler sensor fusion baselines. The model integrates and improves on these models by having reduced-biomass error, better outbreak forecasting ability, and stronger prediction of fertilizer-induced nutrient effects [19]. The model can accommodate counterfactual intervention scenarios, providing decision support for catch allocation, disease management and regulation of nutrient runoff in marine management. This kind of framework is related to sustainable management in several categories [20]. First, it is consistent with a precautionary approach in harvest policies explicitly carrying uncertainty through the model in such things as biomass-disease-nutrient interactions. Second, it may direct early disease warning signals through linking the dynamics of dormant stress and pathogens. Third, it joins land-water interactions: by attributing nutrient stress to fertilizer leaching, it connects terrestrial management to marine ecosystem effects. Given its modular design, BESSO can be expanded or adapted to regional models, different sensors and multi-species situations. Overall, this study fills an important methodological void and develops a decision-based probabilistic

The key contributions of the paper are: ●​ Proposal of a unified Bayesian state-space model that treats fish biomass, disease prevalence, and nutrient load as a coupled latent vector, enabling joint inference across ecological, epidemiological, and biogeochemical domains. ●​ Design of observation models to fuse multi-source heterogeneous data streams (eDNA, CPUE/acoustic, in-situ probes, and satellite-derived indices) within the same sequential inference architecture. ●​ Demonstration via simulation and retrospective calibration that this integrated approach reduces estimation error, enhances disease outbreak prediction, and yields stronger explanatory insight into fertilizer-driven nutrient impacts compared to decoupled or single-sensor baselines The paper is organised as follows: Section 2 provides a review of related work in Bayesian state-space models, fisheries stock assessment, disease modelling and nutrient impact inference with an emphasis on the intersection of this important research gap. Section 3 is devoted to the description of BESSO methodology: from its state-space formulation, with process equations and observation models, up to the inference algorithms (particle filter/PMCMC building). Section 4 gives the experimental setups (simulation scenarios; retrospective calibration on real or semi-synthetic datasets) and baseline comparisons along with evaluation metrics. Although higher-order models can account for time dynamics or spatial behavior [18,19], we are not aware of any model attempting joint estimation of acroporid biomass and disease prevalence and nutrient loads under a common likelihood function.
