The particle filtering algorithm used the systematic importance resampling scheme to provide a smooth update along with the stability of the numerical calculation in sequential measurements. Diagnose and visualize functions were executed through Matplotlib and ArviZ which allowed assessment of convergence, inspection of the posterior densities and analysis of traces with MCMC chains. The experiment was conducted in a synthetic deep-sea fishery ecosystem adjusted to realistic oceanographic and biological conditions. Each simulation cycle was 30 days long, and spanned a steady 10 yr period, fitting satellite-based SST and chlorophyll data with eDNA and acoustic CPUE observations. Environmental and biological parameters were initialized from literature-informed priors: intrinsic biomass growth rate , carrying capacity 𝑟= 0. 32 , nutrient stress coefficient , pathogen transmission rate 𝐾= 1. 2 × 10 5 β = 0. 014 , and disease decay constant . The observation variance was set λ = 0. 008 δ = 0. 002 σ 2 adaptively using the maximum-likelihood estimates of residual errors. Computing efficiency was assessed using simulations on a 64-core high performance node equipped with 128 Gigabytes of RAM, allowing for parallel sampling with 50k particles per iteration. Modular implementation enabled us to dynamically enable further sensor types, e.g. dissolved oxygen probes or a turbidity sensor, without modifying the core state-transition equations. Coarse-fine resolution may also pave the way for inclusion of multispecies interactions in future, as this methodology provides an ideal route to shared nutrient dynamics or predator–prey coupling within a unified Bayesian framework. Interpretability was maintained through a posterior probability summary, ranking of parameter sensitivity and decision thresholds based on credible intervals, to maintain the actionability of model outputs for fishery management. Stochastic forecasts of decreases in biomass, disease outbreaks, or nutrient accumulations can therefore be used to develop early warning indicators for quota allocation, habitat conservation and reduction of nutrients lost through runoff. The results emphasize the combined effectiveness of eDNA sensors, nutrient stress modeling and disease dynamics to achieve both high predictive accuracy as well as ecological interpretation. 5.2 Discussion The BESSO framework provided evidence for the effectiveness of the integrated Bayesian state-space approach to management of deep-sea fisheries. The model also performed better than baseline and single-sensor predictions across all primary metrics tested, translating into a reduction of 22.8% in biomass estimation error, an improvement of disease prediction accuracy by 19.3%, and an increase in explanation for nutrient impact prediction by 24.7%. These advances are achieved through the combined assimilation of different types of data – including eDNA signals, CPUE records, satellite-derived chlorophyll and SST proxies, and in-situ water-quality measurements – into a unified representation of the latent state that encodes feedbacks between fish biomass, disease incidence and nutrient load. The ablation study further strengthens our point on each module’s contribution to predictive performance, and it can be seen that decoupled or partial modeling might miss some important system dynamics. Counterfactual scenarios analysis had shown BESSO’s value in managing actively, and enabled policy makers to assess to which extent decreasing fertilizer input production or fishing pressure could influence ecosystem health. In summary, the framework generates interpretable, probabilistic outputs that can be used to inform targeting of sustainable catch sharing and disease mitigation strategies, as well as nutrient management, rendering BESSO a strong decision-support platform in addressing both ecological and operational dilemmas in complex marine systems.

text: VI Conclusion The BESSO framework is an advancement in integrated fisheries management, by including fish biomass, prevalence of disease, and nutrient dynamics. Preliminary tests using simulated and retrospective calibration cases demonstrated (compared to a regression model and single sensor models) a 22.8% reduction in estimation error for biomass, 19.3% improved accuracy of prediction of disease outbreak, and explanatory power for fertilizer-induced nutrient effects at an increase of 24.7%. The assimilation of heterogeneous observations (eDNA assay, acoustic CPUE data and satellite-derived chlorophyll and SST proxies, in-situ water-quality) into a Bayesian state-space framework enabled reliable latent states estimates with quantified uncertainty. Ablation studies validated the importance of each module as they showed that eDNA signals, nutrient-induced stress modeling, and disease propagation dynamics were all necessary for accurate prediction. Counterfactual scenario analyses further illustrated the suitability of BESSO for forecasting forthcoming fisheries interventions, catch allocation planning and nutrient management strategies. Its modular structure and interpretability allow for the transfer of the species-independent approach to other animals or environmental conditions as a strong decision-supporter. The future of BESSO could include extending the model to multi-species interactions, incorporating real-time sensor networks in order to continuously monitor fisheries, and developing adaptive management and responses under potential climate change scenarios in deep-sea systems for more sustainable and resilient deep sea fisheries. text: A Few-Shot Contrastive Learning Framework for Industrial Dataset Cleaning Using Cross-Domain Embedding Optimization Abstract- The accuracy of computer vision models across various applications in industry and environment is severely compromised by dataset noise and class imbalance. However, existing cleaning frameworks are not suitable for limited-label scenarios, where datasets gathered from heterogeneous sources have inconsistent visual quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new algorithm—IndusCleanNet, a few-shot dataset cleaning mechanism based on supervised contrastive learning and cross-domain embedding optimization. The model operates in two stages: the first stage uses an EfficientNet backbone pre-trained with contrastive loss on the NEU Surface Defect Dataset to enhance texture and structural cues and the second stage uses prototype-based clustering and embedding distance regularization to identify defective, irrelevant, or redundant samples through few-shot fine-tuning. The final cleaning decision is made by a lightweight attention-guided autoencoder ensemble that limits feature redundancy and improves anomaly detection precision. Our experimental results show that IndusCleanNet obtains a 96.84% cleaning accuracy that is higher by 5.71% compared to the original contrastive cleaner and improves defect classification by 17.92% over unfiltered datasets. These results validate the algorithm’s efficacy in maintaining data integrity while significantly improving downstream prediction reliability. The proposed method thus establishes a robust, domain-independent cleaning mechanism applicable to large-scale industrial vision datasets and other non-medical imaging tasks. Keywords: Few-shot learning; Contrastive learning; Dataset cleaning; Industrial defect detection; EfficientNet; Cross-domain adaptation. I Introduction The performance of data-driven industrial systems is often limited by the integrity and relevance of visual datasets when it comes to successful defect detection, anomaly recognition, and predictive maintenance [1]. When working with industrial image corpora, poor lighting conditions, class frequencies, and sensor-related noises affect the generalization capabilities of any model [2][3]. Furthermore, the multi-sensor and multi environment-based data are more likely to produce too many redundant or irrelevant samples that only increase the difficulty of obtaining an optimal training model [4][5]. Moreover, in many life systems and manufacturing as well as inspection plants, there is an excess of unlabeled or poorly labeled data that is generated regularly. Considering that data annotation severely lacks both economically and temporally, several low-supervision, automated methods for data preparation are urgently required [6]. The existing applied techniques are ineffective for life system data since the statistical and clustering-oriented cleaning methods fail to capture the texture dependencies and defect-related clues [7]. It leads to a growing tendency to use a

text: learning-oriented approach that not only generalizes well cross-data types but also adapts effectively to the few -shot learning settings due to data sparsity [8]. Few-shot learning has emerged as a prominent paradigm in the recent past for handling rigid data conditions through the integration of meta-learning and contrastive optimization principles [9][10]. It has critical applications in the broader field of industrial vision as visual errors often emanate from microscopic changes in the material texture, slight variance in lighting in different capture settings, and changes in operations. Contrastive learning enables models to generate discriminative, domain invariant embeddings by pushing dissimilar samples apart and pulling those from the same category together [11]. However, the model’s capacity to learn quality embeddings as determined by the stability of the output is significantly compromised in industrial datasets due to varying defect morphologies. The use of few-shot techniques in the contrastive embeddings sub-field is especially challenging when used to refine the embedding results in error as the work scope expands to eliminate irrelevant images; thus, the current work is severely undermined in this regard. These issues necessitate a model capable of learning stable, refined embeddings by aligning the embeddings from the different domains into a single space to achieve intra-class compactness and inter-class separability [12]. We present IndusCleanNet, a few-shot contrastive learning framework for industrial dataset cleaning in low-labeled and cross-domain scenarios [13][14]. IndusCleanNet utilizes a pre-trained EfficientNet backbone also on the NEU Surface Defect Dataset, allowing the model to capture fine textural details of industrial defects. It leverages a two-stage pipeline, where the model first approaches supervised contrastive loss to learn discriminative embeddings before few-shot fine-tuning to minimize embedding distances between clean samples and noisy samples [15][16]. Prototype-based clustering is designed to separate the defective, irrelevant, and noisy samples while embedding regularization boosts the adaptation’s stability. An attention-guided autoencoder ensemble enhances decision trustworthiness by post-cleaning outputs, removing feature redundancy, and boosting anomaly sensitivity [17]. The combined use of representation learning, clustering intelligence, and attention-based feature reconstruction provides a robust, consistent, and domain-agnostic cleaning strategy for industrial visual data represented. For reasons, this paper is inspired by the need to improve the quality of data for succeeding industrial vision tasks, given the role of training data fidelities in the reliability of predictions and system vagility [18]. While qualified and balanced data improve the rate of convergence, it also enhances robust decision in the presence of operational variances in the real-world [19], [15]. The following three specific industrial data challenges; namely, the heterogeneous noise, class imbalance, and domain inconsistency are uniquely addressed by IndusCleanNet. The learning-based architect balances both the feature representation and the data integrity by binding few-shot adaptability with cross-domain contrastive learning [20]. An explicit improvement in data quality and accuracy of defect classification are observed. text: Figure 1: Overall Architecture of IndusCleanNet – Contrastive Pretraining and Few-Shot Fine-Tuning Framework 3.1 Data Acquisition The NEU Surface Defect Database was deliberately chosen as a benchmark for the Selection of CNN-Based Clustering Core of the IndusCleanNet Framework. I chose this dataset due to its rich representation of real-world industrial problems, specifically in the area of metal surface defect detection. In the metal surface defect detection area, data inconsistency such as variance in image capturing conditions and natural variation such contrast, roughness, and illumination, in addition to texture complexity, occurred more frequently in images. The NEU-CLS dataset also provides the ideal platform to train and evaluate the dataset cleaning algorithms. These images are actually surface images taken under various conditions of roughness, contrasts, and illuminations which are all types of intrinsic noises likely to occur during production. The NEU-CPS dataset strikes a balance between the ideal situation of a laboratory environment and natural variation, guaranteeing that the model will be faced with the same kind of noises that are present where manufacturing plants are. Furthermore, the dataset’s availability through Kaggle (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kaustubhdikshit/neu-surface-defect-database) provides transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility—qualities essential for a robust academic study. In addition to the above reasons, the choice of using the NEU-CLS database from other larger commercial datasets or proprietary datasets is also due to its moderate size, which makes it suitable for few-shot learning paradigms. Specifically, NEU-CLS allows simulating limited-labeled industrial under few-shot setups efficiently, as annotating large-scale datasets is often time-consuming and labor-intensive. Hence, by utilizing NEU-CLS the current study maintains methodological relevance, computational viability, and domain adaptiveness – which are all crucial to prove the generalization ability of IndusCleanNet in practical industrial settings. In daily industrial practice, new data from different production lines or distinguished visual environments render the learned model non-generalizable over the target hardware, causing the feature responses to be unstable and the performance to degrade. To take it into account, a domain-invariant feature alignment technique is incorporated via Maximum Mean Discrepancy -based optimization. The MMD approach minimizes the distributional distance between source embeddings and target embeddings within a reproducing kernel Hilbert 𝑍𝑠 𝑍𝑡 space (RKHS). The MMD loss is mathematically expressed as in Eq.11: ​ ​ ​ (11) 𝐿𝑀𝑀𝐷= 1 𝑛𝑠𝑖=1 𝑛𝑠 ∑ϕ 𝑧𝑖 𝑠 ( ) − 1 𝑛𝑡𝑗=1 𝑛𝑡 ∑ϕ 𝑧𝑗 𝑡 ( ) |||| |||| |||| ||||𝐻 2 Where represents a kernel-induced mapping and is the associated Hilbert space. By ϕ ·( ) 𝐻 minimizing this loss, the model is encouraged to align high-order statistics between the two domains, driving down the discrepancy in embedding distributions and learning model structure consistency. This aligns the pretrained EfficientNet and fine-tuned prototype clusters to novel datasets in one-stop shopping without the full retraining. Besides, the MMD constraint can be seen as a distribution regularizer that encourages a smoother embedding manifold in which source and target features cohabit the same latent subspace. The learned texture and pattern descriptors can be more general, allowing for recognition of new surface anomalies under varying illumination conditions, noise levels, sensor equipment, etc. . Moreover, a gradient reversal layer is implemented to enhance domain invariance in an adversarial training framework. The GRL enables feature adaptation with a corrective action by endorsing the feature extractor to a domain discriminator in an aggressive optimization process. The 𝐹 𝐷 discriminator seeks to classify whether a feature originates from the source domain or the target domain, and the feature extractor is trained to fool the discriminator, leading to domain-agnostic feature extraction. The experimental environment was developed in Python 3.10 leveraging the Tensorflow and Pytorch backends. The source data for this study was the NEU Surface Defect dataset, preprocessed, and split into 70%, 15% validation, and 15% test data to balance its proportional distribution relative to the frequency per class. The training set employed data augmentations like random cropping, horizontal flipping, Gaussian blurring, etc. to introduce visual disruption to artificial industrial vectors and promote visual dissimilarity among the samples. Under the same clustering and few-shot learning settings, the ablation study progressively ablated critical components: Contrastive pretraining, prototype clustering, and cross-domain optimization: Figure 1 shows the results. Excluding contrastive pretraining reduced the cleaning accuracy to 91.13%, indicating that the process is critical in learning the ability to differentiate defective patterns in textures from industrial surfaces. Omitting prototype clustering reduced the cleaning accuracy to 93.20%; thus, the module is sufficient in tuning inter-class relationships within few-shot learning assumptions. Omitting cross-domain embedding optimization reduced the cleaning accuracy to 94.50%; the findings suggest that the process is adequate for aligning features into a stable representation across dissimilar domains. The cleaning accuracy was highest when all modules were integrated, the IndusCleanNet, with a cleaning accuracy of 96.84%, showing that the combined effect of the three modules minimizes noise, enhances intra-class consistency, and promotes stable domain adaptation during industrial dataset cleaning. text: 5.2 Discussion Overall, the experimental results support the above claims and show the advanced model capability and generalization of IndusCleanNet in industrial dataset cleaning and downstream defect classification. Concretely, it would obtain the highest accuracy and feature purity in the performance comparison with existing models. This result proves the strength and the effectiveness of the hybrid architecture that combined the contrastive pretraining, the prototype-based clustering, and domain alignment, which we have also verified that the later one makes the dataset more generalizable for the training process to reduce the influence of the mislabel and the noise data. The increased accuracy rate in the defect classification further shows the correlation between the data purification process and the learning model. Ultimately, IndusCleanNet is an easily distributed and an efficient solution to industrial data intelligence that paves the way to high-integrity machine learning in manufacturing. VI Conclusion In conclusion, the proposed IndusCleanNet achieved remarkable results with 96.84% of cleaning accuracy, F1-score of 0.96%, and 0.90% feature purity ratio, thus outperforming the current models in industrial dataset cleaning. By combining contrastive pretraining, prototype-based clustering, and cross-domain embedding optimization, the model could effectively reduce noise, improve data quality, and enhance the performance of downstream defect classification by 17.92%. Overall, these results prove the robustness and generalizability of all the proposed frameworks across different domains heterogeneity thus establishing IndusCleanNet as an efficient few shot learning cleaning framework. The future work of this model includes extension to multi-modality datasets, including temporal defect learning, and self-supervised adaptation to continue the operational performance in evolving industrial environments. text: Abstract-Predicting user trust in conversational agents remains a significant challenge. Most existing models fail to capture both the temporal dynamics of trust formation and the nuanced interplay between emotional, behavioral, and contextual signals. To address this, we present ConTrust, a deep learning architecture specifically designed for the Conversational Trust Dataset, which contains 3,909 conversations (26,329 turns total, with 12,569 agent turns annotated for trust). Unlike traditional regression or shallow learning approaches, ConTrust integrates six key innovations. First, a trust-aware self-attention mechanism adaptively weights conversational cues based on their trust relevance. Second, an LSTM-based conversation memory module models longitudinal trust evolution. Third, we fuse textual, temporal, and behavioral features through multi-modal integration. Fourth, hierarchical attention captures dependencies at both turn and conversation levels. Fifth, multi-task learning jointly optimizes trust, emotion, and engagement predictions. Sixth, adaptive loss weighting dynamically balances these competing objectives. Extensive evaluations demonstrate ConTrust's substantial improvements over established baselines. While ensemble methods achieved R²=0.946 (RMSE=0.401), and strong learners like Random Forest (R²=0.944) and XGBoost (R²=0.938) performed competitively, ConTrust reaches R²=0.982 with RMSE=0.248. Crucially, 90% of predictions fall within ±0.5 error—a clear advance in trust modeling. Beyond these metrics, ConTrust offers interpretability by revealing how trust evolves with sentiment polarity, emotional congruence, and engagement intensity. This research contributes a scalable, domain-adaptable framework for trust prediction, establishing ConTrust as a foundation for reliable conversational agents in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, education, and customer support. Keywords-ConTrust, conversational trust prediction, trust-aware attention, conversation memory, multi-modal fusion, hierarchical attention, multi-task learning, adaptive loss weighting, deep learning, human-AI trust

Interestingly, dissatisfaction often traces back to seemingly minor conversational missteps-delayed responses, emotionally misaligned phrasing, or overly generic engagement behavior [5][6]. Traditional supervised models, trained on isolated utterances, have consistently struggled with trust signals precisely because trust accumulates gradually rather than emerging from single turns [7][8]. text: Trust remains a cornerstone of sustainable human–AI interaction, particularly as conversational agents transition from informational tools to emotionally and socially responsive partners. This study introduced ConTrust, a novel deep learning framework that models trust as an evolving, context-dependent phenomenon rather than a static attribute. By integrating Trust-Aware Self-Attention, Conversation Memory, and Multi-Modal Fusion mechanisms, ConTrust holistically captures linguistic, temporal, and behavioral signals within multi-turn dialogues. Experimental evaluations conducted on the Conversational Trust Dataset—comprising over 3,900 annotated conversations and 26,000 dialogue turns—demonstrated the framework’s superior predictive fidelity, achieving R² = 0.982 and RMSE = 0.248, with 90% of trust predictions falling within a ±0.5 margin of error. Beyond numerical performance, the framework provides interpretability and psychological validity by revealing how emotional alignment, response latency, and engagement intensity influence human trust trajectories. The Bi-LSTM-based Conversation Memory Module proved especially effective in capturing longitudinal trust evolution, validating that temporal continuity and sequential coherence are essential determinants of trust perception. Similarly, the Adaptive Loss Weighting (ALW) mechanism ensured balanced learning across trust, emotion, and engagement tasks, enabling ConTrust to generalize across diverse dialogue contexts such as healthcare, education, and customer service. From an operational standpoint, the introduction of ConTrust-Fast, a lightweight variant with a 60% parameter reduction, demonstrated that computational efficiency need not compromise trust-prediction accuracy—achieving comparable R² values (0.972–0.98) with significantly lower latency. This underscores the scalability of the proposed architecture for real-time trust assessment in production environments and embedded conversational systems. Looking forward, future research will explore cross-domain transfer learning, multilingual adaptation, and reinforcement-driven trust calibration, wherein agents dynamically adjust their conversational strategies based on real-time trust feedback. Integrating explainable AI (XAI) modules into ConTrust will further enhance transparency, allowing users to understand why an agent is perceived as trustworthy or not. Ultimately, this work lays the foundation for designing ethically aligned, emotionally intelligent, and context-aware conversational agents that can build, sustain, and justify human trust in complex interaction ecosystems.

text: Hierarchical Privacy-Hardened Federated Defense (HPH-FedDef): A Hybrid Edge-Cloud Federated Framework for Privacy-Preserving Intrusion & Malware Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems Abstract- The coordinated nature of the cyber-physical attacks and the state of the art of malware in the emerging modern CPS requires the design of collaborative and privacy-aware frameworks of intrusion detection. We present a novel algorithm: Hierarchical Privacy-Hardened Federated Defense (HPH-FedDef) that combines hierarchical device-to-edge-to-cloud federated learning topology, adaptive differential privacy noise scheduling, encrypted update similarity screening and reputation-weighted robust aggregation to provide resilient detection in distributed locations in CPSs. Each Local Device computes lightweight temporal autoencoder anomalies and feature updates for peers to perturb differentially, encrypt, and send for secure aggregation, while each Edge Node stores a tamper-evident ledger to audit and weight-client contributions. It provides further aggregation of consensus with trimmed-mean consensus for global models and releases these signatures in a manner that preserves user privacy at the cloud tier. HPH-FedDef improved upon traditional federated averaging by 9.4 % in average detection F1-score, with 96.7 % under cross CPS datasets and malware collections and non-IID distributions within 15 % malicious client poisoning scenarios, while also ensuring less than 2.3 % membership-inference success (compared to 9.1 %). Fixing the latency overheads for secure aggregation to be less than 12% of baseline makes the approach practicable for near-real-time CPS deployment. Such findings show that HPH-FedDef enables practical and secure joint attack and malware detection in distributed CPS at the proof-of-concept level, filling important gaps in the federated CPS security research landscape. Keywords-Hierarchical Federated Learning, Privacy-Preserving Intrusion Detection, Cyber-Physical Systems Security, Differential Privacy, Robust Aggregation Techniques I Introduction On the other hand, modern cyber–physical systems today behave like well-coordinated, interdependent digital–physical infrastructures which transport sensitive operational data and accommodate diverse devices working under the above critical latency constraints. Coordinated cyber and physical threats targeting these environments further amplify the potential for cyber intrusions and malware to exploit communication gaps, resource limitations and restrictive data-sharing policies. Existing studies highlight the limitations of centralized detection architectures, as they open the systems to confidentiality risks and bottlenecks when device-level data
label: human

text: cannot be transmitted due to regulatory or bandwidth-related constraints [1], [2], [4]. Research additionally emphasizes that sophisticated attackers employment obfuscation methods and delayed household time manipulation strategies, making distal discovery from nodes with varying processing capacities more difficult. With the expansion of CPS infrastructures toward the more autonomous and inter-connected Industry 5.0 environments, there is an urgent need for decentralized defenses that are privacy-preserving and that can provide a long term resilience against adversarial conditions [8], [19], [21]. Federated learning has proven to be a promising direction for decentralized intrusion detection used to guide platform users on the decoupling of model refinement in a non-disclosure way when it comes to raw device telemetry [9]. Overcoming these hurdles is a major step forward, but deployment in hostile CPS may be years away due to a host of unaddressed challenges. The static differential privacy setting typically comes either at the cost of model accuracy degradation or violently breaks the stable differential privacy bound with dynamic data dynamics [1], [12], [17]. Therefore, edge-centric aggregation increases bandwidth and communications efficiency but cannot detect malicious updates (or poisoned gradients) that can subvert global learning [3], [31], [39]. On the other hand, while homomorphic encryption and secure aggregation secure model exchanges, the induced overhead complicates matching real-time responsiveness while also reducing insight into insider manipulation efforts [14,15,27]. In addition to these, CPS heterogeneity, multiple temporal patterns of anomalies, and non-IID (Independent and identically distributed) distributions also worsen the stability of global learning behavior resulting in unresolved trade-off between privacy-preservation and reliable detection performance in distributed environments [7], [13], [30]. To mitigate some of this tension, hybrid edge–cloud strategies have been suggested that enable scale through cross multi-tier infrastructures albeit at the cost of introducing limited communication [24], [33], [34]. However aggregation nodes still have blind spots, where clients can gain a false sense of trust and cause the model parameters to converge to a poisoned one. While reputation-based scoring, behavioral filtering, and strong aggregation are shown to contain poisoning [10], [16], [26], they have been applied within a hierarchical CPS deployment. Furthermore, the detection of malware within federated settings is more challenging due to the existence of polymorphism methods that change the appearance of malware, encrypted payload transport, and behavior tailored based on target environments, which ultimately yield a lack of reproducibility of detection across heterogeneous nodes [22], [23], [29]. This shortcoming highlights the lack of a unified framework that can address at the same time some: (i) intrusion indicators; (ii) malware signatures; (iii) privacy constraints; and (iv) adversarial poisoning in multi-layered CPS architecture. As CPS
label: human

text: infrastructures become more heterogeneous, new operational constraints arise, such as hard timing constraints, lightweight model requirements, and the need to provide verified integrity checks at hierarchical aggregation layers. Targeted poisoning attacks regularly break performance guarantees for traditional federated averaging, leading to increasing calls for privacy-preserving mechanisms with adaptive noise infusion [5], [20], [38], secure similarity screening [18], and transparent auditability [36]. The CPS environment needs to synergistically combine multi-level defense mechanisms, including (i) privacy hardening in local environments, (ii) mutual trust assessment in mid-level environments and (iii) resilient model coordination in the environment between the entities. The above context drives the design of a Hierarchical Privacy-Hardened Federated Defense (HPH-FedDef) which is aimed at jointly addressing the privacy protection, adversarial robustness and near real time detection requirements in distributed cyber-physical infrastructures. What: The paper's main contributions are as follows: ●​ A comprehensive federated defence architecture with two levels of coordination and fair privacy guarantees, which operates at device, edge, and cloud levels, integrates temporal anomaly extraction on-device, encrypted comparison on the edge, and robust global aggregation, in order to provide coherent detection among heterogeneous cyber-physical systems (CPS). ●​ A novel adaptive differential privacy noise scheduler, which adaptively varies the perturbation strength according to both the gradient sensitivity and the temporal context, providing partitional inference safety at a low cost of stable detection performance under non-IID setup and attacks. ●​ This one provides a reputation-weighted and tamper-evident aggregation strategy that assesses the reliability of clients through a ledger-based consistency score, and it not only allows to withstand poisoning attempts but also preserves low-latency model fusion found in CPS environments. 1.1 Organization of the Paper The paper first introduces related works, and then positions the proposed framework against the background of existing research in the areas of federated intrusion and malware detection, privacy-preserving aggregation, and hierarchical CPS defense strategies. The methodology section subsequently elaborates on the HPH-FedDef architecture, e.g., modeling temporal anomalies, adaptively regulating noise, encrypting similarity screening, and aggregating reputation-weighted. The experimentation section of the paper includes datasets, non-IID setups, poisoning attack models and the evaluation metrics used, while the results section presents detection performance, privacy leakage evaluation, latency measurements and
label: human

text: robustness evaluation. The paper ends with final thoughts, considerations, and expected future research directions. II Related works Mahmud et al.(2024) a federated intrusion detection model was proposed in [1] where the general behavior is refined using FedAvg while the sensitive IoT data remains on local devices, and where collaborative learning enables high accuracy without global data exposure. This solution showed that in IoT scenarios, privacy can be maintained while providing intrusion detection even in resource bounded environments. Khan et al. Building on this line of work, Zhao et al. (2021) presented PC-IDS, a privacy-preserving scheme that pre-processes the raw SCADA data before analysis. They utilized a tuned probabilistic neural network with low-computational complexity for effective anomaly classification [2]. They showcased a design with preprocessing and hybrid optimization to minimize data leakage and enhance the reliability of detection. Soomro et al. The good news for secure collaboration is that this approach proved to be more reliable than centralized IDS frameworks. Keshk et al. (2021) through perturbation, authentication, cryptography and machine learning collectively addressed confidentiality of CPS, and mapped approaches across a broad set of privacy-preserving strategies [4] The review highlighted that a multi-layered approach to privacy would be more effective than a single-method defense. Keshk et al.(2022) Building on this, they recently proposed ICA-based data transformation as a way to reshape the information about the CPS while preserving the utility of the data and providing a data-centered method to disclosing CPS oriented databases that attained an ideal disclosure, which from our evaluations led to better preservation of sensitive features than four traditional disclosure methods [5]. They concluded that transformation-based privacy can preserve analytical utility over CPS datasets. Alqaralleh et al. Proposing the use of an optimization driven feature selection and a Dirichlet Variational Autoencoder for CPS anomaly detection, (2022) developed XAIIDS-FSDVAE, a model for recognizing unseen threats with lower levels of false positive [6]. Results demonstrated that explainable variational learning can enhance robustness against evolving intrusion behaviors. In 2025, Rahmati and Pagano proposed an encrypted aggregation and GRU-based sequence modeling, it enables federated anomaly detection framework for IoT with a trade-off between communication cost and threat detection accuracy to improve the security of the IoT [7]. In [8], (2022) reviewed vulnerabilities in Cyber Physical Systems (CPS) and outlined defense mechanisms that operate across both physical and cyber spaces, stating that as the use of CPS diversifies, integrated protective modeling is necessary. Through their work, CPS security became framed as an emerging ecosystem that needed foundational resilience. Then, Althobaiti et al. (2021) proposed a cognitive computing intrusion detection system (IDS) based on biological foraging feature selection and GRU classification for industrial CPS, which realized effective feature assaying and good detection performance thanks to the skill of optimization-guided learning [9]. In doing so, the two spoke to the increasing level of relevance that federated deep learning has in the contemporary threat landscape. Alazab et al. Ntizikira et al. SP-IoUAV is a multi-layer UAV intrusion model that is built based on federated learning, differential privacy, and secure computation, which can immediately respond to anomalies in real-time (2023) [13]. This method attained nearly complete detection and demonstrated how privacy-preserving learning contributes to the resilience of UAVs under attack. They found that for high-sensitivity networks, encrypted training pipelines are still possible. Spathoulas et al. (2021) proposed inter-organizational alert clustering using homomorphic encryption which allows multiple entities to collaboratively assess potential threats without disclosing any of their underlying private data [15]. The results confirm scalable cross-organizational privacy in IDS communication. Kumar et al. Their results confirmed that adaptive DP strategies can outperform static noise schedules under non-IID threats. 2.1 Research Gap Across the existing literature, federated and privacy-preserving intrusion detection has advanced significantly, yet notable research gaps remain. Current works mainly secure local training or encrypted aggregation but rarely integrate hierarchical multi-tier defense spanning devices, edge, and cloud, leaving CPS ecosystems vulnerable to coordinated cross-layer attacks [1–17]. Most solutions handle either intrusion or malware detection, not joint multimodal threat detection required for modern CPS environments. Furthermore, while many studies use differential privacy, cryptography, or secure key exchange, few frameworks combine these with robust aggregation and reputation mechanisms to counter poisoning and adversarial model manipulation. Another persistent gap is the limited ability of existing models to operate efficiently under non-IID heterogeneity and partial device compromise, conditions common in real CPS. Consequently, there is a need for a unified, privacy-hardened, adversary-resilient hierarchical federated framework that ensures end-to-end security while maintaining real-time performance across distributed CPS infrastructures. III Proposed Methodology This proposed method uses a layerwise federation learning pipeline for device, edge, and cloud layers to enable privacy-preserving and robust threat detection mechanism in crowded cyber-physical system(CPS) environment. The temporal autoencoders at the device tier are lightweight yet effective in extracting signatures of the anomalies and outputting local compressed gradient updates, which are perturbed locally with adaptive differential privacy schedules for optimal balance between privacy and utility [18]. Protected updates are sent to edge nodes to be filtered by encrypted similarity screening, which eliminates malicious or low-quality contributions, and reputation-weighted aggregation for further robustness against poisoning attempts [19]. The cloud tier receives the aggregated edge models and applies a trimmed-mean consensus mechanism to refine the global parameters, which is proved to be robust to coordinated adversaries behaviours [20]. Lastly, the cloud transmits (privacy-worn) threat signatures and refreshed model parameters back to edge and device tiers, forming a cyclic, clear and scalable learning process that is amenable to heterogeneous, real-world CPS conditions [21]. text: Figure 1: Architecture Diagram for the Proposed Model 3.1 Dataset Selection TON_IoT Dataset: This dataset is proposed for cyber-physical system and IoT security research and is a publicly available dataset widely referenced by the community [42]. This dataset is useful for validating various intrusion and malware detection frameworks & it consists of heterogeneous telemetry data from IoT and IIoT sensors, OS logs for Windows and Linux devices, and Network traffic. The dataset covers virtually every attack methods such as DoS, DDoS, ransomware, data injection, backdoors, MITM and others, that provides researchers with wide range of threat landscape for analysis. We selected TON_IoT because it provides a realistic CPS simulation configuration, hierarchical architecture which mimics device-edge-to-cloud communication, and publicly available formats that are preprocessed ensuring reproducible research. Due to its heterogeneity and dynamic nature, as well as its non-IID and the imbalance between benign and malicious events, it is an ideal candidate for the evaluation of realistic distributed datasets to test privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks. The dataset is openly accessible via the UNSW Research page at https://research.unsw.edu.au/projects/toniot-datasets and a mirrored version is available on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/codymlewis/TON_IoT_network, enabling straightforward download and integration into experimental workflows.

text: Figure 3: Flowchart for the Proposed Model IV Implementation Details 4.1 Experimentation In the experimentation phase, we tested the practical operation of the proposed HPH-FedDef framework under various aspects: performance, privacy guarantees, and adversary resilience across heterogeneous CPS environments. Abstract—Motivated by the emerging non-IID nature of a wide class of IoT and industrial distributed learning scenarios, we create a realistic IOT-Clusters dataset based on federations of multiple open-source datasets representing IoT, industrial CPS, and UAV telemetry and federate them across realistic simulated device clusters to deliver non-IID distributions of dataset owners. We design experiments to evaluate the detection, F1-score, false-positive rate, utility loss caused by DP, and robustness with different poisoning strengths (5–20% malicious clients) in terms of accuracy. We also evaluate the latency overhead incurred by secure aggregation, the effectiveness of reputation-based filtering, and the resilience of global convergence to adaptive differential privacy. As comparative baselines, we include FedAvg, DP-FedAvg, Krum, and conventional hierarchical FL models to show how HPH-FedDef
label: human

text: outperforms them in the presence of a subset of malicious clients and limited resources. 4.2 Experimental Setup Our experimental arrangement includes a six-tier simulation framework with 100 to 300 virtual cyber-physical system devices (edge sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) systems), five to 10 edge servers, and a cloud aggregator developed using TensorFlow Federated and PyTorch FL framework in Python. We run lightweight temporal autoencoders at devices with mini-batch sizes of 16–32, and at edges we run encrypted similarity screening and reputation scoring. Differential privacy budgets are within ε ∈ [0.5, 3.0], while secure aggregation preserves confidentiality using homomorphic encryption. We run training on a system with a GPU (e.g., RTX 4090/3090) which is running the Ubuntu 22.04 environment, and emulate the communication, and use variable bandwidth latencies between these interfaces to better reflect the actual CPS constraints. The dataset is split into 70%, 15% and 15% training, validation and testing respectively among the clients, with a non-iid, imbalanced partition of the triple as per the common behavior of CPS. 4.3 Evaluation Metrics ●​ Accuracy- Measures how correctly HPH-FedDef identifies benign and malicious CPS events across distributed nodes. ​ ​ ​ ​ (24) 𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦= 𝑇𝑃+𝑇𝑁+𝐹𝑃+𝐹𝑁 𝑇𝑃+𝑇𝑁 ​ ●​ Recall- Evaluates the framework’s ability to detect true cyber-attacks without missing stealthy or low-frequency intrusions. ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (25) 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙= 𝑇𝑃 𝑇𝑃+𝐹𝑁 ●​ F1-Score- Captures the balance between precision and recall, reflecting reliable detection under non-IID and adversarial conditions. ​ ​ ​ ​ (26) 𝐹1 = 2 × 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛×𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛+𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 ●​ Energy Consumption- Quantifies the computational overhead on devices during local training, DP noise addition, and encrypted communication. ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (27) 𝐸= 𝑖=1 𝑁 ∑𝑃𝑖× 𝑡𝑖 ( ) ●​ Privacy Budget (ε)- Defines the allowed information leakage per DP-SGD update, controlling how strongly gradients are obscured during FL. ​ ​ ​ ​ (28) 𝑃𝑀𝐷 ( ) = 𝑜 ( ) ≤𝑃𝑀𝐷 ' ( ) = 𝑜 ( )

Without similarity screening, the poisoning vulnerability sharply increases and leads to robustness dropping by 8.4% under 15% malicious clients. Thus, providing both privacy protection and real-time operation, as it can still achieve an F1-score of 96.7% with 2.3% privacy leakage and role latency overhead of no more than 12%. The hierarchical architecture to lower communication cost and enhanced resilience to 15% poisoned clients demonstrates the significance of similarity screening and reputation-weighted aggregation. Third, the adaptive DP ensures accuracy under non-IID data distribution, overcoming a critical drawback of existing FL-based IDS solutions. In summary, these results confirm HPH-FedDef as a strong, scalable, and privacy-hardened defense framework for the emerging CPS threat landscape. VI Conclusion Evaluation results prove that the integration of hierarchical learning, adaptive noise control, and multi-tier verification endow HPH-FedDef with a solid foundation for developing a robust and privacy-hardening intrusion detection framework for distributed CPS. It maintained the 96.7% F1-score, lowered successful membership-inference down to 2.3%, and kept latency overhead below 12%, making it a good candidate in online industrial and IoT scenarios. This demonstrates the power of encrypted similarity checks and reputation-weighted aggregation, as 15% malicious client poisoning is enough to withstand. Lowering the communication cost to 88 KB down demonstrates the feasibility of privacy and efficiency at the same time in resource-constraint scenarios. Its adaptive DP and edge-layer screening strategies can be considered as effective also as proven with an enhanced stability under non-IID data distributions. The unified secure aggregation, context-aware weighting, and multi-layer refinement features closed remaining gaps in federated CPS defense in an integrated framework. Should protect distributed heterogeneous cyber physical infrastructures HPF-FedDef is modular and scalable tool and could be used for protecting distributed heterogeneous cyber infrastructures. In future work, we will integrate our framework into large-scale multi-domain CPS ecosystems and bolster the zero-knowledge validation modules with tools that enhance threat transparency of the infrastructure. text: A Sociocognitive Structural-Flow Framework for Explainable Pre-Assault Prediction through Micro-Action Algebra and Counterfactual Intent Simulation Abstract- We introduce SENTINEL, a novel neuro-symbolic sociocognitive framework for interpretable pre-assault prediction in dynamic and multi-agent worlds. In contrast to these conventional deep learning methods that learn superficial correlations, which serve as a building block of the atomic behavior model for action composition, SENTINEL applies MAA to encode fine-grained behavior micro-atoms and STF modeling to uncover causal influences among temporal micro-action sequences. The RHSE unit is able to effectively model the collective interactions among multiple subjects and can well address crowded parts or partial occlusions. Additionally, the transparency is enhanced with the Counterfactual Intent Simulator (CIS) which creates counterfactual “what-if” scenarios and explains "why" a decision was made and establishes operator trust: interpretability. The system is based on a survival-guided Early-Time Risk Calibration Loss, while preserving probability consistency of threat estimation. Experiments on benchmark datasets like RWF-2000, XD-Violence and the proposed PreAssault-CHI present strong performance gains with 96.84%, early prediction accuracy, 94.31% causal edge precision rate and 92.75% counterfactual explanation fidelity. In addition, the model achieves a 93.12% fairness parity among demographic subgroups and achieves a 38% decrease in false-positive alarms compared to previous RNN-based and transformer-based baselinesี่. These results highlight SENTINEL’s ability to provide timely, interpretable, and ethically aligned early-warning signals for security-critical environments, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and cognitive transparency in human-AI decision collaboration. Keywords- Pre-assault prediction, micro-action algebra, structural temporal flow, relational hypergraph, counterfactual reasoning, early warning, explainable AI, causal modeling, multi-agent interaction, calibrated risk prediction, ethical surveillance, human-AI collaboration. I Introduction Anticipating violent behavior in advance is a challenging problem and interesting to a variety of domains including human-robot interaction, surveillance, behavioral science, and human-AI fusion [1],[2]. Earlier research on anticipation of early action has demonstrated that preparatory cues—minimal body movements, changes in gaze direction, oscillographic micro‐actions—convey information about intent substantially before actual aggression [3],[4]. This in turn has led to the development of a catalogue of known pre-attack (pre-assault) behavioral and physiological indicators including posture, tension in limbs, altered breathing or facial expression, body orientation toward others [5],[6], scanning behaviors (e.g. looking for threats) defensive displays and verbal cues. However, these signals are typically considered as higher level information or latent features by present model formulations and architectures in the context of recurrent or convolutional networks which stop short deliberately of disentangling minimal atomic behaviors ("micro-actions")
label: human

text: before an assault [7]. Second, Causal structure within the sequence steps—how one micro-action causes or depends on another—is rarely specified explicitly resulting in lack of interpretability and potential overly associative conclusions [1],[14]. Ethical considerations also complicate the use of “black-box” predictors: trust is lost when operators or those affected cannot explain why a prediction has been made, especially with respect to demographic or social variation [8], [9]. The additional obstruction caused by human presence in a crowded or partly occluded environment creates even more challenges. The effects of these conditions—there being audience or no audience, limbs and interruptions from the environment—are too obscure the micro-actions and situational changes in their world. And social interaction models which consider the structural relations between multiple agents also show promising results, such as hypergraph representations and relational encoders by learning interactions among all different agents besides pair wise or scene representation baselines [10], [11].If you do not model the interaction graphs, you face the challenge of signal mixing or context collapse- i.e., micro-acts of one agent are mixed with those of others or buried social signals may coexist. The temporal flow of actions—an ordered sequence of preparatory behaviors—necessitates modeling not merely the correlation between events, but their causal antecedence, so as to justify interventions or alarms based on more than an increase in accuracy alone, accordingly making sense of how risk develops [12],[13]. Another gap in existing literature is lack of counterfactual reasoning: knowing that an assault is predicted is insufficient unless one can examine “what if” alternatives, showing how changes in behavior or context would alter outcome [14],[15]. Counterfactual models have been used in other domains (e.g. healthcare, safety) to increase transparency, but seldom in pre-assault risk prediction. Also, calibration of early risk: high stakes environments require high sensitivity to early signs without overwhelming false positives [16],[17]. Loss functions that discount late recognition or that encourage early detection while maintaining probabilistic consistency are needed but under-explored. Finally, fairness across demographic subgroups—across gender, ethnicity, age, body type—must be measured, since many visual/behavioral models exhibit bias [18],[19],[20]. This research proposes a framework that addresses all the above: atomization of micro-actions with algebraic structure, explicit temporal causal flow, relational encoding of multiple agents, counterfactual explanation modules, early-time risk calibration, and fairness assessment. Extensive experiments on datasets including RWF-2000, XD-Violence, and a newly collected PreAssault-CHI dataset allow evaluation of early prediction accuracy, causal structure precision, and explanation fidelity. The results show strong performance under each measure, lower false positives, and the robustness of parity across racial groups. The paper is characterized by the following innovative contributions: ●​ Formalization of Micro-Action Algebra (MAA) and Structural Temporal Flow (STF) modules, capturing the minimal behavioural atoms and its connected causal effect to support intelligible chaining of micro-actions within pre-assault chains. ●​ Relational Hypergraph Social Context Encoder (RHSE) combined with a Counterfactual Intent Simulator (CIS) to obtain scenario-level explanations (“what if
label: human

text: this micro-action were different?”), so that they can output reliable predictions even when crowded or occluded. ●​ Construction of an early-time risk calibration loss with fairness constraints, trained to maximize the early detection of threat while minimizing both false positive rates and demographic parity across groups in various datasets. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we discuss the related works on pre-assault activity prediction, causal model and explainable surveillance and point out the limitations of existing methods. Section 3 introduces the proposed SENTINEL framework including specific formulation of MAA, STF, RHSE, CIS and Early-Time Risk Calibration Loss. Section 4 discusses the experimental settings: datasets, preprocessing, evaluation metrics. The results and comparison to existing benchmarks along with interpretability and fairness analysis are presented in Section 5. However, popular approaches tend to focus on isolated micro-actions or coarse motion patterns and fail to encode the causality between sequential actions, which hurts its interpretability in challenging multi-agent scenarios [2,5,11]. The skeleton-based and two-stream models enhance action perception except occlusion, rapid changes and relational gestures when interacting between people [5,11]. Explainable counterfactual reasoning for “what-if” scenarios is mostly missing, which undermines trust and transparency [12,14]. Whereas material-based modeling has illustrated the power of a structured fine-grained representation to produce some levels of stability/resilience [1,3,8,10,15], this way of doing things was never transferred completely to behavioral prediction. Moreover, the issues of fairness and early-risk calibration are mostly unexplored. Filling this gap would mean creating a formal system for combining micro-action algebra, temporal causality, multi-agent relational reasoning, counterfactual interpretability and ethically aligned early-warning signals. III Proposed Methodology The proposed methodology presents a neuro-symbolic sociocognitive model that combines Micro-Action Algebra (MAA) [20], Structural Temporal Flow (STF) and Relational Hypergraph Social Context Encoding (RHSE) in order to enable interpretable pre-assault predictions [19, 20]. The MAA discretizes human motion into a set of atoms of behaviors to allow the algebraic manipulation with micro-actions and represent illations about intentions over time [21]. The STF subpart formalizes causal links between these successive micro-actions, it shows how previous behavioural cues stochastically curve next intending

text: [22],[23]. At the same time, RHSE module encodes collective interactions in a multi-agent environment by relational hypergraphs, enabling the model to learn grouplevel dynamics and social context dependencies [24]. For interpretability, a Counterfactual Intent Simulator (CIS) generates counterfactual paths and offers “what-if” explanations on why the model made a decision in human cognitive-friendly style [25]. Moreover, an Early-Time Risk Calibration Loss ensures early warning capabilities by requiring that confidence in future prediction matches its probability before it actually happens, thereby enforcing a calibrated and fair risk assessment. Altogether these components constitute an end-to-end reasoning pipeline that spans symbolic interpretability to deep causal inference, enabling the system to localise, explain and justify early incipient signs of assault around natural/simulating human scenarios. In it, we first pre-process the raw video frames of surveillance footage, which are converted into organized sequences of pose vectors and motion gradients via keypoint detection and optical flow computation. These lower-level motion features are subsequently discretized into atomic units by MAA module, encoding the symbolic encodings of elementary performance 𝑎𝑖 𝑡 action. The STF module captures causal temporal transitions among those micro-actions by a graph-based temporal differentials and a gradient-based dependency matrix, whereas the RHSE constructs high-order hyperedges encoding relational proximity and social tension dynamics between multiple interacting agents. In the training, all sub-modules are jointly optimized in an end-to-end multi-objective fashion with the total loss consisting of causal consistency loss, temporal flow regularization, fairness constraint and survival-based calibration objective. We optimise it by AdamW with cosine annealing rates and gradient clipping to ensure stable learning in multi-agent temporal domains. Hyper-parameters, such as the temporal window size , causal sparsity weight , fairness (τ = 12) (λ = 0. 03) coefficient , and alignment factor have been empirically tuned via (γ = 0. 05) (α = 0. 1) grid search to achieve convergence stability. The entire pipeline is coded in PyTorch 2.2 using parallel graph computations on the NVIDIA A100 GPU, with the use of mixed precision computation that helps to speed up convergence and at the same time keeps numerical values stable. This joint training scheme provides co-adaptation at symbolic, probabilistic, and relational level acting as a cognitively plausible and temporally accurate pre-assault detection mechanism which naturally leads to the experimental validation stage. text: A Causal Neuro-Symbolic Judicial Reasoner Integrating Defeasible Logic and Counterfactual Analysis for Transparent Legal Decision-Making Abstract-The exponential growth of data-driven courts has raised the urgency for transparency, accountability and causal-explanation in automated legal decision-making. The current neural-symbolic frameworks are largely focused on text-driven inference and fail to encode causal relationships, rule exceptional cases or compute interpretable reasoning trails. To address these limitations, in this study CausaLexNet is developed as a novel process-based Causal Neuro-Symbolic Judicial Reasoner which unifies causal graph-based learning with defeasible legal logic for explainable and counterfactual decision-making. The proposed model utilizes a Structural Causal Graph to encode factual interdependences between legal clauses and allows for counterfactual reasoning via cause–effect analysis. A Heterogeneous Case Graph (HCG) using a Relational Graph Attention Network (R-GAT) captures multi-relational interactions between statutes, precedents and case outcomes. The DSM, a hierarchy of norms including exceptions, is introduced in order to formalize legal norms and to maintain based normative consistency by means of conflict resolution. A Probabilistic Logic Interface (PLI) serves as a translator between uncertain neural representations and formal symbolic proofs, enabling probabilistic rule grounding. By experimenting on benchmark legal datasets such as CUAD, Pile of Law, and the Caselaw Access Project, we show that our CausaLexNet performs 94.67% in outcome prediction accuracy, 92.14% in faithfulness to quality explanation, and 90.83% in robustness against counterfactual perturbations which is better than existing neuro-symbolic baselines by a large margin of 7–11%. The combination of causal reasoning, defeasible logic and counterfactual interpretability makes CausaLexNet a groundbreaking approach for explainable AI-based judicial decision-making with legal coherence. Keywords-Causal Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning, Defeasible Logic, Counterfactual Legal Analysis, Structural Causal Graph, Graph Neural Network, Probabilistic Logic Interface, Explainable AI, Legal Decision Support, Transparent Judicial Systems, Trustworthy AI I Introduction The increasing prominence of artificial intelligence in legal systems has raised profound concerns about transparency, interpretability and normative coherence when it comes to algorithmic decisions. The rising tendency to use data-driven algorithms to predict legally significant decisions and assess the materiality of evidence has exposed a deficiency of relational power in our currently available computational machinery [1]. It should be noted that while the average neural architecture has been shown to have sufficient reasoning depths for interpreting large amounts of legal text it may indeed fail to bridge computational inference and normative legal principles [2]. The judiciary’s use of black-box predictive models may alienate the public, particularly when prescriptive determinations are not fundamentally grounded [3]. Such lack of explicit causal explanation impedes the systems from explaining why a decision was made, thus impacting the ability to determine fairness,
label: human

text: consistency and legal justification [4]. In light of the increasing pressure for accountable AI at a global scale, models that reason under legal uncertainty and explain their causes are necessary [5]. We believe our networks allow humans to inspect the prediction process and its relationships with the law, providing interpretable causal pathways. Therefore, a model shift is needed and it should be from text-based statistical learning to a system that joint logical reasoning for causation, symbolic deduced by domain formalization and probabilistic reasoning in order to ensure its fitness for automatic judicial decisions [6]. Recent breakthroughs in neuro-symbolic AI have addressed the interpretability challenge through a joint representation of formal reasoning structures and neural ones [7]. However, to the best of our knowledge, the existing frameworks still are mainly data-oriented with syntax relations dominative while causality among legal concepts have not been seriously considered [8]. Legal systems are complex hierarchical structures of norms, exceptions and defeasible rules that cannot be learned solely inductively [9]. As an example, a rule clause may limit its range of application under certain circumstances but can be overruled using even more important principles which require support for dynamic rule evaluation mechanisms [10]. The lack of structured causal models in deployed neuro-symbolic systems restricts their ability to reason on counterfactuals, which is a critical element for testing hypothetical legal scenarios and checking whether the reasoning has led to robust outcomes [11]. How to handle these drawbacks is what an hybrid casual neuro-symbolic framework should provide, capable of being able to learn from various legal knowledge sources and at the same time be interpretable and support formal logical consistency [12]. By engraining causal structure within symbolic legal reasoning, the reasoning is not only explainable but also amenable to changes in jurisprudence [13]. To address these challenges, the current work presents CausaLexNet, a Causal Neuro-Symbolic Judicial Reasoner aiming at reconciling causal graph learning with defeasible legal logic. The framework builds a structural causal graph (SCG) to model interconnections between legal clauses, statutes and precedents, which facilitates counterfactual analysis through implementing cause–effect reasoning [14]. In particular, due to the complex multi-relational nature in legal text, a Heterogeneous Case Graph (HCG) based on a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT) is further involved [15]. Moreover, the Defeasible Symbolic Module (DSM) represents the reasoning by encoding rule precedence and active knowledge normative hierarchy, in such a way that the system still complies with the legal standard of interpretation [16]. By incorporating a Probabilistic Logic Interface (PLI), the model is shown to successfully connect uncertain neural embeddings with symbolic proofs, enabling probabilistic grounding of legal rules without losing interpretative clarity [17]. It is the unification of causal, probabilistic and symbolic logic that gives AI its integrated structure, capable of supporting both data-driven methods’ statistical variability and normative clarity sophistication [18]. However, the proposed model not only is empirically accurate as a predictor, but also explains why judges made their decisions. Experiments show the practicability and theoretical perfection of CausaLexNet. Experimental study on benchmark datasets including CUAD, Pile of Law and Caselaw Access Project
label: human

text: further demonstrates its superior performance in terms of outcome prediction, explanation faithfulness and robustness to counterfactual perturbation case [19]. Tracking steps of reasoning along causal chains enables lawyers and judges to know why certain clauses in the model drive predictions, providing accountability in automated legal analytics. Defeasible logic is also introduced in the model to represent normative exceptionalism installed for the purpose of bridging a gap between legal consequences of rules and human reasoning. This dual factual and counterfactual interpretability aspect makes CausaLexNet a key contribution of transparent legal AI. The findings not only support the importance of causal interpretability, but also contribute to a wider discussion around trustworthy AI governance in law [20]. Through the combination of explainability and formal legal semantics, the project paves the way for a new generation of interpretable and normatively consistent systems in judicial reasoning. The main contributions of the paper are as follows: ●​ Causal-Neuro-Symbolic Integration: Presents CausaLexNet, a unified architecture that fuses causal graph learning with defeasible logic to produce transparent, causally based judicial decisions. ●​ Defeasible Symbolic Reasoning Module: Realizes an infrastructural hierarchy of legal logic-based modules that is able to resolve contradiction of rules and deals with normative exceptions in general and it provides for consistent interpretations of the law across different legal domains. ●​ Counterfactual and Probabilistic Reasoning: Integrates counterfactual reasoning and probabilistic logic grounding to reason about causal relationships and judge hypothetical legal situations with interpretive accuracy. The rest of this paper is organised as follows. Related work is presented that has sought to advance understanding in neuro-symbolic legal reasoning, causal modelling and defeasible logic. Section III methodology describes the composition of CausaLexNet, which consists of the Structural Causal Graph, Heterogeneous Case Graph and Defeasible Symbolic Module. The experiments section covers the dataset, training settings and evaluation metrics used to evaluate how well the framework performs. The experimental results and discussion section provides the numerical experiments, in which comparison advantages in interpretability and robustness are discussed. Finally, we summarize the key findings, discuss their implications for judicial transparency and outline possible future directions of causal and defeasible reasoning in AI-driven law. Previous work has highlighted hybrid interpretability [1], ethical frameworks [11], blockchain integration for accountability [12] and neuro-symbolic reasoning [16] but most of them concentrate on single technologies rather than the comprehensive analysis. Existing legal AI models find it challenging to combine statistical prediction with conceptually sound, defeasible reasoning that accommodates hierarchical rule exceptions and counterfactual evaluation [4,16,19]. In addition, the regulatory framework as GDPR shows that quality of explanations is not sufficient for high risk automated decisions [10], and indicates the need to develop multi-layered transparency mechanisms. There is also little focus on numerical reasoning and multi-relational dependencies in legal scenarios, which makes models susceptible to biased or partial conclusions [19]. Together, these constraints form the gap: there is no current system that provides all of causal, probabilistic and symbolic inference with benefits such as hierarchical exception handling and counterfactual analysis for transparent AI-based decisions which are legally robust. This gap motivates the pursuit of an end-to-end framework to address all these challenges at once, while ensuring that a unified deployment architecture is provided for interpretable, accountable and normative-compliant results. III Methodology​ The CausaLexNet approach, which combines neuro-symbolic causal reasoning with defeasible legal logic and counterfactual interests to foster transparent, interpretable pro-lingua judicial decision-making. Complementing recent progress on magnitude-aware legal reasoning [19] and neuro-symbolic frameworks for prediction of judgments [16], the system introduces a Structural Causal Graph (SCG) which encodes factual and causal dependencies between legal clauses and precedents, enabling counterfactual inference over hypothetical scenarios [20]. A Relational Graph Attention Network based Heterogeneous Case Graph (HCG) which captures multi-relational interactions between the statutes, cases and outcomes in legal context are used to learn informative relationships [21]. Norms are formalised using a Defeasible Symbolic Module (DSM), which captures priority and exception rules in a hierarchically structured DSM for recourse to bridging the ontological gap between symbolic and numerical reasoning – an approach inspired by investigations that bridge symbolic with numerical/logical reasoning in legal AI [22,23]. Another approach is to reconcile uncertainty on representations from neural networks through a Probabilistic Logic Interface (PLI), connecting deep learning embeddings with symbolic proofs and enabling probabilistic grounded rules [24]. This combination of SCG, HCG, DSM and PLI constitutes an end2end cognitive framework to produce legally consistent, counterfactually stable and explainable judgments that extends what has been done more recently in the hybrid neuro-symbolic AI for legal context [25]. First, the SCG captures factual and causal relations between legal clauses, statutes, and references to precedents which adds a structured representation of how facts contribute to outcomes. In the HCG, concept embeddings are causal embeddings that model interactions between cases, statutes and verdicts in a multi-relational fashion using relational attention mechanisms. When attending, R-GAT directly gives ‘attention’ to neighbors so that the model can pay attention to precedent cases and statute priors which are directly relevant with given legal questions. Such integration ensures that the neural presentation is context-sensitive and relation-aware to generate embeddings reflecting structural as well as semantic complexity in court data. Subsequently the solutions computed for SCG and HCG are reconciled by symbolic-reasoning in a DSM (descriptive semantic model) that incorporates hierarchical priorities, rule exceptions and conflict resolution strategies. By combining the generated probabilistic neural embeddings with formal symbolic rules via a PLI on top of them, it enables us to quantify such attendance probability for each rule’s applicability to an instance and thereby obtain a more flexible grounding in legal decisions. This stacked integration ensures that each layer contributes a visible and interpretable degree of freedom to the decision making: SCG gives causal understanding, HCG patterns relationship influence, DSM enforces normativity consistency, PLI provides uncertainty aware probability reasoning. Altogether, this architecture enables support for counterfactual reasoning to ask “what-if” questions, while maintaining legally coherent and human understandable reasoning trails. In this way the framework endorsed end-to-end XAI in the judicial domain to assure that decisions are not only correct, but can be audited, traced back and compliant with ethical and legal guidelines. text: The experiments of CausaLexNet show that the joint use of causal reasoning, relational graph attention, defeasible symbolic logic and probabilistic grounding significantly increases not only predictive performance but also interpretation in legal decision-making. The model systematically performed better than neural-only, symbolic-only, and hybrid baselines with 94.67% accuracy, 92.14% explanation faithfulness and 90.83% robust in presence of counterfactual perturbation—all measures demonstrate promising high-stake judicial decision reliability. The ablation study revealed that all modules make distinct contributions: SCG capturing factual interdependencies; HCG describing relational nuances between statutes and precedents; DSM enforcing normative consistency; and PLI bridging uncertainty and formal proof. Such findings show that both neural and symbolic approaches are insufficient for balancing accuracy with transparency and CausaLexNet’s neuro-symbolic combination makes a good starting point to achieve explainable and accountable AI-based legal reasoning. The capacity to perform counterfactual analysis, and ambiguity of the model’s decision capability regarding decision stability even in presence of perturbations is particularly desirable for real-world judicial applications satisfying interpretability, causal justification and robustness. Taken together, these results reinforce the necessity of a multi-component neuro-symbolic system for providing trustworthy and transparent legal AI tools. VI Conclusion In summary, we present CausaLexNet, a Causal Neuro-Symbolic Judicial Reasoner that seamlessly connects Structural Causal Graphs, Heterogeneous Case Graphs, Defeasible Symbolic Modules and Probabilistic Logic Interfaces to ensure transparent (interventions & explanations), robust & legally coherent decision-making. Experimental results on popular legal datasets, including CUAD, Pile of Law, and the Caselaw Access Project illustrate that CausaLexNet achieves 94.67% prediction accuracy for outcome prediction (which measures how often the model agrees with human interpretation in labeled texts), 92.14% faithfulness in explanation quality (by comparing features brought up by CausaLexNet as opposed to human) and superior robustness at 90.83% against counter factual perturbations than existing neuro-symbolic counterparts by a margin of 7-11%. Ablation studies further verify the importance of every module in prediction accuracy and interpretability, among which the causal reasoning, relational attention, normative logic and probabilistic grounding cooperate to improve the fidelity in decision making for the model. CausaLexNet not only overcomes some restrictions of neural-only or symbolic-only approaches but also provides a pathway to explainable AI in legally sensitive applications for which reasoning is built on uncertainty about legal truth. Its interpretive explanation and stability on acquired cases under hypothetical case changes demonstrates its practical significance for real world judicial applications. In the future, we will work on cross-domain adaptive learning, to cope with new legislation and laws being ruled and promulgated, improve multimodal legal data interpretation, as well as adapting our model to the multi-jurisdictional context. These developments seek to reinforce transparency, accountability and robustness in AI-enhanced law reasoning. References
