text: An Adaptive Lightweight Online and Energy-Aware Gaussian Mixture Model for Processor-Based Embedded Systems Using Sensor and Machine Learning Abstract-The increasing integration of machine learning into embedded systems necessitates models that are computationally efficient, adaptive, and capable of performing real-time analysis within strict resource constraints. Traditional Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) applied to sensor data in embedded environments suffer from limited adaptability, high energy consumption, and scalability issues in dynamic conditions. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes a novel algorithm titled ALOE-GMM (Adaptive Lightweight Online and Energy-Aware Gaussian Mixture Model), specifically designed for processor-based embedded systems such as the NXP FRDM-K64F. The proposed ALOE-GMM framework incorporates incremental Expectation-Maximization for continuous learning, adaptive component birth-death control for dynamic clustering, and quantized fixed-point arithmetic to ensure low memory utilization. Additionally, an incremental Principal Component Analysis (PCA) module enhances feature fusion and dimensionality reduction, optimizing sensor-level computation. Experimental validation using multi-sensor datasets demonstrates a real-time inference accuracy of 97.83%, a processing latency reduction of 41%, and a 28% improvement in energy efficiency compared to conventional GMM implementations. Furthermore, memory consumption was reduced by 34%, ensuring suitability for microcontroller-class processors with limited resources. The ALOE-GMM approach thus establishes a scalable, resource-aware paradigm for embedded machine learning applications, enabling intelligent local decision-making without reliance on cloud resources. This framework is poised to advance real-time anomaly detection, industrial monitoring, and environmental sensing in next-generation embedded platforms. Keywords-Processor-based embedded system, sensor fusion, lightweight machine learning, Gaussian Mixture Model, online EM algorithm, incremental PCA, energy efficiency, real-time inference, TinyML, ALOE-GMM I Introduction Thanks to the development of more and more sophisticated sensor devices along with the availability of low-resource embedded platforms, the possibility to offload tasks at the network's edge instead of exclusively relying on cloud computing connectivity has risen in popularity [1][2]. Motivation for this work with embedded systems is that they are being used to accomplish high-level functions using information from various sources while imposing strong limitations on processing power, memory, and energy [3][4]. In such a scenario, the unsupervised and semi-unsupervised learning approaches which can account for the dynamic changes in sensor patterns are of special importance. Conventional methods, such as static clustering or batch-trained classifiers, are often unsuccessful when the statistical characteristics of sensor readings or environmental states drift over time, or when the system needs to respond in real time using limited resources [5] Integration of lightweight sensor-level feature processing with self-adjusting model complexity and fixed-point
label: human

text: arithmetic has been demonstrated to be an effective means for increasing responsiveness, efficiency, scalability and autonomy in embedded decision systems. Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) have been widely used for representing complex probability densities and addressing multimodal sensor inputs in the context of anomaly detection, clustering, and classification [6][7]. The EM algorithm used with GMMs (EM-GMM) is a flexible approach for GMM model parameter estimation [8], but it requires numerical computation in full-precision data format, iterative manipulation of sensor measurements and offline calculation (for standard implementations) — consequently impractical for embedded platforms that have limited computational resources. Recent studies show that incremental mixture models are a promising candidate for on-line learning in non-stationary environments [9][10]. Yet, many of those designs focus on high end microprocessors and disregard the direct inclusion of: energy awareness, fixed point quantization, dynamic control over components and sensor fusion through low dimensional representation. Addressing these gaps is crucial in order for the GMM-based approaches to achieve practical implementation on microcontroller-class processors for real-time sensory-driven applications [11]. Distributed sensor fusion has its own set of challenges: The heterogeneity of data streams, the intermittent nature of sampled information, the different noise characteristics and drift effects all will lead to changing distributions in data over time [12][13]. Dimensionality reduction methods, such as incremental PCA, provide a way to compress and decorrelate the features while still keeping discriminative information. The insertion of such modules in the signal path before the mixture-model classifier module can lower computational and memory overhead, and improve inference latency [14]. At the other extreme, birth and death of mixture components is a powerful means to accommodate changes in cluster structure over time that occur without introducing new parameters constantly [15][16]. When coupled with fixed-point arithmetic, and energy aware scheduling, the outcome is a paradigm which preserves real-time and resource constraints of embedded monitoring systems in both time-efficient precision and ensuring a reasonable level of accuracy [17][18] In this work, we provide a holistic design and implementation of an ALOE-GMM for processor-based embedded systems such as the NXP FRDM-K64F [19]. The proposed method consists of incremental EM, adaptive general mixture-component control, sensor-level fusion and reduction through incremental PCA, and quantized fixed-point arithmetic for ultra-low-latency and low-energy inference on microcontrollers. Comprehensive experiments on multi-sensor data show that our method not only preserves the high detection accuracy but also gains obvious improvements on latency, energy consumption and memory overhead over traditional GMM approaches [20]. These results place the embedded anomaly detection, industrial monitoring, and environmental sensing applications that may not have access or do not require cloud connectivity. Key contributions of this work: ●​ Development of an online incremental EM-based Gaussian mixture framework with adaptive component birth/death control optimized for microcontroller-class embedded hardware. ●​ Integration of an incremental PCA module at the sensor-fusion level, coupled with quantized fixed-point arithmetic implementation, to reduce memory and computational load while preserving inference accuracy.

On one hand, the advanced models focus on either hardware acceleration [1][10][11], or model compression [4] and few works present a unified solution combining online learning, adaptive model control, and quantized arithmetic suitable to continuous operation with low resources. From nearly all previous publications, there is in general no capability of self-evolution for the static architectures that are used [3][8][17], which leads to poor performance under non-stationary data. Additionally, energy savings in embedded systems have typically not been central to design as much as it has been layered and approached post-design or pushed through the use of some form of sparse inference models that only loosely couple computational load to available energ[13][15][18]. Although probabilistic and neural models have been successful in isolation, there is a lack of combined technologies that integrate incremental probabilistic inference with dimensionality reduction for sensor fusion under real-time constraints. This gap highlights the necessity of an adaptive, lightweight and energy-driven probabilistic model which can maintain high accuracy, low latency and memory efficiency across various embedded platforms—an observation that motivates the proposed ALOE-GMM framework. III Proposed Methodology We propose an integrated framework known as Adaptive Lightweight Online and Energy-aware GMM (ALOE-GMM) that achieves successful compromises between (i) adaptiveness, (ii) light weight in terms of computation, and (iii) energy saving for processor-based embedded applications. It is based on continuous probabilistic learning by an Incremental EM algorithm, and the model grows incrementally with new sensor data with no need for full re-training passes [20]. To maintain scalability with the dynamic mixture of data, an adaptive component birth-death process adaptively controls the number of Gaussian components in order to minimize unnecessary calculations and stabilization convergence in an online manner [21]. On the other hand, provided a stream of input data and a set of features, a progressive Principal Component Analysis (PCA) component can compress and
label: human

text: fuse features continuously to minimize the dimension of feature representation while keeping discriminative power intact [22]. In order to save memory and energy, all the numerical operations are performed with quantized fixed-point arithmetic to make the model more compatible with microcontroller class processors. The framework even provides an energy-profiling layer in charge of profiling the computation frequency and adjusting inference scheduling according to power budget constraints, which makes its real-time performance consistent under limited powers [23]. Overall, this approach provides a coherent probabilistic background for adaptive, energy-conscious and online decision making in future embedded machine learning systems. Figure 1: ALOE-GMM: Adaptive Lightweight Online and Energy-Aware Gaussian Mixture Model Architecture for Embedded Systems 3.1 System Architecture and Data Flow The ALOE-GMM is implemented on an embedded hardware platform targeting energy-efficient, real-time learning and decision making. The execution is directed to the NXP FRDM-K64F development board, which boasts an ARM Cortex-M4 processor core, a clock speed of 120 MHz and built-in floating-point unit that enables for quick mathematical calculations in low power conditions. The structure is established on hierarchically functional layers, which include five functional ones: sensor acquisition, pre-processing, online feature fusion, adaptive GMM-based inference and decision output control. The first layer provides the interface between multi-modal sensors for acquiring environment or visual information using communication protocols such as I²C and SPI on-board. Subsequently, the data are preprocessed in the pre-processing layer, including filtering, normalization and time-stamping
label: human

text: to remove transient noise and sensor drift. The concatenation is fed to the embedded ALOE-GMM inference core for on-the-fly adaptation of the GMM’s Gaussian components due to data drift and novelty. Inference results are transferred out through the UART, or stored in on-chip flash memory for post-processing. Continuity of the firmware at execution and synchronization level between these modules is achieved with FreeRTOS, promoting a deterministic task scheduling and non-blocking code. This hierarchical ModelZoo architecture allows the processor to process data flow continuously with low latencies and minimized energy consumption, making it independent of external computation when entering training or inference modes. The CIFAR-10 image database was chosen as the experimental benchmark for evaluating the real-time intelligent classification performance of this embedded framework. CIFAR-10 is a standard dataset to test embedded ML systems on, made of 60,000 images in ten categories (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship and truck) evenly distributed over the pipeline. There are each picture of size 32×32 pixels, very compact and rich in information that can be used to evaluate the low-power, memory-poor processor. The dataset includes 50,000 samples for training and 10,000 samples for testing (90:10 ratio) which supports full generalization and adaptive learning validation. Being moderately complex in nature, the dataset has potential applicability to modelling of probabilistic boundaries within real world embedded scenarios where illumination level variance, object occlusion and background noise can cause fluctuation on inference stability. CIFAR-10 is additionally chosen for the fact that it can be used with feature compression and incremental learning, enabling the ALOE-GMM to manifest adaptive component control as well as great quantized arithmetic performance. Compared with those larger scale datasets requiring excessive GPU memory and bandwidth, CIFAR-10's realistic trade off between human perception diversity and computational feasibilities makes it ideal for testing out the developed lightweight embedded framework when practical hardware limitations are taken into account. 3.2 Dataset Preprocessing Prior to feeding image data into the ALOE-GMM framework, a systematic pre-processing pipeline is employed so as to stabilize, normalise, and expedite learning in the embedded platform. text: 4.1 Experimental Setup and Validation The NXP FRDM-K64F development board was using an ARM Cortex-M4 processor in addition to 256 K SRAM and 1 M flash memory. The board was along the lines of a microcontroller-class embedded platform [20]. Multi-sensor input streams were simulated by making use of the CIFAR-10 dataset. This reference collection has 60,000 color images in 10 classes. With 48,000 images 80 % used for training and discriminant learning, 12,000 images 20% were put aside as test data. The CIFAR-10 is optimal for embedded vision systems to evaluate lightweight online learning and feature fusion, since it incorporates varied image categories and has a dimensionality that is not too high. According to processor limitations, the dataset was preprocessed by normalization, centering of the mean, and fixed-point conversion. By using incremental PCA, we managed to reduce the 3,072-dimensional feature space to 64 dimensions. This allows for efficient computation of the Mahalanobis distance during EM updates. A small number of components initiates the mixture components of Gaussians; birth–death measures dynamically control it from then on. The whole process (including preprocessing, PCA projection, EM updating, component control and fixed-point computation) was implemented in C/C++ for the Cortex-M4, optimized on the reservoir itself. With internal sensors and an external profiler, power consumption and energy efficiency were monitored to record inference latency, memory occupation and classification accuracy. Batches of 128 images were processed as they arrived, forming the basis for evaluating real-time adaptability, incremental learning and embedded feasibility. 4.2 Training Strategy The ALOE-GMM framework employs a set of carefully tuned parameters to balance accuracy, resource usage, and real-time adaptability on the FRDM-K64F embedded platform. The initial number of Gaussian components was set to 5, allowing the model to adaptively 𝐾 grow or shrink via the birth–death mechanism. The novelty threshold for creating new components was set at 0.05, while the minimum component weight for ϵ𝑛𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑙 π𝑚𝑖𝑛 elimination was 0.01, monitored over a sliding window of 50 iterations. The incremental PCA retained the top 64 eigenvectors to reduce dimensionality from 3,072 (CIFAR-10 images) while preserving 95% of the variance. The learning rate for incremental covariance α updates was 0.01, and the EM convergence threshold was set to to ensure stable 10 −4 posterior updates [28][30]. The training strategy was fully online and incremental. The dataset was fed in mini-batches of 128 images, allowing the EM algorithm to update the Gaussian parameters π𝑘, µ𝑘, Σ𝑘 continuously without storing previous batches. PCA eigenvectors were updated incrementally with each batch to adapt the feature space dynamically. The adaptive component control ensured that the number of active components remained compact, which directly reduced memory usage and inference latency. Quantized fixed-point arithmetic was applied throughout training to minimize energy consumption while maintaining parameter precision.

Ablation studies verify the indispensable role played by each subsystem; multi-metric comparisons show that SPLVP, FPGA-SVM, CNN-TPU, M-RLS, MosAIc, and ECG models perform worse in accuracy, latency, energy use and memory size. Based on these results, future work will be directed towards introducing heterogeneous multicore, real-time industrial IoT anomaly detection and dynamic environment adaptive sensor selection. text: A Proactive Quantum-Adaptive Digital Twin Framework with Reinforcement Learning for Ultra-Resilient Healthcare IoMT Abstract- The rapid proliferation of Internet-of-Medical-Things (IoMT) deployments in healthcare has heightened the demand for ultra-resilient, quantum-safe, and adaptive Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs). Based on our previous Quantum-Trust IoT (QT-IoT) architecture that integrated QKD with self-healing trust management, this work proposes a Proactive Quantum-Adaptive Digital Twin IoMT (PQDTI–IoMT) architecture. The virtual model will integrate digital twins, Deep Reinforcement Learning and federated anomaly learning to support quantum-resilient predictive and adaptive security orchestration in medical settings. In the edge–fog layer, each sensor node has a digital twin, which provides real-time what-if simulations for routing, healing and anomaly response before deployment. A quantum-adaptive DRL algorithm is proposed to dynamically control trust-aware clustering and energy-constrained routing, while federated anomaly learning improves detection performance across heterogeneous devices without information leakage of patients' privacy. Integrated hybrid post-quantum cryptosystems with QKD to provide protection against both quantum channel loss and adversarial ML attacks. We conduct comprehensive NS-3 and Cooja simulations with 50–100 nodes and show that within the network, PQDT-IoMT attains 41% better anomaly detection accuracy, 47% shorter healing latency and a prolongation of the lifetime by as much as 29% compared with QT-IoT. In addition, trust convergence stabilizes 36% faster, and packet delivery accuracy is maintained at 97.8%, which outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines such as LEACH-TM, DGTTSSA and BlockWSN. This interplay of proactive healing (based on digital twin), quantum safe trust re-adjustment, and federated anomaly intelligence is the special feature in PQDT-IoMT that marks an evolutionary step away from reactive self-healing architectures. The architecture provides a strong foundation for 6G-based patient centric and mission critical IoMT services. Keywords-Quantum Trust, Digital Twin IoMT, Self-Healing Networks, Federated Anomaly Detection, Deep Reinforcement Learning, Post-Quantum Security, Edge-Fog Computing, Healthcare WSNs, 6G Resilience I Introduction​ The proliferation of Internet Medicated Things (IoMT) has brought about health services provisioning remote diagnostics, continuous monitoring and wise clinical decision-making in distributed sensor infrastructures. However, this rapid integration generates and enhances opportunities on resilience, privacy and security in areas of mission critical controllers particularly on trustworthiness relation between WSNs and patients’ vital signs [1]. Quantum computers can also obsolete the traditional cryptographic solutions, since both classical and quantum attackers are not secure for IoT-networked systems in cost-effective medical scenarios [2][3]. As a result, there is a growing need for being able to predict failures, deal with adversarial anomalies and ensure trust in communications. The digital twin being cited as a key enabler, which created the virtual look-alike of the physical twin so that predictive
label: human

text: analysis, proactive healing and real-time adaptation were possible [4][5]. However, in the context of healthcare IoMT where device heterogeneity and sensitive data are dominant, there is a lack of research on orchestrating quantum-resilient digital twins. The transition from reactive healing paradigms to proactive intelligent-based approaches entailing trust recalibration, energy-aware routing and quantum-secured communications is considered as a pivotal step towards ultra-resilient healthcare infrastructure [6][7]. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning has been demonstrated to endow the network optimization with dynamic decision making under uncertainty and adversarial environment [8][9]. The potentiality of such networks using DRL architecture can be enhanced through adaptive routing, trust-aware clustering, and predictive service when handling anomalies in distributed IoMT systems is a great possibility. Combination of DRL and federated anomaly learning becomes significantly crucial in domains such as healthcare where the privacy-preserving collaboration across heterogeneous nodes is a critical requirement [10][11]. For federated learning, the machinery learns across devices without sharing raw patient data hence increasing detection performance and complying to medical data's governance [12]. Therefore, the proposed models may have the advantages of DRL and federated learning for resolving self-healing at network-level by using a predictive mechanism on one hand, and benefiting from privacy-preserving intelligent models on another side. Together with digital twins, these tools allow simulation of different types of attack on a virtual network before any action is taken to mitigate the threats on the real network. This marks a shift in the threat model from reactively holding back opportunistic pathology to proactively defending against IoMT infrastructure that continues learning, adapting, healing before vulnerabilities reach macroscopic proportions [13][14]. The foundation for quantum secure primitives is built with these security provided building blocks. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is an information-theoretically-secure protocol exploiting the nature of quantum mechanics, but it suffers from channel fragility and scalability issues, and can be vulnerable to denial-of-service attack [15]. To be able to overcome these challenges, the hybrid PQC schemes are designed to improve the fallback protection of QKD for channel errors against machine learning based adversaries [16]. The integration of QKD with post-quantum primitives therefore leads to multi-layer resiliency against different threat landscapes, accelerating the trust convergence in the large-scale healthcare IoMT deployments. By weaving this dual defense into the digital twin environment, healthcare networks are endowed with a proactive armor surpassing cryptographic robustness and continuity of services [17]. Furthermore, the ability to imbibe the healing responses in a digital twin layer ensures quick trust re-calibration, lower latency in anomaly detection and steady packet delivery accuracy even under network variations. This integration epitomises a new model of anticipatory healing, one where Q&R is framed not only as recovery but more importantly as an ongoing, quantum-adapted response [18]. In this context, the PQDT-IoMT proposed framework provides an original approach that fuses quantum level security, digital twin orchestration, deep reinforcement learning and federated anomaly intelligence together. Into the edge–fog layer the digital twin of all the physical sensor nodes is deployed, one-to-one relationships with each node for what-if simulations on routing, clustering and anomaly response before deployment. Trust-aware, energy-sensitive
label: human

text: routing is scheduled by a DRL-driven engine, and federated anomaly detection improves the accuracy of alerting without exposing sensitive patient data. Hybrid post-quantum cryptographic primitives are well suited for functional complementarity of QKD and hence enables robustness, even in presence of quantum channel failure. Through comprehensive simulations, the proposed framework is shown to be valuable in heterogeneous healthcare WSN applications: performance parameters like anomaly detection accuracy, healing latency, network lifetime and trust convergence are significantly enhanced with respect to state-of-the-art works [19]. The innovation is rooted in combining proactive digital twin-based healing with post-quantum trust recalibration and federated anomaly intelligence – thereby taking a step further beyond reactive self-healing architectures and setting the foundation for ultra-resilient, 6G empowered healthcare ecosystems. The main contributions of this paper are: ●​ We will also develop a PQDT-IoMT framework that includes digital twin orchestration, DRL-based trust management and energy-aware routing for predictive healing in health WSNs. ●​ The novel contribution is a federated anomaly learning mechanism to improve detection accuracy for heterogeneous devices under the constraints of medical data privacy and robustness against adversarial attacks. ●​ Designing a hybrid quantum security model that integrates QKD with post-quantum cryptographic primitives to provide security for IoMT systems from quantum channel failures and machine learning based adversaries. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: related works on quantum-safe IoT, digital twin frameworks, reinforcement learning applications and federated anomaly detection are discussed respectively in Section II. The methodology of the proposed PQDT-IoMT framework, which consists of digital twin orchestration, DRL-based clustering and a hybrid quantum trust model is described in section III. Experimental setup is in Section IV that includes NS-3 and Cooja simulator environments, performance metrics, and healthcare IoMT scenarios. Section V offers some numerical results and discussions, comparing serving efficiency with QT-IoT, LEACH-TM, DGTTSSA, BlockWSN baselines. Section VI is closing the paper with the main findings, implications and research directions of the study. II Literature Review The advanced realization of 6G and beyond networks have led the industry towards smart network management for high bandwidth low latency applications such as remote surgery, augmented reality, and autonomous health care systems. Tran et al. (2025) introduced Network Digital Twins (NDT) as a candidate technology for creating virtual counterparts of physical networks, facilitating simulation of failures, operation policies, and large-scale networking optimisation in real-time [1]. This method enables predictive planning and proactive network maintenance, which is critical for mission-critical healthcare IoMT deployments where service availability directly influences patient outcomes. Han et al. (2024) stressed the role of predictive maintenance and dynamic monitoring in medical cyber-physical systems. Their combination of swarm robotics with fog computing and extreme learning machines was able to assess device health in real time, reducing downtime

Their SafeTwins solution is based on blockchain and NFTs, presented a proof-of-concept that improved telemedicine services as well as emphasized design trade-offs of secure, robust DT-enabled healthcare systems [19]. 2.1 Research Gap​ Although significant progress has been made in the development of digital twin–enabled
label: human

text: IoMT architectures, quantum-secure protocols, and AI-based predictive analytics, many key challenges have yet to be solved. The majority of current solutions share their emphasis on security in the blockchain or quantum cryptography [5][15], and predictive power by use of AI and federated learning [6][7][18], few attempts to incorporate them together as a whole for to serve as alert system stand alone in its preventive perspective. Second, although task offloading and energy efficiency have been investigated in 6G-ready settings [9], dynamic anomaly detection and trust recalibration in near real-time across diverse IoMT devices is yet to be studied. The state-of-the-art digital twin solutions do not integrate with federated anomaly intelligence or quantum-adaptive trust for simulating isolated device behaviours, hindering their scaling and effectiveness in large-scale mission-critical clinical applications [14][19]. Likewise and in most cases, they do not consider satisfactorily the confluence between energy-aware routing, cyber-physical resiliency and predictive healing to ensure network lifetime sustainability as well as an operative continuity in hyper-resilient healthcare systems. These are the gaps that this chapter tries to point out, i.e., a full-fledged model based on unified proactive DT simulations, quantum-resilient security capabilities and federated anomaly detection/reinforcement learning–based adaptive control frameworks in accomplishing anticipatory patient-centric ultra-resilient IoMT ecosystems. III Methodology​ The PQDT-IoMT framework utilizes digital twin modeling, DRL (Deep Reinforcement Learning), and federated anomaly detection with the aim of realizing ultra-resilient healthcare operations. Each physical sensor node has a digital twin in the edge–fog layer for real-time what-if simulations for routing, energy management and predictive healing prior to live deployment [20]. A quantum-adaptive DRL engine is developed for real-time optimization of clustering and routing to ensure trust-awareness degree in addition to energy efficiency, by tuning network trust with the respect to anomalies and adversarial attacks [21][22]. For controlling model adaptation and anomaly detection on diverse device populations, federated anomaly learning combines the model updates without transmitting raw data to increase accuracy of identifying unforeseen behaviors over network [23][24]. Furthermore, hybrid post-quantum cryptographic primitives will have a role alongside quantum key distribution (QKD) to protect the communications from classical and quantum adversaries [25]. Integrating predictive simulation, adaptive intelligence, and quantum-resilient security, the proposed approach offers a comprehensive and preemptive control framework for sustaining operational continuity, reducing healing latency and prolonging network lifetime in mission-critical IoMT systems. Figure 1 illustrates the overall architecture of the proposed PQDT-IoMT framework integrating hybrid quantum security, federated meta-learning, and distributed trust management.

With the coordination of all these modules, The whole PQDT-IoMT achieves 97.8%accuracy,1.0% latency and 3.2%QBER, which presents overall excellence of our hybrid layered-design. 5.3 Discussion To summarize, the proposed PQDT-IoMT architecture has made a substantial improvement over trust mechanisms for IoT in security and performance aspects. When used in combination with hybrid QKD + PQC encryption, it realizes nearly the lowest possible ( 1s for real-time secure communication), quantum-secure communication. Federated meta-learning boosts the anomaly detection accuracy to 97.8%, which outperforms all baselines. Secondly, the trust optimization layer can promote the convergence rate and thus prolong network lifespan; this evidence assured that the system can scale well with dynamic edge conditions. Insights from ablation study also suggest that both the cryptographic and trust modules form a most stable and power-effective combination. In combination all these findings validate the effectiveness and future readiness of PQDT-IoMT in addressing the next gen IoT cloud security and trust management challenges. VI Conclusion In summary, the proposed PQDT-IoMT approach offers a new era in ultra-resilient healthcare IoMT by incorporating QDT-ADT, deep reinforcement learning and federated anomaly detection. Comprehensive simulations demonstrate its superiority in terms of the anomaly detection accuracy 41% higher, healing latency 47% faster, network lifetime 29% longer, and the packet delivery precision that preserved at a level of 97.8%, if the trust convergence is reduced to converge up to 36% faster than current solutions. Next steps will concentrate on the extension of the framework to real 6G-driven hospital deployment, integration of explainable AI for clinical decision support and optimization of energy-aware protocols for further increasing scalability as well as reliability toward the patient. text: A Neuro-Symbolic Multimodal Framework for Transparent, Ethical, and Trust-Aware Human-AI Collaboration in Recruitment Systems Abstract-The growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in recruitment has enhanced candidate screening efficiency, yet challenges in fairness, interpretability, and recruiter trust remain unresolved. This research introduces NeuroTrustNet, a novel neuro-symbolic multimodal framework that combines deep neural learning with symbolic reasoning to deliver transparent and human-aligned recruitment intelligence. The framework processes heterogeneous data—textual resumes, voice interviews, facial micro-expressions, and behavioral gestures—through a transformer-based Cross-Modal Alignment Network (CMAN), creating unified semantic embeddings. Candidate–Skill–Organization relationships are captured via Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), while DeepProbLog enforces rule-based symbolic reasoning to ensure ethical compliance, fairness, and explainability. A Trust-Aware Human Feedback Engine employs interactive reinforcement learning to adapt recommendations based on recruiter input, improving interpretability and mutual understanding. The NeuroTrust Index (NTI) quantifies fairness, consistency, and recruiter acceptance, dynamically adjusting AI autonomy. Experimental evaluation on multimodal recruitment datasets demonstrates 95.3% fairness compliance, 93.7% decision interpretability, and 92.5% recruiter acceptance, outperforming conventional neural-only approaches by 12–18% across these metrics. These results confirm that NeuroTrustNet effectively mitigates bias propagation, enhances transparent reasoning, and fosters trust-aware human-AI collaboration. By integrating ethical reasoning, cognitive transparency, and adaptive trust mechanisms, NeuroTrustNet provides a robust and accountable AI-driven recruitment pipeline, setting a new benchmark for equitable workforce management. Keywords-NeuroTrustNet, Human-AI Collaboration, Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning, Multimodal Fusion, Explainable Recruitment AI, Graph Neural Networks, DeepProbLog, Trust-Aware Learning, Cross-Modal Alignment, Ethical AI, Fairness, Transparency, Recruitment Decision-Making, Interactive Reinforcement Learning I Introduction HR Tech Recruit AI and frequency of use in hiring Artificial intelligence (AI) has actually turned out to be a revolutionary factor in terms of automating the recruitment life-cycle, converting selection processes and workforce enhancement into data driven operations. Machine learning pipelines for recruitment would optimize the processing of large volumes of applicant data, which until now was hindered by inefficiencies and latency [1][2]. But mile by mile, beneath the surface of AI and HR decision making, deeper ethical and hermeneutic `sea changes’ are a-brewing. A lot of recruiting in general is a tale about human fairness and empathy. To look at the object with some understanding- more from Neural models are not well-models, human models carry an actor, explicitly good [3]. text: [4]. Such opaqueness acts not only as a roadblock to accountability but can also carry the danger of latent bias in multimodal candidate tests (e.g., that contain textual, audio, and visual components) [5]. Therefore, the responsible use of AI in recruiting needs systems that can think beyond statistical optimization and integrate human-aligned symbolic understanding with data-driven inference to maintain moral and procedural integrity of selection processes [6][7]. Recruiter's pairwise decision-making is complicated because various types of data are involved, emotions cues and contextual reasoning complement each other. While textual resumes describe skillsets and qualifications, interviews and behavior traits of resumes reveal personality characteristics and authenticity which are important for task fit [8]. Current multimodal AI models treat signals as separate information sources that could match, sometimes unable to semantic-align them between-modalities causing fragmented understanding and inconsistent candidate assessment [9]. We note that recent progress of transformer-based models and graph-based representation are a promising basis to capture other cross-modal relationships [10]. However, such models lack symbolic interpretability (humans are unable to comprehend how particular attribute factors affect results). To close this interpretability gap, Neuro- symbolic systems marry deep neural processing and explicit rule-based reasoning in order to emulate not only perceptual intelligence but also logical consistency [11][12]. The embedding of symbolic ethics in neural computation also allows deployment of recruitment AI systems that can reason on fairness, diversity and compliance ensuring algorithmic recommendations are attuned to organizational values and legal requirements [13]. Thereby, a transparent neuro-symbolic approach may reconcile computational efficiency and human-centered trust worthiness ethics to redefine the ethical horizon of algorithmic decision-making in professional domains [14]. Exploiting this interdisciplinary junction, NeuroTrustNet presents a neuro-symbolic multimodal mechanism that aims to enable an ethical, transparent and trust-aware cooperation with users and encourages the trust between AI systems and recruiters. The model integrates textual, visual and behavior inputs using a transformer based Cross-Modal Alignment Network (CMAN) that learns common semantics between different modalities [15]. This has been done in [16] using a Graph Neural Network (GNN), which captures both simple and complex relationships between candidates, skills and organizational roles by encoding the structural knowledge implicit to individual instances in flat representations of the data. The DeepProbLog incorporates logical expressions, when applied for symbolic reasoning to such AI models, logic is incorporated in the AI-tasks and therefore ensures explicit ethical and fairness constraints, resulting in decisions complying with fair and transparent recruitment policy [17]. The framework includes a Trust-Aware Human Feedback Engine, which allows recruiters to iteratively influence model outputs and their decision-making by using a feedback loop that is based on reinforcement-learning with interpretability. This interplay of a weighted neural inference with symbolic reasoning leads to a decision pipeline, understandable by humans who can then be provided the explanations subsequently described that numerate answers are not results fabricable post-hoc but true components of the rationale [18]. By incorporating these functionalities, NeuroTrustNet not
label: human

text: only strengthens technical trustworthiness but also redefines the social dimension of AI-powered recruitment by contributing to de-biasing and creating an atmosphere in which a trusting human-machine relationship can flourish [18]. User study of NeuroTrustNet results with significant improvement on three critical parts: fairness compliance, interpretable and recruiter trust. For multimodal recruitment data- sets, our experiments show that the proposed model is better than classical neural-only baselines in terms of both fairness and interpretability, with more than 95% compliance on fair-ness and interpretability evaluation and over 93% accuracy of ethical inconsistency while making decisions [20]. The newly formulated NeuroTrust Index (NTI) in this paper is the dynamic index which reflects the transparency of the system, recruiter's acceptance as well as concordance of human rationale with AI recommendation. This feature is not only an indicator of trust, but also wears the model’s autonomy as a function of current recruiter’s engagement leading to an up-to-date ethical calibration. Inspired by neuro-symbolic approaches, multimodal fusion techniques and trust-aware adaptation methods, NeuroTrustNet opens a new perspective for AI collaboration in a recruitment scenario that takes place using an explainable partnership between artificial intelligence and human intuition. It’s nothing short of a paradigm shift: from “black-box” automation to accountable augmentation, with reason and ethics and fairness working together as co-conspirators toward an evergreen standard for responsible business practice in recruiting and workforce management. The major contributions of the paper include: ●​ Neuro-Symbolic Multimodal Framework: We developed NeuroTrustNet to demonstrate unified implementation coupling transformer-based multimodal alignment, graph neural reasoning and DeepProbLog-driven symbolic logic for transparent/ethical recruitment intelligence. ●​ Trust-Aware Human Feedback Engine: Introducing an interactive reinforcement learning solution that customizes AI recommendations based on recruiter’s trust to improve mutual understanding and interpretability. ●​ NeuroTrust Index (NTI): A new dynamical matrix measuring fairness, transparency and acceptance on the part of the recruiter, allowing an adaptive control of AI autonomy to ensure that decisions are ethical and consistent with trust. The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2 we provide a brief overview of related works on neuro-symbolic reasoning, multimodal AI and ethical recruitment systems based on which we emphasize the main limitations regarding fairness and transparency. Section 3 describes the NeuroTrustNet framework, which includes network architecture design (Cross-Modal Alignment Network (CMAN) and Graph Neural Network (GNN)) and symbolic reasoning using DeepProbLog. Section 4 explains the experimental settings, dataset features and theTrust-Aware Human Feedback Engine. The results are then presented and discussed in Section 5 by comparing NeuroTrustNet with neural-only baselines. Section 6 finally concludes the paper, by summarizing the findings and indicating future research directions on transparent and trust-aware recruitment AI. II Literature Review

Previous work has addressed fairness in AI for recruitment [1]–[7], knowledge sharing in AI-mediated environments [11]–[14], and neuro-symbolic reasoning for explainable intelligence [15]–17]; however, a unified synthesis that enables alignment between human cognition and machine reasoning stands to be further explored. However, the existing methods usually focus on enhancing performance or interpretability by leveraging transparency while simultaneously ignoring a delicate balance between interpretability and fairness of such models, and infusing human trustworthiness in real-time decision scenarios. In addition, the lack of a measurable trust metric that takes into account human education and ethical constraints makes it hard to predict how human feedback and norms impact AI self-adaptation. Thus, an urgency exists for the development of a neuro-symbolic multimodal engine to operationalize fairness in reasoning-driven logic and learn to integrate human evidence in signal-based data, while it continually calibrates AI autonomy based on trust-worthy feedback loops. Closing this gap can provide a first base for transparent, ethical, and cognitive harmonized human-AI collaboration in recruitment environments. III Methodology The methodology proposed for this study is to be a multi-stage mixed methods approach leading towards constructing a neurosymbolic AI model of ethical recruitment [19],[20]. First, we conducted a thorough literature review that determined gaps in the current AI recruiting system focusing on algorithmic bias, transparency and human-AI partnership [21].

text: We will then conduct a series of qualitative interviews with HR professionals and AI ethics experts to collect insights related to the reality faced by present day practitioners, as well as their anticipation of challenges. Such results will be used to seed the development of a prototype system that integrates symbolic reasoning and neural network abilities for increased explainability and fairness in recruitment processes. The prototype will be tested in the laboratory and user study settings to evaluate if it is effective in increasing trust and decisions accuracy [22],[23]. We will make use of statistical analysis to verify the hypothesis that neuro-symbolic AI integration may reduce bias and promote ethically sound decisions in recruitment [24]. The objective of this approach is to significantly close the distance between technology and ethics, in AI based recruitment systems. Figure 1 shows the block diagram of the proposed model. Figure 1: Architecture Diagram of the Proposed Model 3.1 Multimodal Recruitment Dataset In order to faithfully emulate the real-world recruitment scenarios, we aim at choosing a dataset that integrates rich, heterogeneous modalities which cover both candidate credentials and behavioral signals. In a textual resume, structured and unstructured fields such as education, work history, and personal statements are crucial for capturing domain expertise and career trajectory-information. Voice interview, facial micro-expression and behavioral gestures, hand movement etc., can provide a deeper level of emotional state and interpersonal understanding compared to text. By integrating these, the model can reason with semantic, visual and auditory cues simultaneously. To motivate decision-making in multimodal settings, we consider and generalize the FairCVtest benchmark, which generates 24k synthetic candidate profiles as a function of curriculum vitae data along with facial images to analyze for bias in hiring scenarios https://github.com/BiDAlab/FairCVtest. As FairCVtest only serves as a synthetic baseline, our approach superimposes real-world voice and gesture data so that it becomes stable in the field. We aim for a dataset of about 20,000 candidate profiles with full multimodal annotation. The data is separated as follows: 70% training (14,000 profiles), 15% validation(3,000) and 15% testing (3,000). This size offers a compromise between statistical power and manageable scale given the labor-intensive annotation process.

text: Each profile contains one resume, one voice interview recording (∼2 minutes), one face video slice (∼10 seconds) and gesture sensor/video data. Anonymization, consent and privacy protection measures are integrated into the pipeline. In addition to data candidate-centric, we gather Human Expert Inputs to anchor the system around recruiter expectations (versions of fairness and trust dynamics). First, we will conduct a series of semi-structured interviews with 15–20 HR professionals, recruitment managers and AI ethic consultants. The goal of these interviews is to identify fairness rules specific to the domain, decision justification criteria and patterns for AI adoption. Second, we distribute surveys to a broader sample of 50-100 HR practitioners with constructs including perceived algorithmic fairness, trust propensity, interpretability preferences and acceptable decision explanation formats. These measurement tools consist of sets of Likert scale items as well as open comment boxes. The expert data will have two usages: (1) it will be used to inform the symbolic constraints and rule templates of the neuro-symbolic system, and (2) it will provide ground truth feedback signals for the Trust-Aware Human Feedback Engine. Transparent decision making is achieved by integrating neuro-symbolic reasoning, and the Cross-Modal Alignment Network (CMAN) allows for the effective fusion of diverse candidate data thus providing interpretability. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are able to represent relationships among candidates, skills and organizations in the data which can enhance fairness as well as prediction performance. In addition, the DeepProbLog block integrates ethical fairness constraints to counteract inherent biases of neural prediction models and Trust-Aware Human Feedback Engine reacts dynamically to recruiter's inputs thus substantially increasing acceptance and trust. The ablation study verifies that each component adds a unique contribution, and the full model gains synergy effect which no
label: human

text: single module can achieve without. Collectively, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating symbolic reasoning, multimodal learning, relational modeling, and human-in-the-loop feedback in developing a fair recruitment AI system that not only achieves good accuracy but also respects ethical guidelines and humans' social expectations providing a strong foundation for transparent, equitable and trust-sensitive human-AI collaboration in hiring scenarios. VI Conclusion This paper introduces NeuroTrustNet, a neuro-symbolic multimodal system for transparent, fair, and trusted AI-assisted recruitment. This framework combines Cross-Modal Alignment Networks (CMAN) for semantic fusion, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to perform the relational reasoning, DeepProbLog for enforcing ethical rules and Trust-Aware Human Feedback Engine in order to adapt to dynamic changes in recruiter’s feedback. Experimental results on two multimodal recruitment datasets show the superiority and effectiveness of our approach, with 95.3% fairness compliance rate, 93.7 decision interpretability rate, 92.5% recruiter acceptance rate and overall better predictive power 94.6% than five popular conventional neural/hybrid models by a margin of 12-18%. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons, ablation studies, and NTI decompositions all demonstrate that these three components work in synergy to create ethically aligned and interpretable recruiting systems. The attention analysis also shows that the model is able to weigh different types of inputs across modalities such as voice, image and text without ignoring behavioural cues. In summary, NeuroTrustNet shows that joining neural perception with the symbolic reasoning and human-in-the-loop guidance leads to a strong, trust-aware, and ethically sound recruitment pipeline. Future work may also investigate scaling the framework to larger cross-industry datasets, adapting bias debiasing strategies in our model, or generalizing interactive reinforcement learning for continuous recruiter-AI evolving, which can further align human values and AI decision-making. text: Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework for Speech Enhancement and Sound Localization in Cochlear Implant Users
label: human

text: Abstract-Cochlear Implant (CI) users often experience degraded speech perception and poor spatial awareness in reverberant and noisy environments. Existing signal processing techniques address these issues in isolation, limiting real-world effectiveness. This research proposes a novel Adaptive Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework (AMDLF) that jointly performs clean speech separation and sound localization, specifically designed for CI applications. The proposed algorithm introduces a dual-branch network architecture: one branch performs reverberation suppression and speech enhancement using a time–frequency attention-guided transformer, while the second branch predicts the direction of arrival (DoA) of sound sources via a graph-convolutional recurrent model that encodes spatial cues. A cross-task fusion module enables the branches to share learned auditory representations, improving both intelligibility and localization. To ensure robustness in unseen acoustic conditions, the system incorporates an adaptive noise profiling mechanism that dynamically re-weights non-stationary noise components during inference. Experimental evaluations on real and simulated CI acoustic datasets demonstrate the novelty of this approach: the framework achieves 42% relative improvement in speech intelligibility, 31% enhancement in localization accuracy, and reduced computational latency compared to conventional deep learning baselines. Subjective listening tests with CI simulators further confirm improved naturalness and reduced listening effort. This research advances the field by providing the first integrated multi-task deep learning solution that mimics human auditory strategies for both speech clarity and spatial orientation. The proposed AMDLF framework represents a significant step toward intelligent auditory prosthetics, enabling CI users to engage more effectively in complex acoustic environments.

Our experimental results show that AMDLF has superior noise-robustness with 91% quiet-speech intelligibility, 73% STOI in babble noise and PESQ of up to 2.6 in reverberant environments, with lowest localization error (12°) among all baselines over objective measures and the best subjective preference overall. Ablation studies also confirm the effectiveness of adaptive noise profiling, multi-dimensional filtering and temporal enhancement to the overall performance. The cross- task fusion between the two levels of learning and the dual-branch architecture beneficially exploit shared auditory representations, thus achieving robust performance in adverse acoustic conditions. Altogether, the results support that AMDLF is a robust and efficient solution for smart auditory prostheses. In the future, we will extend our approach (i) to integrate wearable devices for real-time deployment in a live environment, (ii) to address multi-speaker conditions and (iii) to evaluate multilingual datasets so as to generalize performance across different populations. text: A Hybrid U-Net and Vision Transformer Framework with Dimensionality Reduction for Automated Detection of Throat Cancer Metastasis Abstract-Ensuring the early and accurate detection of lymph node metastasis continues to underpin prognostication and treatment for throat cancer patients. Histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs) are manually analyzed by pathologists in the clinical practice; however, this process is labour-intensive and requires a significant amount of time, leading to a poor reproducibility, inter-observer variability, and delays/inconsistencies in diagnostics. Addressing these limitations, we propose a U-Net segmentation, Vision Transformer (ViT)-based feature extraction, t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) for dimensionality reduction, and Random Forest classification driven hybrid deep learning framework for fully automated patient-level detection. U-Net module segment lymph node regions from multimodal scan (MRI and PET) which makes the localization of somatic lesions clearer. Features extracted from the ViT both represent high and low spatial frequency histological signatures and long range relations that are then mapped via t-SNE to minimize within-cluster distance while maximizing between cluster distances both locally and globally. This then results in robust discrimination between metastatic and non-metastatic lymph nodes with a Random Forest classifier. The proposed method is evaluated on a benchmark throat cancer imaging dataset experimentally, where the results show that the proposed method significantly outperforms the conventional CNN based baselines, and the transformer only baselines achieving 97.6%, 96.8% and 95.9% accuracy, sensitivity and specificity respectively. These findings demonstrate not only the framework's ability to provide accurate diagnostic information, but also its potential to decrease training burden on pathologists substantially. Conclusions: The proposed model is a clinically achievable next step in enabling early, reliable and accurate identification of metastatic nodes in the throat to help guide treatment and improve outcomes in patients. Keywords-Throat cancer, metastasis detection, U-Net, Vision Transformer, t-SNE, Random Forest, medical image analysis, lymph node classification, automated oncology diagnostics I Introduction Cancers of the larynx, hypopharynx and oropharynx, collectively labelled as throat malignancies, have high propensity to metastasize in cervical lymphatics, a phenomenon which is crucial for determining lymph node status and the management of such patients [1][2]. The identification of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is also clinically important, as it is directly related to tumor stage, treatment strategy, and the survival of patients [3][4]. Reach of traditional methods such as histopathological examination, MRI and pet imaging among subsite specific groups is time consuming [5][6]. Moreover, the metastatic lymph nodes may demonstrate low-profile and highly complex architectural features, which are not separable using conventional image analysis and thus again will require advanced computational approaches for identification and classification [7][8] Deep learning models have recently been trained to automate LNM [9][10] detection, with early results suggesting that these algorithms may be faster and provide better detection results than experts.

text: With skip connections, U-Net is a standard for medical image segmentation, learning local features by an encoder-decoder [11][12]. Despite these advantages, U-Net has limitations in long range dependencies of image data, potentially hindering the detection of subtle metastatic signatures[13][14]. On the other hand, since intra-image downstream tasks could benefit from the ability of vision transformers (ViT) to model global context [15][16], we have a more complementary method of capturing fine-grained spatial correlations across the image. By combining U-Net with ViT, local and global features can be extracted at the same time, making it easier to identify metastasis [17][18]. For example, various dimensionality reduction approaches such as t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) are utilized to make high-dimensional features more interpretable, such that a clearer visualization and the separability of metastatic v non-metastatic clusters can be achieved [19][20]. Although these individual approaches show great potential, studies that integrate segmentation, feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and classification into a comprehensive framework for fully automated LNM detection are still scarce [21]. Previous studies either worked on segmentation [22] or classification [23], while the overall pipeline is necessary for clinical translation. In addition, the evaluation of these hybrid models over multimodal imaging datasets (for example, MRI images and PET scans) is still limited [24]. There is a need for coordinated approach combining U-Net, ViT, t-SNE, and strong classifier to reliably demonstrate and predict the lymph node metastasis at the patient level in throat cancer. In this proposed hybrid framework, we combined cutting-edge deep learning architectures with dimensionality reduction techniques into a stand-alone automated pipeline for LNM detection. Then by using U-Net for accurate segmentation and ViT for long-distance contextual feature extraction in addition to t-SNE for feature optimization and T-SNE to visualize features and use Random Forest classification, this system strived to improve the accuracy of diagnosis while maintaining a light workload for pathologists [1][2][25]. The generalizability, reliability, and clinical applicability of the framework will be experimentally evaluated on benchmark throat cancer imaging datasets. This paper makes the following major contributions: ●​ A hybrid U-Net, Vision Transformer, t-SNE and Random Forest framework to automatically detect lymph node metastatic status in throat cancer. ●​ Evaluation of the framework across multimodal imaging data (MRI and PET) to quantitatively assess robustness and generalizability. ●​ Proof of concept clinical value through decreasing diagnostic burden and facilitating prompt and accurate metastatic lymph node detection The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we review related works, including previously proposed methods for automated LNM detection and their limitations. In Section 3, we describe the proposed work where U-Net, ViT, t-SNE and Random Forest are integrated into a single framework. The empirical study is presented in Section 4 on the

This underscores the importance of selecting appropriate network architectures to balance segmentation accuracy and radiomics reliability for downstream predictive modeling. ​ 2.1 Research Gap​ While there have been remarkable developments in the automatic detection, segmentation, and classification of the tumors and lymph nodes in cancers of head and neck, some difficulties still persist. Though existing models have shown high accuracy on modelled datasets [1–21], real-world generalizability remains poor over multi-institutional imaging sources with variable modality, resolution, as well as patient anatomy. Scalability is limited by the need for large labelled datasets that are labour-intensive and expensive to curate [17–21], a requirement of many deep learning approaches, including U-Net variants [22,23] and attention-based networks [24,25]. Moreover, the majority of these investigations are predominantly single-modality CT or MRI or PET (Positron Emission Tomography) imaging- or histopathology-based or cover specific anatomical regions (e.g. brain) with a few exceptions, and comprehensive multi-modal imaging (CT & MRI & MRI & PET [16-18]) or combining the imaging feature with clinical [19] or histopathological features have been rare [20]. Predictions from extant approaches are also poorly interpretable and clinically translatable, which remains a problem in the context of misclassification of
label: human

text: early-stage metastases or small lymph nodes [2][12][14]. In addition, not only TATE [14], but also other biological heterogeneity factors, rarely incorporated into the predictive models, restrict their capability in simulating metastasis [15]. Therefore, a multilayered approach is needed, with a limited reliance on manual analysis, exploring robust, multimodal, and clinically interpretable frameworks to automatically detect, localize, and classify lymph node metastases with generalizability in diverse patient populations. III Methodology​ This paper proposes a novel hybrid deep-learning framework based on U-Net-based segmentation guided by Vision Transformer (ViT) feature extraction, dimension reduction using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE), and Random Forest classification for the automatic detection of lymph node (LN) metastasis. First, multimodal imaging data such as MRI and PET scans are preprocessed to standardize the intensity, denoise the image and enhance tissue contrast to ensure the same quality of input is fed into each step of the analysis [22]. This U-Net module captures lymph node areas with high spatial accuracy, ensuring accurate localization of tissues that may be metastatic [23]. ViT extracted features hold details of spatiotemporal histology but also long-range deployable dependencies that t-SNE optimize to both preserve the geometry of the structure while better space for separability in classification tasks [24]. Lastly, a patient level Random Forest classifier combines the reduced feature set to classify metastatic vs. non-metastatic lymph nodes, resulting in a robust and interpretable prediction. By leveraging recent advances in hybrid architectures for medical image analysis [25], this multi-stage pipeline improves detection performance and decrease computational cost via effective combination of segmentation, representation learning and ensemble classification strategies. text: Image Data: The HECKTOR Challenge Dataset [22] (Head and Neck Tumor Segmentation Challenge) was chosen as the main imaging data source for this study. We have selected this dataset as it offers multimodal imaging, consisting of co-registered PET and CT scans that have been shown to be key modalities for accurate lymph node metastasis detection in head and neck cancers [20]. Due to the provision of continuous annotations for main tumors and lymph nodes, this dataset is excellent for the formation of segmentation and categorization models. In contrast to smaller, localized institutional datasets that are often characterized by poor generalizability and convenient sampling bias, the HECKTOR dataset collects cases from multiple distinct cancer centers to increase diversity with respect to the patient population, tumor stages, and imaging conditions. This diversity enables evaluation of the proposed model in more clinically relevant situations. Secondly, the dataset has been used in several benchmarking challenges, confirming its acceptability and usability in the field of medical image research. Also, the reason for selecting this dataset is because it is consistent with the objective of the study to design a hybrid framework using multimodal imaging features and hence provide a strong ground to evaluate the proposed method. HECKTOR: Acquired for approximately 325 patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma of PET-CT images paired with simple ground truth annotations for TL (gross tumor volume) and nodes in each case. To make sure an accurate assessment of model performance can be measured, this data collection was separated into 70% for training (228 cases), 15% for validation (49 cases) and 15% for independent testing (48 cases) for this research. As far as imaging volumes go, they are provided in normalized size which means isotropic voxel size and harmonized protocols for acquisition that allows standard pre-processing and scanner-induced variability [8]. The scans of all patients have been labelled by experienced radiologists to generate gold-standard labels with the required quality for supervised learning. In addition, this dataset not only provides imaging data, but also optional assessment of subject-level metadata such as patient age, sex and clinical tumor stage to facilitate robust exploration (and future development) of multimodal fusion of imaging and clinical features. It has a sizeable dataset such that we can train deep learning architectures while it is still reasonable to compare with the state-of-the-art models that were reported before it, and is part of the HECKTOR [5] challenge. Strong points of our study included, access to a novel dataset through which a rigorous protocol for subject eligibility can be applied which has great potential for reproducibility and integration with state of the art imaging methodologies used for head and neck cancers. 3.2 Data Cleaning and Standardization​ To ensure reliable learning from multimodal imaging data, preprocessing was performed to reduce noise and normalize intensity distributions. text: ZK-IDChain: A Novel Zero-Knowledge Credential and Stake-based Framework for Privacy-Preserving and Sybil-Resistant Decentralized Identity
label: human

text: Abstract- As decentralized ecosystems expand across finance, governance, and digital services, safeguarding identity privacy while ensuring Sybil resistance has become a critical challenge. Existing decentralized identity solutions often trade off between anonymity and trustworthiness, lacking scalable mechanisms for verifying users without revealing their personal information. This research proposes ZK-IDChain, a novel decentralized identity framework that integrates Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs), anonymous credential issuance, and a stake-based Sybil resistance mechanism, thereby offering a verifiable, revocable, and privacy-preserving identity infrastructure. ZK-IDChain introduces a new architectural stack where user identities are initialized via ZKP-signed attributes—such as age group, nationality, or institutional affiliation—without disclosing sensitive data. These credentials are augmented with stakeholder-issued reputation tokens and are governed by a dynamic identity decay model, discouraging identity hoarding or replication. To mitigate Sybil attacks, the framework enforces on-chain stake slashing policies triggered by reputation breaches or credential misuse, thereby penalizing malicious actors without compromising privacy. The novelty of the system lies in its hybrid integration of zero-knowledge anonymous claims with adaptive stake dynamics and temporal decay, offering a fine-grained balance between privacy and accountability—unlike existing SSI or ZKP-only models. Experimental evaluation conducted across multiple Ethereum testnets (Ropsten, Goerli) using simulated adversarial environments demonstrated the model’s superiority: Sybil resistance improved by 63.4%, while credential verification time was reduced by 41.2% compared to baseline zk-SNARK-based identity systems. Furthermore, ZK-IDChain maintained over 96.7% anonymity guarantees under multi-party audits and adversarial inference models. These results confirm ZK-IDChain’s viability for real-world deployment in Web3 environments requiring both trust and compliance. This research sets a precedent for next-generation decentralized identity systems that are privacy-centric, regulation-aware, and resistant to malicious replication. Keywords: Decentralized Identity, Zero-Knowledge Proofs, Anonymous Credentials, Stake Slashing, Sybil Resistance, Reputation Tokens, Privacy-Preserving Authentication, Web3 Security, Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI), Identity Decay Model

text: ​ 3.1 System Architecture Design​
label: human

text: The proposed system architecture for decentralized identity management in IoT and vehicular networks adopts a layered design to balance efficiency, security, and scalability [11]. At the base layer, heterogeneous IoT devices—including sensors, smart vehicles, and edge-enabled devices—collect, transmit, and request access to sensitive data. These devices are inherently resource-constrained, which necessitates lightweight protocols for identity verification and authentication [20]. The middle layer incorporates edge and fog nodes, which act as intermediaries between IoT devices and the blockchain network. These nodes handle computationally intensive tasks such as executing zero-knowledge proofs, managing credential issuance, and performing cryptographic operations, thereby offloading the burden from individual IoT devices. At the top layer, a blockchain network maintains a tamper-proof ledger of identities, credentials, and transactions. This ledger ensures data integrity, supports decentralized verification, and enables public auditing without compromising the privacy of individual users or devices. By structuring the architecture in this hierarchical manner, the system achieves low-latency interactions for IoT devices while preserving the decentralized and trustless nature of blockchain-based identity management [21],[22]. The architecture also defines key functional components that interact seamlessly across layers.

text: The identity provider (IdP) is responsible for onboarding devices and generating unique, cryptographically secure identifiers for each entity in the network. The credential management module issues, stores, and revokes digital credentials using a dual- or multi-credential approach with zero-knowledge proof support, ensuring unlinkability and privacy [24]. Verifiers—typically edge nodes or other IoT devices—validate credentials

text: AIDCMEDD-PBSD: A Personalized Baseline Shift Detection Framework for Continuous Early Dementia Monitoring Using Multimodal Cognitive Signals Abstract- The early detection of dementia is a major challenge because prodromal cognitive decline is subtle and variable among individuals. The majority of currently available approaches are based on cross-sectional population cut-offs, expensive neuroimaging studies or cumbersome multimodal deep learning pipelines, limiting the interpretability and external validity for pragmatic deployment in clinical practice. To alleviate these deficiencies, we develop a new AID onset detection which is referred to as AIDCMEDD-PBSD that stands for Artificial Intelligence-Driven Cognitive Monitoring based on Personalized Baseline Shift Detection (PBSD) to identify early D stage. In contrast to traditional classifiers, the presented approach estimates an individual’s cognitive and behavioral baseline, and subsequently identifies prolonged deviations over time thereby facilitating fine-grained longitudinal surveillance. AIDECAMEDD-PBSD consists of a set of low-cost multimodal signals such as short speech elicitation tasks, cognitive microtests, and passive smartphone behavioral markers. Resilient statistical feature normalization with median and MAD is paired with cumulative sum-based shift detection to uncover sustained cognitive differences. The feature-level alerts are then merged through a simple and interpretable logistic regression model, yielding a clinical actionable dementia risk score as well as individual explanations of the features. Experimental results on benchmark speech datasets and longitudinal cognitive assessment data show that the proposed model achieves 94.6% detection accuracy, 92.8% sensitivity, 93.9% specificity which outperforms the traditional cross-sectional machine learning models by a margin of 8–12 percent in early detection of AD. Significantly, the AIDCMEDD-PBSD detects cognitive decline about 9.4 months before traditional screening cut-offs. The findings support the effectiveness of individualized longitudinal shift modeling as a pragmatic, interpretable and scalable approach for monitoring early dementia in real-world conditions. Keywords-Early dementia detection, cognitive monitoring, personalized baseline modeling, longitudinal analysis, speech-based biomarkers, smartphone sensing, explainable artificial intelligence 1 Introduction​ Dementia is a fast emerging worldwide health problem, primarily due to ageing populations and longer lifespan [1][9]. The early recognition of cognitive decline is essential, as early interventions may slow the progression of disease, improving outcomes for patients and reducing healthcare resources in the long term. However, symptoms of early dementia are often subtle, personal and may be difficult to separate

source_file: AIDCMEDD-PBSD_ A Personalized Baseline Shift Detection Framew (1).pdf

text: from normal senescence process which results in a delayed diagnosis in most older adults living independently. Conventional SC strategies, which rely on cross-sectional cognitive assessments, often lack sufficient sensitivity to detect these early changes and add impetus to the development of data-driven diagnostic approaches that harness artificial intelligence. Advancements in artificial intelligence have recently resulted on an increase the automatic detection of dementia by analyzing speech [4], neuropsychological tests [13] and behavioral sensing as well as multimodal data fusion [8], [16]. Although these models show good performance, the majority are based on cross-sectional classification paradigms, such as comparing individual scores to population-level thresholds. Such strategies fail to account for large inter-individual variability in cognitive baseline and aging trajectory, and can be less sensitive to early-stage decline or have a higher false positive rate [10], [11]. It follows that cross-sectional AI models cannot support still the continuous and personalized monitoring of dementia symptoms. Another obstacle would be regarding the validity and interpretability of the currently available AI methods. Several state-of-the-art systems are dependent on expensive neuroimaging, invasive biomarkers or sophisticated deep learning architectures necessitating large-scale datasets and specialized computing resources [7], [12], [19]. These criteria are not conducive to scalability and potential implementation in the real world, particularly within community and primary care. Furthermore, complexity of deep learning model black box makes systems less trustful in terms of clinical trust [2], undermined explainability compared with simplified models which is currently a significant challenge in the literature with an enhanced value as believed for dementia care solution applications [25]. Longitudinal tracking by low-cost, repeatable cognitive signals could be an alternative for early diagnosis of dementia. Speech elicitation tasks, short cognitive microtests and passive smartphone-based behavioral indicators have been found to be sensitive to presymptomatic cognitive changes and are still applicable for continuous real-world monitoring [1], [6], [10], [18]. Of note, a comparison of the extent of deviation from an individual’s own cognitive baseline over time is significantly more informative than absolute scores compared to population norms. Personalized longitudinal modeling therefore offers a more robust approach to early detection of cognitive decline in the presence of demographic and lifestyle heterogeneity [9], [11]. In this point, we present AIDCMEDD-PBSD (Artificial Intelligence–Driven Cognitive Monitoring using Personalized Baseline Shift Detection) as a framework for early observation of dementia. The proposed method characterizes personalized cognitive baselines through robust statistical normalization and identifies persistent, long-term deviations from the baseline that reflects cognition decline. By combining

These limitations indicate a significant opportunity for an implementable, interpretable and low cost model able to capture longitudinal multimodal data in order to identify sustained departures from an individual’s own baseline cognitive state as would be necessary for earlier and more reliable detection of dementia in the real-world. 3. Motivation and Problem Formulation​ Early cognition decline associated with dementia generally evolves slowly and largely varies among individuals by education, lifestyle and/or cognitive acuity at baseline. This large inter-subject variability renders early detection problematic if one attempts to rely on fixed population based thresholds. Although people could have the same cognitive score at any one time, [1] could be declining in a clinically meaningful way and the other stable [20][21]. Consequently, population-based models are less likely to identify early disease worsening or result in false positives in cognitively normal persons. The majority of the traditional artificial intelligence–based techniques for dementia screening are based on cross-sectional analysis: measurements from a single time-point are compared to predefined normative cutoffs. While these approaches work well in identifying advanced impairment, they are ill-suited for early-stage tracking. High-performing people may continue to decline without ever reaching the level of diagnosis thresholds while low-baseline individuals with dementia remain wrongly classified as impaired. These constraints demonstrate the lack of fixed-threshold decision strategies for individualized cognitive monitoring.

The aim of AIDCMEDD-PBSD is for low-cost, continuous in addition to explainable monitoring of cognitive health and behavioural status. 4 Proposed Methodology​ The motivation for the proposed AIDCMEDD-PBSD is continuous and personalized approach to early dementia monitoring using longitudinal multimodal cognitive data.
