text: ​ Figure 1: Architecture of the AIDCMEDD-PBSD Framework for Personalized Early Dementia Monitoring Using Multimodal Cognitive Signals 4.1 Multimodal Cognitive Signals To this end, the presented architecture combines non-invasive and cheap—but complementary—multimodal cognitive signals for continuous monitoring. Speech elicitation tasks are capable of capturing language-based and acoustic indicators of cognitive decline, such as diminished lexical diversity [23], variabilities in speech rate [23] and pauses, which appear to be sensitive to early dementia-induced alterations [4], [10], [14]. Cognitive microtests are short repeatable tasks which measure memory, attention and processing speed, allowing for regular monitoring with minimal user burden and literacy bias [2]. Smartphone use attributes, such as typing behavior, activity periodicity, and mobility ubiquity capture the day-to-day functional behavior and were demonstrated to be associated with real-world cognitive decline [1], [3], [18]. For each participant an initial baseline is established based on longitudinal recording during a stable monitoring period in all modalities including speech features, cognitive microtest scores and smartphone behavioral indicators [24][25]. The framework does not employ population values but it generates participant-specific norms allowing to evaluate cognitive changes with respect to an individual’s own historical performance. Integration of the cumulative difference tracking and duration-based validation, the framework effectively reduces false positive cases while preserving sensitivity in detecting early cognitive decline, to allow robust longitudinal monitoring and timely clinical intervention. 4.4 Risk Score Fusion and Explainability​ To interpret the multimodal baseline shift evidence to a clinically interpretable measure, our framework utilizes an easily understandable logistic regression model for risk score fusion. The logistic regression model is chosen because of its interpretability, simplicity and the fact that it yields easy interpretable probabilities for clinicians. Alerts at feature level as directly derived from prolonged baseline shifts across the speech, cognitive mic(row)test battery, and smartphone behavioral patterns are used as input, such that the contribution of each modality can be clearly quantified. The obtained risk score provides a current estimate of the probability for developing future cognitive decline and can be directly translated to clinically relevant subgroups, such as low, moderate, and high probability of this disease outcome. Crucially, model coefficients can provide easily understandable explanations for influence of individual features on a final decision which allows clinicians to connect identified risk to particular cognitive or behavioural changes, promoting trust, interpretability and practical feasibility in real world dementia monitoring. 5. Experimental Setup The recommended AIDCMEDD-PBSD model is examined through the DementiaBank Pitt Corpus, a well-known multimodal dementia dataset (collected on TalkBank repository for public access). The dataset is composed of speech recordings with manually transcribed text along with clinically validated cognitive labels for dementia patients and cognitively healthy controls, appropriate for multimodal cognitive analysis. The corpus is accessible via the official TalkBank interface at: https://dementia.talkbank.org. For the purpose of facilitating a longitudinal-style analysis, speech sessions are per-subject reordered in time and split into baseline and follow-up sections, for personalized baseline construction and deviation monitoring. A subject-independent split approach is used with 70%, 10%, and 20% of individuals for training and baseline modeling, validation, and testing, so that there is no overlap between the subjects. Performance is evaluated in terms of accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, and lead time for early detection, which characterises how much earlier cognitive decline is detected with respect to fixed cross-sectional cut-off thresholds. text: 6 Conclusion​ In this paper, we introduced AIDCMEDD-PBSD for continuous early dementia monitoring with multimodal cognitive signals. Experimental results show the proposed approach attains an accuracy of 94.6, sensitivity of 92.8 and specificity of 93.9 outperforming traditional cross-sectional machine learning models when predicting cognitive decline an average of 9.4 months earlier than what is clinically used for screening thresholds. Modeling individual cognitive baselines and identifying persistent longitudinal deviations, the approach offers a feasible, interpretable, and scalable platform without imposing extra sensors or complex transfer control. It remains to be seen whether such methods can be practically applied in the clinic (requiring large scale real world clinical validation) and combined with adaptation of a system’s baseline information via lifelong learning. text: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserved and Low-Latency Cybersecurity in Cloud-Based Telemedicine Systems Abstract-With the simultaneous explosion of connected medical devices, and increasing real-time patient monitoring capabilities, telemedicine infrastructures have witnessed a tremendous surge in demand for intelligent, adaptive, and privacy-preserving cybersecurity mechanisms‌. In fact, most of the currently available centralized Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) frameworks, that provides high detection accuracy, have high latency, scalability problem and less explainability. This paper proposes a new hybrid architecture HIER-MA-DRL (Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning) to overcome those limitations to facilitate distributed threat detection for edge/cloud environments. The proposed model maintains a balance between quick response for immediate anomalies and global situational observance by integrating lightweight edge agents but also using a centralized DRL coordinator for policy optimization over long-horizons. Moreover, embedded explainable policy distillation mechanisms to guarantee transparency and faithfulness in response to automation. We conduct extensive experimental evaluation using network intrusion benchmark datasets and real-time telemedicine traffic and demonstrate that HIER-MA-DRL achieves a detection accuracy of 99.03%, a response latency of 41.8% lower, and a false positive rate of 36.5% lower than that of the conventional centralized DRL frameworks. We ensure scalability with high data stream volumes due to our hierarchical coordination between agents and we protect patient data privacy using on-device anonymization. In summary, HIER-MA-DRL provides a strong, explainable, and low-latency cybersecurity framework that can be applied to next-generation smart healthcare and telemedicine environments. Keywords-Hierarchical Multi-Agent DRL, Edge Computing, Cybersecurity, Telemedicine, Privacy Preservation, Explainable Reinforcement Learning, Low-Latency Detection, Cloud–Edge Architecture I Introduction Telemedicine and real-time patient monitoring have extremely changed the way healthcare is delivered, introducing a level of interconnectivity among medical devices, cloud and edge nodes on a level we have not seen before. On the other hand, the fast digitalization has enlarged the attack surface of health-care infrastructures and the need for intelligent cyber-security methods that can accommodate privacy concerns [1], [2]. Centralized security won't work because of latencies introduced processing high queued medical traffic, a common occurrence in tele-health applications [3][4], and doesn't also scale. While the combination of distributed learning paradigms and cloud–edge orchestration is an interesting direction to explore, upholding the desired level of speed in anomaly detection with compliance under confidentiality policies for highly sensitive patient environments are Current models may be robust and system-aware [5], but these do not consider hierarchical
label: human

text: mechanisms trading localized decision-making versus global optimisation. As a result, this creates an increasing demand for multi-layer, explainable, and compliant privacy-preserving learning systems able to meet the latency–security trade-off in cloud-based telemedicine environment [6]. Multi-agent reinforcement learning has also been applied as a disruptive adaptive cybersecurity and intelligent network control technology in the rapidly changing digital healthcare ecosystem [7]. Multi-agent systems enable distributed intelligence across heterogeneous healthcare networks by allowing agents to learn from changing contexts [8]. Nevertheless, traditional frameworks rely on centralized training, which introduces the risks of congestion and loss of exposures [9]. It is possible that the multi-agent learning can be embedded into a hierarchical control framework to enable localised anomaly suppression and global policy refinement or convergence. Such a concept is of paramount importance, particularly in latency-constrained applications as remote diagnostics and on-the-fly IoMT devices based on the continuous health monitoring of patients [10]. Furthermore, ensuring transparency and explainability of such learning processes has become a clinical demand and is an obligatory aspect in terms of medical data protection [11]. As such, a hierarchical learning ecosystem architecture including explainable deep reinforcement learning at both the edge and cloud layers can offer an additional antifragile cybersecurity defense in depth [12]. Recent works advocate hybrid cloud–edge deployment architecture in healthcare to reduce data flooding, increase data throughput and preserve privacy for distributed learning [13]. But despite these advances in technology, the telehealth systems are still facing challenges such as data sovereignty, reducing latency and flexible policy synchronizations between agents [14]. Privacy techniques activated at the edge (e.g., anonymization and differential learning) may bear positive potential of preserving patient data [15], however, these methods don’t seem to be highly elastic in such a way when used over heterogeneous network infrastructure hindering the response time [16]. With the shift in complexity of healthcare workloads there is an unprecedented requirement to adopt automated analytics systems that continuously harness high performance computing to focus on prioritizing important security threats [17]. These discrepancies can be reconciled using a hierarchical reinforcement learning approach, while real time decision making is performed by the edge agents, which have been implemented to operate as cloud coordinators and are still able optimize long term policies with experience sharing aggregation [18]. It considers this dis- tributed yet coordinated setup to find the right balance between privacy protection, flexibility, and agility in telemedicine cybersecurity [19]. Cyber Security and telemedicine – Not just a technical problem, but an ethical duty for patient confidence, medical reliability and digital health evolution. Although classical DL-based ID models are often accurate, they are mainly black boxes that lack clinical interpretability and regulatory approval [20]. We integrate explainable reasoning and policy distillation components into our hierarchical multi-agent architecture, which as a result makes it possible for the system to exchange justifications of security decisions in order to obtain transparency in respect automated reactions to security threats. Furthermore, by using slim agents all over edge devices, latency-sensitive functionalities (e.g., anomaly filtering and intrusion flagging) can be performed in real time without sending all events to the cloud. On the other hand, a central coordinator can collect up policies and optimize decision rules to achieve better long term survival. Such a two-layer

text: orchestration can make telemedicine cybersecurity as a self-learning, privacy-preserving and latency sensitive ecosystem. To realize this, the present work develops a Hierarchical Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (HIER-MA-DRL) model that enables cloud–edge intelligence and possesses explainability and privacy protection properties to enhance cybersecurity of next-generation telemedicine systems. The main contributions of this paper are: ●​ H-MAC: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Coordination Our hybrid DRL framework offloads the computational cost of optimal multi-agent coordination in hierarchical structure from edge agents to a central coordinator by taking advantage of local (short-term) threat mitigation responses and global (longterm), OPTimal security learning. ●​ XPD Mechanism: We use the explainable reinforcement learning to transform complicated policy updates into readable decision-rational in reasoning processes, making it more transparent and reliable of telemedicine cybersecurity system response. ●​ Cloud–Edge Integration Combined with Privacy-Preservation & Latency-Optimisation: Incorporates device-side anonymization and federated learning to trade-off between confidentiality of patient data in face of real-time intrusion response, versus scalability being maintained against a backdrop of large-scale medical data. Organization of the paper: In Section II, we surveyed some related works focusing on privacy preservation, hierarchical intelligence, and DRL-based cybersecurity models in the telemedicine infrastructure. The proposed HIER-MA-DRL methodology is described in section III with its hierarchical agent architecture, policy, and explainable distillation. We detail the experimental design, dataset selection, performance metrics, and training parameters to validate detection accuracy and latency reduction in Section IV. The results and analysis, in Section V, compares the performance metrics such as detection rate, false positives, and computational latency of the proposed approach with centralized DRL frameworks. Section VI ends the paper with the main points and implications of the research and challenges for adaptive and privacy-aware cybersecurity in telemedicine. II Related Works Odeh et al. Existing solutions either tackle the problem in a centralized architecture that provides a high learning ability which comes with a high communication overhead and high latency in decisions [2], [3], or based on an edge lightweight framework that leads to a low detection accuracy due to light-weighting computations [5], [8]. While blockchain based [12] and multi-agent models [15] have provided significant improvements over existing systems in transparency and decentralization, at high volumes of telemedicine data streams they also introduce additional synchronization latency and scalability issues. Likewise, hybrid deep learning and reinforcement learning methods [9], [10], [17] demonstrate the potential for adaptive threat detection but also fail to incorporate hierarchical coordination mechanisms to ensure alignment of local edge solutions to global policies at the cloud-level. Additionally, in the context of DRL-driven cybersecurity explainability and interpretability have not been well studied, which not only hinders the trust of decision makers, but also regulatory conformance of medical environments [11]. One that combines edge-level responsive agent, cloud-level policy updating agent and privacy-preserving computing into a comprehensive hierarchical multi-agent DRL framework is thus required to deliver on-time, explainable and scalable cybersecurity for next-generation telemedicine infrastructures. III Proposed Methodology The HIER-MA-DRL approach in the proposed methodology exploits a hierarchical structure of three operational tiers—edge, and fog, and cloud—to realize adaptive privacy-preserved cyber-security in telemedicine environments [20]. At the edge tier, lightweight DRL (Deep Reinforcement Learning) agents conduct continuous device behaviour monitoring, also performing on-device anonymization, to safeguard patient data before it is transmitted. Fog layer serves as an interface to aggregate local threat intelligence and enable coordination between different agents in order to avoid alerts duplication and temporal consistency in responses [21]. At the same time, the cloud coordinator performs long-horizon policy optimization via deep Q-networks and actor–critic models, allowing for global knowledge and adjustment of local agent policies. To ensure that training can be distributed yet still efficient without compromising data privacy, we incorporate federate learning mechanisms into our method to allow training without revealing any raw data to make the model robust without sacrificing confidentiality. Privacy-preserving encryption, adaptive trust scoring, and edge offloading together enable a secure and efficient solution for telehealth environments [22]. Simulation environments mimic real telehealth traffic and agents are trained and evaluated on benchmark datasets for intrusion detection over multiple performance metrics such as accuracy, false positive rate, and response latency. Such an orchestrated multi-layered architecture will ensure the intelligence at local and global policies are consistent, making it further adaptable, scalable, and interpretable for real-time healthcare cybersecurity [23].

text: Attention-Guided Multi-Autoencoder Explainable Network for Breast Cancer Histopathological Image Multi-Classification Abstract- Breast cancer is the most common and pernicious disturbance among women worldwide, thus an early and precise diagnosis pays a pivotal role in the enhancement of a patient's survival rate. Histopathological image analysis is the gold standard for breast cancer diagnosis, but manual examination by pathologists can be time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. In order to overcome these limitations of existing methods, this work presents a new deep learning framework AMAE-GCNet (Attention-guided Multi-AutoEncoder with Grad-CAM Network) for automatic histopathological image based multi-classification of breast cancer. The proposed model is tested on the publicly available annotated BreakHis dataset consisting of 7,909 breast tumor histopathological images which are divided into eight benign and malignant subtypes with different magnification levels. To standardize the images, preprocessing methods such as stain normalization and image resizing are first used. We utilize a transfer learning backbone based on EfficientNet-B4 to elicit deep hierarchical features from the histopathological images. A multi-autoencoder module is therefore included to learn representative compressed latent feature embeddings for reducing unnecessary redundant side information. Moreover, a combined channel–spatial attention mechanism is introduced to emphasize diagnostically important cellular structures but suppress background regions that are irrelevant. These refined feature representations are then processed in a fully connected classifier predicting multiple tumor subtypes respectively. For better interpretability and clinical trustworthiness, we employ Grad-CAM visualization to show the corresponding regions of tissue that drive predictions from individual models. The experimental results show that the proposed AMAE-GCNet framework can achieve 98.72% classification accuracy, 98.41% precision, 98.33% recall and 98.37% F1-score performance, which is superior to some existing deep learning-based breast cancer diagnosis models.

text: Attention-Guided Multi-Autoencoder Explainable Network for Breast Cancer Histopathological Image Multi-Classification Abstract- Breast cancer is the most common and pernicious disturbance among women worldwide, thus an early and precise diagnosis pays a pivotal role in the enhancement of a patient's survival rate. Histopathological image analysis is the gold standard for breast cancer diagnosis, but manual examination by pathologists can be time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. In order to overcome these limitations of existing methods, this work presents a new deep learning framework AMAE-GCNet (Attention-guided Multi-AutoEncoder with Grad-CAM Network) for automatic histopathological image based multi-classification of breast cancer. The proposed model is tested on the publicly available annotated BreakHis dataset consisting of 7,909 breast tumor histopathological images which are divided into eight benign and malignant subtypes with different magnification levels. To standardize the images, preprocessing methods such as stain normalization and image resizing are first used. We utilize a transfer learning backbone based on EfficientNet-B4 to elicit deep hierarchical features from the histopathological images. A multi-autoencoder module is therefore included to learn representative compressed latent feature embeddings for reducing unnecessary redundant side information. Moreover, a combined channel–spatial attention mechanism is introduced to emphasize diagnostically important cellular structures but suppress background regions that are irrelevant. These refined feature representations are then processed in a fully connected classifier predicting multiple tumor subtypes respectively. For better interpretability and clinical trustworthiness, we employ Grad-CAM visualization to show the corresponding regions of tissue that drive predictions from individual models. The experimental results show that the proposed AMAE-GCNet framework can achieve 98.72% classification accuracy, 98.41% precision, 98.33% recall and 98.37% F1-score performance, which is superior to some existing deep learning-based breast cancer diagnosis models. With the incorporation of transfer learning, attention-guided feature refinement and explainable visualization, the model proposed in this study is a robust clinical aid for pathologists performing breast cancer analyses. Keywords: Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Histopathological Image Classification, Transfer Learning, Attention Mechanism, Multi-Autoencoder, Grad-CAM Visualization, Explainable AI, Deep Learning. 1.Introduction​

text: 4.6 Grad-CAM Explainability Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is also integrated into the proposed AMAE-GCNet framework to improve interpretability and clinical reliability through visual explanation of model predictions. Deep learning models often function as black-box systems, making it difficult for clinicians to understand the reasoning behind automated diagnostic decisions. Grad-CAM addresses this limitation by generating visual heatmaps that highlight the most important regions of the input histopathological image contributing to the predicted tumor class. In this approach, the gradients of the target class score are computed with respect to the feature maps of the final convolutional layer. label: human

text: The rapid evolution of intelligent transportation systems has led to the emergence of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), an advanced paradigm that integrates vehicles, roadside infrastructure, cloud platforms, and users through wireless communication technologies. IoV enables a wide range of applications such as traffic management, accident prevention, autonomous driving, infotainment services, and real-time navigation. However, the large-scale exchange of sensitive vehicular data, including vehicle identity, location, speed, and driver behavior, has introduced serious security and privacy concerns. Due to the high mobility, dynamic topology, and open wireless communication environment of IoV networks, they are highly vulnerable to various cyber threats such as impersonation attacks, Sybil attacks, replay attacks, false data injection, and unauthorized tracking. Traditional centralized security architectures rely on trusted third parties and centralized servers, which suffer from single-point-of-failure, scalability issues, and increased latency. These limitations make conventional security solutions inadequate for next-generation IoV environments. To address these challenges, blockchain technology has emerged as a promising solution due to its decentralized architecture, immutability, transparency, and cryptographic security. Blockchain eliminates the need for a centralized authority by enabling distributed trust management among vehicles and infrastructure. However, while blockchain enhances trust and data integrity, it introduces challenges such as high computational cost, storage overhead, and privacy leakage if not carefully designed. In addition, the growing sophistication of cyber-attacks necessitates intelligent security mechanisms capable of detecting malicious behavior in real time. Machine learning and deep learning techniques have proven effective in identifying
label: ai_generated

text: abnormal patterns and malicious activities in dynamic environments like IoV. Furthermore, ensuring data privacy during communication and storage requires robust cryptographic mechanisms with optimized key management. This thesis focuses on developing efficient, secure, and privacy-preserving authentication protocols for IoV networks by integrating blockchain technology with intelligent learning models and optimized cryptographic techniques.

The proposed framework ensures data integrity, vehicle anonymity, and resistance to malicious attacks while maintaining low computational overhead, thereby making it suitable for real-time vehicular environments.

text: Internet of Vehicles environments are exposed to a wide range of security threats, including cyber intrusions, Sybil attacks, and the participation of compromised or malicious entities, which seriously affect the reliability of vehicular communications. When combined with smart contracts, this integration enables automated, tamper-resistant, and secure validation of vehicular transactions without relying on centralized authorities. text: AI-Driven Coral Reef Health Classifier Using Satellite Imagery and Convolutional Neural Network Models Abstract- Coral reefs are the world’s most biodiverse and climate-sensitive marine ecosystem, but monitoring them at scale and over time is difficult due to prohibitively high survey costs, restricted underwater access, and spatial– temporal variability in reef degradation. In this work, we present an AI-based framework for reef health classification using multispectral satellite images and CNN models to automatically assess the reef in a scalable fashion. The proposed model combines atmospheric-corrected satellite imagery with a custom Deep CNN architecture that is capable of capturing fine-grained spectral–spation patterns indicative of healthy and bleached corals, algal dominated, and degraded reef substrates. In contrast to standard thresholding and index-based algorithms, the model can learn discriminative hierarchical features from the raw reflectance images without residing on the manual setting of thresholds, offering robust separability for different water depths and illuminations. Experiments were specialized on publicly available satellite multispectral data acquired over various reef regions, with ground-truth representing cross-validated field investigations. The proposed classifier obtained an overall accuracy of 94.6%, a macro-averaged F1-score of 93.8% and Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 0.91, exceeding the traditional machine learning baselines up to 11.2% in classification accuracy. Additionally, sensitivity analysis reveals great generalization ability between reef systems that are geographically separated, with less than 3.5% drop in performance on cross-region evaluation. The findings establish the potential for satellite-informed deep learning algorithms to achieve accurate, low-cost and nearly real-time monitoring of coral reef health, which can inform proactive conservation practices and long-term climate impact assessment. Our framework provides a transferrable decision-support tool for marine ecologists and environmental managers targeting local and global efforts to reduce reef loss. Keywords: Coral Reef Health Monitoring; Satellite Imagery; Convolutional Neural Networks; Marine Ecosystem Assessment; Deep Learning; Environmental Remote Sensing 1. Introduction​ 1.1 Background and Motivation Coral reef systems are one of the most ecologically important marine environments, having 25% of all marine diversity while accounting for only 1% of ocean space [1][2]. Reefs are not only essential in their ecological role, but are also responsible for valuable ecosystem services including coastal defence, fisheries productivity and tourism-driven economy [3]. Nonetheless, such reef systems are currently threatened
label: human

text: by climate stressors, such as warming sea surface temperatures (SSTs), ocean acidification, sedimentation and human activity. These pressures have been associated with frequent and severe coral bleaching [4][5] leading to rapid declines in live coral cover for many reef regions. Monitoring efforts that can function at a large scale across space and short time intervals are required due to the accelerating rate at which reefs are degraded. Traditional methods of assessment may be inadequate to satisfy this demand, which calls for scalable and automated monitoring of the health of reefs to underpin timely interventions in conservation and management. 1.2 Limitations of Traditional Monitoring Approaches Traditional methods of studying coral reef mostly depends on diver-based surveys, imagery, and manual visual assessment. Although these techniques give rich ecological information, there remain drawbacks due to their expensive implementation [6][7], low spatial coverage, and reliance on expert interpretation. Manual annotation contributes to the subjectivity and inter-observer variability, leading to lack of consistency between studies and sites. In addition, difficulties and time-consuming requirements for field surveys restrict their application for long-term or large-scale reef monitoring, particularly in remote or inaccessible areas. These limitations highlight the necessity for non-biased, automated monitoring frameworks that minimize inter-observer bias and allow for consistent comparisons across reef communities. 1.3 Remote Sensing and Artificial Intelligence for Reef Monitoring With the advent of satellite remote sensing, shallow marine areas have increasingly become environments that can be observed repeatedly in large area from space using multispectral data1. These types of data provide spectral signatures that can contribute to the classification of benthic features [8], but index-based or threshold approaches to their classification are problematic due to differences in water depth, illumination and environmental conditions. CNNs are able to offer a data-driven solution, as they learn in an end-to-end manner the hierarchical spectral–spatial features from multispectral inputs. CNN models work well in modeling complex [9][10], nonlinear patterns of different coral reef health states and are more robust, scalable than classical machine learning. Such combination of satellite with deep learning is a promising path for automatization and large scale health assessment of coral reefs. In spite of the recent advances, much of the work on coral reef monitoring is based on handcrafted features or datasets from individual regions, preventing their use in a wider context. Most of these deep learning algorithms are extended from architectural models with generic and unspecialized architectures to multispectral reef data,
label: human

text: moreover cross-site performance comparison is limited [11]. Moreover, extensive comparisons with classical machine learning baselines are often missing, which prevents from estimating the added value brought by deep models on reef health classification. 1.5 Contributions of This Work​ This work has the following contributions: ●​ A satellite-induced deep learning approach is introduced for large-scale coral reef health assessment based on multispectral satellite images, automating and scaling-up coral reef monitoring. ●​ A tailored CNN architecture is designed to effectively extract spectral–spatial features of various coral reef health states, enhancing the robustness of classification in different underwater conditions. ●​ Extensive experimental validation is performed, including multi-class reef health classification and cross region-generalization studies and against traditional machine learning models with respect to performance. 1.6 Organization of the paper​ The rest of this paper is arranged as follows. Related works on coral reef monitoring based on remote sensing and artificial intelligence is presented in section 2, the dataset and data preprocessing are described in section 3. The presentation of the CNN-based proposed method and experimental setup is given in Sections 4 and 5, respectively, whereas Section 6 is for results and analysis; finally Section 7 describes the conclusions of the study with insights on future work. 2. Literature Review​ Li et al. (2024), which aimed to develop an advanced methodology for estimating live coral cover (LCC) based on deep learning in underwater video data, demonstrating the criticality of LCC as a fundamental indicator of reef health. To alleviate the laborious work of manually analyzing videos, the authors introduced a channel and spatial attention mechanism into the existing PSPNet-based semantic segmentation framework. The model accomplished high segmentation accuracy, thus indicating that deep learning was capable in largely enhancing the efficiency and precision of coral cover estimation. But the use of UAV may restrict scalability to great spatial dimensions, since data collection still depends on in-situ survey [1]. Veeranjaneyulu et al. (2024) used remotely sensed images for coral reef monitoring based on a combined HCNN–SVM approach. Using CNN-based feature extraction connected to SVM classification and spectral indices (e.g., NDVI, CBI), the study achieved high classification accuracies across varied reef datasets. Although the
label: human

text: method performed well, it used hand-designed spectral features and post-CNN classifiers that could limit its generalization to different environmental and geographical Post processing of the saliency maps for automated feature extraction from remotely sensed data settings [2]. Abeysiri Wickrama Liyanaarachchige et al. (2022) provided a temporal view into coral reef health monitoring, focusing on challenges of nonlinear trends and of sudden disruptions in long-term ecological data. Employing semiparametric and interrupted time-series models, the study suggested adaptive monitoring regimes for Scott Reef and showed that improved survey designs could decrease the effort required to monitor without severely reducing information. The framework only supports temporal analysis and fails to include automatic spatial tracking or image classification [3]. Maurya et al. (2023) developed a Stationary Reef Monitoring System (SRMS), which synchronizes photographic monitoring with in situ environmental sensing to sample the fine-scale response of corals under stress. The system identified the difference between satellite-retrieved and in situ temperature measurements, and provided a means to estimate local stress within the observation window. Despite the capability of those systems in situ, they are stationary and not suitable to perform big scale or anywhere coral reef assessment [4]. Singgalen [2024] stressed the need to develop a coherent coral monitoring program in order to inform ecological sustainability and policy development. The study adopted a rapid application development methodology to produce the monitoring application to pinpoint the causes for corals attrition. Although it showcases the necessity for technology-based solutions, most of its focus lies on designing systems and managing frameworks rather than automated remote sensing- or artificial intelligence-based classification of the reef health [5]. Warne et al. (2022) examined recovery dynamics of corals, using the sum of coral cover across the Great Barrier Reef. The research discovered a new two-stage recovery pattern following severe disturbances, suggesting that the recovery may be slower compared to what has been assumed in the past. While the results yield insights on reef resilience, they are based on summary field observations and do not cover automatic recognition or classification of reef health states [6]. Makled et al. (2024) used the FoRAM (Foraminifera Reef Assessment Monitoring) Index, a bio-monitoring method to evaluate coral reef status on the Red Sea coast. The research showed that bioindicators could offer affordable and timely monitoring of water quality and reef health. Nonetheless, bio-indicator approaches typically involve field sampling and are over on the scale of a laboratory analysis making them not practically applicable to large-area long-term in-situ monitoring [7]. Terzin et al. (2024) analyzed the potential of seawater microbial communities as sensitive probes for reef degradation and ecosystem disturbance. The authors presented a conceptual framework to shift from being descriptive microbial studies,
label: human

text: toward predictive reef monitoring. Despite the promise, microbial methods have not yet had real-time operational tools in an international context and are less amenable to being incorporated within large spatial monitoring systems [8]. Ouassine et al. (2025) described the use of YOLOv8 object detection and DeepSORT tracking for automated underwater removable monitor systems to recognize and track coral structures in video transects. We showed that the framework had a strong detection and tracking performance on several datasets and reef habitats. However, the use of underwater video data is not suited for scalable operation and does not exploit synoptic coverage using satellite remote sensing [9]. Jiang et al. (2023) developed a Coral Detection, Ranging and Assessment (CDRA) system to estimate coral cover on video sequences using object detection, stereo vision and tracking. The approach achieved high levels of accuracy in both controlled and field conditions, demonstrating the potential of automation for video analysis. However, like most video-based methods, it is not scalable for large-scale reef monitoring [10]. Jiang et al. (2023) was another review of AI-based surveillance systems for ocean organism health described, with the highlights on multi-source data integration such as sensors, imagery and environmental measurements. Although the review discusses AI revolution for marine monitoring, it does not include specific framework for satellite-based coral reef health classification [11]. Kumar et al. Reyad and Fahmy (2025) studied YOLO object detection for detecting of coral reef health state and diseases from image data. The research showed the potential for real-time coral health monitoring from improved YOLOv5 models. Yet, the emphasis on object-level detection rather than pixel-level or region-wise classification restricts its efficiency in terms of reef-wide health-mapping [12]. Chen et al. (2024) put forward a deep learning model that integrates bathymetry feature in satellite imagery-based coral reef benthic habitat classification process. The model combined bathymetry information and weakly supervised learning, obtaining substantially improved classification accuracy and good generalization ability across regions. This study illustrate the benefit of using ancillary spatial information but needs further bathymetry data which is not always provided at a global scale [11]. Rajan and Damodaran (2023) created a benchmark coral reef database, they also proposed a multitier attention feature fusion network in conjunction with YOLOv5 to detect the health of corals. The model surpassed performance of multiple state-of-the-art detectors, and was shown to be suitable for hardware-based implementation. The method has a competitive performance in detection, but it is also object-based and not designed explicitly for large-scale reef health classification on multispectral satellite imagery [13][14]. 2.1 Research Gap​ In total, the available literature indicates the increasing use of artificial intelligence applied to coral reef monitoring and assessment with underwater imagery, in situ
label: human

text: sensing, and locally remote sensing. However, several methods are still limited by localized spatial coverage of input samples, manually engineered features or acquired underwater samples. Clearly, there is a need for a satellite-based, end-to-end DL solution that can handle largescale multi-class reef health classification across different regions and achieve strong cross-region generalizability – precisely what this paper seeks to address. 3. Dataset and Preprocessing​ 3.1 Satellite Data Source The study is based on Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI) images for coral reef health classification. Sentinel-2 provides an open-access, high resolution, multispectral satellite data at regular revisits and it is suitable for large-scale and near real-time monitoring of shallow water marine ecosystems [15]. The reflectance information covers 13 spectral bands ranging from visible and near-infrared to short-wave infrared spectra that are ideal for discriminating benthic features in clear, shallow waters. For this study, we chose the visible and near-infrared bands (Blue, Green, Red and NIR) because they are known to be sensitive to coral reflectance and benthic composition. Resolution The bands provided are at a 10 m spatial resolution [16], which provides enough detail to analyse reef scales whilst maintaining wide coverage. Sentinel-2 Level-2A products (surface reflectance corrected from atmospheric effects) were downloaded through the Copernicus Open Access Hub (https://dataspace.copernicus.eu). 3.2 Ground Truth Data Coral reef health ground-truth labels were used from publicly available ecological survey and expert annotated-reff maps for the Sentinel-2 acquisition dates. Reef health conditions were defined as categories of healthy coral, bleached coral, algal-dominated areas [17] and degraded reef substrates as per monitoring guidelines. Trained reef monitoring specialist and validated benthic habitat maps were geospatially registered to satellite imagery for the creation of labeled training and test samples. A portion of the labeled regions was held-out for independent testing, in order to evaluate model bias. 3.3 Preprocessing Pipeline A standard pipeline was applied to all Sentinel-2 images for radiometric normalization and spectral–spatial features enhancement [18]. Atmospheric influences were corrected using surface reflectance products [19], with no other adjustments made against water-column attenuation by depth. Vegetation indices were applied
label: human

text: into the purely cloudy-free pixel values from the spectral bands that passed quality control masks and all bands were resampled to a single common spatial resolution. Finally, all spectral inputs were normalized to stabilize CNN training: ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (3) 𝑥 ' = 𝑥−𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑥 ( ) 𝑚𝑎𝑥𝑥 ( )−𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑥 ( ) This preprocessing procedure promotes the CNN to learn robust, depth-normalized and noise-reduced spectral–spatial feature representations associated with coral reef health. 4. Proposed Methodology 4.1 System Architecture The coral reef health classification system we present builds on a fully automated end-to-end pipeline for scalable analysis of multispectral satellite imagery. R2R images are derived from observations acquired during the R2R process, for which surface reflectance Sentinel-2 imagery covering shallow reef areas is collected 19. The resultant images were further processed through a standard pre-processing chain (including atmospheric correction, water-column normalization, cloud masking and spectral resampling) to guarantee radiometric homogeneity between scenes [21]. After preprocessing, the images are split into fixed-sized image patches of reef areas for the model to learn local spectral–spatial patterns with computation efficiency. The patch-wise decomposition is fed into a custom CNN, which automatically learns hierarchical representations from a multispectral input through increasingly higher-level convolutions and poolings. The resulting features are then fed into a classification layer, which classifies each patch according to the pre-defined categories of coral reef health [22]. Lastly, a post-processing fuses patches-level predictions to produce spatially consistent reef health maps for visualizing and quantifying coral reef status at a large scale. Figure 1. This architecture allows for efficient end-to-end learning of discriminative spectral–spatial features from multispectral satellite images and plays a key role in the accurate, scalable classification of coral reef health. 4.3 Training Strategy The Adam optimizer was used to train the proposed convolution neural network, and an initial learning rate of 0.001 was set, it led to stable and rapid convergence when training. The number of epochs was set to 100, and early stopping was used to avoid overfitting when the loss on validation data did not improve for 10 consecutive epochs. A batch size of 32 was chosen to minimize computational time and ensure that the gradients are stable. Dropout regularization of 0.5 was used on the fully connected layers to improve generalization between reef regions. For enhanced robustness, we also used data augmentation operations such as random rotations (±15°) and horizontal/ vertical flipping followed by slight variations in spectral intensity for the training patches. These training parameters allowed for stable learning and better generalization of the model to a variety of coral reef environments from multispectral satellite imagery. 5. Experimental Setup 5.1 Class Definitions The problem of coral reef health classification was posed as a multi-class one involving four ecologically meaningful classes taken from reef monitoring standards. Pristine reef means a reef habitat where live, stony coral dominated, structurally intact and fully pigmented colonies are observed. Bleached coral is a sign of stressed coral colonies, where symbiotic algae has been lost and the colony appears
label: human

text: as pale or white. Algal-dominated zones refer to areas on the reef that are largely dominated by macroalgae or turf algae, either suggesting decreased coral health or a post-disturbance succession. Reef with degraded substrate, groups the non-living components of a reef (rubble, sand, dead structures) commonly associated to long-term destruction of reefs. 5.2 Baseline Models To measure objectively the performance of the proposed CNN, their classification results were reassessed and compared with classical machine learning classifiers. As an effective classification tool handling high-dimensional feature space, SVM with a radial basis function kernel was used. Random Forest (RF) was chosen since it is an ensemble learning method and also known as being resistant to noise. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) were adopted as a distance-based classifier to measure local neighborhood discrimination, and we employed a Decision Tree (DT) model as a simple, interpretable baseline. For comparison purposes, we also trained all other baseline models with handcrafted spectral features extracted from the same multispectral input. 5.3 Evaluation Metrics Standard multi-class classification metrics was used to quantitatively evaluate model performance. ●​ Accuracy is an index to evaluate how many samples are classified correctly among all: ​ ​ ​ ​ (6) 𝐴𝑐𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑦= 𝑇𝑃+𝑇𝑁 𝑇𝑃+𝑇𝑁+𝐹𝑃+𝐹𝑁 ●​ Precision measures the ratio of accurate predicted positive samples to all predicted positives: ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (7) 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛= 𝑇𝑃 𝑇𝑃+𝐹𝑃 ●​ Recall (Sensitivity) : How well the model predicts all the actual positive samples: ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (8) 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙= 𝑇𝑃 𝑇𝑃+𝐹𝑃 ●​ The harmonic mean of precision r and recall p is F1-score, which takes into account both precision and recall: ​ ​ ​ (9) 𝐹1 −𝑠𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒= 2 × 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛×𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛+𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 ●​ The Kappa coefficient of Cohen measures the agreement between predicted and true labels considering chance agreement: ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ (10) 𝐾= 𝑝𝑜−𝑝𝑒 1−𝑝𝑒

Results and Analysis 6.1 Quantitative Results We quantitatively benchmark the proposed CNN-based coral reef health classification framework and compare its performance with baseline traditional machine learning methods (SVM and RF). Table 1 demonstrates the classification results using Accuracy, F1 score and Cohen’s Kappa coefficient. A CNN model had been proposed that outperformed all baseline models by achieving an accuracy of 94.6%, a macro-averaged F1-score of 93.8% and Kappa coefficient of 0.91, which stands for near perfect agreement away from chance level. By contrast, the RF model obtained 85.2% accuracy and 0.81 Kappa value, whereas the SVM model reached 83.4% accuracy with a Kappa of 0.78. These results highlight the deficiencies of handcrafted spectral features for classical models, especially in diverse reef types. The significant enhancement of the presented CNN indicates that it can effectively extract robust spectral–spatial information from the multispectral satellite images. Table 1. The strong diagonal dominance of the model values for all categories suggests that it achieves very high classification accuracy. The healthy coral and the degraded substrate classes have at least 34% of correct classifications, as they present distinctive spectral features. Slight confusion is highlighted between bleached corals and algae dominated areas, which have a similar brightness (reflectance) in some spectral windows, especially for shallow water and
label: human

text: high turbidity conditions. In general, the confusion matrix confirms that the model is balanced and has no class bias. ​ Figure 2. Confusion matrix of the proposed CNN-based coral reef health classification model. 6.3 Cross-Region Generalization To evaluate the generalizability to other regions, cross-region generalization was examined through a model trained on reef data from one region and tested on reef systems located across space. Our CNN also demonstrated great generalization, showing a maximum performance drop below 3.5% in accuracy overall regions. This indicates that the model can capture invariant spectral spatial features independent from specific region and thus capable for large-scale and multi-regional coral reef survey. It is also shown that the proposed method is robust regardless of reef type, water depth and environmental conditions. 6.4 Error Analysis Through error analysis, we find that the majority of misclassifications fail along transitions between reef health class pairs, particularly between bleached coral and algal-dominated regions. These errors are largely the result of spectral signatures that overlap and mixed pixels in satellite imagery, particularly in reef-reef transitions. Further misclassification occurs on water turbidity and variable illumination regions, because those could influence reflectance patterns. However, overall error is relatively low and the misclassifications should have little impact on broader scale reef health
label: human

text: assessments. These errors could be further improved in subsequent study by involving temporal information and auxiliary data, bathymetry. ​ Figure 3. Error analysis of coral reef health classification results. Figure 3. Misclassified sample distribution by coral reef health category. The majority of errors are between bleached coral and algal-dominated regions as a result of similar spectral structures and mixed-pixel issues in Landsat satellite imagery. 6.5 Discussion​ Experimental results show that the proposed CNN-based model can well extract discriminative spectral–spatial patterns from multispectral satellite images to achieve accurate classification of coral reef health conditions. The drastic gain in performance over classical machine learning models further emphasizes the benefit of end-to-end feature learning for diverse reef domains. The strong cross-region generalization also indicates the robustness and scalability of our method for large-scale monitoring. The remaining misclasses were predominantly restricted to spectrally similar reef conditions, and suggest that additional improvements may be possible through consideration of temporal and ancillary data. 7. Conclusion​ This paper proposed an AI-based coral reef health classification pipeline on multispectral Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, designed a tailored convolutional neural network (CNN). Strong classification performance of the proposed model was obtained with overall accuracy of 94.6%, F1-score of 93.8% and Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 0.91, indicating good agreement and reliability to classify IOLs. Comparative assessment with classical machine learning models further validated the
label: human

text: potential of deep spectral–spatial feature learning for reef health analysis. Inter-regional experiments also demonstrated the robustness and transferability of the framework to different reef settings. The findings emphasize the potential of deep learning model from satellite as a cost-effective tool for large-scale coral reef monitoring. Future work will concentrate on introducing temporal analysis, other environmental factors and deep learning architectures in order to increase classification accuracy and predictive capability for the long-term health of reefs. text: A Topology-Aware Selection and Duty Control Algorithm for Comparative Performance Enhancement of Electric Vehicle Power Converters Abstract- The electrification of automotive applications cannot succeed without EV power conversion systems that have a critical impact on drivetrain efficiency, thermal robustness and energy consumption for traction, regenerative braking and charging modes. While significant literature exists in evaluating isolated DC–DC and bidirectional converter topologies, the majority of the studies are focused on static conditions with fixed values which do not capture the highly fluctuating power requirements in practical EV operation. In this paper, we introduce a novel TADS (Topology-Aware Duty and Selection) algorithm for EV power converters that provides an organized and fair comparison while improving systemlevel performance, without introducing computation-intensive or adaptive control strategies. The presented methodology combines few number of industry oriented converter topologies by employing a rule based topology selection strategy that takes into consideration the power requirement, level ratio and the thermal conditions through duty cycle computation for selected topologies. Unlike traditional comparative analysis, which relies on a single 'best' topology assumption, TADS dynamically chooses the best converter topology with respect to different operating conditions such as acceleration, cruising and regenerative braking and charging regimes. The simulation results using standard EV drive cycles show that the average efficiency improvement of the proposed method compared to fixed topology based converter systems is 2.8%, peak switching losses decrease by 18.6%, and the maximum junction temperature decreases by 14.2%. Furthermore, the whole efficiency of the energy use during full-cycle operations is enhanced by 3.4%. These findings confirm that the proposed topology-aware framework is a viable and sized approach to next-generation EV power electronics, providing performance improvements without sacrificing implementation simplicity. Keywords- Electric vehicles, DC–DC converters, power electronics, topology selection, duty cycle control, efficiency optimization, comparative study. 1. Introduction Electric vehicles (EVs) have become a key solution for sustainable transportation by promising to largely mitigate the vehicles’ greenhouse gas emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. On the core of an EV powertrain stands power electronic conversion system [1][2] that mainly controls bi-directional energy flows between battery pack, traction inverter, and auxiliary subsystems [3][4], along with external charging infrastructure [5]. Transistorized dc–dc and bidirectional converters are important
label: human

text: to maintain voltage regulation, efficient transfer of energy and protection of delicate devices against electrical overstress and thermal excursions [6][7]. The efficiency of these converters can directly affect overall vehicle performance, battery life time, thermal reliability and driving range of the vehicle; therefore power conversion have become a critical design concern in current EV architectures [8]. There have been a lot of works focusing on DC–DC converter topologies for EV in recent years, such as buck [9], boost, buck–boost, interleaved, isolated and bidirectional topologies [10]. Although these studies help understand the converter behavior, but also most of the comparison is done under constant operation [11] what means that there is a single topology and direct duty ratio. The above methods do not account for the intrinsic dynamic behavior of the EV, since rapid modes-switches take place among acceleration, cruising at constant speed in steady-state condition, regenerative braking and recharging ones, each one entailing different power and thus DC voltage levels and thermal loads on the converter fringe system [12]. Furthermore, the few current comparative frameworks usually consider individual performance metrics, such as peak efficiency or voltage gain [13] at best and disregard system-level implications over a driving cycle [14]. Advanced control techniques such as model predictive control and artificial intelligence–based approaches have been investigated to accommodate dynamic operation, but with tradeoffs of high computational burden, additional sensing, and limited industrial applicability for wide installation [16], [18], [35]. As a result, there is still an urgent demand for a practical and scalable platform to facilitate fair comparison and efficient utilization of multiple converter topologies under real EV-operating scenarios. To mitigate these limitations, this work presents three research objectives: (i) lack of a consistent framework for dynamic and fair comparison of various converter topologies, (ii) absence of topology-aware duty cycle calculation as a function of varying operating regions and (iii) limited investigations on system-level efficiency and thermal performance across standardized EV drive cycles. Closing such gaps is important for the further development of next generation EV power electronics, which reconciles improving performance with circuit complexity. In this context, this article introduces a new Topology-Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) methodology for the EV power converters. The method includes a library of commercially representative DC–DC and bidirectional converters topologies and uses rule-based selection based on power requirement, voltage step-ratio, and heat-flow limitation. In contrast to traditional studies which consider a single best-fit topology, the TADS method adaptively determines the adequate converter configuration for each working region, and solves for its respective duty cycle in a topologically
label: human

text: equivalent manner. This allows a fair comparative evaluation while obtaining measurable benefits in terms of efficiency, switching losses and thermal stress in relevant driving conditions. The salient features of the paper are: ●​ A Topology-aware duty And Selection (TAD S) algorithm for dynamic selection and fair comparison of EV DC-DC converter topologies at different operating points. ●​ An easy rule based duty and topology control scheme, which increases both efficiency and thermal performance without resorting to complex adaptive or intelligent controllers. The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 presents literature review of the DC–DC converter topologies and comparison studies for EV. The model of the EV power conversion system and the inc-luded converter topologies are presented in Section 3. The proposed TADS algorithm and its rule-based selection logic are presented in Section 4. The simulation setup and evaluation methodology is described in Section 5. Section 6 presents the comparative performance results at representative EV drive cycles. Last, Section 7 ends the paper and discusses some directions for future work. 2. Literature Review​ Rathore et al. (2022) proposed a dedicated stand-alone multilevel DC–DC converter configuration for fast charging in electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles. The design of aimed at high power density and small filter size by generating multilevel output voltages using the voltage doubler rectifier units. Soft-switching was obtained due to resonance between leakage inductance of transformer and parasitic capacitances, opening the possibility to improve efficiency at higher power levels. While the topology had good behavior for fast charging, its design was only tuned at a fixed point and not capable of dealing with the number of operating conditions encountered by EVs in real-world driving cycles [1]. Wang et al. (2021) presented a detailed review on isolated bidirectional dc–dc converter topologies and operation strategies for EV applications. The study categorized the converters as; PWM-based, dual active bridge and resonant type of which several other phase-shift control methods to improve performance have been discussed. The paper appeared to provide useful investigation for topology properties and control strategies, however its main concern is the performance of individual converter with no focus on dynamic topology selection or analytical comparison among systems under different EV operating conditions [2]. González-Castaño et al. (2022) where a composite EV power conversion system with flexible buck–boost DC–DC converter can have wide voltage regulation. The work focused on increasing motor efficiency by means of a flexible DC-link voltage control, and it was verified by thermal simulations,
label: human

text: experimental results, and hardware-in-the-loop tests. Although being an efficient wide input voltage regulation was achieved in [3], the design assumed single topology selection and had no discussion on multi-selective topology according to operating modes. Tekin et al. (2023) presented a single-input multi-output buck–boost converter to obtain many voltage levels typical for EV application. The high voltage gain of the converter was adjustable by the duty cycle and a DSP-based PID controller was adopted for control. Despite the favorable voltage scaling potential of the topology, however, the control approach also remained static and was not tested for further dynamic transitions between several operating conditions such as regeneration and acceleration [4]. Zakaria et al. (2023) designed a hybrid interleaved nonisolated DC–DC converter with lower part count and high voltage gain for renewable energy and medium-voltage applications. The current ripple and voltage stress were also alleviated due to the interleaved implementation, while a PI-based controller was used for voltage regulation. Although the topology yielded high steady-state performance, it could only be used in fixed-use cases and did not meet the requirements of topology adaptability or EV specific duty control [5]. Nassary et al. (2024) analyzed a four-switch boost–buck AC/DC converter focusing on internal dynamic stability and power factor correction for EV charging. The authors introduced a damping RC circuit to solve the instability problem and verified their method by small-signal modeling and simulation. This work emphasized stability-oriented control, but it only concentrated on one converter topology and not comparative or topology-aware strategies [6]. Sangeetha & Ramachandran (2022) provided a wide technical review of EV subsystems such as electric machines, energy storage device and power electronic converter. They focused on propulsion, regenerative braking and energy management converter operation in various vehicles. (2022) provided a comprehensive review of power converter topologies, control strategies and semiconductor devices for EVs. The research contrasted between the AC–DC, DC–DC and the DC–AC converters, while emphasizing advantages of wide-bandgap devices in order to achieve high efficiency and power density. Although the review was in depth, less attention had been paid to component-level optimization rather than system-level topology selection at dynamic EV operation scenarios [8]. Maroti et al. But that work considered fixed preset structures of the converter and couldn't handle dynamic transition between a number of topologies [9]. Hemavathi and Shinisha (2022) studied EV

This comparison demonstrates a lack of a coherent, system-wide methodology which makes evident the need for the presented topology-aware duty and selection process. 2.1 Literature Gap Summary Based on the reviewed literature, there have been remarkable DC–DC and bidirectional converter topologies as well as control methods and charging schemes for EVs. Previous works have investigated many high-efficiency converter topologies, soft-switching techniques and wide voltage-gain range operation mechanisms as well as advanced control strategies in scope of particular applications, like rapid charging, renewable generation integration and vehicle-to-grid scenario. However, in current literature the performance of the converter was tested for a preset operating point and topology, by considering a fixed conduction angle to maximise the transferred energy. Comparative analyses mostly have not taken into account dynamic transitions between modes of EV operation, but often concentrate on static performance criteria or topology level parameters. Moreover, advanced control methods tend to add higher computational complexity and practical deployment difficulties, thereby restraining their applicability in practice. Therefore, it can be inferred that there is no available common and practical framework for network topology dynamic selection jointly with application duty cycle separately in various topologies as well as fair performance comparison at the system level across realistic EV drives. This research gap motivates the design of the presented topology-aware duty and selection scheme. 3. System Model and Converter Topologies​ This section presents unique topology aware power conversion system for electric vehicle (EV) and the DC–DC converter topologies which are incorporated in proposed topology-aware duty and selection scheme. The goal is to provide a consistent system model to fairly compare different converter topologies for dynamic EV conditions.

Proposed TADS Algorithm​ 4.1 Motivation for Topology-Aware Selection Electric vehicle power converters work in very dynamic environments: the power and battery voltage [30][31], operating mode changes continuously during acceleration, cruising, regenerative braking and charging. Since no single DC–DC converter topology operates efficiently for the entire range, thermal performance is compromised due to topology suitability depending highly on both voltage conversion ratio and load level [32]. Losses of conduction and switching increase as a fixed topology is pushed to work at very high duty cycles, resulting in higher thermal stress and reliability problems [33]. Another reason is that the converter also deviates from its optimum working point to a large extent due to battery voltage changing with state of charge. These constraints inspire the topology-aware selection strategy selecting at run time the best converter configuration based on instantaneous power demand, voltage ratio and thermal restrictions and represent the basic elements of the proposed TADS (Topology-Aware Duty and Selection) algorithm. Architecture of the proposed Topology-Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) framework for EV DC–DC power converters​ 4.2 TADS Algorithm Overview​ The Topology-Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) algorithm is a supervisory decision layer which dynamically selects correct DC—DC converter topology and its duty cycle for instantaneous operating conditions [34][35]. Power demand, battery to DC bus voltage ratio and thermal limit constraints are inputs to the algorithm reflecting electrical and thermal states of the EV power conversion system. TADS selects the most efficient topology that avoids high duty cycle operation based on predefined operating regions considering converter characteristics [36]. When the topology has been chosen, a topology- specific duty cycle is calculated based on the respective steady-state voltage conversion relation. The converter topology and the duty cycle command are thereby determined by the algorithm, so that efficient and thermally well balanced operation is achieved without needing advanced adaptive or optimization control strategies. Conclusion​ In this paper, a novel Topology- Aware Duty and Selection (TADS) method is provided for electric vehicle DC–DC power conversion systems that significantly enhances the efficiency and thermal management in dynamic operating conditions. By dynamically choosing the optimal converter topology and calculating duty cycles specific to each topology based on closed-form solutions, the proposed method avoids compromises of dedicated-topology converters with complexity in control design. Simulation results carried out over standard EV drive cycles show that the proposed topology yields 2.8% higher system efficiency, an 18.6% lower peak switching loss and a reduced maximum junction temperature of 14.2%, compared to traditional converter configurations. Furthermore, the overall energy efficiency of utilization is enhanced by 3.4%, validating that the topology-aware approach can optimize system-level performance. Future work will be the experimental hardware validation of the presented concept under real driving conditions as well as an extension of the selection logic to take into account component aging and fault-tolerant operation. More research on multi-objective optimization regarding efficiency, thermal stress and reliability at the same time is also a next step to improve the robustness of power electronics in future generations EVs. text: Hierarchical Radiogenomic Transformer-GNN (HRT-GNN): A Novel Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Enhanced Glioma Diagnosis and Prognosis Prediction Abstract- Accurate diagnosis and prognosis prediction of gliomas, as one of the hottest topics due to the complex spatial heterogeneity of tumor and the multimodal nature of clinical data, have remained challenging. In response to these limitations, we present a new Hierarchical Radiogenomic Transformer-GNN (HRT-GNN) model that combines MRI, genomic, and clinical data in a single predictive architecture. Our proposed method utilizes a hybrid CNN–Vision Transformer backbone to extract high-dimensional spatial features from multi-parametric MRI sequences and employs a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to capture both intra-tumoral subregion interactions and inter-patient radiogenomic relationships. The cross-attention fusion module dynamically aligns imaging features with genomic and clinical embeddings, which allows us to learn interpretable multimodal features. Our model is a multi-task predictor, which allows us to predict molecular subtypes, recurrence risk, and survival altogether. An experimental evaluation on the UCSD‑PTGBM dataset shows that HRT-GNN reaches 98.67% on diagnostic accuracy, 96.21% molecular subtype prediction accuracy, and 0.937 on C-index for survival prediction, averaging 6.8% performance improvement over existing multimodal baselines. Attention-based interpretability emphasizes clinically relevant tumor subregions and genomic associations, which further enhances clinical trust. Our results present HRT-GNN as an interpretable, strong baseline for precision neuro-oncology, linking away from interpretation to imaging, genomics and clinical insights for answering the need for personalized patient care. Keywords-glioma diagnosis, radiogenomics, hierarchical graph neural network, transformer, multimodal fusion, survival prediction, cross-attention, medical imaging, deep learning, precision oncology I Introduction The most common primary malignant brain tumours, gliomas have aggressive growth features, extensive genomic heterogeneity, and significant resistance to standard therapies [1]. Their clinical management remains challenging due to shared radiological signatures, and extreme intratumoral diversity [4]. Conventional diagnostic pathways rely on invasive biopsy and histopathological assessment, but these often do not represent the spatial heterogeneity of the tumour micro-environment, limiting their prognostic and predictive capacity [19]. Molecular glioma reclassification by glioma biomarkers, namely IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion and MGMT promoter methylation, developed over the last decades have revolutionized prognosis evaluations [1][25]. A thorough yet non-invasive tool which can predict histologic, molecular, and survival characteristics, is still sought after [21]. Radiological, genomic and clinical dimensions combined in a single computational framework represent an essential milestone for individualized treatment and early detection of recurrences [5][27]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is still the mainstay imaging technique for glioma assessment, encompassing a range of sequences indicative of
label: human
source_file: Enhanced Glioma Diagnosis and Prognosis Prediction (1).pdf

text: cellularity, necrosis and angiogenesis [23]. Standard radiomics tries to derive quantitative, or semi-quantitative, features from these images that relate imaging phenotypes to genetic mutations, and ultimately clinical outcomes [7][9]. Yet clinical translation has been limited due to manual feature engineering and limited reproducibility between scanners and protocols [18][20]. The introduction of deep learning strategies has started to overcome these challenges by learning high-dimensional representations directly from imaging data in an automated manner [8][10]. However, many existing systems are limited to either MR imaging or genomic input and do not consider interactions across spatial and molecular scales as well as clinical factors, all of which drive disease evolution and progression [14][15]. Thus, models capable of learning from heterogeneous sources while simultaneously maintaining biological interpretability for real-world decision support [2][24].. Recently, transformer and graph-based neural networks have been shown to be quite promising to fill in this multi-modal integration gap [3][6]. Transformers model long range dependencies and contextual semantics in volumetric MRI [4] and GNNs can model non-Euclidean relationships among tumor subregions and across patients [11][12]. Radiogenomic pipelines based on these architectures may uncover interactions spanning multiple scales, between tumour morphology and molecular alterations [13]. However, in most of the previous frameworks the modalities are treated independently or a shallow concatenation is performed without learning structural interdependence [16][17]. Lastly, interpretability is still quite limited and affects the clinical trust and adoption [28]. Towards biologically plausible fusion and clinically interpretable prediction, hierarchical attention mechanisms that can reason across modalities are introduced [26]. This study presents the Hierarchical RadiogenomicTransformer-GNN (HRT-GNN), which aims to bridge these methodological and translational gaps. It features a hybrid CNN–Vision Transformer backbone to extract local and global imaging characteristics; and a GNN component to encode not only intra-tumour spatial relations, but also inter-patient radiogenomic networks. A cross-attention fusion module that aligns imaging, genomic and clinical embeddings for consistent multimodal reasoning. It simultaneously learns a model for multi-task, molecular subtype classification, recurrence risk estimation, and survival prediction with comprehensive clinical utility [5][30]. Extensive experiments on the BraTS 2023 and TCGA-GBM/LGG cohorts demonstrate that it achieves the highest predictive accuracy and interpretability than existing multimodal approaches [31][33]. Finally, attention-based heatmaps allow to promote biologically relevant subregions of tumours and genotype-phenotype associations [29][36], reinforcing its use for translation. This unified model is a step forward in radiogenomic intelligence for precision neuro-oncology [32][35]. The main contributions of the paper are as follows: ●​ Hierarchical multimodal learning architecture: A Unified Framework Incorporating a CNN–Vision Transformer Backbone, A Graph Neural Network for Relational Modeling, and Cross-Attention Fusion for MRI, Genomic, and Clinical Embeddings 6.

With this ensemble based system, diagnostic performances were excellent creating a robust computational model for glioma detection and grade classification. 2.1 Research Gap Although there has been substantial advancement over molecular characterization, integration of radiogenomics, and prediction frameworks based on deep learning [1–18], glioma prognosis modeling still has important gaps. Existing studies are predominantly restricted to single-modality data (e.g., MRI or genomics), or have relied on handcrafted features implying low cross-cohort generalizability. Fusion and attention-based multimodal learning have shown potential [5,6,9], but are generally not biologically interpretable nor cross-clinically consistent techniques of performing integrative learning in heterogeneous clinical datasets. Additionally, the vast majority of existing survival prediction models do not consider the hierarchical interactions between radiomic, genomic, and clinical domains important for capturing tumor behavior complexity. Such limitations highlight the pressing need for an interpretable hierarchical deep learning architecture, with predictive robustness and the capability to integrate multimodal information while retaining biological relevance. III Methodology​ We proposed a new multimodal irradiation architecture, Hierarchical Radiogenomic Transformer-GNN (HRT-GNN), which was able to combine multi-parametric MRI, genomic, and clinical data for glioma diagnosis and prognosis prediction [19]. We describe a pipeline, which utilizes standardized pre-processing of multi-sequence MRI data, including T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR modalities, extracting spatially discriminative features using a hybrid CNN–Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder, where we treat Positional Embedding as learned features. The CNN part adopts localized morphology pattern expression, and the ViT module, which is capable of long-range spatial dependencies modeling within tumor subregions, enables a comprehensive description of tumor heterogeneity [20][21]. These imaging embeddings are hierarchically aligned to genomic and clinical feature embeddings using a Graph Neural Network(GNN) that captures spatial relationships within the tumor, and

The description prior to biological knowledge integrated at different depths enables both strong prediction capabilities and biological interpretability, allowing HRT-GNN to serve as a clinically interpretable deep learning framework for precision neuro-oncology.
