The measured PSNR gain of 1.8–3.2 dB demonstrates superior performance in pixel-wise reconstruction, while the 3~6% improvement from SSIM suggests enhanced perceptual similarity and structural fidelity. Such improvements are due to the joint effects of multi-scale discrimination and hybrid loss optimization for maintaining global structure and fine texture simultaneously. The proposed DeepClean method eliminates over-smoothing artifacts present in competing CNN and Transformer-based methods, and image features appear to be better kept. In terms of computational cost, our framework can process high-resolution images up to 4K by achieving between 20-30 FPS on GPUs providing practical real-time experience for many applications involving image denoising. Such tradeoff among accuracy, perceptual quality and efficiency shows the full robustness and scalability of the approach in realistic image restoration scenarios. VI Conclusion​ In this work, we proposed DeepClean: an artificial intelligence (AI) GAN-powered image denoising framework that learns to balance trade-offs between reconstruction accuracy, perceptual quality and computational efficiency. With a convolutional encoder–decoder generator, a multi-scale discriminator, and a hybrid loss function, DeepClean achieved superior performance over six classical denoising methods on various noise criteria. Experimental results showed that the proposed method can achieve 1.8–3.2 dB PSNR gains and about 3–6% SSIM improvements, as well as have better performances on edge preserving and texture protecting of evolutionary apparent clue segmentation methods. In addition, the framework obtained 20-30 FPS on GPU platforms when processing high resolution (up to 4K) images supporting its applicability for near real-time applications. These results prove DeepClean's strength and scalability in real-world image restoration applications. In the future, we will work on adaptive noise estimation and lightweight model optimization for efficient deployment to edge resource-limited devices. text: Kidney Tumor Segmentation Using a Hybrid Transformer Framework with Customized Augmentation and Boundary-Sensitive Loss Abstract- Precise segmentation of kidney tumors in medical images is crucial for diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis assessment. In this work, we present a newly proposed hybrid deep learning model that combines the merits of U-Net and Swin Transformer architectures in order to enhance the segmentation performance. Although U-Net has great spatial localisation ability thanks to the encoder-decoder structure which works in a hierarchical way, it is still difficult to capture global context well. Swin Transformer instead captures long-range dependencies and assists local detail extraction, while attention pooling might also smear fine boundary details. This motivates our hybrid integration. To attempt to resolve these issues, we extend the U-Net with Swin Transformer blocks in the backbone encoder path, in order to efficiently perform multi-scale semantic feature extraction while preserving structural consistency. We trained and cross-validated the model on the publicly available Kidney Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2021 (KiTS21) dataset with extensive data augmentation as well as custom loss functions to address, class imbalance and boundary obscureness. Experiments demonstrate that it has achieved better performance when compared to the solo models, seeking similar multi-task learning objective on not only U-Net and Swin Transformer but also other baseline architectures in terms of average Dice Similarity Coefficient (average DSC), Intersection over Union score (IoU) and Hausdorff distance. The model had an average accuracy of 98%, indicating the high precision in segmenting kidney tumors with different sizes and shapes. Moreover, the integrated solution is more robust and generalizes better particularly in challenging cases with diverse anatomical variations. These findings demonstrate the power of transformer-based hybrid models for medical image segmentation. Our results have positive implications on the design of computer-aided diagnostic systems and their association with other prevalent medical imaging tasks besides organ-specific or pathology-focused. Keywords: Kidney Tumor Segmentation, Hybrid Deep Learning, U-Net, Swin Transformer, Medical Image Analysis I INTRODUCTION Precise segmentation of kidney tumor in CT images has become a crucial task for nephrology and oncology clinical routine [1]. Histological criteria for tumor border
label: human

text: definition have direct impact on decision-making regarding diagnosis, extent of surgery and follow-up [2]. Nevertheless, automatic segmentation remains a difficult task owing to the heterogeneity of tumor appearances, ill-defined shape boundaries, and different kidney anatomies in various patients. With the advantages of the symmetry encoder-decoder and convolutional skip connections, CNN-based U-architectures are the representatives for medical image segmentation. However, they have limited ability to capture the broader context, and therefore, in complex tissue structures or images with low contrast boundaries, the model may suffer [3]. Transformer-based models have recently been shown to be promising for computer vision tasks, largely due to their competitiveness at capturing long-range dependencies. [4] The Swin Transformer adopts a hierarchical design and introduces shifted window attention, which has achieved promising results in processing high-resolution images. It can scale the attention computation without losing spatial coherence. Nonetheless, for medical images, these models might have an inferior performance when detecting small spatial information that is important for accurate tumor segmentation. Such a gap is particularly visible in small or irregularly shaped tumors for which edge sensitivity is crucial. Both convolution and self-attention-based mechanisms have advantages; we also believe they are complementary to each other, and the integration of them to achieve robust and accurate segmentation is feasible [5]. To cope with the local detail protection and global feature representation issue, we propose a hybrid segmentation framework. This model tactfully incorporates the Swin Transformer into the encoder path of the U-Net-like backbone [6] [7]. Larger receptive fields enable contextual learning over the Transformer modules, and structural and anatomical consistency is preserved at the voxel level in the decoder. This architectural capitulation enables the model to represent rich semantic cues and at the same time preserves the low-level spatial information. The training strategy includes a composite loss function to address the class imbalance and impose contour sensitivity that is prevalent in medical image segmentation challenges [28]. Our model is tested on the publicly available KiTS21 dataset, presenting high-quality annotated kidney tumor CT scan images. Both heavy data augmentation and customized preprocessing are utilized to ensure generalization across different tumor shapes and imaging conditions. Dice Similarity Coefficient, Intersection over Union, and Hausdorff Distance [8] are the quantitative evaluation metrics. The model attains 98% accuracy, which outperforms traditional U-Net, Swin Transformer alone, and other baseline architectures. In addition to numerical improvements, we demonstrate
label: human

text: the model to be significantly more robust across difficult-to-segment tumors, which attests to its applicability to clinical deployment as a consistent and precise tool. 1.1 Background We first confirmed that early diagnosis and treatment are critical for treating one of the most common urological malignancies, renal cell carcinoma. Whilst for expert-drawn manual segmentation of kidney tumors the success is high, it is currently time consuming and observer dependent. The task of automatic delineation of keypoints has increasingly been fulfilled using deep learning models, with the U-Net and its variants being the method of choice due to their localizability and architectural simplicity. However, they still are not able to perceive the high-level context outside their convolutional receptive fields for visually cluttered regions in particular. The Swin Transformer introduces a hierarchical architecture of self-attention, which is more efficient and scalable for visual tasks. Its window-based operation allows localized attention modulation over the overlapping regions, which is more preferable for capturing spatial dependences at different image scales. Nonetheless, for the purpose of organ segmentation learning spatial information can sacrifice fine details in attention pooling especially at boundaries. These compromises provide an opportunity for hybrid modeling, i.e., aggregation of convolutional and transformer models that benefit both from high-level semantic abstraction and low-level structural fidelity in the segmentation results. 1.2 Scope and Motivation In this paper, we present a deep learning hybrid segmentation model for the kidney tumors in terms of structural accuracy and generalization ability. The method solves both boundary vagueness and class imbalance in CT images. We limit the evaluation to the KiTS21 dataset for task-specific validation. The current advanced segmentation methods generally suffer a trade-off between spatial resolution and semantic abstraction. Correct delineation of the boundary of kidney tumor is essential, in favor of decreasing false negative in diagnosis. There is a need for an integrated model that is able to correlate local information with global knowledge and which also extends clinical trustworthiness. 1.3 Objectives and Key Contributions To develop and validate a hybrid deep learning model, including U-Net and Swin Transformer, for better segmentation of kidney tumors. The model aspired to create a trade off between fine-grained localization and context awareness. The performance is
label: human

text: evaluated by standard segmentation metrics on a benchmark dataset. The main contributions of the paper are: ●​ Proposed a mixed-method segmentation model which integrates Swin Transformer blocks into the encoder of U-Net. ●​ Mitigated the problem of class imbalance and boundary ambiguity through a designed loss function and data expansion. ●​ Validated the model on KiTS21 dataset and reached the segmentation accuracy up to 98% together with improvements in DSC, IoU, and Hausdorff Distance. ●​ Quantitatively and qualitatively showed the robustness of the model across various size and shape of different tumors. Unlike previous works, which mainly concentrate on the architectural integration of Swin Transformer with U-Net, our approach focuses on methodological breakthroughs. Specifically, we propose a multi-task composite loss for tumour-boundary sensitive reconstruction, elastic transformation based data augmentation for learning from anatomical variations and intensity-invariant data augmentation to improve cross-scanner robustness. In addition, our pre-processing pipeline supports voxel-wise normalization with structural preservation, which is unique to the Swin-UNETR implementations. 1.4 Organization of the Paper The paper is structured as follows. It starts with the Related Works, where related works about kidney tumour segmentation, from those based on convolutional networks, to Transformer-based models and hybrid approaches. The Methodology section then presents the architecture of the proposed hybrid model, describing the incorporation of Swin Transformer blocks to the U-Net encoder and the design choice for loss function and training pipeline. Experimental In this section, we describe the dataset, preprocessing steps, evaluation metrics and implementation details. The experimental results are described in the Results section with performance evaluation, comparison with baselines, and qualitative segmentation outputs. Finally, Conclusion describes the contributions in this work and future lines of research. II RELATED WORKS Heller et al. (2021) introduced a widespread benchmark (KiTS19 challenge) to assess automatic 3D segmentation algorithms for the kidney and tumor structure from annotated CT images. The challenge released a common dataset and evaluation protocol to stimulate the development of deep learning models in clinical applications. Although the state-of-the-art results have approached clinically relevant kidney segmentation accuracy, tumor segmentation remains challenging with
label: human

text: ambiguous boundaries and heterogeneous morphology. However, a significant challenge lies in the requirement of large amounts of annotated data and the absence of a consensus on the ideal architectures for reproducible tumor segmentation [9]. Da Cruz et al. (2022) proposed a 2.5D CNN model for kidney tumor segmentation in CT images, trying to be suitable for the trade-offs between complexity and memory cost. The approach combines preprocessing, the DeepLabv3+ model with a DPN-131 encoder, and image processing to reduce false positives. Although 3D networks can achieve great segmentation results, they are computationally expensive, so 2.5D networks can be considered as an efficient alternative. The proposed method showed very high accuracy with 99.71% accuracy, even though it had relatively lower sensitivity and Dice scores than those for the full 3D model (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2), suggesting further potential for improvement in the delineation of the tumor boundary [10]. Shen et al. (2021) introduced COTRNet, a convolution-and-transformer network for joint segmentation of kidney, kidney tumor, and kidney cyst on CT images. The model combines the convolutional and transformer layers within the encoder to encode local and global information and share information from the encoder to the decoder using skip connections for better spatial accuracy. Pretrained weights and deep supervision were borrowed for the performance improvement of segmentation. When tested on the KiTS21 dataset, the method reported an average Dice of 61.6%, surface Dice of 49.1%, and tumor Dice of 50.52%, showing promise but also showing a gap in segmenting the precision and the accuracy of tumor boundaries [11]. Zhao et al. (2021) developed a coarse-to-fine-based framework on the nnU-Net for automatic segmentation of the kidney, kidney tumor, and kidney cysts as a potential way to enhance accuracy and efficiency in kidney cancer surgery. The model is a multi-step process, initially setting a coarse segmentation and progressively updating it for better precision. The method obtained 0.9077 average Dice and 0.8262 surface Dice on the KiTS2021 challenge test set and ranked 1st among all the teams. These findings illustrate the ability of the framework to generate good-quality segmentations, which could also be used in clinical practice towards easier preoperative planning [12]. Patel et al. (2024) introduced a complete model for kidney tumor segmentation and classification to support early diagnosis of renal cancer. Their approach applies a 3D-Trans-Residue DenseUnet++ (3D-TR-DUnet++) network for precise segmentation of kidney tumors in the CT images, and afterwards, they perform the tumor classification by using an Adaptive and Attentional Residual Densenet with Gated Recurrent Unit (AA-RD-GRU). This thorough, two-stage method tries to discriminate benign from malignant tumors and provides important knowledge for treatment decisions. We also optimize the parameters of the model by the Modified Crayfish Optimization Algorithm (MCOA) to improve the performance. The
label: human

text: segmentation and classification procedures based on the results of the experiments are superior to other deep learning networks and optimization algorithms, holding great promise for clinical applications in the early diagnosis and treatment of kidney cancer patients [13]. Hu et al. (2024) proposed a new One-to-Multiple Progressive Style Transfer Unsupervised Domain-Adaptive (PSTUDA) framework to segment the kidney and tumor in multi-sequence Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). By unsupervisedly aligning cross-modal features, the proposed method overcomes the issue of labor-intensive annotations in conventional supervised methods. The multi-level style dictionary of PSTUDA can store target-side information at different levels, lightening the load of a single generator in modeling multi-target tasks. Cascading style fusion modules also promote cross-modal alignment as well as structural consistency. Experimental results on the MSKT and KiTS19 datasets achieved substantial improvements, in which the Dice Similarity Coefficients were enhanced not least 1.8% and 3.9%, respectively. It also brought down the model dimensionality to 50% and then cut the computation cost by about 72%, showing the efficiency and feasibility for clinical applications [14]. Raman et al., 2025 evaluated the generalizability of the nnU-NetV2 segmentation model by training on KiTS19 and an independent institutional dataset and testing each model across both cohorts. Models performed best on their native datasets (Dice: 0.85 on KiTS vs. 0.66 external; 0.74 on INST vs. 0.60 external), indicating noticeable performance drops on unseen data. Statistical analyses confirmed significant differences but showed no major variation across tumor size, ethnicity, or gender. The authors conclude that kidney tumor AI models require broader, multi-institutional validation and adaptive strategies to ensure reliable clinical deployment [15]. Choi et al. (2024) presented a Squeeze-and-Excitation (UNEs) model for those scans and developed a model in which transformer layers were replaced by Squeeze and Excitation (SE) layers in order to be more computationally efficient and to automate the detection of tumors detection CT scans in mammograms. The model had better quality in tumor segmentation with the organ and tumor being segmented together, and adding information of the organ improved its performance. The findings of their study also indicate the importance of considering organ context in training for accurate localization and segmentation of the tumor [16]. Deng et al. (2024) proposed the DWR-SegFormer network, which tries to generalize kidney tumor segmentation on CT images into clear cell and papillary renal cell carcinoma. The model encoder is built with MiT-B0 which can focus on the long-range dependence, and the multi-branch DWR decoder are designed to fuse the multi-scale information efficiently to improve

This comprehensive comparison enables a clearer understanding of segmentation accuracy and boundary delineation across existing methods. 2.1 Research Gap​ Although much success has been obtained in segmenting kidney tumors, there are still several challenges that make it difficult to apply these existing models in clinical settings. One major problem is the loss of uniformity in the delineation of the tumor boundary caused by heterogeneous morphological tumor types. Despite the presence of such methods, most (such as those based on 3D CNNs or U-Net architectures) still cannot perform accurate contouring of irregular or very small tumors as a result of limited training data and computational resources. Additionally, models rely on manually annotated datasets that are time-consuming and subject to human mistakes. These limitations obstruct the clinical application and scaling-up of the segmentation systems in real-time. In addition, most existing models do not take into account
label: human

text: the highly variable kidney and tumor sizes among patients, which are likely to have a detrimental effect on the generalization performance across different data sources. To cope with these limitations, in this paper, we propose a novel multi-scale method for precise tumor boundary delineation with a combination of local and global feature extraction. Our model considerably enhances the accuracy of tumor detection at various sizes and shapes, thanks to the integration of the advanced segmentation methods and adaptive attention mechanism. It alleviates the dependence on a large amount of annotated data by using self-supervised learning and transfer learning to handle the problem of the annotation bottleneck. Moreover, the integration of an efficient postprocessing unit reduces false positives, resulting in a more consistent performance between different clinical cases. This method is more robust for providing near real-time segmentation in clinical use and can be applicable to various patient populations. III METHODOLOGY​ The first approach for kidney tumor segmentation is a hybrid deep learning architecture that concatenates the encoding/decoding structure of U-Net with a transformer-based attention model [18]. This model benefits from the U-Net's powerful localization ability to achieve accurate segmentation of the kidney and the tumor boundaries. To better capture the context, we introduce a Swin Transformer into the encoder path so that it is able to capture global dependencies and multi-scale features. The model of the current framework has the advantages of effectively segmenting tumors with different shapes and sizes, which are manifested in solving the border ambiguity of tumors and the morphological diversity. The model is trained with KiTS21 dataset and its class imbalance issue was resolved, so that it can enhance segmentation accuracy. Aside from that, for the complex characteristics of tumor morphology and size, the personalized loss functions (i.e., Dice loss with weight) are used to improve the performance of segmentation [19]. This hybrid strategy has good segmentation performance, and is efficient and can be used in clinical applications where accurate and rapid results are demanded. To guarantee the robustness of the proposedTM segmentation framework, dropout layers and batch normalization were added for preventing overfitting and stabilizing the training process. The early stopping using validation was employed to stop training when performance of the model started stagnating and grid search for hyperparameter tuning optimized various parameters. In addition, a 5-fold cv in the training set was conducted to avoid overfitting and ensure the resulting results generalize well across different data splits. We recognize that, despite serving as a dependable benchmark, the size and diversity of the KiTS21 dataset is limited and we intend to investigate further validation on larger multicenter datasets as well as augmentation and transfer learning to improve
label: human

text: robustness in diverse clinical settings. The structure of the proposed hybrid model is depicted in Figure 1. Obtained from the official Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) challenge, KiTS21 datasets provide a collection of realistic 3D CT scans, with real-world clinical complexities (e.g., renal parenchyma and tumor heterogeneity) present in both the public and private test sets. It consists of heterogeneous cases with different tumor sizes, shapes, and stages, which is a suitable dataset to train a robust segmentation model. Moreover, the publicly available consistent annotation guidelines of the dataset enable reproducibility, cross-study comparison, and large-scale model evaluation [20]. The KiTS21 dataset includes a total of 300 CECT volumes with pixel-wise annotations of CT images for the kidney, tumor, and cyst. For this study, 80% of the data was used for training and the rest for testing; a good mix of tumor complexities was well distributed in both training and testing sets. For each scan, there are volumetric slices with ground truth masks (labels) to facilitate supervised 3D segmentation. Preprocessing included normalization in Hounsfield units, axial slice

Important features, such as voxel spacing, range of intensity, and anatomical homogeneity, were preserved to ensure that data integrity was maintained regarding the model training. 3.2 Data Augmentation and Preprocessing Due to a restricted diversity of available training samples and the necessity to make the model generalizable to unseen data, we have employed an extensive data augmentation pipeline. With a strong pre-processing pipeline in place, here we describe the design of an encoder where Swin Transformer blocks are used to capture long-range dependencies. 3.3 Swin Transformer-Based Encoder The encoder part in this work is built upon Swin Transformer, aiming to incorporate global and long-range context of visual contents more efficiently. Our encoder takes as input full 3D CT patches of size 96 × 96 × 96 voxels created by densely evenly cropped non-overlapping 3D patches prior to the embedding. This architecture maintains the volume context information rather than limiting the analysis to 2D slices or limited 2.5D stacks. Different from traditional CNNs with a shallower and local receptive field size, the Swin Transformers are constructed in a hierarchical manner to gradually harvest context information through windows-based self-attention [22]. Each input CT image is initially divided into non-overlapping patches, which are considered as tokens. These tokens are then embedded linearly and traversed through multiple Swin Transformer blocks. The differences enter the way attention is computed locally within windows and shifted to mediate across windows. This SW Attention mechanism helps the model to store local information as well as global context, which is important for segmenting structures like renal tumor having different size, shape and location. To balance global representation with fine localization, we employ a U-Net-based decoder, which is explained next. 3.4 U-Net Decoder The decoder of the proposed hybrid model keeps the classical U-Net architecture that is known in medical images to perform well in spatial localization. U-Net uses symmetric encoding and decoding paths with skip connections between pairs of corresponding layers on the encoder side and the decoder side. These skip connections play a crucial role in retaining spatial resolution by allowing the decoder to recover fine-grained structural details lost during the encoding (downsampling) process. Without skip connections the decoder would have to work purely on compressed feature maps which may blur or even remove sharp segmentation boundaries – a critical problem in medical images where tumor margins are frequently hard to define. The results of the inferences were considered visually and quantitatively focusing on potential precision in tumor boundaries and volumetric tissue consistency between slices. 4.1 Experimental Setup The whole model was written in Python 3.10 with PyTorch 2.0.1 for deep learning and utilizing CUDA 11.8 to accelerate on GPU. During training, 60% of the images were raw and 40% were augmented. Augmentation was performed on the training set only; validation and test sets were imaged unprocessed. text: 4.4 Ablation Study We analyzed the contribution of each one in ablation studies. Dice decreased from 0.91 to 0.86 after removing Swin Transformer blocks. Accuracy dropped 2.3% without the boundary-aware loss. Overfitting worsened and generalization decreased with removal of elastic augmentations (PR-AUC: 0.89 to 0.84). These findings validate the importance of both architectural and methodological pieces for the performance of the model. V CONCLUSION In this paper, a hybrid DL model combined with U-Net and Swin Transformers was designed for precise kidney tumor segmentation in CT. By integrating the strong spatial localization of U-Net and the powerful global context learning of Swin Transformer, our proposed model substantially overcomes typical challenges in both CNN-based and transformer-only works. The Swin Transformer-based encoder allows richer feature extraction, and the U-Net-style decoder helps preserve significant anatomic features for better tumor boundary delineation. Experiments on the KiTS21 dataset validate that the presented approach achieves superior performance to state-of-the-arts, including U-net, nnU-net, COTRNet , DeepLabV3+ and DWR-SegFormer in terms of Dice Similarity Coefficient, Intersection over Union as well as F1 scores among various-size tumors. Besides, the model also demonstrates increased boundary consistency in terms of Hausdorff distance and reduced variance of prediction, and remains stable in face of difficult conditions like low contrast or irregular tumor contour. Generalization and robustness are further improved by using a customized loss function and heavy data augmentation. Moreover, low bias in volumes suggests potential clinical application for planning treatment. The performance of the model was thus promising but it has only been evaluated on a single dataset. In the future, we will consider validating the method on a larger multi-center dataset and extending our work to achieve full 3D volumetric segmentation over other datasets as well as adding attention-guided refinement modules to gain more accurate boundary and improve its clinical usability. text: MicroPack-HE: A Packing-Aware Lightweight Homomorphic Encryption Framework for Secure Analytics in Resource-Constrained IoT Networks Abstract- The explosive growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has further highlighted the requirement to safely perform data analytics over resource-constrained networks, for which existing encryption primitives are insufficient for supporting in-network computation and traditional homomorphic encryption (HE) is not practically computable. Recently-proposed light-weight HE schemes trade-off either security assurances or architectural overhead by employing adaptive, federated or multi-stage constructions and thus lack deployability on low-power computation devices. To mitigate these challenges, we propose the MicroPack-HE, a new packing-aware lightweight homomorphic encryption framework for resource-limited IoT systems in this work. MicroPack-HE relies on a constraint additive core making it simple to handle first-order aggregation tasks as well as controlling such computational and memory overhead. The main novelty contributes to a fixed-size plaintext packing method, where multiple low-bit sensor samples are packed together into one ciphertext by an efficient bit-level tiling approach, and thus greatly reduces encryption times of the device and the communication cost. In contrast to FHE schemes, MicroPackHE purposefully limits the homomorphic expressiveness such that it only supports addition and one small scaling multiplication for efficient running on 32-bit microcontrollers without specialized hardware. Computationally intensive assistance components are pre-computed and stored at the cloud side, so that the IoT devices do the negligible arithmetic operations in encryption. Experimental results on ESP32-class hardware show that MicroPack-HE reduces encryption latency by 41.6% compared to the off-the-shelf Paillier-based ones and energy demand is 38.2% less per transmission. Effective packing helps save 57.4% the size of ciphertext and network overhead. However, with these improvements the framework remains semantically secure under standard additive HE assumption and accomplishes data integrity without expensive message authentication. The results confirm that MicroPack-HE is a feasible and efficient privacy-preserving analytics approach for emerging IoT networks. Keywords-Lightweight homomorphic encryption, IoT security, resource-constrained networks, ciphertext packing, privacy-preserving analytics, secure data aggregation I Introduction​ The explosive growth of Internet of Things (IoT) has turned the traditional data collection model into these highly distributed, data-intensiveness ecology [1][2], which can enable large-scale sensing, monitoring, and analytics at network edge. The present-day IoT deployments cover wide range of application domains like smart cities [3][4], industrial automation, health monitoring and intelligent traffic system [5], where millions to billions of low-powered sensor nodes incessantly stream sensitive data. Aiming at reducing latency, decreasing bandwidth consumption and alleviating the reliance on cloud computing [6][7], edge-assisted and in network analytics has become extremely important. Nevertheless, such a
label: human

text: migration brings with it huge trust and security issues: raw sensor data are not rarely streamed over untrusted networks or collected by semi-trusted aggregation nodes. Preserving the privacy of data, while keeping the possibility of meaningful computation not a trivial task and poses some fundamental questions on resource-limited environments as an IoT device. Existing encryption techniques, although widely adopted to secure data at rest and during transmission, naturally preclude computation over encrypted values, requiring decryption at intermediate nodes, and hence exposure secrets [8][9]. Homomorphic encryption (HE) can provide a practicable approach since it allows to directly compute over ciphertexts, but the most schemes for HE or even fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) that have been proposed so far involve extremely high computational, memory and energy costs. Such schemes rely upon extensive integer arithmetic, intricate noise control, and multiple ciphertext operations which are not feasible for the low-end microcontrollers found in IoT devices [10][11]. All recent existing light-weight or partially homomorphic solutions even, unnecessarily bring architectural complexity, via adaptive protocols, federated learning paths [8][9], multi-stage encryption etc. reducing the practicality and deployability on resource and communication constrained networks [12]. A crucial but still widely unaddressed vacuum is the need for packing aware: lightweight homomorphic encryption solutions tailored to abide by the data properties and operational needs of IoT sensing workloads. In most real-world applications, sensor readings are low-bit signals that may be collected periodically [13] and naturally lend themselves for aggregation such as addition or averaging. Currently, most of the lightweight HE schemes only encrypt per reading independently and the frequency of encryption is too high that lead to over-inflated communications overheads and superfluous energy consumption. Furthermore, most designs favour cryptographic generality over system efficiency [14], and do not take advantage of fixed-size data representation, bounded-arithmetic and asymmetric workload distribution between devices and the cloud. At present, however, there does not exist a publicly available practical HE framework that is able to jointly optimize computation complexity, ciphertext compactness and deployability onto commodity IoT hardware. To overcome these drawbacks, in this paper, we present MicroPack-HE, which is a packing-aware light-weight homomorphic encryption (LWHE) system suited for secure analytics on resource-constrained IoT networks. MicroPack-HE is designed primarily to support efficient private data aggregation by using a bounded additive homomorphic encryption (BAHE) core combined with a fixed-size plaintext packing approach, which packs multiple low-bit sensor readings into one ciphertext. By deliberately constraining homomorphic expressiveness to addition and a single delicate scalar multiplication, as well as offloading computational expensive mechanisms onto the cloud via precomputation, MicroPack-HE can achieve low device-side overheads while maintaining semantic security under standard additive HE assumptions [15][16]. The key objectives are: (i) to minimize the latency and energy consumption of encryption operations on microcontroller class devices, (ii) to reduce communication overhead via a lightweight ciphertext-packing scheme, and (iii) to substantiate the feasibility of lightweight homomorphic analytics through real-device experiments. The performances demonstrate that

text: MicroPack-HE is a scalable and deployable approach for privacy-preserving analytics in future IoT systems. The rest of this paper is structured as follows. We summarize in Section II the related work including the lightweight cryptography and homomorphic encryption for resource-constrained IoT scenario, and point out the research gap that we fill. Section III describes the system model, threat model and security assumption. Section IV describes the design of the proposed MicroPack-HE, which incorporates the bounded additive homomorphic encryption core, plaintext packing scheme, and processing mechanisms ( encryption/decryption operations, cloud-side precomputation), followed by complexities analysis. Experimental setup and performance evaluation procedures are explained in Section V. Section VI presents the experimental results, comparison with other methods and ablation study. Finally, the last section concludes the paper and points out possible future research directions. II Literature Review Kuldeep, Zhang Dual (2021), problem on data privacy and communication efficiency in internet of things (IoT) was studied via compressive sensing (CS) as a joint compression-encryption scheme. Albeit promising for massive sensor data processing, even computationally-secure CS schemes turn out to be susceptible to ciphertext-only attacks under short signal length due their own recovery conditions, which is common in the case of IoT sensing as in [1]. They addressed this challenge by introducing an energy concealment (EC) based encryption scheme which has the property of providing perfect secrecy and does not rely on an additional secure key delivery channel. Even though their solution reduced energy consumption and memory footprint significantly in comparison to AES on TelosB motes, it does not support computation over encrypted data which limits the application of storing encrypted primitives for secure in-network analytics. Palaparthy et al. (2022) [2] moved to attacking protocol-level lightweight security, conducted a comparative evaluation of IoTsecurity protocols including LSMWP, CoAP with DTLS andefficient cryptographic primitives forconstrained devices. They performed a study of the cryptographic strength, key management resilience, integrity-protection and processing overhead in their work. Although the authors present very interesting trade-offs between security and efficiency, the considered protocols are intrinsically communication-oriented ones, that do not take into account privacy-preserving data processing or encrypted aggregation concepts which are a must-have feature in today's IoT-driven analytics. Thakor et al. (2021) [3] presented a detailed comparison on lightweight cryptographic algorithms developed for IoT devices with limited resources and compared over fifty existing schemes and the most recent NIST new candidates. The analysis performed by them focused on the implementation cost as well as the software and hardware performance, resistance against cryptanalytic attacks. The authors pointed out that, while lightweight cryptography can save a lot of resources in real applications, most schemes only consider the aspects of data privacy and authentication with little or no attention to secure computation or analytics over encrypted data. Ding et al. (2021) [4] focus on IoT security in terms of authentication and presented a lightweight authentication scheme for anonymous entities in the IoT system with elliptic curve
label: human

text: cryptography (ECC) and signcryption. Their scheme lowered the computational and communication costs with a provable security guarantee under the RO model. Despite these benefits, identity authentication is the only secure operation provided by the work and no integration with encrypted data aggregation and privacy preserving computation, which are two functionalities that are more in demand when it comes to IoT based systems for big data. Aljaedi et al. (2025) [5], explored lightweight encryption techniques from the perspective of an unholy trinity that combined quantum encryption ideas, chaotic maps, and metaheuristic learning. Their method had excellent statistical security characteristics and was robust against many attack models. Yet, it is tailored for multimedia content encryption as opposed to low-bit sensor readings, and its computationally expensive nature makes it infeasible for real-time analytics or homomorphic computation on microcontroller-class IoT devices. Li et al. (2021) [6] were one of the first who brought homomorphic encryption to IoT environments and discussed a lightweight privacy-preserving protocol in industrial IoT applications. Under their approach, the use of a user-preserving protocol to perform cryptographic computation over encrypted data in untrusted cloud servers was made possible. While few computational optimisations were proposed, however the scheme comes at a non-trivial overhead and does not take benefit of data packing or bound arithmetic to scale well on tight edge devices. Sheela et al. (2025) [7] Generalized the concept of homomorphic encryption to reinforcement learning centered WSN's via combining HE with Quantum-safe cryptography for the purpose of model parameter aggregation. The framework has the extremely good privacy pros against the attackers and a high network gap, but it comes at a cost of significant architectural complexity involving cooperative decryption and an iterative learning cycle which becomes unsuitable for elementary type sensing nodes having severe energy and memory limitation. Ali et al. (2023) [8] combined homomorphic encryption and block chain technology for better privacy preservation in IoT based health system. Theirs system supported encrypted computation, fine-grained access control and auditability using smart contracts. Even though it is resilient, the aggregated overhead of blockchain and HE makes deployment possible only on moderately powerful nodes; low-power IoT sensors are hence prevented from being involved in encrypted analytics directly. Mohammed et al. (2025) which is a taxonomy based survey on lightweight cryptographic schemes for industrial IoT providing a classification of the schemes based on algorithmic type, deployment situation and performance attributes [9]. Their work also stressed the increase in demand towards hybrid and energy-aware secure solutions while it reveals a dearth of scalable cryptographic constructions that trade-off computation, communication, and security for heterogeneous IIoT environments. Zhang et al. (2024) [10] introduced an anonymous data sharing scheme for resource-limited IoT devices by utilizing elliptic curve operations and blockchain based integrity checking. The comparative advantage of the scheme is that it is more efficient in terms of computation costs with privacy and revocation using elliptic curve instead to bilinear pairings. But, as with other data-sharing platforms, its focus is primarily on secure transmission and verification, not encrypted data analytics. Active and passive homomorphic encryption integration with federated learning for smart cities was addressed by Alqazzaz (2025) [11], they proposed an optimization technique to

Although it works at system level, the strategy assumes relatively powerful edge nodes and is not applicable to microcontroller-level IoT things with respect to iterative model updates and encryption-heavy workloads. Radhakrishnan et al. [12] ran the AES-128, SPECK and ASCON algorithms on constrained IoT boards in a comparative analysis of lightweight cryptographic algorithms. They concluded that while some algorithms obtain a favorable performance, all the approaches are essentially non-homomorphic and require decryption prior to processing -at least partially- sensitive data during computation. Their construction showed better computational efficiency than that of traditional public-key systems. However, the encryption and decryption latencies still are too high for continuous sensing applications, and no packing mechanism is adopted to decrease transmission overhead. Thabit et al. (2022) [14] proposed a dual layer lightweight homomorphic cryptosystem for cloud computing that makes use of symmetric encryption and multiplicative homomorphism. The approach enhances security and execution time compared to classical cloud cryptosystems, however it is targeted for the cloud environment and disregards the limited hardware of IoT end devices. Halder and Newe (2022) [15] introduced SmartCrypt - a symmetric homomorphic encryption technique for storage and analytics of secure IIoT timeseries data. Their system showed significant improvements in query processing and scalability. However, SmartCrypt targets cloud-assisted architectures and does not specifically minimize encryption frequency or ciphertext size at the sensor level. Amgbara et al. [16] surveyed lightweight machine learning models for personal IoT security, and discussed the tradeoff between model complexity, accuracy and resources. Even though its main focus lays in anomaly detection and intrusion prevention, there are still existing unsolved issues regarding data privacy and encrypted processing that are beyond the reach of a purely ML-based only approach. Hendaoui et al. (2025) [17] introduced EPAD, a PP anomaly detection method that merges optimized homomorphic encryption with federated learning. While EPAD greatly reduces computational cost compared with the traditional HE based IDS systems, it still relies on federated learning facilities and encrypted model exchanges which only holds for ultra-limited IoT nodes. Finally, Hsu et al. (2023) [18] focused on secure group communication in Internet of Medical Things and presented a lightweight group key agreement protocol using XOR operation and symmetric polynomial. Their scheme acquires low computational and communication overhead, but it only supports secure key establishment without the support of encrypted data aggregation and computation. 2.1 Research Gap Overall, the related works show that there has been a great development in lightweight cryptography (PRF), authentication and privacy preserving IoT protocols. Nevertheless, existing works either (i) do not enable computation over encrypted data, (ii) are based on heavy homomorphic or federated architectures, or (iii) do not consider optimizing the computation results for low-bit sensor workloads as well as for reducing the size and

text: frequency of encryption operations. This gap in the state-of-the-art supports the justification for a packing-aware, bounded homomorphic encryption scheme which allows efficient secure aggregation in a way which can be realized on microcontroller-class IoT devices and this is precisely the goal achieved by our MicroPack-HE framework. III System and Threat Model The system follows a three-tier IoT architecture consisting of resource-constrained sensing devices, aggregation gateways, and a cloud-based analytics server. IoT devices are assumed to be ESP32-class microcontrollers with 32-bit processors, limited memory, and strict energy constraints, capable of performing only lightweight arithmetic operations without cryptographic acceleration [19][20]. Each device periodically collects low-bit sensor readings and encrypts them locally before transmission. Gateways forward and aggregate encrypted data without accessing plaintext, while the cloud performs homomorphic aggregation and supports cryptographic precomputation. The adversary is modeled as honest-but-curious, where gateways and cloud servers follow protocol specifications but attempt to infer sensitive information from observed ciphertexts or aggregated outputs. The attacker may passively eavesdrop on communication channels but is not assumed to compromise device hardware or secret keys. The primary security goals are to ensure confidentiality of individual sensor readings during transmission and aggregation [21][22], and to maintain data integrity through lightweight authentication mechanisms. Under these assumptions, MicroPack-HE enables efficient privacy-preserving data analytics while adhering to the strict resource limitations of IoT devices. 3.1 Preliminaries 3.1.1 Additive Homomorphic Encryption Additive Homomorphic Encryption (AHE) allows the addition of ciphertexts representing plaintexts and for the decryption of the result in-order to be equal to a sum of plaintext values. Some, (but 𝑚1 𝑚2 not all) such schemes also allow an encrypted value to be multiplied by a small public scalar. Unlike fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) [23][24], AHE does not require costly noise management and ciphertext refresh operations, which is more suitable for energy and resource-constrained IoT devices. MicroPack-HE leverages this bounded additive homomorphic property to enable secure aggregation of sensor reading and uniformly limit the set of allowed operations in order to decrease computational and storage overhead. 3.1.2 Security Assumptions Security definition for MicroPack-HE MicroPack-HE assumes semantic security in the standard model of additive homomorphic encryption, ciphertexts are indistinguishable under chosen-plaintext attacks (IND-CPA). The framework runs in an honest-but-curious adversarial setting, where intermediate gateways and cloud servers adhere to protocol

We do not assume there is any collusion between the cloud and compromised devices, and that private keys are protected in IoT devices. Integrity in LS-AP encourages keeping lightweight message authentication codes so that ciphertext tampering and replays with respect to the homomorphic engine is detectable. 3.1.3 Microcontroller Constraints The intended deployment targets for MicroPack-HE are microcontroller devices in the ESP32 class with tight RAM and flash constraints, and strict energy requirements. Such devices have no hardware support for large integer arithmetic and cryptographic acceleration, and consequently conventional public-key encryption or fully homomorphic encryption are impracticable. Therefore, encryption operations should be lightweight, in terms of computations, memory occupancy and execution time predictability [26][27]. MicroPack-HE Framework Design 4.1 Design Overview The Micropack-HE is click-mining oriented, and has been 8202built to be privacy preserving data aggregation tool for IoT type of environments which involves sensors working in ultra constrained computational, memory and energy circumstances [28][29]. In contrast with traditional lightweight cryptosystems that concentrate only on secure transmission and provide no support for encrypted computation [2], or homomorphic frameworks which introduce significant overhead due to high arithmetic complexity and architectural layers [6], MicroPack-HE follows a minimalistically-computation-aware design philosophy. The approach is based on the bounded additive homomorphic encryption core which only allows addition and a small scalar multiplication, and does not require a fully homomorphic expressiveness otherwise imposed by FHE-based approaches [14], thus avoiding the computational cost of such fully expressive schemes. In addition to minimising the encryption frequency and communication overhead, MicroPack-HE makes use of fixed-sized plaintext packaging scheme where multiple low-bit sensor readings are combined into one plaintext based on bit-level tiling technique, selected due to less-entropy of periods and typicality representation in IoT data streams [30]. We intentionally offload computational overhead key-related precomputations and parameter setup to the cloud layer, as it has been observed that the use of cloud can greatly increase system efficiency while maintaining security assumptions [15]. On the device side, encryption uses exclusively simple modular arithmetic that runs on ESP32-type micro-controller which provides predictable time of execution and modest energy requirements. With concerted efforts in the optimization of cryptographic expressiveness, packing efficiency and workload balance, MicroPack-HE strikes a realistic point between security, deployability and practicality that has not been achieved by previous lightweight encryption [3] or homomorphic IoT framework [7]. text: A Continuous-Time Causal Graph Learning Framework for Predicting and Mitigating Cascading Failures in Global Supply Chains Abstract- Global supply chains face increasing exposure to rapidly propagating disruptions triggered by geopolitical conflicts, climate-related shocks, and operational instabilities. Existing predictive approaches, including recent causal graph neural networks, remain limited by static causal structures, discrete-time reasoning, and post-hoc counterfactual analysis. These constraints reduce their ability to anticipate high-velocity cascade effects and to recommend proactive, cost-effective interventions. This work introduces CT-SCaLE, a novel Continuous-Time Structural Causal Learning Engine that unifies Neural ODE-based temporal dynamics, end-to-end differentiable causal structure learning, and counterfactual contrastive representation learning into a single predictive and decision-support architecture. CT-SCaLE learns both the evolving causal topology and the temporal propagation dynamics of disruptions, allowing the model to capture time-varying influences, multi-tier propagation patterns, and realistic feedback loops that traditional DAG-based causal GNNs cannot represent. Evaluations on SupplyGraph and Time-Series Risk datasets show that CT-SCaLE improves disruption prediction accuracy by up to 14.7%, increases early-warning lead time by 22%, and reduces simulated cascade size under optimized interventions by 31.4%, significantly outperforming advanced baselines. A central novelty is a built-in intervention planner based on models that uses multi-step counterfactual simulations to discover the minimum-cost actions that can mitigate or steer cascading failures. This addresses a crucial unmet need, predicting not just disruptions, but actionable causal explanations and mitigations. By incorporating prediction, explanation and intervention optimization in a continuous time framework, CT-SCaLE opens a new frontiers for supply chain analytics driving more resilient and adaptive global operations. Keywords-Causal Graph Neural Networks, Supply Chain Resilience, Neural ODEs, Causal Discovery, Counterfactual Learning, Cascading Failures, Intervention Optimization, Graph Machine Learning, Risk Prediction, Continuous-Time Modeling I Introduction Global supply chains have become complex and highly-linked, multi-level networked systems with localized disruptions cascading to system levels. The recent past has demonstrated that cascading failures are no longer rare, slow-moving outliers but high-velocity events grounded in geopolitics, extreme climate and infectious disease as well as infrastructural fault lines. Trade barriers, port closures, energy scarcity and regional conflicts now spread across borders within days or even hours rather than the previous months, quickly overpowering conventional risk cushions and recovery systems [1], [2]. Empirical works on the flow of global shipping, commodity trade, and supply chains of critical materials show how disturbances tend to trigger non-linear ripple effects whereby losses propagate well beyond the directly disrupted nodes [3][4][5]. Although organizations are paying more attention to making resilience more resilient, they tend toward a reactive rather proactive response. It waits till the disruption occurs before stopping the propagation of
label: human

text: failure [6], [7]. This increasing disparity between rate of disruption and latency to a decision underscores the importance of predictive models that can foresee cascading failures before they happen and direct interventions in time. There is previous work that used machine learning and network analysis to predict supply chain risks, utilizing graph representations to capture inter-firm relationships and disruption spillover [8][9][10]. However, the vast majority of graph machine learning methods remain essentially correlation-based [11][12], learning statistical relationships rather than causal dependencies in failure propagation. Recently, the advanced causal graph neural networks employ a static directed acyclic graphs and implicitly assume that the causal effects are time-invariant and acyclic [17], [18]. There are some obvious flaws with this kind of assumption that do not correspond to the reality of supply chains: 1) asset strength scores change over time in real-world networks, as do loop/circuit counts; 2) sources of disruption appear and disappear when looking at the graph locally changes in response to human activity. Discretetime models increase unresponsiveness still more by binning events into coarse time bins, which may miss early cascades or see late ones [11][12]. In addition, counterfactual reasoning in previous models tends to be used post factum to rationalize predictions as opposed to being embedded into an optimization approach that considers actively identifying and evaluating prevention strategies under cost and timing constraints [15][16]. Consequently, existing approaches fall short in providing the real-time decision-driven approach for addressing cascading failures. To overcome these shortcomings, in this paper we present CT-SCaLE (Continuous-Time SCaLing Engine), for cascading failure prediction and mitigation in global supply chains. In contrast to prior methods, CT-SCaLE learns simultaneously the changing topology of causal supply chain networks and the continuous-time evolution dynamics of shock spreading. The proposed framework uses Neural Ordinary Differential Equations to represent high-resolution temporal change and design time varying causal influence, delayed effects and feedback-based escalation. The parsing of causal structure is then trained within the end-to-end pipeline, and can therefore adapt its causal graph as network conditions evolve. Crucially, CT-SCaLE is intervention-aware: it natively includes counterfactual reasoning in the learning and decision cascade, allowing for simulation and evaluation of pro-active mitigation measures over retrospective justifications. By integrating prediction, causality, and intervention planning in the presence of disturbances into a continuous-time framework, CT-SCaLE is positioned to satisfy the needs common to contemporary supply chains that are susceptible to disruptions. II Literature Review 2.1 Cascading Failures and Systemic Risk in Supply Chains Global supply chains are characterized by high levels of interdependence, which naturally render them susceptible to cascading failures, in which isolated perturbations spread throughout layers and geographies. Early system-oriented investigations inform the ways in which national contingencies such as pandemics, climate catastrophes, cyber attacks, and geopolitical spats can turn multiple supply chain layers fragile to congested bottlenecks and extreme shortages (Khan et al., 2022) [1]. These systemic risks have been accentuated by the growing use of outsourcing and lean operating practices that improve efficiency at the cost of resilience. Yang et al. (2021) [2] quantitatively investigated this issue by constructing a model of underload-driven cascading failures and showed that demand shocks can induce out-of-proportion system collapse despite mechanisms including safety stock and backup suppliers. Subsequent to this, network cascading failure models have been used for large-scale physical and trade networks. Xu et al. (2024) [3] studied the impact of port-level disruptions within the Global Container Shipping Network and demonstrated that single-node failures could lead to traffic redistribution and overload across maritime logistics networks. (2021)[5] studied the disruption in the global plastic waste trade and showed that capacity overloads spread across international trade networks if reactions are not coordinated. These works taken together support the finding that cascading failures are highly nonlocal, nonlinear and network-structure dependent—and yet we still rely on static models, using but not learning from networks. 2.2 Ripple Effect Analysis and Recovery-Focused Strategies Related studies have investigated the ripple effect by simulating propagation of disruptions in multi-echelon supply chains and analysing post-disruption recovery strategies. KEk et al. [4] employed discrete-event simulation for the analysis of disruption propagation in the copper sector and reported limited sourcing flexibility and lack of adequate safety stock as dominant amplification factors. Manupati et al. Further analyzed recovery strategies in complex supply chain networks and employed blockchain-enabled smart contracts and genetic-algorithm optimization to examine pre- and post-disruption decision-making (2022) [6]. Although these methods can offer significant managerial guidelines, they mainly aim at optimizing responses after disasters break out but not predicting or controlling cascade onset in the early stage. Organizational and managerial aspects Park and Singh (2023) [7] stressed the significance of risk alert tools using big data analytics impact, as they demonstrated empirically that strong IT and analytical capabilities are correlated positively with firms’ capacity to anticipate risks. However, these alert tools usually function as early-warning systems and do not explicitly simulate how risks spread through a supply network in an interdependent manner. Moreover, other reviews on resilience in various domains such as automotive, pharmaceuticals, shipping, semiconductor suggest the importance of proactive adaptive mitigation strategies though they do not provide a comprehensive causal-dynamic prediction framework (Maheshwari & Jaggi, 2024 [10] ), Xiong et al., 2025 [11]). 2.3 Data-Driven Risk Prediction and Digital Supply Chain Surveillance Given the rapid increase in heterogeneous digital data types, machine learning and artificial intelligence have recently been playing significant roles in supply chain risk analytics. Brintrup et al. (2024) [12] proposed the idea of Digital Supply Chain Surveillance, use AI to uncover hidden dependencies and increase visibility across an opaque supply networks. Related work has utilized the event-driven IoT data and deep learning in order to predict logistics failure during natural hazards, with high prediction accuracies but dominated by black-box sequence models (Alzahrani & Asghar, 2023 [13]). Fraud detection is another area where ML has been considered useful in detecting unusual transactions, or operational quirks (though predominantly correlated detection rather than causally for intervention planning) (Lokanan & Maddhesia, 2025 [8]). Finally, system-level modelling methods have also been proposed for the evaluation of infrastructure-supply chain interdependencies. Oliver et al. (2022) [15] integrated model-based systems engineering (MBSE) with discrete-event simulation to assess

By contrast, in the context of power [Salehpour et al., 2022] and smart grid networks [Ghasemi et al., 2023], similar cascading failure analyses show that considering heterogeneous role composition and component dependencies results in better prediction performance. Although refined methodologies have been developed, these frameworks are still domain specific and do not include learning of generalizable mechanisms to evolve acausal structure. 2.4 Graph Neural Networks and Network-Aware Prediction Models Graph learning is such a powerful paradigm for capturing inter-firm dependencies and spread of disruption. Yang et al. (2024) [18] utilized graph-based models and showed that inter-firm relations enhance the predictive value for post-hazard firm-level sales changes, compared to non-network-based baselines. Further extending GNNs with neurosymbolic reasoning Kosasih and Brintrup (2022) [19] (GNNR), discoveries of hidden supply chain relationships that improve structural visibility can be made. These approaches validate the benefit of relational learning, but are mainly for a purely static or discretetime analysis, without taking into account the causal dynamics. Recent research is becoming more aware that predictive accuracy alone suffices neither for risk prevention. Wyrembek et al. (2025) [17] stated that causal machine learning is key to intervention planning, where decision-makers can reason over “what if” situations corresponding to alternative managerial interventions. But existing methods relying on the causal GNNs often utilize static or slowly evolving causal graphs, are applicable only to acyclic relations, and treat counterfactual analysis as a post process rather than integrated with dynamic decision making. 2.5 Research Gap and Motivation Throughout the literature, three drawbacks remain. To begin with, existing cascading failure research is based on static simulation models that are incapable of prediction and adaptation. Furthermore, the machine learning and GNN-based methods we study mainly cover correlations or static network effects, making it difficult to model time-varying causality and feedback loops. Third, despite its potential, causal and counterfactual design is still not real-time assisted intervention optimization at risk prediction tasks, making it impractical for proactive cascades suppression. This motivates the design of a causality-driven learning framework for continuous-time setting, which can simultaneously predict disruption propagation and optimize mitigation actions together, where this is the basis of our proposed CT-SCaLE model. III Problem Formulation To do this, we define a global supply-chain network infusing dynamics and causality into it as a dynamical system evolving continuously with time. The aim is to forecast the initiation and spread of cascading disruptions [14], as well as to recommend the best interventions to minimize their consequences given resources and budget limitations.

The prediction is evaluated on the SupplyGraph dataset by employing same training–testing splits for fair comparison. An illustration of the relative accuracies can be seen in Figure 6. Figure 6. Prediction Accuracy Comparison Across Models Figure 6 demonstrates that the proposed CT-SCaLE framework obtains the best prediction accuracy compared to all other tested models. Although Classical Static and Temporal GNNs show some improvements in the performance, they suffer from discretely defined representations of supply chain evolution. The causal GNN can do better than Si, but is limited by static DAG. The non-causal ODE model has smooth temporal learning but does not have causally specific temporal dynamics. In comparison, the performance of CT-SCaLE is better than all baselines with an accuracy gain of about 14.7% compared to the weakest GNN baseline. This finding supports that incorporating causal dynamics in continuous time is able to improve the reliability of predictions in complex and fast evolving supply chains. 6.4 Early-Warning Performance Comparison A timely warning is needed in order to avoid fast disruption propagation as observed in multi-echelon supply chains. text: 6.8 Limitations and Future Work While CT-SCaLE show promising predictive and intervention performances, it may suffer from the issue of data sparsity in multi-tier supply chains since incomplete visibility restricts the accuracy of learned causal relationships. Furthermore, causal identifiability in continuous-time still remains a challenge under strong confounding and when the external conditions are changing rapidly, highlighting the necessity of richer multimodal integration. In the future, we will further improve the real-time deployment efficiency and other time dimension indices, such as adaptive updating, streaming inference and scalable causal structure learning in order to monitor massive dynamic global networks continuously. VII Conclusion In this paper, we presented CT-SCaLE, a causal learning framework in continuous time that incorporates prediction, explanation and intervention planning for how to counter cascading failures in global supply chains. In contrast to the discrete and correlation-based models, in CT-SCaLE changes in causal influence over time and rapid spread of disruption may be captured, allowing better risk management. Experiments makes a 14.7% improvement in the prediction accuracy, increase the lead time of early warning by 22%, and decreases the size of cascade spread by 31.4% comparing to advanced baselines. Combining causal rationale with real-time intervention optimization, CT-SCALE is steering Supply Chain Analytics away from the bands of forecast toward an actioned, control-oriented resilience. text: Blockchain-Integrated Lightweight Machine Learning Framework for Real-Time Threat Detection in IoT Networks Abstract:

text: The explosive growth of IoT networks has raised stakes for cyber threats, demanding effective, scalable and powerful systems to detect them. This paper introduces a new Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) model using edge computing, which combines the blockchain technology and lightweight Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to protect the IoT environment. The solution adopts the decision tree (DT) and K-Nearest Neighbors, to carry out on-the-fly energy-efficient threat classification that tackles limitation of resources in IoT. Features are extracted and dimensions reduced using PCA so that accurate detection with low overhead can be performed. A simplified blockchain is provided to securely record and log network activity and threat events, as while smart contracts automate responses to threats like isolating infected devices or alerting administrators. For low-latency, we deploy Machine Learning (ML) models to the edge of the network for on-premise reasoning, which can quickly detect and mitigate malware. In addition, adaptive model retraining based on periodically aggregated edge data provides robustness against shifting threat patterns. The Lightweight Blockchain-Based Threat Detection (LB-TD) framework presents several advantages, such as secure and unmutated logging, real-time actioning as well as scalability for large IoT networks with a classification accuracy over 95%. Featuring the simplicity of traditional ML algorithms as well as the tamper-resistance of blockchain, our solution provides a practical and efficient mechanism to protect IoT networks against new cyber threats.

text: 3.4.2 K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is yet another simplistic algorithm, selected due to its ability to learn the outliers as it is based on distance from closest point in feature space. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) – New instance is to be classified based on its proximity to the k-nearest instances (neighbors?) in the training dataset. The new point is classified according to the most frequent class of its k-nearest neighbors. This approach works in sparse or high variance data such as most of the IoT networks where network traffic and device behavior can be significantly different. In this structure, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) works by measuring the distance (typically Euclidean or Manhattan) between the input features of a new sample and features of previously supported instances. Afterwards, the point is assigned a label that corresponds to its most common among nearest neighbors. Specifically, as a type of abnormal detection approach, KNN is well adapted to anomaly detection as it compares new data with two profiles about normal and attack behaviors for recognition of outlierness different from the normal or attack pattern. K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is simple and needs very few computations, it is therefore well adapted for implementation on the edge devices that has limited resources in terms of computation and power. Also, due to K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)’s capability on complex decision boundaries, it is likely to be useful for finding minor anomalies from normal pattern which might lead to sophisticated attack.
