text: MindTrace-ID Personalized Cognitive Drift Modeling for Early Mental Health Risk Detection Using Longitudinal Clinical Interviews Abstract-Early detection of mental health decline continues to be a challenge owing to significant inter-individual differences, delayed toxicity profile and the reliance on population-based emotional cues by current artificial intelligence models with limited clinical interpretability. To overcome these drawbacks, in this paper we consider MindTrace-ID, a personalized mental health detection framework capturing cognitive drift with longitudinal micro-behavioral and textual signals rather than the static sentiment ones. This method builds a personalized cognitive baseline for each subject and dynamically scores deviations in terms of syntactic complexity, semantic coherence, interaction rhythm, as well as response latency. These disparate indicators are adjudicated using a drift-aware adaptive inference strategy that prioritizes temporal deviation trends over absolute emotional polarity. To provide transparency and clinical relevance, MindTrace-ID incorporates an interpretable reasoning level which encodes detected drifts in behavior to cognitive markers (e.g., attentional instability, cognitive slowing). The framework performance is tested on the publicly available DAIC-WOZ data base of longitudinal records of interviews with clinical annotations for depression assessment. Results show that our proposed detector obtains a global detection accuracy of 91.6%, which significantly outperforms deep learning baselines trained on population data by 7.8% and simultaneously improved the early-stage risk detection-recommend recall from 79.2% to 88.4%. There are increased benefits for personalized baseline modeling which also decreases false positive rates by 32.5%, and ablation analysis shows that drift cognitive modeling yields a performance increase of 19.3% when compared to static representations. These results demonstrate that personal cognitive drift analysis is a reliable, interpretable, and scalable approach for early clinical intervention in proactive monitoring of mental health. Keywords: Mental health detection; Cognitive drift analysis; Personalized baseline modeling; Explainable artificial intelligence; Longitudinal behavioral analysis; Depression risk assessment 1 Introduction Mental health diseases, such as depression and anxiety, are growing worldwide however detection often comes late due to gradual emergence of symptoms and high inter-patient variation [1][2]. This diagnostic assessment is common to depend on the one-time clinical assessments or self-reporting questionnaires [3], and it suffers from
label: human

text: subjective bias, less frequent monitoring, as well as late detection of symptoms. Such methods are likely to miss the protracted behavioural and cognitive changes that precede clinical diagnosis by many years [4][5]. Recent AI solutions demonstrate some promise on automating MH assessment, yet most existing models capture population-level emotional patterns and fail to be sensitive to individual behaviour trajectory. Consequently, they are subject to misclassification and delayed risk recognition. Most importantly, mental health decay is indicated in subliminal and gradual cognitive anomalies rather than immediate emotional transformations, therefore demanding kinematic aware and personalized detection mechanisms. 1.1 Gaps in Existing AI Approaches The latest AI based mental health detection techniques have been mainly based on sentiment analysis, emotional polarity and static text representations from single interactions. These methods are effective in recognizing emergency cases of emotional distress [6][7] but have low performance for the early cases where signals are weak or inconsistent. Static embeddings also overlook longitudinal dependencies by which a temporary emotional stage can be differentiated from the persistent cognitive decline. Furthermore, most DL models are used as black-box systems with limited interpretability and clinical understanding. As individual baseline modeling is not available here meaningful deviation analysis cannot be performed, since changes in behaviour are compared to norms and not an individual historical standard. Therefore, current methods do not have drift-informed reasoning and clinical interpretable outputs needed for robust early mental health monitoring [8]. 1.2 Core Idea of MindTrace-ID In order to address such issues, we present a personalized mental health detection framework referred as MindTrace-ID that learns the cognitive drift along longitudinal clinical interviews [9]. It formulates a personalized cognitive baseline for each user and dynamically measures distortions in various micro-behavioral and linguistic parameters, including syntactic complexity, semantic coherence, coupling pace, latency-of-response. MindTrace-ID captures dynamic changes in cognition that are reflective of early stage risk, by focusing on the temporal pattern of aberrant emotional state rather than the absolute emotional state. An explainable reasoning layer additionally translates detected drift patterns to interpretable cognitive markers, offering a transparent and clinically relevant evaluation. 1.3 Contributions​ The contribution of this paper is summarized as: ➢​ A novel cognitive drift modeling framework personalized to early mental health risk estimation is presented, using individualized baselines and
label: human

text: longitudinal behavioral analytics rather than population-based sentiment mechanisms. ➢​ A multi-index longitudinal feature representation and a drift-aware adaptive inference module is presented to model and prioritise sustainable syntactic, semantic, temporal, and interaction-level behavioral changes. ➢​ An explainable reasoning layer is introduced to translate the detected cognitive drift patterns into clinically interpretable markers, and comprehensive testing on the DAIC-WOZ dataset shows that our model can achieve better accuracy, early-stage recall and lower false positive rate. The rest of the paper is structured as follows. Related work and the research gap that justifies the proposed approach are studied in Section 2, while Section 3 details the dataset and preprocessing steps. Section 4 introduces the MindTrace-ID approach, Sections 5 and 6 describe experimental setup and results analysis, while we finish with discussion and future work in Section 7. 2 Literature Review​ Ding et al. (2025) evaluated the decision-point trade-offs of machine learning and deep learning in mental health disorder recognition from social media text. They compared the traditional machine learning methods (logistic regression, random forest and LightGBM) with deep learning architectures like ALBERT and GRU networks. The authors showed that although both models reached similar performance on medium-sized datasets, machine learning models could provide better interpretability (feature importance) while deep learning ones were more robust to complex linguistic patterns. The study also pointed out that model selection should trade-off between performance, interpretability and dataset size and computation efficiency, stressing the on-going tradeoff of explaining patterns mental health detection systems [1]. Tiwari et al. (2024) studied stress detection from EEG signals and they have reviewed a full list of signal processing method, feature extraction technique and machine learning approach used in this field. Their work highlighted the need for non-invasive and real-time monitoring of physiology parameters to detect stress at an early stage, and addressed issues such as signal noise, inter-subject difference, and system scalability. While they demonstrated efficacy, the approaches described above depended on specialized hardware, and did not consider behavior or language context, thus were unsuitable for large scale cheap monitoring of mental health [2]. Matthews et al. (2022) studied loneliness as a general risk factor of mental health problems based on large scaled longitudinal cohort samples in the United Kingdom and New Zealand. Using the UCLA Loneliness Scale, we showed that loneliness can effectively classify individuals at-risk for depression, anxiety and self-harm providing classification accuracy comparable to well established
label: human

text: sleep-quality measures. Although clinically relevant, the method depended on questionnaire-based screening and lack of time-varying behavior change susceptibilities highlight a need for continuous and personalized diagnostic frameworks [3]. A deep learning-based proof-of-concept system for relapse detection and estimation of depression based on audiovisual channels from clinical interview videos was suggested by Othmani and Zeghina (2022). Their similarity-based anomaly-detection method compared audiovisual patterns extracted from depression-free and depressed states, thereby allowing us to predict relapse without any user involvement. On the DAIC-WOZ dataset we obtained good accuracy, but instead of individual-based baseline drift modeling, matching for similarity was emphasized and little explanation as to what changed in terms of underlying cognition [4]. Wang et al. (2024) investigated on-device artificial intelligence for depression detection using wearable internet of things. Their work underscored the benefits of leveraging psychophysiological data, such as sleep and activity, in continuous monitoring of mental health and showed better performance with ensemble learning. Even if the results are promising, wearable-based solutions rely on sensor availability and adherence, and they usually fail to take into account the linguistic and interaction-level behavioral cues that can be found in clinical interviews [5]. Hinduja et al. (2022) leveraged social media users as distributed social sensors and presented a proactive discord monitor system through Twitter data. They used LSTM-based models to identify individuals at risk in the early stage combined with intensive text preprocessing and sentiment analysis. Although successful in monitoring at the population level, we employed population level patterns and personal temporal baselines were absent which did not show its full potential for personalized early intervention [6]. Sharma et al. (2023) developed a multimodal emotional detection based on text, audio and video signals, relying on transfer learning and decision-level fusion. Their EmoHD model achieved state-of-the-art results on the benchmark datasets by aggregating heterogeneous affective cues. However, the model was for discrete emotion recognition but not continuous cognitive change over time, and no personalized drift analysis was made for early risk-detection of mental health [7]. Lin et al. (2024) were able to perform a large meta-analysis for the detection of mental health problems in sexual minorities on mainland China. Their results exposed wide variance in detection rates as a function of measurement instruments, cut-offs, and demographic moderators. The study stressed that context-aware and population-sensitive methods of assessment were essential by implication, the inadequacies of one-size-fits-all detection strategies [8]. Sharma et al. (2022) proposed an EEG-based stress detection method based on the entropy features and an evolutionary-optimized support vector machine. Providing high accuracy on the
label: human

text: short-time EEG signals, the paper showed that it is feasible to detect stress quickly. However, dependence on physiological indexes and hardware-based configuration limited the scalability, and could not mitigate behavioral or linguistic expression of deteriorating mental health [9]. Lin et al. (2023) combined external psycholo-gical knowledge to social-network-based mental health detection models by including diagnostic criteria and mild screening instruments. Their knowledge-sensitive model enhanced classification performance and reduced the dependence on data-driven decision forums. Although this methodology improved interpretation, it did not explicitly model longitudinal behavioral drift or individual baselines [10]. Yang et al. (2022) proposed tough interpretable mental health analysis as a text generation task and founded instruction-tuned large language models. Their MentaLLaMA network provided human-level explanations in addition to predictions, which help address the interpretability problem. However, it depended on the enormous first-step training data and was mainly based on social media text but not historical clinical engagement [11]. Nawindah and Wulandari (2023) have designed a mobile-based self-screening application as an attempt in order to assist the adolescent mental health assessment. Their app, Smart-Senyum also enhanced awareness and early recognition of mental health conditions in young people. The system was however based on self- reported questionnaires and did not have continuous behavior monitoring features [12]. Olawade et al. (2024) conducted an extensive analysis of the applications of AI-based technologies in mental health care, with a focus on early detection, personalized medicine and ethical aspects. The importance of privacy, bias and transparency in the application of AI to mental health were emphasised as key challenges that need to be addressed when designing explainable, responsible AI systems for mental health applications [13]. Tutun et al. (2023) developed an AI-enabled DSM-5 decision support tool, which simplified classical mental health assessment tools through reducing questionnaire length and enhancing diagnostic accuracy. This approach successfully identified candidates for removal; however, its design was focused on the questionnaire and it did not take advantage of longitudinal behavioural or linguistic signals [14]. Hybrid deep learning architecture based on textual and audio features has applied in depression detection by Marriwala and Chaudhary (2023) on DAIC-WOZ dataset. Their results showed that this approach works well in the case of audio-based CNNs. However, the model primarily focused on predictive accuracy rather than interpretability and did not include any explicit approach to model personalized temporal cognitive drift [15]. 2.1 Research Gap​ While earlier works have investigated textual, physiological and multimodal techniques in machine learning and deep learning models for mental health detection, there are several important open questions remain. Current methods are largely based
label: human

text: on aggregated sentiment across the population or static feature representations, which can have limited capacity to describe individual difference and subtle cognitive shifts that precede manifest symptoms. For most models, the focus is placed only on isolated transactions and lacks longitudinal carry-over, which clouds the ability to separate temporary emotional states from consumed mental health. Moreover, a large number of deep learning–based approaches tend to be black boxes providing a restricted clinical interpretability and generated trust in practical applications. To tackle those aspects, MindTrace-ID proposes personalized baseline modelling and longitudinal cognitive drift analysis based on micro-behavioral and linguistic cues, accompanied by a drift-aware inference strategy and an explainable reasoning layer for accurate early-stage, clinically interpretable mental health risk detection. 3 Dataset and Preprocessing​ 3.1 DAIC-WOZ Dataset​ The Mind-Trace-ID is tested using the DAIC-WOZ dataset, which includes video-recorded structured clinical interviews with a human interviewer to diagnose depression [16]. The interviews are conducted semi-structurally and conversationally, allowing subjects to describe freely their thoughts, life stories and experiences without limitation. This longitudinal interview format allows the consideration of cognitive and behavioral change as it occurs, rather than discrete emotional expression. Each patient has a depression severity score provided by the Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8) [17][18], which is a clinically tried and tested screen scale. Here, PHQ-8 scores are binarized into two classes: depressed and non-depressed subjects, here used for evaluation only. The proposed solution does not aim at estimating depressions scores in a conventional way, and unlike traditional methods it aims at modeling personalized behavioral deviations instead over time. 3.2 Data Cleaning and Feature-Oriented Segmentation​ Interview transcripts are broken into discourse-level utterances to maintain conversational structure. The above properties facilitate the suggested cognitive drift analysis through construction of baseline for each subject and tracking their temporal deviation. 4 Methodology​ 4.1 System Overview​ The proposed MindTrace-ID framework is designed to be completed in a structured pipeline, starting from the input of longitudinal clinical interview transcripts and extracting micro-behavioral and linguistic features. These features are utilized to create an individual cognitive baseline for each subject, which can then be used as a reference for further analysis [21]. This is used to calculate drifting of cognitive function from the individual baseline over time, and an adaptive inference system integrates these drifts for computing a score on mental health risk. Ultimately, an interpretable output layer that relates the identified drift patterns to clinically interpretable cognition markers leads to transparent and actionable monitoring. The model does not treat all deviations equally, but it gives more weight to the drift patterns that are consistent across windows, which reduces the effect of sudden changes in behavior. These temporally persistent deviations are accumulated to develop a continuous mental health risk score [6][7], which allows for stable and early detection of emerging risk while also reducing the number of false positives. 4.6 Explainable Reasoning Layer The explainable reasoning translation layer interprets quantified cognitive drift patterns into clinically relevant cognitive markers to enable informed decisions. Disturbances in interaction rhythm and response latency are correlated with attentional instability and cognitive slowing [14], sustained decrease of syntactic complexity and semantic coherence indicate disorganized reasoning. By directly relating behavioral drift to these established cognitive markers, the framework allows clinicians to comprehend which factors contribute to the predicted risk. 5. Experimental Setup​ 5.1 Baselines Compared To verify the performance of the proposed MindTrace-ID framework, we chose several representative baseline methods for comparison. CNNs, captures local n-gram patterns in the interviews transcripts, and Long-term Short-term Memory (LSTM) networks models sequential dependencies in linguistic data. Transformer-based models are listed to represent the latest contextual embedding methods, which employ self-attention mechanisms for modeling the long-distance dependencies. Moreover, we include sentiment-only models that make use of polarity and affective lexicon features to capture emotion-centric mental health detection methods that are commonly used. Together, these baselines span static, sequential and contextual modeling. 5.2 Evaluation Metrics We evaluate the model performance through standard classification measures such as accuracy, precision, and recall for overall detection robustness. Early detection specifically For early-stage risk identification, we calculate the ‘early detection‘ recall measure by calculating the recall performance on initial interview segments before peak symptoms. We also report the false positive rate as an estimate of model

This all-sided test can help to have a balanced view of prediction performance and practical application. 5.3 Implementation Details We implement all models on PyTorch deep learning framework and train them by the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.0001. The maximum length of all input sequences is set to 512 tokens and batch size is fixed at 16 in order not to exhaust the available memory. All the experiments are implemented on a workstation with an Intel Core i7 processor, 32 GB RAM and NVIDIA RTX 3080 GPU (10GB VRAM). If used at the subject level, a stratified 5-fold cross-validation approach is applied, to ensure generalization and prevent data leakage; while hyperparameters are tuned on different validation folds. 6 Results & Discussion ​ Figure 2. text: 6.1 Ablation Study An ablation study is performed to estimate the importance of some components in proposed approach. text: Abstract— The rapid growth of social media platforms has resulted in massive volumes of user-generated content, offering valuable insights into public opinion, consumer preferences, and emerging social trends. However, the informal writing style, context-dependent expressions, and noisy nature of social media text pose significant challenges for traditional sentiment analysis techniques. To address these issues, this study proposes a Context-Aware Sentiment Analysis framework using a Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Network (Bi-RNN) with an Attention Mechanism. The bidirectional architecture captures sequential dependencies in both forward and backward directions, ensuring that contextual nuances surrounding each word are preserved. The attention mechanism further enhances performance by assigning dynamic importance to sentiment- rich tokens, enabling the model to focus on words that contribute most to sentiment polarity. Pre-trained embeddings are employed to initialize lexical representations, while regularization techniques mitigate overfitting. Experimental evaluation on benchmark datasets such as Twitter Sentiment140 and IMDB reviews demonstrates that the proposed model achieves superior accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores compared to baseline methods including CNN, LSTM, and Transformer-based models. On Twitter Sentiment140, the model attained an accuracy of 91.5% and F1- score of 90.7%, while on IMDB reviews, it achieved 93.8% accuracy and 93.2% F1-score. These results highlight the ability of the proposed framework to effectively handle short, noisy, and context-heavy social media text while providing interpretable sentiment predictions. The study emphasizes the potential of context-aware attention-driven recurrent architectures in advancing sentiment classification for large- scale social media analytics.

text: The explosion of social media platforms such as Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram has transformed the way individuals express opinions, share experiences, and influence public discourse. Millions of posts are generated daily, providing a rich source of data for analyzing sentiment trends in domains such as politics, marketing, and healthcare. However, the informal language, use of slang, abbreviations, emojis, and context-dependent expressions inherent in social media make sentiment classification a challenging task for conventional computational methods [1]. Sentiment analysis, often referred to as opinion mining, seeks to identify and classify the polarity of text into categories such as positive, negative, or neutral. Traditional approaches relying on lexicons and machine learning models such as Naïve Bayes or Support Vector Machines have demonstrated reasonable performance but are limited by their dependence on handcrafted features and inability to effectively capture sequential context [2]. These shortcomings have motivated the shift toward deep learning-based approaches, which automatically learn hierarchical representations from raw text data. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have shown promise in capturing sequential dependencies in natural language. Yet, standard RNNs face limitations such as vanishing gradients, which hinder their ability to model long-range dependencies. To address this, bidirectional RNNs (Bi-RNNs) extend the architecture by processing text in both forward and backward directions, thereby capturing the full context of a sentence. This feature is particularly useful in social media texts, where the meaning of a sentiment often depends on preceding and succeeding words [3]. Attention mechanisms further enhance RNN performance by allowing the model to dynamically focus on sentiment-rich tokens within a sequence. Instead of treating all words equally, attention assigns higher weights to contextually significant words such as “amazing,” “disappointing,” or negations like “not good.” This not only boosts classification accuracy but also improves interpretability by revealing the model’s decision-making process [4]. In this study, we propose a context-aware sentiment analysis framework that integrates a Bidirectional RNN with an Attention Mechanism to effectively classify sentiments in noisy and diverse social media text. The model leverages pre- trained embeddings for semantic richness, Bi-RNN for capturing long-range contextual dependencies, and attention for emphasizing key tokens. We evaluate the framework on benchmark datasets such as Twitter Sentiment140 and IMDB reviews, achieving significant improvements in accuracy and F1-score compared to CNN, LSTM, and Transformer-based baselines. text: II. LITERATURE SURVEY
label: human

text: Lexicon-based sentiment analysis approaches have long been popular due to their interpretability. Resources such as SentiWordNet and AFINN provide pre-assigned polarity values for words, enabling rule-based classification. However, these methods fail to adapt to the informal style and evolving vocabulary of social media, where sarcasm, emojis, and abbreviations dominate [11]. Machine learning models such as Naïve Bayes, SVM, and Maximum Entropy improved sentiment prediction by using statistical features like TF-IDF and n-grams. Although effective on structured datasets, these models struggle with short, noisy, and context-dependent texts typical of Twitter and Facebook posts [12]. The emergence of distributed embeddings such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText transformed sentiment analysis by providing dense semantic representations of words. These embeddings capture similarity and context beyond surface- level frequency features, significantly improving classification performance across large-scale datasets [13]. Deep learning architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were introduced for text classification and sentiment analysis. CNNs excel at capturing local n-gram patterns but are limited in handling long-term dependencies, reducing their effectiveness on longer reviews or multi- sentence posts [14]. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including LSTM and GRU variants, became the next milestone in sentiment classification. These architectures modeled sequential word dependencies more effectively than CNNs. However, their unidirectional processing limited the capture of contextual cues spanning both past and future tokens [15]. The development of Bidirectional RNNs (Bi-RNNs) addressed this limitation by processing text in both forward and backward directions. This bidirectional context enhanced the classification of ambiguous sentences, such as those involving negations or sarcasm, commonly observed in social media text [16]. To further improve interpretability and performance, attention mechanisms were integrated into RNN-based architectures. Attention models assign dynamic weights to sentiment-rich tokens, ensuring the network focuses on critical words like “fantastic,” “awful,” or “not good,” leading to improved accuracy and transparency [17]. Recent research has explored hybrid architectures combining CNNs, Bi-RNNs, and attention modules. These models leverage CNN for local phrase-level features, Bi-RNN for contextual sequence modeling, and attention for focusing on important tokens. Such hybrids have consistently outperformed single-architecture models in sentiment classification tasks [18]. Transformer-based models such as BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet have recently achieved state-of-the-art results in NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis. Their self-attention mechanism enables them to capture long-range dependencies without recurrence. However, their high computational cost and memory requirements make them less suitable for real- time sentiment monitoring in large-scale social media streams

text: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
label: human

text: The performance of the proposed Context-Aware Bi-RNN with Attention framework was systematically evaluated on benchmark datasets including Twitter Sentiment140 and IMDB movie reviews. The experiments were designed to validate the effectiveness of bidirectional sequence modeling and attention integration in handling noisy, context- dependent social media texts. The dataset was split into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% testing, ensuring balanced representation of positive, negative, and neutral classes. Preprocessing retained negation terms and mapped emojis into sentiment tokens, preserving the expressive nature of social media posts. The model was implemented in TensorFlow/Keras, optimized using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.001, and trained with a batch size of 64. Dropout and early stopping techniques were applied to minimize overfitting and enhance generalization. On the Twitter Sentiment140 dataset, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 91.5%, precision of 91.2%, recall of 90.3%, and F1-score of 90.7%. In comparison, CNN and LSTM baselines recorded 87.2% and 88.9% accuracy, while a Transformer-based model achieved 90.4%. These results confirm that the bidirectional context modeling and attention weighting enable superior performance in short, noisy texts typical of Twitter. For the IMDB reviews dataset, which contains longer and more structured content, the model achieved 93.8% accuracy, 93.5% precision, 92.8% recall, and an F1-score of 93.2%. This demonstrates the robustness of the proposed framework across varying text lengths and complexities. Notably, the Bi- RNN component captured long-range dependencies within reviews, while the attention layer ensured that sentiment-rich words and phrases were emphasized. An ablation study was also conducted to measure the contribution of each component. Removing the attention mechanism reduced accuracy by nearly 2%, while excluding bidirectional processing led to performance drops of more than 3%. The complete Bi-RNN with attention model consistently outperformed these simplified versions, validating the necessity of each module. Furthermore, confusion matrix analysis revealed that most misclassifications occurred between neutral and mildly positive or negative instances, reflecting the inherent ambiguity of social media text. Despite these challenges, the proposed model maintained balanced performance across classes, highlighting its ability to generalize well. Overall, the results confirm that the context-aware Bi-RNN with attention achieves superior accuracy, robustness, and interpretability compared to existing sentiment classification models, making it highly suitable for large-scale social media analytics applications.

text: Abstract— The explosive growth of social media platforms has created vast repositories of user-generated content, where sentiment polarity detection plays a crucial role in understanding public opinion, consumer behavior, and emerging trends. Traditional machine learning models often fail to capture long-range dependencies and nuanced contextual cues in such dynamic data. To address these limitations, we propose an Enhanced Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) with Multi-Level Attention Layers for fine-grained sentiment polarity detection. The framework integrates a hierarchical attention mechanism that operates at the word, sentence, and document levels, enabling the model to selectively emphasize semantically rich features while suppressing irrelevant noise. This multi-level attention not only improves interpretability but also enhances the ability to capture subtle variations in sentiment expressions, including sarcasm and context shifts. Comprehensive experiments were conducted on benchmark social media datasets such as Twitter Sentiment140 and SemEval, demonstrating that the proposed approach achieves superior accuracy, F1-score, and robustness compared to conventional RNNs, CNN-based sentiment classifiers, and transformer baselines. The results confirm that our model effectively balances context preservation and computational efficiency, offering a scalable solution for real-time sentiment monitoring in social media analytics. Keywords— Sentiment polarity detection, Social media analytics, Enhanced recurrent neural network (RNN), Multi-level attention mechanism, Context-aware sentiment analysis, Natural language processing (NLP).

text: I. INTRODUCTION
label: human

text: The rapid expansion of social media platforms has transformed the way individuals express opinions, share experiences, and influence public discourse. Platforms such as Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram generate massive amounts of user-generated content daily, reflecting sentiments that are highly valuable for applications ranging from political campaign monitoring to consumer product analysis [1]. Analyzing this vast textual data to determine sentiment polarity—whether positive, negative, or neutral—remains a critical challenge in natural language processing (NLP). Conventional sentiment analysis approaches primarily relied on lexicon-based techniques and shallow machine learning classifiers. These methods often struggled to capture contextual nuances such as sarcasm, irony, or evolving word usage in dynamic social media environments [2]. With the advent of deep learning, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) models gained popularity for their ability to model sequential dependencies in text. However, their limitations in capturing long-range context and interpretability have restricted their effectiveness in complex sentiment tasks [3]. Recent advancements introduced attention mechanisms, which significantly improved performance in sequence modeling tasks by allowing models to focus selectively on informative parts of input text [4]. Despite these improvements, single-level attention may overlook hierarchical relationships in language, such as the interplay between word-level, sentence-level, and document-level features. This limitation necessitates the exploration of multi- level attention architectures for more comprehensive sentiment representation [5]. The heterogeneity of social media data, including informal grammar, slang, emojis, and multilingual expressions, further complicates sentiment polarity detection [6]. Standard RNN models often fail to generalize across such noisy and diverse inputs, which reduces their robustness in real-world deployments. This motivates the development of enhanced RNN frameworks that incorporate sophisticated attention mechanisms capable of extracting sentiment cues at multiple levels. In recent years, hybrid deep learning models combining CNNs and RNNs have been explored to capture both local and sequential dependencies [7]. While these models improve accuracy, they often suffer from computational overhead and lack interpretability in terms of identifying which features contribute most to sentiment polarity. Addressing this gap requires architectures that balance accuracy, efficiency, and transparency in predictions. Our proposed Enhanced RNN with Multi-Level Attention Layers framework addresses these challenges by integrating hierarchical attention mechanisms. At the word level, attention highlights important tokens within a sentence; at the sentence level, it identifies sentiment-rich sentences within documents; and at the document level, it consolidates global sentiment context [8]. This hierarchical strategy enables the model to preserve nuanced semantic information while filtering out noise inherent in social media content. The interpretability provided by multi-level attention mechanisms is particularly valuable for applications in sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, where decision-makers require not just accurate predictions but also clear explanations of model outputs [9]. Furthermore, the hierarchical structure enhances generalization across datasets with varied linguistic and cultural patterns. Extensive experiments conducted on benchmark datasets such as Twitter Sentiment140 and SemEval demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over baseline RNN, CNN, and transformer-based classifiers. Evaluation metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score consistently highlight the robustness of the enhanced architecture under diverse conditions [10].

Early research efforts primarily focused on lexicon-based approaches, where sentiment dictionaries were employed to assign polarity scores to words and aggregate them at the sentence or document level. However, the reliance on manual feature engineering limited their scalability and effectiveness in handling the noisy, diverse, and dynamic nature of user-generated content. Deep learning models revolutionized sentiment analysis by enabling automatic feature extraction from raw text. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were particularly effective in capturing local dependencies and short phrases, offering competitive results in sentiment classification tasks [13]. Nonetheless, CNNs struggled to preserve long-range contextual relationships, a critical factor for nuanced sentiment detection in social media discussions. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their variants, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), emerged as powerful architectures for modeling sequential dependencies [14]. These models excelled in capturing temporal patterns in language, making them more effective than traditional classifiers. Yet, standard RNNs faced challenges such as vanishing gradients and limited interpretability, restricting their ability to handle complex sentiment nuances. To address these issues, attention mechanisms were introduced as a significant innovation. By allowing models to selectively focus on sentiment-rich words or phrases, attention enhanced both accuracy and interpretability in sentiment analysis tasks [15]. However, most early implementations relied on single-level attention, which often overlooked hierarchical dependencies across multiple linguistic levels. The emergence of hierarchical attention networks (HANs) demonstrated the potential of multi-level attention mechanisms. Still, their application to noisy and short-text social media environments remained underexplored, indicating a gap for further research. Transformers and pretrained language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, have recently gained traction in sentiment analysis for their ability to capture global dependencies and contextual embeddings [17]. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on many benchmark datasets, their heavy computational requirements and lack of real-time adaptability pose challenges for large-scale social media monitoring. Hybrid models that combine CNNs, RNNs, and attention layers have also been explored to leverage the strengths of each architecture. text: PCOS Risk Detection and Personalized Recommendation System Using CatBoost Classifier with Hormonal and Lifestyle Health Indicators Abstract- Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is common endocrine disorder among women of childbearing age and it is a condition commonly overlooked as the symptoms are heterogeneous and varies largely in terms of clinical presentation. In this work, we proposed an intelligent PCOS risk identification and personal recommendation system with the use of CatBoost classifier, for accurate and accessible early diagnosis. The present model included the most important hormonal vessel markers, such as luteinizing hormone/follicle-stimulating hormone (LH/FSH) ratio, prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), in addition to lifestyle and anthropometric vessels parameters: body mass index (BMI), physical activity level, sleep quality and nutrition. CatBoost is chosen due to its built-in capability of handling categorical variables in an efficient manner and avoiding overfitting without much prior processing. The model is trained on fine-tuned feature engineering of a well-annotated clinical dataset, and associated performance tests indicate an accuracy of 96.3%, precision of 95.8%, recall of 96.9%, F1-score of 96.3% and an AUC (area under the ROC curve) as high as 0.97, thereby indicating its high predictive capacity as well as strong stability. The system also provides intelligent recommendations about lifestyle and healthy living by dynamically creating recommendations based on individual risk profiles, in a very user-friendly way. The solution proposed allows early prevention, increases PCOS enlightenment and aids proactive health experience. This system combines traditional clinical screening and explainable machine learning-based digital healthcare, providing utility for patients and clinicians. The majority of existing approaches have been concentrating on maximizing the classification accuracy by leveraging complex ensemble or deep architecture, which usually suffer from elaborate feature engineering, optimization heuristics and multimodal data (e.g., ultrasound images), leading to higher computational cost and lower scalability in routine screening [1], [3], [5], [9]. text: transparency into the learning process limiting explaining the model during both training and inference [4], [8]. Furthermore, many methods take a poor account of the categorical nature of lifestyle attributes and rely extensively on an manual encoding or aggressive feature selection that might bring in bias and limit generalization across different populations [2], [7], [12]. In addition, the majority of the currently available models concentrate on only PCOS classification, and do not extend predictive outcomes to individualized lifestyle or health advice, which limits their use for early intervention and self-care interventions [6], [10], [13]. To overcome these limitations, in this study we use a CatBoost-based learning framework as an approach that naturally handles categorical features and prevents overfitting as well as offering stable predictions which can be easily interpreted when using tabular clinical and life style information. By combining valid risk detection with a user-specific recommendation module, it closes the gap between high-performance PCOS prediction and practical, user-oriented decision support for accessible and actionable digital screening without the need for costly or invasive diagnostics [14]. III Methodology 3.1 Overall System Architecture The general design for the proposed PCOS risk estimation and individual recommendation model-based CNN system is realized as a Model Based Pipeline, where the model summary chain provides an end-to-end structure with sub-model level interchangeability across data collection [15][16], interpretation, and decision support. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the process starts with user data acquisition through the structured interface reporting hormonal parameters, anthropometric measures and lifestyle-related factors. The collected data are pre-processed including missing value imputation, normalization, and categorical feature processing, for the purpose of data consistency and quality. The processed feature set is inputted forward to a CatBoost based classification module, which effectively captures the complex non-linear patterns and deals with categorical attributes automatically when making prediction on individual PCOS risk levels [17]. Depending on the risk category that is estimated, a recommendation machine is triggered to create an individualized lifestyle and health advice according of the user profile. Finally, the system discloses risk assessment scores and corresponding recommendations in a user-friendly decision support front end which supports accessible, transparent and proactive PCOS screening for both consumers and healthcare providers.

By integrating risk prediction and individualized lifestyle advice, the proposed system facilitates the transition from computational diagnosis to concrete healthcare assistance, allowing for timely interventions and making well-informed decisions. Future work will involve validation and implementation of our proposed framework on larger more heterogeneous, multi-center data sets and incorporation of longitudinal as well as wearable sensor data to improve the real time monitoring and clinical efficacy in PCOS. text: ProtoExplain-LM: A Prototype-Guided Explainable Vision–Language Framework for Trustworthy Plant Leaf Disease Identification Abstract-In a word, it is the necessity to identify the plant leaf disease in an accurate way apart from explainable for sustainable agriculture, early diagnosis and circular of information for farmers as well as agronomists. Despite the promising classification performance, the recent deep learning methods have had little practical impact due to their lack of interpretability, sensitivity under real-world imaging conditions and actionable explanations. Furthermore, the available explainable AI (XAI) methods are generally limited to qualitative saliency maps and do not furnish case-based evidence or agronomically meaningful interpretation. To rectify these gaps, we present the method ProtoExplain-LM, a new prototype-assisted explainable vision–language pipeline for plant leaf disease recognition. The proposed approach forms a light- weight convolutional feature extractor that is connected with a class-specific prototype learning, which supports case-based visual reasoning by comparing discriminatory leaf areas to learned disease prototypes. In contrast to typical black-box models, ProtoExplain-LM is explicitly grounded for each prediction on a small number of representative visual prototypes. A large language model (LLM) is used for structured explanation generation: it maps prototype activations, certainty estimates, and context metadata to brief diagnostic explanations and treatment recommendations in natural language. Extensive experiments on benchmark PlantVillage Dataset indicate that ProtoExplain-LM achieves 98.12% classification accuracy outperforming the traditional CNN based models by 4.6% under cross-dataset evaluation. The proposed framework further achieves an explanation fidelity of 92.4%, signifying high consistency between visual evidence and model prediction, along with low inference latency for edge deployment. These findings demonstrate the reliability and interpretability of ProtoExplain-LM to provide reliable, transparent and actionable plant disease diagnosis, linking state-of-the-art performance with on-farm agronomic trustworthiness. Keywords- Plant leaf disease identification, Prototype learning, Explainable artificial intelligence, Vision–language models, Large language models, Deep learning, Precision agriculture I Introduction​ Leaf diseases are primary threats to the global agricultural yield due to direct loss in quality and quantity of crops leading to food epidemiological concern [1], [2]. Early disease detection is one of the most important and effective methods for precision agriculture, because it can facilitate rapid intervention and then minimize economic loss [3], [4]. Driven by increasing application of digital farming solutions, image based plant disease detection has been considered as a practical and scalable alternative to conventional field level inspection approaches [18], [21]. However, accurate disease monitoring is still a challenging task as it is affected by illumination changes, complex background, visual similarity of diseases and the limited number of expert agronomists especially in remote and resource-constrained areas [8], [19].

text: Conventional diagnosing of plant disease depends heavily on visual inspection by farmers or experts [5], [6]. It is a time-consuming and subjective process, with high human errors. Furthermore, manual methods are not adequate for large agriculture areas or a variety of crops. To resolve these challenges, deep learning models, especially CNNs, have been extensively employed for automatic plant leaf disease identification. Recent works demonstrate that CNN-based and transfer learning models can reach high accuracy in several crops and disease categories [1], [3], [7], [10]. More advanced architectures, such as DenseNet [6], EfficientNet [16], and attentionbased models[38], which further enhance robustness as well as generalize in real world scenarios. Despite their good results, the real applicability of these models is still reduced by their black-box nature. One notable limitation of most prevailing deep learning models is that they are in the form of black-box predictor, which can only provide prediction outputs without showing why a decision is made. The absence of interpretability undermines the user's confidence, which is especially important in agricultural decision-making due to potential erroneous diagnoses that cause false treatments and higher degree of damage on crop [21], [22]. Finally, in [36], National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA) of the United States Department of Agriculture-funded plant disease detection systems have been proposed with XAI methods including Grad-CAM [38] and saliency map visualization for increased transparency. Although such methods emphasize the critical image parts, they are generally qualitative and have little agronomic significance. Moreover, saliency based explanations are not case-based reference or practical methods for farmers to understand and use directly [19][40]. Another drawback of popular methods is the lack of case-based reasoning, which is often applied by agricultural experts in disease diagnosis [15]. Disease diagnosis in practice is usually based on the comparison of observed symptoms with previous cases, which does not fit for most of deep learning models. It has been observed that the plant-disease identification systems currently available, seldom promote natural-language explanations which are easily understandable regarding their diagnosis generation process. Despite the fact that LLMs are powerful in reasoning and explainable generation, their utility for integrating visual disease evidence with agricultural setting has not been fully investigated. To meet these challenges, we present ProtoExplain-LM, a prototype-lead explainable vision–language technique for accurate plant leaf disease diagnosis. The main contributions of our work are: (i) a prototype-guided visual reasoning, where disease predictions are connected to prototypical leaf representations for transparency and case-based explanation; (ii) a vision–language integration system, which uses an LLM to produce clear human-readable diagnostic explanations and agronomic recommendations based on visual evidence. (iii) comprehensive experimental evaluation that shows the effectiveness of our approach in learning more discriminative features and better explaining image classification together with low inference time for practical and on-edge agricultural applications.

Although some works employ explainable AI (XAI) tools such as saliency maps and class activation visualizations, these explanations are qualitative and pixel-based, and loosely connected to human diagnostic decision-making. None of them explicitly utilize prototype-based learning to semantically ground predictions on typical disease cases or provide a case-based rationale that the users may refer to when comparing their own current symptoms with learned reference patterns. Moreover, despite recent breakthroughs in deep learning for diagnosis, large language models (LLMs) have yet to be incorporated to convert visual evidence into structured and natural

III Methodology The ProtoExplain-LM system model is designed based on a modular vision–language system framework for accurate and interpretable plant-leaf disease identification. Starting from an input leaf image [22][23], a lightweight convolutional feature extractor is firstly trained to distinguish subtle visual appearances between classes and preserve fine-grained lesion properties. The feature maps are then fed into a class-specific prototype learning module to learn representative disease prototypes that matched localized image regions, which supports case-based visual reasoning via similarity comparison [24][25]. The final disease classification is produced based on the prototype activations and prediction confidence scores obtained. To improve human interpretability, the activated prototypes are sent along with contextual metadata to an explanation generator powered by a large language model that synthesizes the visual evidence into short-form, human-readable diagnostic explanations and treatment insights. This end-to-end architecture integrates model decisions with visual prototypes in explainable manner and achieves fast inference time [26], which is applicable for interpretable and deployable agricultural decision support system. ​ Figure 1. In general, the ablation study demonstrates the necessity of synergistically incorporating prototype learning, vision–language alignment and language-based explanation for accurate, transparent and trustworthy plant leaf disease diagnosis. 5.3 Limitations and Future Work​ Despite the favorable experimental results out of ProtoExplain-LM, some limitations persist which provide directions for future research. The existing framework is mainly tested on RGB leaf levees and the robustness of that might be decreased under extreme imaging conditions like heavy occlusion, motion blur, or infections in its early stage with small visual symptoms. Moreover, the dependence on a fixed number of class-specific prototypes might restrict usefulness in unseen diseases or rare variants. In the future, we will extend our pipeline to multimodal inputs (e.g., hyperspectral, thermal imagery) for early detection and increased accuracy in diagnosing the disease. Additionally, future work will investigate dynamic and transferable prototype learning for continual learning within new crops and diseases, and multilingual as well as region-specific explanation generation in order to facilitate better usability across spatially diverse farming communities. VI Conclusion​ In this work, we presented a prototype-guided explainable vision–language framework for reliable plant leaf disease identification, named ProtoExplain-LM. The proposed model bridges the interpretability gap between high classification performance and interpretability by combining class-specific prototype learning, vision–language alignment, and an LLM-based explanation generator. Extensive experiments conducted on the PlantVillage dataset show that ProtoExplain-LM obtains 98.12% of classification accuracy, surpassing previous CNN-based models and explanation-oriented methods and achieving a high explanation fidelity score of 92.4%, which reports strong visual evidence - model decision alignment. Furthermore, the pipeline has been used to have low inference latency (About 45ms per image) and can be deployed practically in real-time and edge-based agricultural scenario. These findings validate the accurate, interpretable and actionable detection in plant diseases diagnosis offered by ProtoExplain-LM for judicious decision-making towards precision agriculture. text: Dual-Attention Hyperbolic Feature Fusion Network for Robust Pre-Harvest Crop Disease Detection Abstract- Detecting crop disease in the pre-harvest stage is important to reduce yield loss and make sure sustainable agricultural production. We present a novel, Dual-Attention Hyperbolic Feature Fusion Network (DAHFF-Net) capable of robust and efficient crop disease classification on the publicly available PlantVillage dataset with 54,306 images across 38 different disease categories from 14 crop species. Unlike conventional convolutional models that utilize Euclidean feature representation only, this framework incorporates EfficientNet-B4 for hierarchical feature extraction, a spatial–channel attention mechanism to focus on lesion-specific region and a hyperbolic embedding layer that improves inter-class separability in a non-Euclidean latent space. We also propose a curvature-adaptive margin loss function to enhance the decision boundary discrimination of visually similar diseases. DAHFF-Net was extensively evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation and obtained the tradeoff classification accuracy of 99.21%, macro F1-score of 98.87% and precision of 98.65% outperforming the baseline architectures including ResNet50 (97.42%), Vision Transformer (98.03%) and standard EfficientNet (98.36%). The proposed model further reduces parameter complexity by 18.4% and inference time by 22.7%, allowing it to be deployable in edge-based precision farming systems. Using Grad-CAM interpretability analysis, our method shows significant improvement in localization of infected regions with 16% increase in intersection over union (IoU) compared to baseline models. We emphasize the potential and impact of hyperbolic feature learning with attention mechanisms for efficient, high-fidelity pre-harvest crop disease extraction through our findings. Keywords: Hyperbolic Representation Learning, Dual-Attention Mechanism, Pre-Harvest Crop Disease Detection, EfficientNet-B4, Precision Agriculture. 1. Introduction​

text: Due to their powerful ability of hierarchical feature learning, CNNs have been widely used in the research of plant disease classification [9][10]. Architectures based on state-of-the-art approaches like ResNet, DenseNet and EfficientNet have been used for the same taking input both kind of texture characteristics multi-scale as well as colour characteristics on leaf images [11]. Using transfer learning techniques, which took advantage of pre-trained weights learned from training on large image datasets, the classification results were improved. These approaches were extended on agricultural vision tasks through self-attention-based transformer models that are capable of modelling long-range dependencies across the leaf surfaces. Although this approach produces comparable performance [12][13], it has inherent limitations. Many of the approaches above, however, project representations into a Euclidean latent space where distances grow linearly and hierarchical class relationships are not preserved as accurately as we could. Conclusion​ In this study, we proposed DAHFF-Net: a Dual-Attention Hyperbolic Feature Fusion Network for accurate and efficient pre-harvest crop disease detection. text: Dual-Attention Hyperbolic Feature Fusion Network for Robust Pre-Harvest Crop Disease Detection Abstract- Detecting crop disease in the pre-harvest stage is important to reduce yield loss and make sure sustainable agricultural production. We present a novel, Dual-Attention Hyperbolic Feature Fusion Network (DAHFF-Net) capable of robust and efficient crop disease classification on the publicly available PlantVillage dataset with 54,306 images across 38 different disease categories from 14 crop species. Unlike conventional convolutional models that utilize Euclidean feature representation only, this framework incorporates EfficientNet-B4 for hierarchical feature extraction, a spatial–channel attention mechanism to focus on lesion-specific region and a hyperbolic embedding layer that improves inter-class separability in a non-Euclidean latent space. We also propose a curvature-adaptive margin loss function to enhance the decision boundary discrimination of visually similar diseases. DAHFF-Net was extensively evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation and obtained the tradeoff classification accuracy of 99.21%, macro F1-score of 98.87% and precision of 98.65% outperforming the baseline architectures including ResNet50 (97.42%), Vision Transformer (98.03%) and standard EfficientNet (98.36%). The proposed model further reduces parameter complexity by 18.4% and inference time by 22.7%, allowing it to be deployable in edge-based precision farming systems. Using Grad-CAM interpretability analysis, our method shows significant improvement in localization of infected regions with 16% increase in intersection over union (IoU) compared to baseline models. We emphasize the potential and impact of hyperbolic feature learning with attention mechanisms for efficient, high-fidelity pre-harvest crop disease extraction through our findings. Keywords: Hyperbolic Representation Learning, Dual-Attention Mechanism, Pre-Harvest Crop Disease Detection, EfficientNet-B4, Precision Agriculture. 1. text: 2.1 Research Gap​ However, despite significant progress that has been achieved on AI applications for crop disease identification, several major gaps have yet to be addressed. As a result, there are limitations to existing deep learning models that are primarily designed for classical Euclidean feature spaces and fail in modeling hierarchical yet fine-grained mutually relational relationships among visually similar disease classes. While attention mechanisms and lightweight architectures led the way towards localization and more efficient parameterization, these predominantly integrate to provide better performance within the framework of existing end-to-end systems, not employing any established non-Euclidean embedding techniques that could help in achieving a deeper separability between classes. Moreover, the present loss function is only focused on Euclidean manifolds and lacks a complementary adoption of curvature-aware optimization for reliable separating boundaries in nearby disease categories. Additionally, there exist several of these models that achieve very good benchmark accuracy but are not robust to subtle differences in intermixed classes and have high computational cost which is a concern for real-time edge deployment. Such gaps motivate us to propose a unified framework which seamlessly combines attention based feature refinement, hyperbolic space representation learning and curvature adaptive discriminative optimization for robust and scalable pre-harvest crop disease detection. 3.Methodology 3.1 Overall Architecture of DAHFF-Net The authors propose DAHFF-Net, an end-to-end architecture consisting of hyperbolic feature extraction and lesion-aware attention refinement mechanisms [21] followed simultaneously by the ability to learn in non-Euclidean spaces. We begin by resizing an image of a leaf to 380 × 380 pixels and feeding it to the EfficientNet-B4 back-bone for deep hierarchical feature extraction when starting the processing pipeline. The efficientNet-B4 model constructs a high dimensional feature representation with compound-scaled convolutional blocks and learns multi-scale spatial and texture patterns [23]. Then, the feature maps go through a dual
label: human

text: attention block consisting of two branches, channel and spatial attention [22], [23], which adaptively recalibrate the feature responses by focusing on informative lesion areas while also suppressing elements in the background that can represent noise. Next, a hyperbolic transformation layer maps those cleansed feature maps into a hyperbolic embedding space to exploit its properties for better modeling of the hierarchical class relations and increased inter-class separability compared with classical Euclidean embeddings [24][25]. Hyperbolic ontology level separation based discriminative learning is further enhanced via curvature-adaptive margin loss in hyperbolic manifold which ions out the decision boundaries of examples from the same class on visual similarity basis and lead to breakage/ separation of structure appropriate disease category as well. Then, a softmax classifier takes the optimized embeddings and maps them into class probabilities from which disease prediction is derived. We present a sequential pipeline leveraging computationally efficient architecture tightly coupling feature extraction, attention based refinement, geometric embedding & classification ready for use in precision agriculture. The architecture of the proposed model is illustrated in Figure 1. ​ Figure 1: Overall Architecture of the Proposed DAHFF-Net Integrating EfficientNet-B4 Backbone with Dual Spatial–Channel Attention for Robust Pre-Harvest Crop Disease Classification ​ 3.2 PlantVillage Dataset​ To evaluate the performance of the proposed DAHFF-Net model comprehensively, we use a common benchmark dataset in plant classification studies- PlantVillage dataset which is publicly accessible. text: A Semantic Confidence–Aware Intuitionistic Fuzzy Ranking Algorithm for Product Evaluation Using Online Reviews Abstract-Online product reviews have become an important source of consumer purchase decision making, but effectively ranking competing products from the large-scale, opinion-rich review data is a challenging task due to semantic ambiguity, sentiment uncertainty and reviewer subjectivity. State-of-the-art rating methods only base on single value sentiment or intervals obtained by classifier randomness which cannot fully represent the confidence, strength and reliability of expressed reviews. To overcome these issues, this paper presents a novel technique called Semantic Confidence–Aware Intuitionistic Fuzzy Ranking (SICA-IFR). The model capitalizes on both contextual semantic representations and confidence-aware sentiment modeling to enhance robustness and interpretability in product ranking. At first, the context em- beddings are utilized to encode the attribute-specific review texts with fine-grained semantic information retained. Afterwards we use more than one sentiment classifiers, such as positive, neutral and negative orientations. Unlike traditional ensemble methods, SCA-IFR embodies a semantic agreement in its framework that evaluates multi-classifier consensus and the intensity of opinion, thus enabling it to produce confidence-weighted sentiment intervals. These ranges are represented using intuitionistic fuzzy sets where support, opposition and hesitance present in the online reviews are considered. In addition, the algorithm includes a data-aware adjustment of attributes weight, to reconcile user preference with sentiment dominance discovered in review. Final product evaluations are performed by an intuitionistic fuzzy TOPSIS model. Experimental results on real-world product review datasets show that our model SCA-IFR significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art review-based ranking algorithms, with approximately 8.7% improvement in average ranking accuracy, about 12.4% reduction of the rank variance and around 10.1% increase of decision stability in different sentiment distributions. These findings validate that the suggested method gives more reliable and consumer-oriented product rankings, for which it is applicable for intelligent decision-support systems in e-commerce environments. Keywords-Product ranking, Online reviews, Semantic confidence, Intuitionistic fuzzy sets, TOPSIS, Sentiment analysis, Decision support systems I Introduction​ The recent growth of online shopping has changed the way people discover [1][2], assess and purchase goods. Today's purchase decisions are heavily influenced by online reviews, which reflect real experiences [3][4], perceived value and product deficiencies. In contrast to conventional star-rating systems, textual reviews also duplicate rich information, such as feature-specific view-points of users and the emotional tone used in their expression. The task of mining such information out and transforming it into trustworthy product rankings is thus crucial for recommendation systems, consumer decision support, and intelligent marketplace management [5][6]. Nonetheless, it is challenging to build a good product-ranking model due to dynamic reviews, large scale and rich opinions of review data.
label: human

text: While abundant review information can be taken advantage of, there are still a few open issues associated with the current ranking methodologies [7][8]. Natural language reviews are ambiguous First, natural language review can be ambiguous since it conveys meaning based on context, sarcasm or implicit sentiment in different ways. Second, sentiment in reviews is inherently uncertain: users often express positive and negative opinions within the same review, posing polarity assignment as a challenging problem. Third, reviewing is subjective and findings may be relative to the review expectation of readers based on usage scenario and writing style as well [9][10]. Last but not least, the majority of prior systems involve relatively less study on modeling confidence in predicted sentiments for the lack of quantisation of opinion extraction. In the current review-based ranking models [11], sentiment information is often collapsed into only one score which oversimplifies complex feelings and throws away important reliability clues [12]. Some recent work tries to correct for uncertainty by providing interval estimates on the basis of classifier randomisation, although these intervals rarely correspond accurately to semantic alignment between classifiers [13][14]. On the other hand, fuzzy and intuitionistic fuzzy reasoning have been studied about decision making under uncertain information; however, how to use these methods in combination with contextual semantics of labels and classifier confidence is insufficiently paid attention with them. Hence, rankings produced by these methods may vary given different sentiment distributions and might not accurately reflect the customer attitude [15]. To compensate these deficiencies, in this paper we propose a Semantic Confidence–Aware Intuitionistic Fuzzy Ranking (SCA-IFR) algorithm to effectively evaluate products based on online reviews. The proposed model integrates context semantic representations and confidence-aware sentiment modeling to represent the opinions with both their meaning and reliability. Our method begins with encoding attribute-level review texts with contextual embeddings that capture fine-grained semantics [16][17]. We finally use several sentiment classifiers and aggregate their output with a semantic agreement mechanism to measure the level of positivity or negativity from the opinion. The confidence-weighted intervals are formulated as intuitionistic fuzzy sets so that the explicit representation of support, opposition, and indecisiveness can be kept in reviews [18][19]. Finally, a data-driven weighting approach and an intuitionistic fuzzy-TOPSIS method leads stable and explainable rankings of products. We can summarize the main contributions of this work as: ●​ A holistic semantic confidence-aware framework that combines context word embeddings with multi-class sentiment modeling for capturing both opinion meaning and the confidence of opinions. ●​ A semantic-agreement–based intuitionistic fuzzy modeling approach, capturing for support, opposition and hesitance with confidence weighted sentiment intervals. ●​ An intuitionistic fuzzy TOPSIS ranking method which is capable of generating consistent, understandable and consumer- oriented product rankings under different sentiment states. In line with these contributions, the study is guided by the following research objectives:
label: human

text: ●​ To build a review-ranked model with consideration of semantic context, sentiment uncertainty and classifier confidence. ●​ To develop a confidence-conscious intuitionistic fuzzy representation model for hesitation and disagreement on opinions. ●​ To evaluate the proposed framework against advanced models ranking approaches and to verify its improvement in accuracy, robustness, and decision stability. 1.1 Organization of the paper: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews existing studies on review-based ranking, fuzzy decision models, and confidence-aware sentiment analysis. Together with these advances, the overall achievements illustrate steady progress of fusing fuzzy logic, psychological modeling and data-driven sentiment processing in building more realistic decision-support systems. 2.5 Gaps Identified Despite the great achievements in previous work, two significant limitations are shared. ●​ While predicting sentiment, most models predict the sentiment of a sentence as a discrete value and do not consider the uncertainty caused by classifier disagreement, linguistic vagueness, and contextual variation. ●​ There are few such models jointly considering semantic under- standing and confidence, particularly in the case of intuitionistic fuzzy structures to handle not only strength of agreement, but also strength of doubt. These deficiencies provide the motivation for devising the SCA-IFR framework, which explicitly considers contextual semantics, classifier consensus and confidence-weighted intuitionistic fuzzy modeling to produce more stable and credible rankings of products. III Methodology​ Our proposed SCA-IFR framework converts raw online reviews into a reliable product ranking based on unified pipeline that fuses semantic modeling, classifier confidence and intuitionistic fuzzy reasoning. First, the reviews are preprocessed, and then correlated with product attributes. And the remaining part of each attribute-specific textual segment is encoded by contextualized embeddings to retain fine-grained semantics [17][18]. These encoded representations of the text are then evaluated by multi-class sentiment classifiers, each of which creates a separate probability distribution for positive, neutral, and negative attitudes. We employ a semantic agreement measure to estimate the inter-classifier agreement and how well classifiers align with contextual semantics, computing confidence-weighted sentiment intervals. These spans are then transformed into intuitionistic fuzzy values, which explicitly reflect on the support, opposition and hesitation [19][20]. Finally, based on user preferences and sentiment dominance, the weight of the attribute is obtained via an intuitionistic fuzzy TOPSIS algorithm to calculate closeness coefficients that rank the products. This combination results in a robust, interpretable and real consumer judgment consistent SCA-IFR ranking computation.

IV Implementation details 4.1 Datasets We validate our approach using the Cleaned Amazon Sales and Reviews Dataset taken from Kaggle, which is made up of a set of curated product records along with the corresponding review data extracted from the Amazon electronics marketplace (CSV format, UTF-8 encoded). This dataset has 4,854 product–review tuples, each representing a review of some product out of its 4,467 products with the following attributes: name and brand (product detail), price and discount percentage (product trading status), numerical rating and text review from users of the product (user sentiment toward that product) as well as cleaned review text and sentiment label. Since the dataset has already gone through pre-processing (non-preference, missing value treatment and fields standardised) it can be directly used for sentiment modelling and ranking analysis. In the case of machine-learning experiments, the data are split 80:20 resulting in a training set with 3,883 instances and a test set containing 971 instances; thus we can evaluate classifier performance and stability downstream. 4.2 Experimental Setup​ The purpose of these experiments was to test the efficacy of the proposed SCA-IFR framework for ordering products based on online reviews. We experimented with the Kaggle cleaned dataset of Amazon sales and reviews that consists of 4,854 review records for 4,467 products with 11 attributes. Pre-processed YourDailyMenu review text were loaded, that include lemon juice.and then tokenized and lower-cased with punctuation, URL stop-word removed. We extracted contextual semantic representations using a pretrained BERT base model (hidden size = 768) that was fine-tuned on the training corpus learning rate, 2 × 10 −5 batch size 16, max sequence length = 128. As a comparison, we also trained an SVM with RBF kernel and a Bi-LSTM network (hidden size = 128, dropout = 0.3). For neural models we used cross-entropy loss, and Adam optimizer and early stopping based on validation loss. The numbers of training and test samples were 3,883 and 971 respectively in the ratio of 80:20. The output of all classifiers was calibrated to probability distributions and these were then used to calculate the semantic agreement and confidence-weighted intervals. The intuitionistic fuzzy decision matrices thus obtained were standardized and ranked by the proposed IFTOPSIS approach. For comparison with robustness, we also confronted SCA-IFR using (i) sentiment ranking by a single classifier, (ii) classical fuzzy TOPSIS, and (iii) since we have only confidence values on the intuitionistic fuzzy set without any representation of the degree of hesitance or extremism over reference values for alternatives in IFset. VI Conclusion This work presented a Semantic Confidence-Aware Intuitionistic Fuzzy Ranking (SCA-IFR) model for product rating based on online reviews. Combining the bag of words with topical semantic embeddings, multi-classifier sentiment estimation process and a Semantic Agreement Measure and intuitionistic fuzzy TOPSIS model, can more effectively measure the meaning of as well as the reliability in expressed opinions. Empirical results on real review data indicate that the SCA-IFR is superior to other existing ranking methods, with improvements of 8.7% in average ranking accuracy, 12.45% in average reduction of ranking variance and 10.1% in decision stability over others are observed. Results show that confidence-aware modeling approach yields more robust and interpretable ranks, which are closer to consumer' judgment. As future work, we will investigate how to integrate the reviewer credibility and fake-review detection into the ranking approach.
