text: I Introduction​ Neoplasms, degenerative conditions, traumatic injuries and compressive syndromes of the spinal cord are one of the leading causes of neurological disability worldwide. Early identification is essential for the patient from a medical point of view [1], because late or delayed recognition may lead to permanent spinal cord injury and lasting dysfunction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) are the most common tools used in routine spinal evaluation, which provide supportive information related to soft-tissue integrity and osseous structures, respectively [3], [5]. Despite these advancements, the precise reading of spinal imaging remains difficult because of complex structure of spinal cord, subtle beginning-stage changes in pathology and major inter-observer difference between radiologists[2], [9]. Recent development of artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning has revealed great potentials for the automatization of spinal image analysis, for example detection of spinal cord compression (SCC), tumor type prediction, and degenerative processes assessment [9], [11], [16], [22]. The majority of the existing works are mainly based on CNNs using single-modality MRI or CT [23], [28]. Although the models have yielded promising results in commonly defined tasks, they generally are insensitive to early-stage or subtle lesions, especially for heterogeneous clinical scenarios [12], [33]. In addition, the CNN-based structures tend not to have abilities such as the ability to model long-range spatial dependencies and cross-structural relationship between different elements which are crucial for comprehending complex spine anatomy. Recently, transformer-based models are employed as effective alternatives to medical image analysis tasks with the self-attention mechanism that can to encode global contextual information. Applications of transformers in spinal imaging GAN 10 also demonstrate better performance for soft tissue segmentation and disease classification [12], [39]. However, transformation based approaches with current transformers still heavily rely on modality-isolated processing or use simple multimodal fusion techniques such as feature concatenation and late decision level adaptive combination. These approaches do not explicitly make use of anatomical correspondence in MRI and CT scans, which might capture irrelevant or even anatomically inconsistent feature interactions [13], [32]. Multimodal MRI–CT fusion may dramatically improve the identification of spinal pathology through integration of complementary soft tissue and bony structural information. But the ideal fusion requires accurate anatomical alignment and region-wise feature interaction for clinical relevance. For spinal imaging, the
label: human

text: combination of vertebral level localization with cord centerline information provide a natural anatomical framework to guide cross-modal feature integration [41]. However, anatomy-guided multimodal learning is rarely studied in the existing models for spinal cord diagnosis. To overcome these limitations, we present an Anatomically-Guided Cross-Modal Residual Transformer (AG-CMRT) to accurately and early detect spinal cord pathologies from multi-modal MRI–CT scans. The proposed work proposed an anatomy-aware fusion that is equivalent by aligning modality-specific feature representations within a shared anatomical coordinate space with reference to spinal cord centerlines and vertebral-level localization. A residual transformer model with anatomically selective cross-modal attention mechanism gives rise to neurophysiologically significant feature interactions, while respecting modality-specific attributes. Moreover, a multi-task learning approach is used to jointly train spinal cord segmentation, lesion detection and vertebral-level localization which can increase robustness under insufficiently annotated data. The main contributions in our work are concluded as follows: ●​ We proposed a new anatomy-based fusion framework of cross-modality (MRI and CT), which incorporates MR-CT anatomic priors at the level of vertebrae and spinal cord. ●​ A persistence transformer with anatomically bias crossmodal attention for clinically consequential feature interaction to improve sensitivity of lesion. ●​ A multi-task learning scheme for simultaneous spinal cord segmentation, lesion detection and vertebral labeling to enhance diagnostic reliability. ●​ Extensive experimental validation on public spinal MRI datasets and the CTSpine1K dataset, showing that our multi-modal boosting method can outperform state-of-the-art single-modality and traditional multimodal baselines. 1.1 Objectives ●​ To construct a MRI and CT images-based deep learning model for early and rapid identification of spinal cord diseases. ●​ To develop an anatomy guided attention mechanism that attends to the important target regions of spinal with both vertebral level and spinal cord information. ●​ To test the proposed method on spinal MRI and CT images, we compare it with state-of-the-art methods. The rest of this paper is structured as follows. Related works on the spinal cord imaging, deep-learning based spinal pathology analysis and multimodal medical image fusion could be found in Section II. Then, the methodology of AG-CMRT is introduced in Section III, where dataset introduction, preprocessing, network design
label: human

text: and learning-based anatomy guidance as well as the training strategy are elaborated. The experimental configuration and the quantitative results, comparative experiments, ablation studies and statistical analysis were shown in section IV. Section V presents the results, limitations and future work, while Section VI concludes with a summary of main findings and clinical implications. II Literature Review Spinal cord disorders, including neurodegenerative diseases, trauma, neoplasms and degenerative diseases can cause severe disabilities when not diagnosed at an early stage. Khamaysa et al. (2025) pointed out that there are diseases with no reliable biomarker, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and early diagnosis and follow-up of these diseases are difficult, discussing the increasing importance of quantitative spinal cord imaging for diagnosis and prognosis [1]. This highlights the clinical requirement of imaging-based techniques capable of detecting small changes in the spinal cord. Recent advancement in artificial intelligence has been prompted to the development of computer-aided tools for spinal imaging. Martín-Noguerol et al. (2023) summarized the application of AI technology on MRI and CT (vertebral labeling, segmentation, trauma detection, and pathologic cord evaluation). The author suggested that AI could enhance diagnostic accuracy of MRI/CT by easing radiologist’s workload [2]. Nevertheless, the authors pointed out that anatomically sensible segmentation and consistent feature extraction are still major barriers in clinical adoption. CT and MRI have complementary roles in the assessment of the spine. Hussain et al. (2023) reviewed imaging protocol of spinal trauma, suggesting that CT excels at evaluating osseous structures, while MRI is superior for assessing injury severity and prognosis of spinal cord [3]. Similarly, Santiago et al. (2022) emphasized the importance of this interpretation and selection of CT and MRI in diverse congenital, degenerative, inflammatory, and tumoral spinal entities [5]. These reports suggest that over-reliance on a single imaging modality could restrict the diagnostic capability. The stability of MRI as the modal image in spinal cord pathology persists. De Paiva et al. (2023) and Won et al. (2022) reported high diagnostic performance of MRI for common spinal cord tumors but with lower sensitivity to rare pathologies and complicated anatomical manifestations [4], [10]. Haynes et al. (2023) also substantially demonstrated that advanced MRI methods, like spinal cord fMRI, allow for important functional findings but could benefit from technically challenging analysis procedures to address technical shortcomings [6]. Deep learning-based methods have shown a growing interest in analysis of spinal MRI. Biercher et al. (2021) showed that CNNs can identify a variety of SC
label: human

text: pathologies on MR, with model performance decreasing for less prevalent conditions caused by sample size (i.e. training set stratification) [7]. Merali et al. (2021) proposed a CNN-based method for identifying cervical SCC and obtained high diagnostic value, showing potential clinical value of AI-assisted interpretation [9]. Recently, Haim et al. (2024), Ito et al. (2023), and Shahzadi et al. (2023) adopted deep learning in pathology differentiation, tumor detection and lumbar stenosis classification successively and the task-specific performance was good [12], [15], [16]. However, despite these promising results, prevalent models are majority MRI-only and adopt CNN architectures with a local receptive field. CT-dl has emerged as a promising tool for structural and compressive spinal pathology. Kuah et al. (2022) emphasized the importance of CT in metastatic spinal cord compression, and it also suggested that deep learning might contribute to shortening diagnostic lag [8]. Hallinan et al. [11] found that the performance of experienced clinicians was matched by a CT-based deep learning model on detection of epidural spinal cord compression [12]. Nevertheless, these CT-based models are not sensitive for intramedullary and soft tissues. To circumvent these challenges, there have been attempts at developing multimodal imaging. Dobrocky et al. (2023), they showed that fusion of cross-sectional imaging increases diagnostic comprehension for neuro-vascular spinal pathologies [13]. Lecouvet et al. (2022) also emphasized the auxiliary diagnostic tasks for detection of minimal residual disease with MRI and PET/CT, stressing the clinical relevance of multispectral fusion [17]. However, current deep learning research mostly uses general kinds of fusion mechanism without anatomically explicit guidance. 2.1 Research Gap The existing deep learning methods on spinal cord imaging are single-modality based, CNN-based and non-anatomy constraint. Models built using MRI perform well in analysis of soft tissue, whereas models constructed from CT offer strong structural assessment; however, neither is able to provide complete diagnostic imaging coverage. Furthermore, the current multimodal fusion techniques lack explicit consideration of the spinal anatomy to guide feature interaction. This obvious research hole encourages the creation of anatomy-aware, transformer-based multimodal frameworks such as the proposed AG-CMRT for early and accurate spinal cord pathologies detection. III Materials and Methods As our main contribution, we present a single and unique end-to-end unified architecture that combines MRI and CT modalities to analyse spinal cord pathology -referred to as Anatomically-Guided Cross-Modal Residual Transformer (AG-CMRT)
label: human

text: [22][23]. As illustrated in Fig. 1, MRI and CT images are encoded by modality-specific encoders to retain their complementary features first. Concurrently, a convolutional encoder captures soft tissue and intramedullary features from MRI scans, coupled with a parallel encoder that learns bony structure and vertebral features from CT volumes. These encoders are separately trained to avoid premature feature dilution, while preserving source modality-specific diagnostic cues. The generated features are projected into a common imaging coordinate system based on spinal cord centerlines and vertebral levels that guarantees spatial correspondences across modalities. Feature representations in this anatomically aligned space [24] [25] are tokenized and forwarded into a cross-modal residual transformer, which leverages anatomical guided attention to fuse clinically meaningful features. This flexible architecture ensures that information from any modality can interact productively across modalities while conforming to anatomy and providing the building block for accurate multi-source learning, and robust spinal pathology detection. An overview of the full AG-CMRT architecture including modality specific encoding, anatomical alignment and anatomy-guided cross-modal fusion is depicted in Figure 1. In addition, the available dataset is composed of 9 MRI examinations on lumbar spine T2-weighted sagittal and axial scans in both DICOM and JPEG formats. The database is supplemented with verbose radiologic reports, containing patient demographics, detailed clinical history including complaints and preliminary diagnosis and follow-up

All the patients are anonymised and informed written consent for publication of data was received. This was chosen due to its quality of annotation, availability in sagittal and axial views and the English composition relevance for soft tissue and intramedullary pathology assessment. 3.1.2 CTSpine1K Dataset CT data were obtained from the publicly available CTSpine1K [41], which is a large-scale spinal CT database collected from multiple hospitals. This data set comprises 1,005 CT volumes annotated with the locations of over 11,100 individual vertebrae across the cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine. Each CT volume is voxel-level vertebral segmented and vertebral level labeled, which is ideal for learning bony anatomy and spinal curvature position. CTSpine1K is selected because of its large scale, variety of types and severities for spinal diseases, as well as high-quality vertebral annotations conducting a strong supervision for vertebral localization and structural feature leaning. 3.1.3 Multimodal Fusion Strategy The Spine MRI Dataset and CTSpine1K were combined in the proposed unified multimodal learning framework to take advantage of complementarity between them. Unlike CT, MRI can be used to visualize the marrow and provide good soft tissue contrast for visualizing spinal cord compression and degenerative changes, whereas there is superior bony anatomy detail provided by CT. While the datasets are not perfectly paired at patient level, anatomical correspondence was attained through vertebral-level localization and spinal region matching that supports successful cross-modal fusion. This joint dataset approach helps alleviate the scarcity of paired MRI–CT data and enables the proposed model to gain anatomically consistent representations across both modalities, promoting robust multimodal spinal pathology analysis. 3.2 Preprocessing Pipeline​ All imaging data were preprocessed using a standardized processing pipeline to obtain cross-modality consistency and anatomical alignment before model training [24]. text: IV Experimental Setup 4.1 Hardware & Software​ All experiments were conducted on high-performance computing workstation with a NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (24GB VRAM), an Intel Xeon processor and 128GB system memory. The proposed AG-CMRT method was implemented by Python 3.9 and PyTorch v1. 13, with CUDA 11. x with GPU support CUDA and cuDNN. Model training, testing and evaluation were performed on Linux. We used standard scientific and medical imaging libraries (e.g., NumPy, SciPy), as well as tools for preprocessing, augmentation and evaluation of data (i.e., SimpleITK [16] and MONAI. The model was trained on this version of the software stack for better transformer based model training and reproducibility in experiments. 4.2 Cross-Validation Protocol and Statistical Significance Testing To ensure the robustness of our model and avoid overfitting with the limited number of MRI images, we employed a fivefold cross-validation scheme at patient-level for Spine MRI Dataset, in which the same patient’s data was ruled out from training set to testing set. In each fold, 80% of the data samples were used for training and 20% for testing, with an internal validation sample extracted from the training set to select the model. The CTSpine1K dataset splits were fixed across folds to ensure consistent distribution on the vertebral level. Statistical significance on the performance differences for AG-CMRT and baseline methods were calculated with paired two-tailed t-test over normal distributed metrics and Wilcoxon signed-rank test over non-parametric comparisons. text: 5.1 Discussion This study demonstrates that it is possible to achieve a significant enhancement of the detection and delineation from SC lesions compared with single modality same as conventional fusion techniques applying anatomy-based multimodal fusion. The proposed AG-CMRT further enhances the detection sensitivity and accuracy of lesion segmentation by leveraging vertebral-level and spinal cord anatomical priors to regularize cross-modal attention. Ablation experiment demonstrates the importance of both residual learning and anatomy-guided attention in the performance improvement, especially for early detection of lesions. Although the absence of full paired MRI–CT data remains a limit, the findings emphasized that AG-CMRT could be considered as an effective and meaningful framework for early spinal pathology diagnosis. 5.2 Limitations and Future Work However, this study is limited by the use of partially unpaired MRI/CT and retrospective data, which may also impact generalizability to other institutions. In the future, we plan to validate the proposed AG-CMRT framework on larger fully paired multi-center data sets. The use of longitudinal imaging data would enhance the sensitivity to disease progression and treatment response. Furthermore, broadening the approach to other spinal levels and classes of pathology will increase its clinical utility. VI Conclusion In this work, we proposed an Anatomically Guided Cross Modal Residual Transformer (AG-CMRT) for multimodal MRI–CT spinal cord pathology prognosis solving limitations of mono-modality and naïve fusion. By leveraging anatomical priors with vertebral-level localization information and spinal cord centerline guidance, the proposed model obtained a lesion detection sensitivity of 93.4%, a lesion segmentation Dice score of 76.8%, and a spinal cord segmentation Dice of 91.6% superior to other baselines in comparison results. These findings indicate that anatomy-aided cross-modality fusion can enhance the sensitivity of small or early lesions. In general, AG-CMRT offers both a solid and anatomically realistic platform to support early diagnosis and clinical decision-making in the assessment of spinal cord pathology. text: A Novel Distribution-Driven Federated Framework for Evaluating Healthcare IoT Data Anonymization under Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Abstract- The explosion of the Internet of Things (IoT) in healthcare has offered parallel opportunities as well, such as continuous patient monitoring and data-driven clinical decisions; however, it also raised concerns about privacy. There are many anonymization methods available for securing sensitive healthcare IoT data and their evaluations have been mostly performed discretely in prior work, with only a limited number of studies quantifying privacy–utility trade-off in an integrated and clear manner. This paper presents HAPED-QA-FL (Healthcare Anonymization Performance Evaluation using Distributional Quality Assessment with Federated Learning), an evaluation framework for privacy, where one does not leverage federated learning as a security tool but as a distributed analytics engine to evaluate the impact of anonymization on model utility across healthcare at scale without centralizing raw data. Anonymization is evaluated by the framework at two complementary levels, i.e., distribution-driven analysis that employs statistical divergence, entropy-based information loss, and quasi-identifier uniqueness; coupled with federated performance validation in which anonymized datasets are collaboratively analyzed to infer utility loss and re-identification risk under realistic IoT healthcare scenarios. A generalised privacy–utility equilibrium score (PUES) is proposed to rank anonymisation schemes with respect to their data-utility preservation, information loss and the re-identification risk. Experiments conducted on real-world healthcare IoT datasets show that the introduced framework provides a more stable and interpretable solution method to anonymization evaluation over traditional single-metric based solutions, providing a scalable and domain-adherent way for privacy support in healthcare IoT data management. Keywords: Healthcare IoT, Data Privacy, Data Anonymization, Federated Learning, Privacy–Utility Trade-off, Information Loss, Re-identification Risk, Distributional Assessment I Introduction​ The introduction of the Internet of Things (IOT) in Healthcare changed how clinical data are acquired allowing for continuous monitoring, personalised treatment and real-time decision support [1][2]. Wearable sensors, intelligent medical devices and remote patient monitoring systems have created the flood of heterogeneous data streams that move across hospitals [3] diagnostic centers [4] and cloud platforms. Although these features enhance the quality of life for patients, they also lead to a new degree of exposure of personal health data [5][6]. Even when direct identifiers do
label: human

text: not exist in the released data, combinations of quasi-identifiers can still enable an individual to be re-identified, resulting in privacy threats being long-term and hard-to-treat [7]. Given that healthcare facilities are more and more relying heavily on big data analytics, there is an urgent need for evaluation frameworks that guarantee privacy while preserving the analytic value of data [8][9]. Several research works have suggested anonymization techniques to mitigate privacy risks in healthcare IoT data but they were evaluated separately and by using incomplete features [10][11]. Some assessments consider only privacy and do not consider how much utility is lost of the data, while others use centralized learning techniques that are impractical if agencies can’t share their data. Therefore, the trade-off between data utility [12][13], information loss and reidentification risk is not easily quantified by one easy-to-understand metric [14][15]. To address these problems, we present HAPED-QA-FL, a distribution-supported framework for quantitatively assessing anonymization process. The framework also does not adopt federated learning as a security technique or for collaborative computation. This permits the evaluation of the impact of anonymization on model performance in a multi-institutional setting without sharing raw data across sites [16][17]. Through the integration of distribution-based metrics and federated validation, this approach offers a straightforward and operationally feasible path for selecting anonymization methods that ensure privacy without compromising valuable clinical information [18][19]. 1.1 Background & Motivation Healthcare IoT environments gather ongoing physiological, behavioural and contextual information which constitute extremely sensitive details of patient’s life. The traditional anonymization research works hardly consider their distributed, high-dimensional [20][21] and dynamic aspects. We thus need a structured, reproducible methodology to assess anonymization methods under realistic health care deployment scenarios. 1.2 Privacy problems in Healthcare IoT However, anonymized datasets are also likely to be privacy-threatening as individuals can still be re-identified through linkage attacks [21], quasi-identifier matches [22], and distributional inference. The risk is multiplied when data is shared between different entities and used together on analysis – resulting in privacy assurance being more of a continuous process rather than just a one-off exercise. 1.3 Limitations of existing anonymization evaluations Most prior evaluations: ●​ Analyze anonymization techniques independently,

III Proposed HAPED-QA-FL Framework​ 3.1 Design Philosophy and Objectives The core motivation of HAPED-QA-FL is the observation that privacy-threats derived from healthcare IoT data not only are rooted in the data distribution rather than only model or algorithmic basis. The datasets in Healthcare IoT are inherently heterogeneous, high- dimensional and evolving over time and span in nature – pertains to physiological signals, context attributes, behavioral characteristics obtained from various environments. Anonymization modifies the statistical distribution of such data, in terms of attribute distributions, correlations etc., and by that has impact on privacy exposure as well as analytical utility [23][24]. But much of the prior evaluation research assesses anonymization effectiveness indirectly via accuracy on downstream models or isolated privacy metrics, without considering what anonymity does to the data distributions. This leads to a distribution-relying philosophy for evaluation, i.e., one should examine the quality of anonymization in terms of statistical divergence, entropy-based information loss and uniqueness of quasi-identifiers, before performing any learning-oriented assessment. Through grounding evaluation at the data level, HAPED-QA-FL allows for transparent and model-agnostic analysis of privacy–utility trade-offs that arise in previous anonymization and privacy-preserving data mining work due to fragmented and non-uniformed evaluation methodologies [1], [3], [32]. This is especially important in healthcare IoT domains, where even small distributional deviations can lead to clinically meaningful analytical errors [25]. Consistent with this philosophy, HAPED-QA-FL deliberately focuses on non-learning metrics as the initial evaluation stage. Model-based evaluations are often influenced by architecture, hyper-parameter selection and optimization dynamics which can bias assessment while not clearly reflecting the underlying effect of anonymization on data quality. Non-learning metrics, on the other hand, offer a fixed and comparable way to measure information leakage and re-identification risk irrespective of prediction accuracy in line with recent privacy vs utility trade-offs studies [6], [35]. Hence, federated learning is only adopted in HAPED-QA-FL as a
label: human

text: supplementary validation approach to explore how anonymity data take effect on a realistic distributed healthcare analytics scenario without centralizing the raw patient data[26][27]. It is important to note that federated learning is not presented as a security and privacy-preserving tool per se, but rather as a joint evaluation platform that emulates real multi-institutional healthcare deployments [7], [12], [16]. Therefore HAPED-QA-FL is framed as an assessment tool and not as a privacy enforcement policy, aiming at ranking anonymization techniques according to their suitability for preserving data utility, minimizing information loss and decreasing re-identification risk in federated healthcare IoT scenarios. This separation of evaluation from enforcement helps achieve better interpretability (with a hierarchical analysis), scalability, and domain adherence, mitigating challenges that were noted in previous federated and anonymization-focused research [8], [10], [32]. 3.2 System Architecture Overview​ The proposed HAPED-QA-FL structure adopts a modular, serial stream pipeline that allows us to evaluate healthcare IoT data anonymization in orderly series under practical distributed scenarios. The pipeline starts with raw healthcare IoT data, extracted from a variety of sources such as wearable sensors, smart medical devices, and remote patient monitoring systems. Such datasets are characterised by direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers and sensitive clinical values under complex temporal and statistical relationships. The data are processed by an anonymization module in the first phase on one hand, using well-known k-anonymity–based generalization, suppression [28][29] and clustering-based anonymization techniques and attribute-stored transformations [2], [15], [18] depending on configuration of privacy presets. Crucially, this module is applied independently from the learning algorithm and thus the anonymization process cannot be corrupted by optimization bias of a specific model. By factoring out the anonymization at this stage, the framework enables proper comparison between different techniques while retaining the original analytical purpose of the dataset, which has been a common criticism in previous healthcare anonymization research [1], [22]. Once anonymized, such transformed data enter the distributional quality assessment phase, which represents the analytical core for our architecture approach. At this point, the framework analyzes how anonymization affects the statistical properties of healthcare IoT for data with non-learning-based metrics including a distance between original and anonymized distributions [3], information loss via entropy based metrics, and uniqueness analysis over quasi-identifiers [25] [32]. These provide an interpretable and model independent view of privacy exposure and data degradation, addressing a concern in prior works on the evaluation of privacy-preserving data mining and anonymization about fragmented or single-metric assessment
label: human

text: practices [6], [35]. Then, the anonymized datasets are put through federated utility testing in which federated learning is used to collectively assess model performance between several healthcare sites without sharing raw data [7], [12], [16]. This step estimates the reality of the anonymization effect on analytical utility in a realistic multi-institutional setting. Finally, the outcomes of both distributional assessment and federated validation steps are combined together into a single Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES) which balances utility preservation, information loss [30], and re-identification risk jointly. Consolidating multi-dimensional evaluation results into a single value, expressed in human-readable values, the proposed architecture provides an opportunity for objective comparison/ranking of anonymization techniques [31]; it is a direct response to the lack of any unified, scalable evaluative mechanism across current healthcare IoT privacy literature [8], [10], [32]. System Architecture of HAPED-QA-FL Illustrating Distributional Assessment, Federated Utility Validation, and Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Scoring 3.3 Distribution-Driven Anonymization Assessment The first analytical phase of HAPED-QA-FL aims to analyze distribution-based anonymization evaluation, which measures the effect on statistical structure of healthcare IoT data caused by privacy protection process. Unlike model-based evaluations, this step works on data distributions rather than models for transparency and interpretability. The difference between the original and anonymized data distributions is quantified using statistical divergence. In their essence, divergence metrics like the KL-divergence or JS-divergence quantify redistribution of probability mass over attributes after anonymization. For the case of healthcare IoT data, that include various physiological signals and contextual features which usually follow nonuniform distribution and are correlated, small distortion in this kind of distributions would lead to large impacts on deeper analytics. By
label: human

text: examining divergence, the model assesses whether anonymization maintains or distorts global data structure at a level of distortion that may impact clinical relevance. Previous work has identified that distributional changes due to the anonymization process are a significant but sometimes overlooked contributor to utility loss, especially in high-dimensional and streaming healthcare data [3], [25], [32]. Besides distribution similarity, HAPED-QA-FL incorporates the loss of information (entropy) as a metric to measure how much data detail is withheld through anonymization. Entropy indicates the amount of uncertainty in the values of data. Anonymization techniques, like generalization and suppression, typical tends to increase entropy by coarsening the data [33][34]. At the same time, high entropy would indicate better protection of privacy but also more potentially useful information that gets lost that is needed for an accurate analysis. Thus, entropy-based analysis can balance the gain of privacy and loss of data utility, which has been a key issue in privacy–utility trade-off studies[1][6][35]. In addition, a quasi-identifier uniqueness analysis is applied to determine the re-identification risk using the frequencies of unique combinations of attributes as in the anonymized file. In healthcare IoT datasets, features such as age brackets, timestamps or device reference numbers can serve as quasi-identifiers for linkage attacks if distinct patterns persist [35]. From the reduction or preservation of these unique combinations due to anonymization, the framework estimates remaining disclosure risk, but does not perform cost-intensive attack simulations [2][26]. Statistical discrepancy, entropy based information loss and uniqueness of quasi-identifiers as such yield a complete non-learning evaluation layer. This layer is built on several pieces that the privacy risk and degradation of data quality are captured in distribution level, ensuring a good integrity to evaluate how much utility one would achieve through federated learning [36]. 3.4 Federated Learning-Based Utility Validation Following the distribution-based evaluation, HAPED-QA-FL leverages federated learning to verify data utility in real-world distributed healthcare IoT settings. In this phase, each federated client corresponds to a healthcare provider or an IoT data source and could be in the form of a hospital, clinic, or a geographically distributed patient monitoring system. Each client has its own tepid dataset local and trains a model independently, thus raw patient data is never shared nor centralized. This configuration is close to actual healthcare implementation [37] due to legal and institutional constraints which make it impossible to directly share the data between organizations.
label: human

text: This approach of training models locally on anonymized data allows the framework to approximate how anonymization affects prediction performance in realistic deployment scenarios, as opposed to assuming analysis from ideal (centralized) systems as is sometimes criticized in federated health analytics research [7], [12], [39]. The model architecture and the learning task need to be the same across clients (to make fair comparison), while differences in performance, should be attributed only to the anonymization methods rather than a mismatch of models. The aggregation of HAPED-QA-FL is also designed to be a minimalist one, that is aimed to compare performance and not provide additional privacy protection or security. Model-updates or performance-metrics are aggregated and analyzed to quantify the extent of deviation in accuracy, convergence, and stability induced by different anonymization techniques. Our approach is fundamentally different from the conventional federated learning systems which complete tasks by focus on secure aggregation [9], encryption or defense against attacks [10,12]. Rather, we take the approach that federated learning is a means to an end it can be used as a tool to observe how anonymization affects results when analytics are applied in distributed healthcare. The federated learning is employed solely for the assessment of downstream utility in a practical scenario. The decoupling of utility evaluation and security mechanisms helps to ensure that anonymization quality is not tangled with security characteristics in HAPED-QA-FL, so the evaluation would be more clear. This perspective is supported by recent works that demonstrate the sensitivity of federated learning to variations in data preprocessing and availability, while it rarely has been employed as a quantitative measure for determining the quality of anonymization [6], [16], [35]. Through this federated validation phase, the framework offers practical deployment-time guidance on how anonymization decisions impact real-world healthcare IoT analytics without imposing superfluous system complexity or security assumptions [38]. 3.5 Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES)​ Anonymization in healthcare IoT data There are several goals for anonymizing the healthcare IOT data and they conflict with each other. These objectives are maintaining the utility of the data for analysis, minimising information loss and reducing the potential to re-identify individuals. Downstream use of such data would most likely to be reported in most other studies using different measures which makes it hard to interpret and compare the anonymization. It makes the evaluations always mixed if there are no clear or objective criteria. For instance, one anonymization approach offers strong privacy protection with much loss of utility and the other technique preserving the data utility still admits some threat for releasing data. With no one objective evaluation measure, there is a need for practitioners to decide which criteria they want to optimise and live with choices based on application-specific
label: human

text: assumptions, a limitation well known in the context of privacy–utility trade-offs [1], [6], [35]. Toward a larger perspective, a combined measure of privacy and utility should be defined for evaluating the anonymization methods -- Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES) which is proposed by HAPED-QA-FL. By aggregating evaluation scores into a single number, PUES ensures easy comparison across anonymization techniques, datasets and deployment settings but without the risk of over-simplifying the underlying trade-offs [39]. The rationale of PUES is to tune the trade-off between three important factors for anonymization quality: data utility, information loss and re-identification risk. Data utility refers to anonymized data that can still provide meaningful analysis as assessed through federated learning within distributed healthcare IoT environments. Information loss measures how much the data is altered by anonymization [40], and was quantified through entropy-based and distribution-based measures, such that a lower information loss means better preservation of valuable information. The re-identification risk is the remaining portion of individuals that can be identified from anonymized data, which are calculated as quasi-identifier uniqueness and distribution-level exposure [2], [26], [32]. PUES integrates these three factors in a manner that applies the benefits to anonymization algorithms that preserve high analytical utility, and the punishments to those with severe information loss as well as residual privacy risk. Unlike the concentration on an individual metric, PUES achieves a middle ground compromise between competing objectives, which is more practical for healthcare data governance and regulatory compliance. Through its provision of an open and unified evaluation metric (PUES), PUES can be used to make informed decisions about anonymization approaches, addressing the absence of comprehensive evaluation mechanisms observed in previous healthcare IoT privacy papers [8], [10], [35]. IV Experimental Setup and Evaluation Metrics 4.1 Healthcare IoT Datasets Description To carefully assess the proposed HAPED-QA-FL scheme under real-world deployment scenarios, it utilizes the healthcare IoT datasets in a representative manner that showcases the diversity and sensitivity as well as distributed properties of contemporary medical data systems. Typical data in healthcare IoT are produced by wearable sensors, medical smart devices and remote patient monitoring systems. These sources generate multi-faceted records recording physiological values, context and the passage of time. Typically, these data sets include direct identifiers and quasi-identifiers (e.g., age groups, timestamps, device IDs, location specific attributes as well as sensitive clinical information). Therefore, they continue to be at risk of being re-identified after simple de-identification. Anonymization in healthcare IoT
label: human

text: data is particularly effective, but previous research indicates that the effectiveness of anonymization in healthcare IoT data strongly depends on types of data items and dimensionality, distribution patterns [3], [5], [32]. Evaluation of anonymization methods with realistic datasets are even more important than those based on simplified or synthetic ones. Consistent with experiences in privacy protection and federated healthcare studies, the datasets introduced in this study are derived from real-world or popular benchmark healthcare IoT sources such as enable experiments across multiple institutions [7], [12], [31]. These datasets contain structured clinical information in addition to series of time-dependent sensor readings depicting realistic patient monitoring. Data related attributes are divided in ident for identifiers, quasi-identies and sensitive variables aiming at a controlled application of anonymization methods like generalization (or suppression) or clustering-based transformations [2], [15], [18]. Furthermore, the datasets do not only have skewed distributions, but some attributes are also strongly correlated, a fact that is crucial for assessing relative statistical divergence and entropy-based information loss by anonymisation. By doing this, we do bridge the gap and confront directly a limitation of previous studies [1], [22], [35], which have utilized oversimplified or low-dimensional datasets and thus didn’t capture realistic privacy–utility trade-offs in healthcare settings. To model decentralized healthcare environments, each dataset is further partitioned over multiple clients, where each client corresponds to a single healthcare provider or a different IoT data stream. These data sub-sampling are designed to maintain the local characteristics and heterogeneity of the data, as well as account for realistic differences in patient populations, device varieties and measurements collection protocols across institutions [7], [16], [39]. Of significance is that raw data are left with each client during the entire process, and at no time is it engaged for distribution-based analysis nor federated utility validation. The proposed setup respects regulatory, and practical constraints such as those usually occurring in healthcare IoT systems, but at the same time it allows an objective evaluation on how anonymization algorithms impact data utility information loss, and re-identification risk level for the federated setting. 4.2 Anonymization Techniques Evaluated In order to guarantee the all-round and fair evaluation of privacy–utility trade-offs in IoHT data, the proposed HAPED-QA-FL framework assesses on a heterogeneous and widely followed class of anonymization methods. These methods cover classical privacy models and utility-aware data-centric approaches which are often adopted in healthcare data release and analysis. These are the classical methods for
label: human

text: anonymization, including k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness that have been identified for comparison due to their maturity and wide use in healthcare data sharing context [2], [18], [22]. These attacks work largely based on the generalization and suppression of quasi-identifiers for risk reduction in re-identification. Although effective for preventing the direct linkage attacks, existing approaches have shown that by enhancing the anonymization strength in such models, a significant amount of information is lost and thereby the analytic utility can be decreased significantly​, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional IoT data sets [1], [3], [35]. Their presence establishes the base-line for how classic privacy guarantees expect to work in distribution-driven and federated evaluation. Both, generalization and suppression techniques are extended to be independent components being evaluated by their own right separately of how they influence data distributions and utility. These are intuitively appealing to practitioners, and thus of interest in healthcare scenarios due to ease of use and regulatory interpretability but they known to distort distributions of attribute values as well as inter-variable relationships when used excessively [2], [25]. Micro-aggregation techniques are also applied [15],[24], wherein records are clustered into groups and replaced by the group means in order to be less sensitive (i.e. have low identifiability) to individual identity while maintaining useful statistical properties. Micro-aggregation is known to provide better preservation of utility over pure suppression but it can be very sensitive to cluster quality and data heterogeneity, which becomes specifically relevant for the evaluation in a distributed healthcare IoT setting [32]. Last, the architecture compares utility-aware and attribute-centric anonymization strategies that take into consideration of importance of an attribute, and distribution characteristics of data in adjusting privacy strength. Such techniques balance the preservation of analytic useful information, and the anonymisation of less important quasi-identifiers in an effort to identify a good privacy–utility trade-off [1], [15], [37]. Both of these approaches are now understood to be more appropriate for healthcare analytics, because wholesale de-identification can reduce the clinical validity. It is worth noting that cryptographic approaches, as well as differential privacy mechanisms, are not examined in this paper as our main task for HAPED-QA-FL is to study how the anonymization effectiveness occurs at data level rather than integrity by introducing noise or encryption. By passing these spectrum of anonymization techniques through a single, distribution-informed and federated abstraction, the work allows an unfettered comparison of their capabilities as well as weaknesses which can guide real-world deployments of healthcare IoT.

These metrics are model-agnostic and are computed prior to federated learning–based validation to ensure that evaluation is not biased by learning dynamics. The selected metrics focus on three complementary aspects: distributional distortion, information loss, and residual re-identification risk. 4.3.1 Statistical Divergence Statistical divergence calculates the difference in the probability distributions of original dataset , and anonymized dataset  ; it measures how much anonymization 𝑃 𝑄 distorts the original data structure. For healthcare IoT datasets, high growth of entropy may hurt clinical interpretability and predictive accuracy. 4.3.3 Quasi-Identifier Uniqueness When records are anonymized, the quasi-identifier (QI) uniqueness is the fraction of records that continue to be able to be uniquely identified with combinations of quasi-identifiers. Let be the number of all records and be the number of 𝑁 𝑈 records whose QI combination are unique. This quantity is of concern in healthcare IoT data, where age ranges, timestamps and sensor meta-data can serve as powerful quasi-identifiers. 4.3.4 Role of Distributional Metrics in HAPED-QA-FL In this way, statistical divergence, information loss via entropy and quasi-identifier uniqueness together form a full distribution-based measure of anonymization quality. These measurements demonstrate the extent to which anonymization warps the data distribution, and how much useful information has been sacrificed in order to maintain privacy of individual identities - without relying on model performance at all. They are the critical inputs of the Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES). PUES leverages these distribution-based statistics and the federated learning–based utility evaluation to compute a unified ranking for anonymization methods that applies in realistic healthcare IoT deployment scenarios. 4.4 Federated Learning Configuration​ In the considered HAPED-QA-FL framework, federated learning mirrors real healthcare environment in terms of multi-institution IoT settings, yet only leverages for data utility analysis and not to realize PPA. Each federated client is a unique health care organization or an IoT data source (hospital, clinic, remote patient monitoring system). Each client locally trains a model on its own anonymized data alone. Models results or performance metrics are pooled across all clients using a federated averaging approach, typical of federated learning in healthcare. All clients share the same learning task, model structure and training settings. This way any differences in model recall can be attributed to only the anonymization techniques used on the data, and not on the models. Note that federated learning process does not explicitly involve secure aggregation, encryption or differential privacy. This is by design, as our objective is to study the effect of anonymization on analytics at scale in
label: human

text: a distributed setting, not to achieve stronger confidentiality. It allows for a transparent and unbiased assessment of how good anonymization performs in terms of preserving utility when faced with realistic IoT healthcare deployment. 4.5 Evaluation Protocol and Baselines The evaluation protocol in this study is designed to ensure a fair, reproducible, and technique-agnostic comparison of anonymization methods under the proposed HAPED-QA-FL framework. For each healthcare IoT dataset, anonymization techniques are applied independently using consistent parameter settings, after which evaluation proceeds in two sequential stages: distribution-driven assessment followed by federated utility validation. In the first stage, anonymized datasets are compared against their original counterparts using statistical divergence, entropy-based information loss, and quasi-identifier uniqueness to quantify privacy exposure and data distortion. In the second stage, the same anonymized datasets are used as inputs to the federated learning configuration described in Section 4.4, where downstream analytical utility is measured through aggregated performance indicators. Baseline comparisons include (i) non-anonymized data to establish an upper-bound reference for utility, and (ii) classical single-metric anonymization evaluations that rely solely on privacy strength or model accuracy, reflecting common practices in prior studies [2], [6], [35]. By combining these baselines with the proposed Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES), the evaluation protocol enables objective ranking of anonymization techniques while highlighting the limitations of isolated or centralized evaluation approaches commonly adopted in existing healthcare IoT privacy research. V Results and Discussion 5.1 Experimental Results Overview This section describes the empirical evaluation of HAPED-QA-FL framework on various healthcare IoT datasets and anonymization techniques. The findings are presented, preserving the two-tiered assessment principle of the approach by first discussing distribution-based anonymization verification and second discussing federated learning-based utility validation. This systematic presentation provides insight into the interpretation of how anonymization impacts data properties at the distribution level and what is transferred to downstream analytical performance in realistic distributed healthcare scenarios. All the anonymization methods were tested under the same conditions according to the procedure described in Section IV. Results are presented with statistical divergence, entropy based information loss, quasi-identifier uniqueness, federated utility measures and the joint Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES). The findings expose common patterns across datasets, which suggest that
label: human

text: anonymization techniques with lower distributional distortion and less uniqueness in quasi-identifier tend to preserves better federated utility. These results confirm the main hypothesis of this paper – distribution-oriented analysis is a strong predictor of downstream utility behavior in federated healthcare IoT analytics. 5.2 Distribution-Driven Anonymization Analysis The distribution based analysis reveals that disparate anonymization schemes lead to distinct impacts on the statistical characteristic of healthcare IoT data. Conventional k-anonymity methods lead to a great increment of the statistical divergence with high anonymization degree, indicating that as the data set is more aggressive distorted from its actual distribution. This issue is particularly acute with attributes having a large number of unique values, and time-based features where heavy generalisation can nullify key relationships between attributes necessary for clinical understanding. It is found that the tendency also holds for the information loss by entropy-based analysis. Methods that strongly rely on data suppression result in the greatest increase of entropy, which represents loss of detail and granularity. Microaggregation and attribute-based anonymization techniques on the other hand present much smaller entropy increases, which means that it is possible to preserve higher levels of useful information while still creating a reduction in disclosure risk. A QI uniqueness analysis also indicates that while all anonymization methods compromise identifiability to some extent, the attribute-aware anonymization approaches are better at reducing the residual uniqueness of records in a manner that is less harmful in terms of data distortion. These findings support the finding that privacy strength alone is not a good indicator of quality when judging anonymization quality and distribution-based measures are key to achieving balance between privacy and data utility. ​ Figure 2. Such a model trained in high-divergence anonymized data will converge slower and make worse predictions on patients from participating healthcare organizations. Such degradation is pervasive among different organizations, suggesting that anonymization-induced distribution shifts cause harm to the stability of collaborative learning. Train loss is plotted against federated rounds for a range of anonymization methods, gradient shading of the curves indicates a strategic smoothing-effects. Attribute-centric anonymization has lower final loss and faster converge rate, indicating a smaller distributional disruption as well as better learning stability. These results demonstrate empirically that anonymization effects, identified over the distribution directly affect the utility of a federated model and justify the inclusion of a distribution-driven analysis for making learning-based evaluations. 5.4 Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES) Comparison The Privacy-Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES) is a comprehensive measure of anonymization performance taking into account federated utility, information loss, and re-identification risk. In all the datasets examined, PUES rankings can effectively discriminate between anonymization techniques that trade off between privacy and utility conductively as opposed to overpro Existing classical anonymization schemes

text: have lower ranking, owing to their high degree of information loss and degraded federated performance, albeit with strong privacy guarantees. ​ Figure 5. Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES) Comparison Across Anonymization Techniques The PUES of different anonymization methods under our HAPED-QA-FL is presented in Figure 5. PUES is a combined normalized score by federated analytic utility, entropy-based information loss and quasi-identifier re-identification risk. Traditional techniques, such as the k-anonymity and suppression, result in smaller PUES due to their higher utility loss in distributional distortion and information loss. Micro-aggregation presents a more favorable trade-off between obfuscation and statistical balance, as the statistical structure is preserved at the cost of identifiability. The attribute- centric anonymization approach has the highest PUES, because it achieves a better balance between privacy and utility through well-controlled anonymizing of important attributes while maintaining acceptable downstream federated learning performance. These results endorse the suitability of PUES as an objective typological measure for anonymization strategies in health-IoT systems. 5.5 Discussion and Key Insights The obtained experimental results show that considering anonymization in the context of isolated privacy or utility measures yields a partial and possibly unjustified view. Distribution-centric analysis provides the means for grounding impact of anonymization and early hints for downstream analytic behavior. Federated validations on top of these models bring the presented findings closer to realistic healthcare deployment and guarantee that the evaluation results are still operationally relevant. One of the main observations that can be abstracted from this study is that anonymization-induced distributional distortion, instead of a sole feature despreading
label: human

text: power, plays as the primary force outworking utility loss in federated healthcare card games. By assuming such correlation, HAPED-QA-FL fills the gap between data-level privacy quantification and system- level utility measurement. As a result, the presented framework facilitates evidence-driven anonymization selection and defines a scalable evaluation process that is in line with regulatory and operational restrictions of healthcare IoT ecosystems. 5.5 Ablation Study 5.5.1 Purpose of the Ablation Study Ablation study is further performed to quantitatively measure the contribution of each key part in the HAPED-QA-FL framework to the accurate and robust anonymization evaluation. In contrast to typical performance ablations which tend to concentrate on model accuracy, this work explores the effects of deleting or modifying each individual component of our framework on both PUES and interpretability of anonymization assessment. In particular, the analysis discuss the need for (i) distribution-driven metrics; and (ii) federated utility validation (iii) conforming to a unified scoring aggregation confirming the architectural design choices of our framework. 5.5.2 Ablation Configurations Ablation Study The ablation study considers four controlled variations of the proposed framework to estimate the contribution made by each component. Complete HAPED-QA-FL consists of distributional assessment, federated utility validation and PUES, the full evaluation pipeline. The without distributional estimation variant uses only federated utility, and the without federated validation distance variant looks at anonymization solely through the lens of distributional metrics. Finally, the without PUES aggregation variant calculates individual metrics separately without ensemble ranking, which emphasizes the necessity of equilibrium based scoring. The ablation settings are summarized in Table 2 to analyze the contribution of each component for the proposed HAPED-QA-FL framework. It shows that the removal of any one of distributional assessment, federated utility validation or unified PUES aggregation causes anonymization evaluation to be incomplete when it comes to completeness, interpretability and ranking reliability and hence justifies the full design of such a framework. For the absence of analysis driven by distribution, federated learning alone could not explain why some anonymization procedures made data less useful. This results in an unstable output, which varies with different training data. However, without federated validation, the framework does not consider how anonymization affects real-world analytics in distributed healthcare IoT like environments. Moreover, deletion of the combined Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES) leads to inconsistent performance results. Here, the anonymisation methods are differently ordered in accordance with which particular metric is chosen. This supports the claim that UES is needed to optimally trade-off privacy against utility, and generate agnostic ranking of anonymization techniques. In conclusion, we provide the most robust, interpretable and practically meaningful analysis on a full HAPED-QA-FL framework of combining distribution-level analysis with federated utility validation through a unified equilibrium score. 5.5.4 Discussion, Implications, and Future Directions​ This study reveals that distribution-based metrics are a better measure of the quality of anonymization as compared to privacy score or prediction accuracy alone. These measures directly illustrate the extent of how anonymization alters underlying data trends that would in turn be leveraged for healthcare IoT analytics. An important novelty of this work is to leverage federated learning as an evaluation base, rather than a solution for protecting privacy. This facilitates the practical
label: human

text: measurement of utility loss in a multi-institution scenario without conflating privacy enforcement and performance evaluation. The introduced Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES) is a transparent and simple measure to guide hospitals, data holders and regulators towards the selection of anonymization techniques that are able to balance on data usefulness with privacy need. There are some limitations to this study, though. It does not have an explicit re-identification attack of its own, it is not compared with other results using differential privacy methods and covers only structured healthcare IoT data. Further steps in this direction will involve adapting this model to include multimodal data such as medical images and clinical text, the use of anonymization techniques based on differential privacy, as well as the study of adaptive anonymity strategies driven by PUES feedback. In addition, the model will be further aligned with healthcare laws such as HIPAA and GDPR to facilitate its deployment in practice. VI Conclusion​ In this paper, we proposed HAPED-QA-FL that is the first distribution-driven federated approach for assessing healthcare IoT data anonymization in the context of united privacy-utility equilibrium. Inspired by the shortcoming of previous evaluation methods based on isolated metrics or centralized assumptions, the proposed framework combines distribution-level profiling and federated learning–based utility validation to formulate a transparent and deployment-aware evaluation process. By examining statistical divergence, entropy-based loss in information and uniqueness of quasi-identifiers before learning, and then homologizing by downstream performance on federated tasks, HAPED-QA-FL reflects how anonymization transforms the shape of data properties and real-world analysis. We unite these insights in an interpretable single measure, the Privacy–Utility Equilibrium Score (PUES), that allows to objectively rank anonymizations and to overcome conflicting measures. Experimental results show that attribute-centric and microaggregation approaches strike a better balance between privacy and utility, while classical methods lead to significant distributional distortion and reduction on data utility. In summary, HAPED-QA-FL is an evaluation framework, not a privacy enforcement system; its value spreads from offering a scalable, interpretable, and regulator-compatible approach for evidence-based choice of anonymization in distributed healthcare IoT scenarios. text: CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION TO BLOCKCHAIN-BASED PRIVACY-PRESERVING AUTHENTICATION IN INTERNET OF VEHICLES 1.1 Background
label: human

text: The rapid evolution of intelligent transportation systems has led to the emergence of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), an advanced paradigm that integrates vehicles, roadside infrastructure, cloud platforms, and users through wireless communication technologies. IoV enables a wide range of applications such as traffic management, accident prevention, autonomous driving, infotainment services, and real-time navigation. However, the large-scale exchange of sensitive vehicular data, including vehicle identity, location, speed, and driver behavior, has introduced serious security and privacy concerns. Due to the high mobility, dynamic topology, and open wireless communication environment of IoV networks, they are highly vulnerable to various cyber threats such as impersonation attacks, Sybil attacks, replay attacks, false data injection, and unauthorized tracking. Traditional centralized security architectures rely on trusted third parties and centralized servers, which suffer from single-point-of-failure, scalability issues, and increased latency. These limitations make conventional security solutions inadequate for next-generation IoV environments. To address these challenges, blockchain technology has emerged as a promising solution due to its decentralized architecture, immutability, transparency, and cryptographic security. Blockchain eliminates the need for a centralized authority by enabling distributed trust management among vehicles and infrastructure. text: The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) represents a critical component of modern intelligent transportation systems, enabling vehicles to exchange information with surrounding entities to improve safety, efficiency, and driving intelligence. Through continuous communication among vehicles, roadside units, cloud services, and edge platforms, IoV supports applications such as collision avoidance, traffic optimization, and autonomous decision-making. However, the open and highly dynamic nature of vehicular communication significantly increases exposure to security threats and privacy risks. Authentication plays a vital role in ensuring that only legitimate vehicles and infrastructure entities participate in IoV communication. Without strong authentication mechanisms, malicious nodes can inject false messages, impersonate trusted vehicles, or disrupt network operations, potentially leading to severe safety consequences. Conventional authentication schemes, which rely heavily on centralized authorities and static trust models, are often inadequate in large-scale and rapidly changing vehicular environments due to high latency, limited scalability, and vulnerability to single-point failures. To overcome these challenges, decentralized security frameworks based on blockchain technology have been widely investigated. Blockchain enables distributed trust establishment, immutable record keeping, and secure verification of transactions without requiring a central authority. Nevertheless, blockchain-based IoV systems introduce new challenges, including computational overhead, storage complexity, and privacy exposure when sensitive data is recorded on transparent ledgers. These limitations necessitate the integration of privacy-preserving mechanisms and efficient authentication designs. In recent years, intelligent learning techniques such as machine learning and deep learning have been adopted to enhance IoV security by identifying malicious behaviors through data-driven analysis. These models can adapt to evolving attack patterns and improve detection accuracy in dynamic environments.

text: The rapid growth of intelligent transportation systems has led to the development of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), where vehicles, roadside units, and cloud servers communicate continuously to support applications such as traffic safety, autonomous driving, and real-time navigation. While IoV improves transportation efficiency and user experience, it also introduces serious security and privacy challenges due to its open wireless environment, high vehicle mobility, and large-scale data exchange. Traditional centralized authentication mechanisms depend on trusted authorities, which suffer from scalability issues, high latency, and single-point-of-failure problems, making them unsuitable for dynamic IoV scenarios. Blockchain technology has emerged as a promising solution by enabling decentralized, tamper-resistant, and transparent authentication without relying on a central entity. However, blockchain alone cannot effectively handle intelligent and evolving cyber-attacks such as impersonation and false data injection. To overcome this limitation, intelligent learning models are required to detect malicious behavior accurately. In this context, this chapter presents an efficient privacy-preserving authentication scheme that integrates blockchain technology with a Hybrid Adaptive Network (HANet) to provide secure, scalable, and intelligent authentication in IoV networks. The proposed framework ensures data integrity, vehicle anonymity, and resistance to malicious attacks while maintaining low computational overhead, thereby making it suitable for real-time vehicular environments.

text: Internet of Vehicles environments are exposed to a wide range of security threats, including cyber intrusions, Sybil attacks, and the participation of compromised or malicious entities, which seriously affect the reliability of vehicular communications. Prior studies have emphasized that traditional rule-based and cryptographic security mechanisms alone are insufficient to handle such intelligent and evolving attacks in IoV networks (Ali et al., 2021). Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool in this context, as it enables systems to learn complex patterns from data and identify abnormal behaviors with high accuracy. Blockchain provides an immutable and decentralized ledger, while machine learning enhances decision-making by analyzing transaction behaviors and network traffic. When combined with smart contracts, this integration enables automated, tamper-resistant, and secure validation of vehicular transactions without relying on centralized authorities. However, existing approaches still face limitations in terms of detection accuracy, computational efficiency, and adaptability to large-scale IoV environments.
